passages.title: Created from a single soul: reverence Allah and the ties of kinship
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah an-Nisāʾ opens not with a law but with a summons: **be conscious of your Lord** — the One who brought the entire human race out of a single soul, then out of that soul its mate, and then spread from the two of them countless men and women. Ayah 1 is a single verse, but Maʿārif ul Qurʾān describes it as the introduction to the injunctions that follow: before Allah lays down the rights of orphans, of relatives and of wives, He first establishes *who we are to one another* (one family, from one father and one mother) and *who is watching* (Allah, always). Its purpose, the commentary says, is to dissuade human beings from becoming usurpers of Divine rights, and at the same time — by telling them they are all children of the same father — to make love, mutual sympathy and concern the working basis of common life. The two commands of taqwā and the reminder of the wombs are the hinge on which the whole sūrah turns.

## Where this sūrah stands

Sūrah an-Nisāʾ was revealed in Madīnah. Ibn Kathīr reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās (through al-ʿAwfī), and Ibn Marduwyah recorded similar statements from ʿAbdullāh bin az-Zubayr and Zayd bin Thābit.

Its weight in the eyes of the Companions was enormous. Al-Ḥākim records in his *Mustadrak* that ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd said, "There are five Ayat in Surat An-Nisa' that I would prefer to the life of this world and all that is in it" — and he listed:

- **4:40** — *"Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of an atom."*
- **4:31** — *"If you avoid the great sins which you are forbidden to do."*
- **4:48** — *"Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him (in worship), but He forgives except that (anything else) to whom He wills."*
- **4:64** — *"If they (hypocrites), when they had been unjust to themselves, had come to you."*
- **4:110** — *"And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Al-Ḥākim also records Ibn ʿAbbās saying, "Ask me about Surat An-Nisa', for I learned the Qur'an when I was still young" — a ḥadīth al-Ḥākim graded as authentic by the criteria of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, though neither collected it.

**The link with the previous sūrah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes the seam: Sūrah Āl ʿImrān closed with an exhortation to taqwā, and an-Nisāʾ begins with taqwā — now in the form of a command. Āl ʿImrān had dealt with some of the battles, with the manner of treating antagonists, with the condemnation of misappropriating battle spoils, and with several other matters. The early part of an-Nisāʾ turns inward, to the rights owed to *one's own people*: orphans, relatives and wives — what the scholars call *ḥuqūq al-ʿibād*, the rights of the servants of Allah.

## Why a sūrah of family rights begins with the fear of Allah

This is the single most illuminating point Maʿārif ul Qurʾān makes about ayah 1, and it deserves to be felt rather than skimmed.

Some rights, it explains, are *justiciable* — their fulfilment can be enforced through law. Common transactions of buying and selling; the rights involved in lease, tenancy and wages: these can be settled through mutual agreements and arbitration, and if one side falls short, the shortfall can be legally retrieved and enforced.

But the rights this sūrah is about are not like that. The rights of those in one's own charge — children, parents, husband and wife, orphans — and the rights of other relatives that fall upon each other, all "depend upon civilized behaviour, respect, loving and caring, and above all on that genuinely heartfelt desire to do what is good for them." These are behaviour patterns, the commentary says, which cannot be weighed on a scale of things. And determining them "fully and perfectly through mutual agreements is also much too difficult."

So what is left? Maʿārif ul Qurʾān answers that there is simply no other method of fulfilling them **except having the fear of Allah and the fear of what would happen in the life to come.** That is taqwā — and the truth of the matter, the commentary states plainly, is that this power of taqwā is more effective than the combined powers of government and law. That is why the sūrah opens with `يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمْ` before it opens with a single ruling.

## The words themselves

**"Ittaqū" — fear.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān renders its sense as *fear acting against your Lord* — the wary, protective caution of someone who does not want to be found on the wrong side of the One he depends on. Ibn Kathīr glosses the later command "have Taqwa of Allah" as: *protect yourself from Allah by your acts of obedience to Him.* Taqwā, then, is a shield you build out of obedience. And Ibn Kathīr opens his comment on the verse by noting that Allah here commands His creatures to have taqwā of Him by worshipping Him alone, without partners.

**"O mankind."** The address is not "O you who believe." It is `يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ` — which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān points out, takes in all human beings, men or women, whether present at the time the Qurʾān was revealed or born at any point right through to the Day of Doom. The rights of kinship and the dignity of the weak are not a sectarian arrangement; they are owed by human beings as human beings.

**"Your Lord" — why *Rabb*?** Alongside the command *ittaqū*, the word chosen is *Rabb*, selected out of the most fair names of Allah — and the choice carries an argument. The fear enjoined here, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, has a justification and a wisdom of its own: the Being totally responsible for man's nurture, the manifestations of Whose Lord-worthiness he witnesses every moment of his life, certainly deserves all the awe one is capable of. The very thought that anyone could rise in antagonism and defiance against Allah is, in the words of the commentary, terribly dangerous.

**A living Sunnah.** Because *ittaqū rabbakum* carries the sense "fear acting against your Lord," Maʿārif ul Qurʾān suggests this may be why the Prophet ﷺ used to recite this verse as part of his address when solemnising a marriage. Reciting it in the khuṭbah of nikāḥ is therefore, the commentary says, a perennial revival of his Sunnah.

## One soul, one mate, countless descendants

`خَلَقَكُم مِّن نَّفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ` — "created you from a single person." Ibn Kathīr identifies that person as Ādam, peace be upon him: Allah reminds His creatures of His ability, in that He created them all from one.

`وَخَلَقَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا` — "and from him He created his wife." Ibn Kathīr says this is Ḥawwāʾ (Eve), created from Adam's left rib, from his back while he was sleeping. When Ādam woke and saw her he liked her and had affection for her, and she felt the same toward him. Ibn Kathīr then cites an authentic ḥadīth (he does not name the collection here): *"Woman was created from a rib. Verily, the most curved portion of the rib is its upper part, so, if you should try to straighten it, you will break it, but if you leave it as it is, it will remain crooked."* The teaching is one of patient acceptance rather than forcible correction.

`وَبَثَّ مِنْهُمَا رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَاءً` — "and from them both He created many men and women." Ibn Kathīr: Allah created from Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ many men and women and distributed them throughout the world in various shapes, characteristics, colours and languages — "In the end, their gathering and return will be to Allah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out what this design was *for*. It was quite possible to create humanity in more than one way; but Allah chose one way and one form, a very particular one — all human beings from the one and only human being, Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him) — and by doing so "tied all of them in a strong bond of brotherhood." Therefore it is not only the fear of Allah and the fear of the Ākhirah that demand our allegiance to the Lord of all creation; this bond of brotherhood between human beings itself requires that the rights of humanity — mutual sympathy, wellbeing, the collective good — be fully discharged. And it follows, the commentary insists, that between one person and another **let there be no one high or low in race or caste, in colour or language**, and that all such distinctions never be made the criterion of good or bad, nobility or meanness.

Ibn Kathīr says the same in a single sentence: Allah mentioned that He created mankind from a single father and a single mother *so that they feel compassion for each other and are kind to the weaker among them.*

## "Through Whom you demand your mutual rights" — and the wombs

`وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ الَّذِي تَسَاءَلُونَ بِهِ وَالْأَرْحَامَ`

Ibn Kathīr reports two readings of "through Whom you demand your mutual (rights)," and they complement each other:

- **Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan:** it refers to when some people say, *"I ask you by Allah, and then by the relation of the Raḥim"* — that is, by the womb-relationship between us. You invoke Allah's name, and the blood tie, to press your claim on another person.
- **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk:** "Fear Allah Whom you invoke when you conduct transactions and contracts."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sharpens the moral edge of this: is it not the case that a man demands his rights from others *in the name of Allah*, and exacts what he wants from them by it? It means that the one who expects others to fear Allah should do that himself as well. You cannot make Allah's name your leverage in claiming and then forget it when it is your turn to give.

**"And the wombs."** On `وَالْأَرْحَامَ`, Ibn Kathīr reports the position of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ar-Rabīʿ and others: revere the womb by *not cutting the relations of the womb*, but keep them and honour them. And Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that this closing word stands as a warning that any shortcoming in taking good care of near relations — whether on the father's side or the mother's — must be avoided.

The word repays a moment's attention. *Al-arḥām* is the plural of *raḥm*, the womb — the mother's womb is the home of the child until it is born, and since that womb is the source of blood relationship, maintaining relations along that line is called *ṣilat ar-raḥm* in Arabic (literally, the umbilical link or bond). Its converse — showing carelessness and indifference toward that natural linkage of blood — is *qaṭʿ ar-raḥm*, the severing of the tie. The Qurʾān does not merely say "be good to relatives"; it names the organ that made you kin, and tells you to hold it in awe.

## From the Sunnah: the weight of kinship

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that the noble aḥādīth have laid great emphasis on the bonds of kinship, and gathers several narrations (citing *Mishkāt*):

- The Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever likes to have his livelihood made plentiful and his age extended for him should maintain good relations with his near of kin."* (Mishkāt, p. 419) Two benefits, the commentary notes: the merit of the Hereafter is vouchsafed, and this fair treatment of one's kin has its benefits in this life as well — it removes straitening from a person's livelihood and blesses his age with more good years.
- Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām ؓ said that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madīnah al-Ṭayyibah and he presented himself before him, the very first words of his that fell into his ears were: *"O men, make a practice of greeting each other with salam, and feed people (for the pleasure of Allah), and treat near relations well, and pray by night while people sleep - you will enter Paradise in peace."* (Mishkāt, p. 108)
- Umm al-Muʾminīn Sayyidah Maymūnah ؓ freed her bondwoman, and when she told the Prophet ﷺ about it he said: *"Had you given her to your maternal uncle, your reward would have been greater."* (Mishkāt, p. 171) Islam motivates people to free slaves and rates it as one of the finest acts of merit — and still, treating relatives fairly was given more importance.
- *"Charity to the needy is just charity, while to a near relative it becomes twofold: charity and kinship."* (Mishkāt, p. 171) A simple change in the end-use of charity, the commentary observes, yields two types of merit.

And the warnings on the other side are stern: *"A breaker of (blood) relationships shall not enter Paradise"* (Mishkāt, p. 419), and *"Mercy shall not descend upon a people among whom there is a breaker of (blood) relationships"* (Mishkāt, p. 420).

Ibn Kathīr also records what this verse looked like in the Prophet's ﷺ own practice. Muslim records in his *Ṣaḥīḥ* from Jarīr bin ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī that a delegation from Muḍar came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he saw the state they were in — wearing striped woollen clothes due to poverty. After the Ẓuhr prayer he ﷺ stood up and gave a speech in which he recited this very verse, "O mankind! Have Taqwa of your Lord, Who created you from a single person," to the end of the āyah, along with *"O you who believe! Have Taqwa of Allah. And let every person look to what he has sent forth for the tomorrow"* (59:18) — and he encouraged them to give charity, saying, *"A man gave Sadaqah from his Dinar, from his Dirham, from his Sa' of wheat, from his Sa' of dates."* Ibn Kathīr notes the narration was also collected by Aḥmad and the Sunan compilers from Ibn Masʿūd. **This is the verse in action:** recited not in a classroom but in front of hungry people, to open the pockets of those who had something.

## "Surely, Allah is always watching over you"

`إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا`

Ibn Kathīr: it means He watches all your deeds and sees your every circumstance — as Allah says elsewhere, *"And Allah is Witness over all things"* (58:6). He cites an authentic ḥadīth (again without naming the collection here): *"Worship Allah as if you see Him, for even though you cannot see Him, He sees you."* This part of the āyah, he says, encourages a sense of certainty that Allah is always watching, in a complete and perfect manner.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the practical consequence. Divine watchfulness implies awareness of whatever there is in human hearts — intentions, scruples, motives, everything. So things done half-heartedly, or merely formally, or for fear of possible embarrassment before people, without any genuine desire to serve, remain acts unacceptable to Allah. And note where the āyah places this: right at the end, as the answer to *why* Allah should be feared at all — because He is watchful over everyone, always.

The commentary adds an observation about the Qurʾān's method that is worth carrying into the rest of the sūrah: Allah does not introduce laws in the sheer cold print of the governments of this world. He puts them forth in the manner of education, training and affection, not restricting Himself to the word of law alone but combining it with the grooming of minds and hearts.

## Living it

Read as one movement, ayah 1 asks four things:

1. **Fear acting against your Lord** — not a distant deity, but the Being totally responsible for your nurture, whose Lord-worthiness you witness every moment of your life.
2. **Remember your origin.** One father, one mother. Difference in shape, colour, characteristic and language is Allah's distribution throughout the world, not a ranking. Compassion — especially toward the weaker among us — is the stated purpose of that shared descent.
3. **Do not use Allah's name only when claiming.** If you invoke Him, and the tie of the womb, to secure what you want from others, then fear Him when others' rights fall due from you.
4. **Guard the womb-ties.** Avoid any shortcoming in taking good care of near relations, from the father's side or the mother's. Give to a relative before a stranger where you can, and never let a blood tie go cold.

And then the seal: **Allah is ever Watchful.** He sees not only whether you did it, but how, and why. That is the discipline the rest of Sūrat an-Nisāʾ is built on — and it is why, immediately after this verse, the second verse emphasises the rights of orphaned children and establishes rules to protect their property.

passages.title: Orphans' property and just marriage limits
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat deal with wealth and marriage where one person holds power over someone who cannot defend themselves — an orphan with an inheritance, a girl with no father to negotiate her marriage, a wife owed her dower, a dependant not yet able to manage money. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the join with ayah 1: an orphan's guardian is usually a relative, so this is still the rights of kinship.

## Ayah 2 — the property that is not yours

Maʿārif opens the word *yatīm*: literally the lone or unique one, which is why a pearl alone in its shell is called *ad-durr al-yatīm*, "the orphan pearl." In Islamic law a *yatīm* is a child whose father has died, and a hadith in *Mishkāt* states that orphanhood ends with puberty.

"Give the orphans their property." Ibn Kathīr: their wealth is surrendered in full at adolescence, and no part may be used or confiscated. Maʿārif reads it through ayah 5: handover comes only once maturity and sound judgement are established, so the command here is to **guard** the estate for its proper time. Refraining is not enough — the guardian must actively protect and conserve it, and cover the child's maintenance from his own means.

**"Do not exchange the bad for the good."** Saʿīd bin Al-Musayyib and Az-Zuhrī: do not substitute a weak animal of yours for a fat animal of theirs. Ibrāhīm An-Nakhaʿī and Ad-Dahhāk: do not give bad quality for good. As-Suddī describes the caretaker who takes a fat sheep from the orphan's property and leaves a weak one of his own, saying "a sheep for a sheep." Why this needed forbidding on its own, says Maʿārif: the *count* is unchanged, so the man tells himself he has not *taken* anything, only *exchanged*. It also covers any deal the guardian strikes with a third party that leaves the orphan worse off.

**"Do not devour their wealth into your wealth."** Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Muqātil bin Hayyān, As-Suddī and others: do not mix the two so that you eat up both. Maʿārif: either keep the orphan's property separate and spend from it separately, or, on a joint budget, keep accounts clear enough to be certain nothing of the child's was spent on you. "Eat" is broad — in common usage every act of using up is called "eating up," so every unlawful use is covered. The phrasing also hints such men generally had lawful wealth of their own, which makes stooping to the orphan's share more shameful, not less.

The verdict: *innahu kāna hūban kabīran.* Ibn ʿAbbās called it a major, substantial sin; Ibn Kathīr notes the same from Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Qatādah and others. Maʿārif records from Ibn ʿAbbās that *hūb* comes from the Ethiopian language, where it means "major sin," and the same in Arabic.

## Ayah 3 — the loophole, and the story behind it

Ayah 3 closes the cleverest workaround of all: marry the orphan girl yourself, and her property quietly becomes household property. Maʿārif: every excuse, device or stratagem set up to usurp the property of the orphan is impermissible.

Al-Bukhārī recorded from ʿĀ'ishah that a man was taking care of a female orphan and married her although he did not desire to marry her; her money was mixed with his and he was keeping her portion from her — and this ayah was revealed about his case. Maʿārif's telling of the narration in *Sahīh al-Bukhārī* adds that he had a fruit farm in which the girl held a share, and rather than give her a dower from his own pocket, took her share in the farm.

Al-Bukhārī also recorded ʿUrwah bin Az-Zubayr asking ʿĀ'ishah what it meant. She answered — "O my nephew!" — that it concerns the orphan girl who lives with her guardian and shares his property, whose wealth and beauty may tempt him to marry her without the adequate dowry another suitor might have given. Such guardians were forbidden to marry them unless they treated them justly and gave the most suitable dowry; otherwise they were ordered to marry other women. Afterwards, she said, people again asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and 4:127 was revealed — its phrase "yet whom you desire to marry" catching the guardian who does *not* want to marry his ward because she is neither wealthy nor beautiful.

So: *if you fear you cannot be equitable with the orphan girls, marry from the women who are good and lawful for you.* Ibn Kathīr: such women are plenty, as Allah has not restricted him. Maʿārif notes where enforcement sits: the injunction is not placed on the government as laws usually are; people are commanded to fear Allah and do right — though the authorities must still see that no such violation occurs, and use the force of law where it does.

## The ceiling of four

Ibn Kathīr notes that 35:1 speaks of angels with wings "two or three or four," which does not mean no angel has more, since there are proofs that some do — but here the ayah specifies what men are permitted of wives. So, as Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of scholars stated, four is the limit; had more been allowed, the ayah would have said so.

The Sunnah settled it. Imām Ahmad recorded that Ghīlān bin Salamah Ath-Thaqafī had ten wives when he became Muslim, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him, "Choose any four of them (and divorce the rest)" — collected up to that statement by Ash-Shāfiʿī, At-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, Ad-Dāraqutnī and Al-Bayhaqī. Ibn Kathīr's inference: they had all embraced Islam with him, and still only four could remain — so if that is the ruling for a man who already had more than four on entering Islam, marrying more than four is forbidden all the more. Maʿārif adds Qais ibn al-Hārith al-Asadī, who had eight wives when he embraced Islam and was told, "Keep four of them and divorce the rest" (Abū Dāūd).

Maʿārif draws the legal consequence: a marriage contracted to more than four women in a single offer and acceptance is void from the outset, no one having the right to more than four. Marriages within the four are valid — but any failure to treat the wives equally and justly is a grave sin, and an aggrieved wife can seek redress in an Islamic court.

## "Then only one"

Ibn Kathīr: if you fear you cannot do justice between your wives by marrying more than one, marry only one, or be content with what your right hands possess — an expression, Maʿārif cautions, carrying very special conditions which generally do not exist these days, so calling a relationship outside marriage "ownership" to license it is patently unlawful.

*Dhālika adnā allā taʿūlū* — "that is nearer to your not deviating." Ibn Kathīr glosses *taʿūlū* as doing injustice, and records that Ibn Abī Hātim reported the same from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀ'ishah, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatādah, As-Suddī, Muqātil bin Hayyān and others. Maʿārif traces *adnā* to a root meaning nearness, and *taʿūlū* to a root meaning inclination or tilt — here a tilt ending in injustice.

Why "nearer to" justice rather than "safe from" it? Because, Maʿārif answers, some men inflict all sorts of injustice on even one wife. Fewer wives lowers the danger; complete deliverance comes only when one wife's rights are fully given and she is treated fairly and generously.

**The apparent clash with 4:129.** Some set this beside "you will never be able to do perfect justice between wives even if it is your ardent desire" and conclude plural marriage must be impossible in principle. Maʿārif answers that 4:3 concerns justice in what a man can do by choice — personal expenses, parity in overnight stays — while 4:129 concerns the heart's inclination, which is not chosen; and even there the Qur'an says *do not tilt the full tilt*, so total indifference toward the other wife is never permissible. He also asks: if the aim were to close plural marriage altogether, why speak of "two, three, four," and why frame the second clause around *fear* of injustice, when on that reading injustice would be certain? The Prophet ﷺ treated his wives with full equality in everything within his control, and still supplicated: "O Allah, this is my apportioning in what I control. So, do not hold me accountable in matters You control and I do not." Maʿārif also cites a hadith (*Mishkāt*): anyone who has two wives and cannot fulfil their rights equally and justly shall be raised on the Day of Doom with one of his shoulders drooping down.

## Ayah 4 — the dower as her right, given gladly

"Give the women their *saduqāt* as a *nihlah*." ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying *nihlah* refers to the dowry. ʿĀ'ishah, Muqātil, Qatādah and Ibn Jurayj said it means obligatory — Ibn Jurayj adding "specified." Ibn Zayd said that in Arabic *nihlah* refers to what is necessary, and drew from it the command: **do not marry unless you give your wife something that is her right** — no one after the Prophet ﷺ may marry a woman except with the required dowry, nor by giving false promises about it.

Maʿārif shows this one word working against three pre-Islamic abuses:

1. **The dower went to her guardians, not to her.** Hence "give *the women* their dowers" — husbands hand it to their wives themselves; and guardians who receive it must give it straight to the girls, putting none of it to personal use without their permission.
2. **It was paid sourly, like a fine.** A man who saw no way out would pay unwillingly, as though paying a penalty. *Nihlah* in Arabic usage means giving cheerfully — and obligatory rights are to be discharged in good cheer.
3. **Husbands pressured wives into "waiving" it.** Hence the closing clause: *if they, of their own pleasure, remit any part of it to you, take it and enjoy it.* Extracting forgiveness by pressure is futile — nothing is forgiven that way. Only her genuinely free choice makes it lawful.

Maʿārif quotes Mullā ʿAlī Qārī (*Mirqāt Sharh Mishkāt*): the dower is called *saduqah* because the root *sadaqa* signifies truth — it shows the true attitude of the husband toward his wife.

Maʿārif cites the Prophet ﷺ (*Mishkāt*): "Beware, do no injustice. Remember, a person's property is not lawful for another unless it be through his sweet will." It applies the principle beyond the dower — to sisters and widows quietly written out of an inheritance, and to donations for mosques and religious schools, which may not be accepted if given under social or legal pressure rather than freely. Maulānā Ashraf Thānavī's test for a real waiver: put the dower into her hands as its owner first; if she then gives it back of her own sweet will, it is truly given — and what is required is the willingness of the whole self, not a calculated show of contentment.

## Ayah 5 — do not hand wealth to those who cannot hold it

Ayah 5 heads off a misreading of ayahs 2 and 4: that property must go to its owner even when he cannot yet protect it. The Salaf differed over who the *sufahā'* — the unwise — are: Ad-Dahhāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that it refers to children and women, and similar from Ibn Masʿūd, Al-Hakam bin ʿUyaynah and Al-Hasan; Saʿīd bin Jubayr said the orphans; Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said women. Ibn Kathīr treats the ruling as broader than any one group: it applies because of youth, and in insanity, erratic behaviour, weak intellect or weak religious practice, and in bankruptcy, when creditors ask that a bankrupt's property be put in escrow.

Ibn ʿAbbās: do not hand over the wealth Allah made you responsible for and made a means of sustenance; hold on to it, take care of it, and be the one who spends on them for clothes, food and provision. Maʿārif preserves his fuller version: when a ward insists on taking possession, explain honestly and reasonably, in a way that neither breaks their heart nor causes the property to be wasted — *all of this is there for you; just grow up a little more and you will have it all.* That is the "kind and just word" the ayah commands — glossed by Mujāhid as kindness and keeping good relations, while Ibn Kathīr notes it commands kind treatment *in deed* toward family and dependants too, not only good words.

Maʿārif draws out the positive side: property is worth protecting, wasting it is a sin. It cites the Prophet ﷺ (*Bukhārī*, *Muslim*): "Whosoever is killed while protecting his property is a shahīd."

## Ayah 6 — test them, then hand it over before witnesses

**"Test the orphans."** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Al-Hasan, As-Suddī and Muqātil bin Hayyān read *ibtalū* as testing their intelligence. Maʿārif turns this into three stages — before puberty, after puberty, and after *rushd* (self-reliance and discretion in one's own affairs) — in the first, the guardian trains the child through small assignments of buying and selling conducted on his own. From this Imām Abū Hanīfah deduced that transactions entered into by a minor with his guardian's permission are sound, valid and operative.

**"Until they reach the age of marriage"** — the age of puberty, according to Mujāhid; the majority hold it comes when the child has a wet dream. Abū Dāūd recorded in his *Sunan* that ʿAlī memorised from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "There is no orphan after the age of puberty." Alternatively fifteen is taken as the age of adolescence: in the Two Sahīhs, Ibn ʿUmar reported that he was presented to the Prophet ﷺ on the eve of Uhud at fourteen and not allowed to fight, then again on the eve of Al-Khandaq at fifteen and allowed; ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz, hearing this, said, "This is the difference between a child and an adult." Maʿārif's summary: real maturity is tied to signs, not to a count of years; where no signs appear, jurists differ — some fix eighteen for boys and seventeen for girls, others fifteen for both, which is the Hanafī *fatwā*.

**"If you perceive in them sound judgement."** Saʿīd bin Jubayr explained *rushd* as being good in their religion and wise with their money; Ibn Kathīr reports the like from Ibn ʿAbbās, Al-Hasan Al-Basrī and others among the imams. Maʿārif adds a grammatical point: *rushdan* is indefinite, so a reasonable measure of understanding suffices — full and perfect sense is not the standard. Some jurists leaned toward withholding property until full understanding is established, even if that lasted a lifetime; Abū Hanīfah's verification is that the deficiency meant here is the effect of childhood, gone within ten years of maturity — so at twenty-five the property is handed over regardless. Those who remain simple or slow in their dealings are not deprived on that account; genuine insanity is governed by a separate rule.

**The guardian's own hand.** "Do not consume it wastefully and hastily, fearing they will grow up" prevents two things, says Maʿārif: spending beyond normal need, and starting to spend long before any need arises, in a hurry, because the guardian sees the handover coming and his control ending. Then compensation: whoever among the guardians is rich should take no wages; whoever is poor may consume what is just and reasonable. Ibn Abī Hātim recorded that ʿĀ'ishah said this was revealed about the guardian of the orphan and pertains to whatever work he does for the estate — Al-Bukhārī also collected it. Imām Ahmad recorded from ʿAmr bin Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that a man said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "I do not have money, but I have an orphan under my care," and the Messenger ﷺ said: "Eat from your orphan's wealth without extravagance or wastefulness, or mixing it, and without saving your money by spending his." For the self-sufficient guardian, Maʿārif says, the service is an obligation and payment for it is not permissible; for the poor guardian with no other livelihood, a reasonable amount covering his basic needs is allowed — a rule Maʿārif extends to those who administer endowments (*awqāf*), manage mosques and religious schools, or hold public office, on the same condition: in proportion to need.

**Witnesses, and the Witness.** When the property is released, take witnesses — Ibn Kathīr: so that none can later deny that he received his money; Maʿārif adds that these should be reliable, upright people, so no dispute follows. Then: *and Allah is All-Sufficient in taking account.* Ibn Kathīr: Allah suffices as Witness, Reckoner and Watcher over the guardians' work for orphans and over what they hand back, whether whole or diminished. Which is why Muslim recorded in his *Sahīh* that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Abū Dharr! Verily, you are weak, and I love for you what I love for myself. Do not become a leader of two nor assume guardianship of an orphan's property."

passages.title: Fixed shares and fear for one's own heirs
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 7–10: Fixed shares, and fear for your own heirs

These four ayat take the property of a dead man and place it under the protection of Allah.

## The world these ayat walked into

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: before Islam, orphans and women — "the weaker links in the human chain" — had no rights recognised, and no power existed to wrest a conceded right from men. The working principle of the pre-Islamic Arabs, reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: the one deserving of inheritance is he who rides a horse, fights the enemy and collects the battle spoils. A girl was excluded outright, major or minor; a boy too, if still a minor. Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Qatādah: the idolaters used to give adult men a share of inheritance and deprive women and children of it — and Allah revealed ayah 7.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the family behind this. In the blessed time of the Prophet ﷺ the Companion Aws ibn Thābit (may Allah be pleased with him) died, leaving two daughters, a minor boy and his wife as his inheritors. Two cousins on his father's side took the whole property and gave them nothing — the wife and daughters ruled out for being female, the boy for being a minor. The widow asked them at least to marry the two orphaned daughters, so she would be relieved of that concern; they refused. She went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him her sad story and the destitution of her children. The verse of inheritance had not yet been revealed, so he ﷺ withheld his response, his heart at peace that this unjust practice would be removed through divine revelation. Then ayah 7 was revealed. When the second verse of inheritance came later in this sūrah with the details of the shares, the Prophet ﷺ gave the wife one-eighth, half of the rest to the son and the other half to the two girls equally, and excluded the cousins, who were not the nearest of kin as compared to children.

Ibn Kathīr adds another woman's voice: Ibn Marduwyah reported that Jābir said Umm Kujjah came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah! I have two daughters whose father died, and they do not own anything" — and Allah revealed ayah 7.

## Ayah 7: reading the words closely

The ayah says: *For men there is a share in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left. And for women there is a share in what the parents and the nearest of kin have left, be it small or large — a determined share.*

**"al-wālidān" and "al-aqrabūn."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two principles of inheritance from these words. *Al-wālidān*, "the two parents," names the bond of birth between children and their father and mother. *Al-aqrabūn*, "the nearest of kin," names kinship in general, and on the correct interpretation covers every kind of family relationship: birth, wider family, and relations established through marriage. Parents were named separately for their importance; but the second word also makes *nearness* the criterion, not the bare fact of being related. If mere kinship sufficed, every estate would have to be spread over the entire human population — everyone descends from one father and mother, Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ (peace be upon them) — leaving each an insignificant particle, no good to anyone. So the nearer is preferred over the farther, and in the presence of the nearest the farthest gets nothing; but where several are all nearest at once — parents alongside children, or a wife — all share, though the *nature* of their nearness differs.

Since the right to inherit depends on being related, and a girl is born to her parents exactly as a boy is, there is no sense in depriving a small child or a girl.

**Why the sentence is said twice.** Allah could have merged the clauses — "for men and women both there is a share." Instead each entitlement gets its own independent sentence, at apparent cost of repetition. That is the point, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: a woman's right in inheritance is quite independent, and as important as the right of men.

**"Be it small or large."** This corrects the custom of assigning certain things to certain heirs — a horse or a sword inheritable only by young males as of right, others deprived. Everything the deceased owned, big or small, carries the standing right of all the heirs, and no heir may keep anything for himself before the estate is formally distributed by the rules.

**"naṣīban mafrūḍan" — a determined share.** Two implications. First, the shares fixed for each heir in the Qurʼān were determined by Allah: nobody may add, delete, change or transpose them by personal opinion or analogical deduction. Second, the ownership passing to an heir is *automatic and compulsory* — it needs neither his acceptance nor his satisfaction. Even if he declares he will not take his share, he owns it in the sight of the Sharīʿah; as owner he may then gift, sell or distribute it by the rules of the Sharīʿah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws one more line from *al-aqrabūn*: distribution goes by nearness in kinship, not need. The nearer relative is more deserving than the farther even if the farther is poorer and needier, because any other criterion could never harden into settled law — poverty, need and usefulness are not permanent, conditions change, claimants multiply, and nothing could be settled firmly. On this basis the much-discussed case of the orphaned grandson resolves itself: in the presence of a son the grandson is not "the nearest," so he does not inherit — and other arrangements have been made for his needs, one of them in the very next ayah. This position, clarified by the Qurʼān and the Ḥadīth, has been held by the entire Muslim Ummah — whether the grandson's own father is dead or alive — and opposed by none but some contemporary, westernised modernists.

## Ayah 8: those at the edge of the room

Notice the beauty and delicacy of the arrangement, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the just rule that the nearer excludes the farther, and alongside it a whole ayah devoted to their disappointment — for not everyone knows the details of the share system, and every relative would like something.

Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: when poor relatives ineligible for inheritance, along with orphans and the poor, attend the division of an estate that is sometimes substantial, "their hearts will feel eager to have a share," seeing each eligible person assume his portion while they are desperate and given nothing. Ibn Kathīr: Allah, the Most Kind, the Most Compassionate, therefore commands that they be given a share, as an act of kindness, charity, compassion and mercy for them.

**Is this obligatory?** The scholars differed, and Ibn Kathīr lays the views side by side. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said this ayah was not abrogated; Ibn Jarīr recorded from him that it still applies and should be implemented. Ath-Thawrī said that Ibn Abī Najīḥ narrated from Mujāhid that implementing it "is required from those who have anything to inherit, paid from whatever portions their hearts are satisfied with giving away"; similar was reported from Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Mūsā, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān bin Abī Bakr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ash-Shaʿbī and al-Ḥasan. Ibn Sīrīn, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Makḥūl, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿAṭāʾ bin Abī Rabāḥ, az-Zuhrī and Yaḥyā bin Yaʿmar said this payment is obligatory. Others said it refers to bequest at death; others said it was abrogated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds it not obligatory but commendatory — a moral obligation on those receiving shares to give some voluntarily, which becomes charity for them and a means of reward from Allah.

**The right frame of mind.** Wealth is coming to you without any effort of yours, simply through the mercy of Allah — so, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, your heart should beat with the urge to give whatever you can. It draws the parallel with *"Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, and give its due on the day of harvest"* (al-Anʿām 6:141). The arrival of distant kin, orphans and the needy at the division is no cause of irritation but an opportunity sent by Allah to compensate someone else's sense of deprivation. The excluded grandson is such a case — his uncles and paternal aunts should be pleased to give him something each from their shares.

**"and speak to them a fair word."** This closing clause covers the case where those given something are dissatisfied and demand a share equal to everybody else's. That demand is unjust and contrary to the Sharīʿah, so it cannot be satisfied — but the answer must not be crude or wounding. Explain the rules politely: they have no fixed share, and what they received was a gift. One condition: the gift must come from the adult heirs present, out of their own shares, not the undivided estate — such gifts from the shares of minors and absent heirs are not allowed in the Sharīʿah.

## Ayah 9: measure it against your own children

*And let those fear who, if they left behind weak offspring, would be afraid for them.*

Ibn Kathīr reports two ways of taking it. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said it refers to a man near death who dictates a will harming some of his rightful inheritors: Allah commands whoever hears such a will to fear Allah and direct the dying man to what is right and fair, being as eager to protect that man's inheritors as he would be with his own. Similar was reported from Mujāhid and several others. It was also said — Ibn Jarīr from al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās — that guardians should have *taqwā* of Allah when taking care of an orphan's wealth. Ibn Kathīr calls this a sound opinion, supported by the warning that follows in ayah 10: just as you would want your offspring treated fairly after you, treat other people's offspring fairly when given responsibility for them.

**From the Sunnah.** The Two Ṣaḥīḥs record that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited Saʿd bin Abī Waqqāṣ during an illness he suffered from. Saʿd said, "O Messenger of Allah! I am wealthy and have no inheritors except a daughter. Should I give two-thirds of my property in charity?" He ﷺ said, "No." Saʿd asked, "Half?" He ﷺ said, "No." Saʿd said, "One-third?" The Prophet ﷺ said, *"One-third, and even one-third is too much."* The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then said, *"You'd better leave your inheritors wealthy rather than leaving them poor, begging from others."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as the Prophet ﷺ doing what ayah 9 asks — stopping a disposal that would have consumed or curtailed the heirs' shares.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also brings under the ayah the duty of guardians to protect orphaned children's property and hand it over in full when they come of age, never letting the least negligence touch it.

## Ayah 10: what is really being swallowed

*Indeed, those who unjustly consume the property of orphans only consume fire into their bellies, and they will be burnt in a blazing Fire.* Ibn Kathīr: consuming an orphan's wealth without a right is consuming fire, which will kindle in your stomach on the Day of Resurrection.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that many commentators read this metaphorically — devouring an orphan's property is *like* stuffing your stomach with fire, because that is what will happen to him in the Hereafter. But those with deeper insight and proofs, it says, do not support a figure of speech here at all: whatever is eaten unlawfully from an orphan's property is in reality nothing but fire, though it may not look like it at the time. It is like calling the matchbox in your hand fire, or a piece of arsenic a killer — handling neither harms you, but a slight friction, or one swallow down the throat, proves the speaker right. The Qurʼān's general statements support this: a person's deeds, good or evil, are themselves the trees, flowers and fruits of Paradise or the embers of Hell, different in form now but coming forth on the Day of Judgement in their true shapes — *"and they will find what they did present before them"* (al-Kahf 18:49).

It appears in some narrations, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, that those who devour an orphan's property unjustly will be raised on the Day of Judgement with flames of fire coming out from their bellies through their mouths, nostrils, ears and eyes. It also cites (from Ibn Kathīr, vol. 1, p. 456) that the Prophet ﷺ said a set of people will be raised that Day with their mouths erupting with fire; when his noble Companions asked who these could be, he ﷺ said, "Have you not read it in the Qurʼān?" — and recited this ayah. From the same place it cites Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrating that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"I warn you to abstain from the property of the two weak ones — the woman and the orphan."*

And it is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Avoid the seven great destructive sins."* The people asked, "O Allah's Messenger! What are they?" He said, *"To join others in worship along with Allah, magic, to kill the life which Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, to consume interest, to consume an orphan's property, to turn your back to the enemy and flee from the battlefield at the time of fighting, and to accuse chaste women who never even think of anything harmful to their chastity being good believers."*

**"Yaʼkulūn" — they eat.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the verb. Using an orphan's property in whatever manner — eating, drinking, consuming, utilising — is totally unlawful and a sure cause of divine wrath.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid about how this goes wrong — these are things "hardly a home remains unaffected from." When a father dies, whoever assumes control — an uncle, an elder brother, the mother, a guardian or trustee — postpones distribution for years, spending a little here and there to feed and clothe the children. Then the jointly held property goes liberally on religiously unacceptable practices, customs and wasteful expenditure, then on the guardian's own person, sometimes to the point of manipulating documents to put his own children's names in place of the orphans'. Donations made for orphans in religious schools and orphanages must be spent on them; not doing so is itself a form of "eating up" an orphan's property.

From the rulings Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists:

- **Everything the deceased owned is inheritance** — even the clothes on the body. People give such things away in charity without realising they belong to the estate, though minors and absent heirs have rights in all of it. Distribute first, according to the shares of children, wife, parents, sisters and anyone else stipulated by the Islamic law of inheritance. Then it is up to the sharers to give from their own shares on behalf of the deceased if they willingly wish to; to do so jointly they must all be adults, since a minor's permission is not valid, and nothing may be taken from an absent heir's share without his leave.
- **Charity from the undivided estate is impermissible.** Any expense before distribution — entertaining guests, giving charity and alms — is not permitted and brings no merit or reward for the deceased. Giving from combined property that includes an orphan's share is like taking from someone else's property and giving it away on behalf of the deceased. Better not to do it even with the heirs' permission: a minor's is invalid from the outset, and an adult's may not come from a willing heart — he may say yes only to avoid disgrace.
- **Funeral extras** — the sheet spread over the bier, a prayer mat torn from the shroud cloth and given to the imām — are not part of the required shroud (*kafan*) and may not be bought from the jointly held estate, though someone may cover the cost personally. New utensils to bathe the deceased are usually unnecessary, since those in the house will do; and if bought, breaking them afterwards is not permitted — it is waste, and a loss to orphans and absent heirs whose rights attach to the whole estate.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with an anecdote: a pious elder visited a sick Muslim and had hardly sat a little while when the man died. He immediately put out the lamp burning there, gave someone money to buy oil, and had it re-lit. Asked why, he said the lamp had been under this man's ownership while he lived, and using its light was correct then; but now his heirs have the necessary right over everything he owned, and since not all were present to permit it, the lamp was lit at a personal cost. That is the scruple these four ayat plant — a conscience that will not burn another's oil for a minute without leave.

passages.title: The detailed law of inheritance shares
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:11–12 — The Detailed Law of Inheritance

These two ayat lay down, in Allah's own words, who inherits from a deceased Muslim and how much. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that those entitled were briefly mentioned in ayah 7, with more detail still to come at the end of the sūrah. Ayat 11 and 12 give the arithmetic — first the closest relatives by blood (children and parents), then those joined not by lineage but by marriage (husband and wife), and the siblings through the mother.

What holds the passage together is one insistence: these are not human arrangements. Ayah 11 calls its shares *farīḍatan mina-llāh*, "ordained by Allah," and closes **"And Allah is Ever All-Knower, All-Wise."** Ayah 12 has its own phrase — *waṣiyyatan mina-llāh*, which Maʿārif renders **"All this is prescribed by Allah"** — then **"And Allah is All-Knowing, Most Forbearing."**

## Why this passage matters

Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah, the next, and the last ayah of the sūrah are the three verses from which the science of *al-Farāʾiḍ* — the law of inheritance shares — is derived, together with the hadiths that explain them. Learning it is encouraged, he says, especially the specific matters named in these ayat. Ibn ʿUyaynah said knowledge of al-Farāʾiḍ "was called half of knowledge, because it affects all people." Maʿārif adds that the jurists codified these rulings from Qurʾān and Hadith into a permanent science, *ʿIlm al-Farāʾiḍ*.

## The world these ayat walked into

Ibn Kathir: the people of Jāhiliyyah used to give the males, but not the females, a share in the inheritance. Al-Bukhari records Ibn ʿAbbās describing the old custom — the property of the deceased was inherited by his offspring, while the parents inherited only by his will. Then, says Ibn ʿAbbās, Allah cancelled what He willed of that custom and ordained the shares: the male twice the amount of the female, a sixth for each parent, an eighth or a fourth for the wife, a half or a fourth for the husband.

**Orphaned girls, and an uncle who took everything.** Ibn Kathir reports that Ahmad recorded from Jābir: the wife of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Allah's Messenger! These are the two daughters of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ, who was killed as a martyr at Uḥud. Their uncle took their money and did not leave anything for them. They will not be married unless they have money." He ﷺ said, "Allah will decide on this matter." The ayah about inheritance was then revealed, and he ﷺ sent word to the uncle: *"Give two-thirds to Saʿd's two daughters and one eighth for their mother, and whatever is left is yours."* Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah collected this hadith.

## "For a male, the like of the share of two females"

Something easy to miss in translation, says Maʿārif: Allah did not say "for two females there is a share equal to that of one male," but *li-dhakari mithlu ḥaẓẓi-l-unthayayn* — the girl's share is made the basis for determining the boy's. That wording is the Qurʾān showing visible concern that girls actually receive what is theirs.

Why double? Ibn Kathir: men need money to spend on their dependants, on commercial transactions, on work and on fulfilling their obligations; consequently men get twice the portion. The difference is one of responsibility, not of worth.

Ibn Kathir draws more from the same words: that Allah commands parents to be just and fair with their own children "testifies to the fact that Allah is more merciful with children than their own parents are with them." He recalls an authentic hadith in which a captured woman was looking for her child, and when she found him she held him, gave him her breast and nursed him. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked his Companions, *"Do you think that this woman would willingly throw her child in the fire?"* They said, "No, O Messenger of Allah." He said, *"By Allah! Allah is more merciful with His servants than this woman is with her own child."*

## The children's shares (ayah 11)

- **Sons and daughters together:** each son takes twice each daughter's portion. Maʿārif's worked example: one boy and two girls means the property is split into four: two-quarters to the boy, one-quarter to each girl.
- **Daughters only, two or more:** two-thirds, all the girls equal sharers; the remaining third goes to other rightful heirs — the parents of the deceased, or the wife or husband.
- **One daughter only, with no other children:** one half; the rest goes to other inheritors.

Ayah 11 says *fawqa-thnatayn*, "more than two." Some said it really means two and that "more" is redundant. Ibn Kathir rejects this: **nothing in the Qurʾān is useless or redundant.** Had it been about only two, it would have said, "the share of both of them is two-thirds." How, then, do two daughters take two-thirds? Ibn Kathir points to the Book — the ruling that two sisters get two-thirds — and to the Sunnah: the Prophet ﷺ commanded two-thirds for the two daughters of Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ. "So this is proven in the Book and the Sunnah." Maʿārif makes the same point: two girls are governed by the rule that governs more than two.

## The parents' shares (ayah 11)

Both tafsirs set out three situations:

1. **The deceased left children.** Each parent takes a sixth; what remains goes to the children and the surviving spouse. Maʿārif notes that in particular circumstances some of the remainder returns to the father over and above his fixed sixth — in the vocabulary of al-Farāʾiḍ this is *taʿṣīb* (agnatic kinship). Ibn Kathir's illustration: where the deceased had only one daughter, she takes a half, each parent a sixth, and a further sixth goes to the father.
2. **No children and no siblings, only parents surviving.** The mother takes a third, the father the remaining two-thirds. If a husband or wife survives, that spouse's share is taken out first and the mother's third is calculated from **what remains** — because, says Ibn Kathir, the remaining portion is treated just as the entire legacy would be with respect to the parents' shares.
3. **No children, but surviving brothers and sisters.** The mother drops from a third to a sixth, and where there are no other heirs the father takes the rest. Ibn Abi Hatim records Qatādah's comment on *"if he has brothers, his mother has a sixth"*: their presence reduces her share, **but they themselves do not inherit** — the father, as Maʿārif puts it, is nearer than they are. One brother alone does not reduce her share; more than one does. Maʿārif calls this *ḥajb al-nuqṣān*, and notes it applies whether the siblings are full siblings, from the same father but a different mother, or from the same mother but a different father.

Why should the mother's share fall while the father's is untouched? Ibn Kathir reports the people of knowledge's explanation: it is the father who helps the brothers and sisters of the deceased get married, spending from his own money, while the mother does not spend from hers. "This is a sound opinion."

## "You know not which of them is nearer to you in benefit"

Ayah 11 then says: *"Your fathers and your sons — you know not which of them is nearer to you in benefit."* Ibn Kathir explains that shares are here appointed for parents and children alike, contrary to Jāhiliyyah and early Islamic practice, when the inheritance went to the children and the parents received a share only if named in the will, as Ibn ʿAbbās stated; Allah abrogated that. One may derive benefit in this life or for the Hereafter from his parents of a kind he could not get from his children, and the opposite could equally be true; since benefit could come from either side, Allah appointed a fixed share for each.

Maʿārif presses further: had the distribution been left to human opinion, we would have made *beneficialness* the criterion — and who will prove genuinely beneficial we could never ascertain with certainty. So **nearness of kinship** was preferred to usefulness. These are settled injunctions from Allah; nobody may enforce his own opinion or increase or decrease what has been stipulated. There is no aspect of benefit outside the expanse of His knowledge, and no command He gives is bereft of wisdom. Ibn Kathir renders the closing words: Allah "places everything in its rightful place and gives each his rightful share."

## The spouses (ayah 12)

- **Husband:** half of what his wife leaves if she had no child; a fourth if she left a child — in both cases after payment of legacies and debts.
- **Wife:** a fourth of what her husband leaves if he left no child; an eighth if he left a child. Ibn Kathir notes that if there is more than one wife they all *share* that fourth or eighth rather than each receiving it. Maʿārif says the same, and adds that a child from any marriage, present or previous, triggers the reduced share.

Ibn Kathir notes the rule applies to grandchildren too, even great-grandchildren and further in generation.

Maʿārif observes on the order: the husband's right is stated **first**, perhaps to show its importance, because after his wife's death he becomes part of another family. If she died at her parents' home with her assets there, her people might avoid giving him his share; by naming his right first the Qurʾān has possibly condemned that practice.

**A practical ruling from Maʿārif:** before any distribution, the wife's *mahr* (dower) must be ascertained as paid. If the deceased had not paid it, it is a **debt**, paid first from the whole property like all other debts; only then is the inheritance distributed. Having received her mahr, she still takes her fixed share as a competent inheritor. And if the property left is not more than the dower, all of it goes to her against that debt, and no heir receives any share.

## Kalālah, and the siblings through the mother

The rest of ayah 12 addresses the estate of one who dies in *kalālah*. Ibn Kathir explains the word as a derivative of *iklīl*, the crown that surrounds the head: the person's heirs come from other than the first degree of relative. Maʿārif reports that al-Qurṭubī gathers many definitions, the best known being "a person who dies leaving no ascendants and descendants," and cites al-Ālūsī, author of *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, who traces the word to *kalāl*, "to become exhausted," denoting weakness: every relationship other than that of father and son is weak by comparison. The word came to be applied to the deceased who left no son or father, to such an heir, and later even to the property left behind.

Al-Shaʿbī reported that when Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq was asked about the meaning of *kalālah*, he said: "I will say my own opinion about it, and if it is correct, then this correctness is from Allah. However, if my opinion is wrong, it will be my error and because of the evil efforts of Shayṭān, and Allah and His Messenger have nothing to do with it. *Kalālah* refers to the man who has neither descendants nor ascendants." When ʿUmar became Khalīfah he said, "I hesitate to contradict an opinion of Abu Bakr." Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Ibn Jarir and others. Ibn Abi Hatim records that Ibn ʿAbbās was among the last to see ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and ʿUmar said to him, "What you said was the correct opinion" — that *kalālah* refers to the person who has no child or parents. Ibn Kathir lists this as the view of ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd ibn Thābit, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, Jābir ibn Zayd and al-Ḥakam, as well as the people of Madinah, Kufah and Basra, the Seven Fuqahāʾ, the Four Imams and the majority of scholars past and present — so much so that some declared there is a consensus on it.

The "brother or sister" here means **the sibling from the mother's side**, as some of the Salaf stated, including Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ; Qatādah reported this as the view of Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq. Maʿārif adds that Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqāṣ's recitation of the verse reads *"and he has a brother or sister **from his mother**"*, as reported by al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī, al-Jaṣṣāṣ and others; although this rendition did not reach us through *tawātur* (transmission by very large numbers in every generation), the consensus of the ummah makes it worth acting upon. A further proof: the kalālah ruling at the end of the sūrah deals with full siblings and siblings from the same father, and including them here too would set the two injunctions in contradiction.

One such sibling takes a sixth; more than one, they share a third. Ibn Kathir lists four ways they differ from the other heirs: they take a share on account of their mother; **the males and females among them take the same share**; they inherit only where the estate is inherited in kalālah, having no share if the deceased has a surviving father, grandfather, child or grandchild; and they never have more than a third, however numerous. Al-Qurṭubī, quoted in Maʿārif: there is no place in the whole law of shares where male and female are equal except the inheritance of siblings through the mother.

## Debt, will, and "causing no harm"

Three times this section states that the shares come *after any bequest made or debt*. In wording the will comes first; in practice **debt is paid first**. Ibn Kathir reports that the scholars of the Salaf and the Khalaf agree on this and says it is apparent to anyone who reads the ayah carefully; he elsewhere calls it consensus. Maʿārif cites the report of a Companion (Mishkāt, with reference to Tirmidhi): people recite the ayah with the will mentioned before the debt, "but the Holy Prophet ﷺ has settled debt before will."

Why mention the will first? Maʿārif gives the answer of the author of *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: for emphasis on carrying wills out. The beneficiary of a will has paid nothing for it and is often no relative of the testator, so the heirs may ignore or delay it, not liking to see property they would otherwise inherit go elsewhere. A creditor, by contrast, presses his claim, which the heirs cannot refuse — and not everyone even leaves an unpaid debt behind.

Maʿārif sets out the order of rights on the estate: first shrouding and burial, in accordance with the Sharīʿah and avoiding extravagance and stinginess; then debts; then the will, **up to one-third** of what remains; then the fixed shares. If the debts equal or exceed the property, there is no will to execute and no inheritance to distribute. A will is not enforceable beyond a third; making one for more than a third is not appropriate, and if done to exclude inheritors it becomes a sin. And no bequest may be made in favour of an heir at all — the Prophet ﷺ said in his famous address at his last Hajj, *"Surely, Allah has given every person his right; so there is no will for an inheritor"* (Maʿārif: Mishkāt with reference to Abu Dawud; Ibn Kathir cites the same as an authentic hadith: "Allah has given each his fixed due right. Therefore, there is no will for a rightful inheritor."). Maʿārif notes the narrations carry an exception — *unless the heirs themselves consent*; then the bequest may be executed first, and that heir still takes his fixed share.

Ayah 12 then adds two words: *ghayra muḍārr*, **"causing no harm."** Ibn Kathir: let the will be fair and free of any type of harm, without depriving rightful heirs of all or part of their share, or adding to the fixed portion Allah ordained for some heirs — whoever does this "will have disputed with Allah concerning His decision and division." Maʿārif catalogues the ways damage is done: lying about being in debt so wealth goes to a friend; showing personally owned property as held in trust so it falls outside the estate; making a will beyond a third; falsely saying a loan one gave out was repaid so the heirs cannot collect it; gifting more than a third during the final illness. Anyone who does such a thing to deprive his inheritors is committing something strictly forbidden, a major sin. Although the words appear only with the kalālah ruling, Maʿārif stresses that the rule is general and is understood at the two earlier places where will and debt are mentioned.

## Living it

Maʿārif is blunt about the demand most often evaded: those who do not give shares to sisters on the pretext that they have forgone their right are in error, because sisters usually do not forgo their rights willingly. Done reluctantly, knowing they are not going to get anything anyway, they think — why create bad blood between brothers and sisters? **Such an act of forgiving is not valid under Islamic law. Their claim remains due against their brothers, and those who usurp inheritance are terrible sinners.** Where the girls are minors, the sin is committed twice: usurping the share of a legal heir, and devouring the property of an orphan.

Ayah 12 closes not with *Ḥakīm* but with *Ḥalīm*, the Forbearing. Maʿārif reads it as a warning wrapped in mercy: Allah knows everything and has apportioned these shares knowing everyone's true state. Whoever obeys does not fall outside His knowledge; whoever contravenes — including a dying man who engineers harm against his heirs — will find that conduct appear exactly as it is in Allah's knowledge, and be held accountable. It is quite possible that Allah may not punish him here in this world, because He is Forbearing; but the one who disobeys "should better not deceive himself by thinking that he really got away."

passages.title: The limits set by Allah, and the two ends
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close the long section on inheritance by giving it a seal. Having spelled out exactly who inherits and how much, Allah now names those shares for what they are — **ḥudūd Allāh, the limits set by Allah** — and then places two destinations at either end of them: Gardens for the one who keeps within them, the Fire for the one who steps across. What holds ayah 13 and ayah 14 together is that single image of a boundary line with an eternity on each side.

## "These are the limits set by Allah"

Ayah 13 opens with *tilka ḥudūd Allāh* — "These are the limits (set by) Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains what "these" refers to. The *farāʾiḍ* — the fixed, obligatory shares of inheritance just laid down — **are** Allah's set limits. As he puts it, this includes what Allah has allotted for the heirs "according to the degree of relation they have to the deceased, and their degree of dependency on him. Therefore, do not transgress or violate them."

That is worth sitting with. On Ibn Kathir's reading, the fractions in the preceding ayat are not accounting conventions or a rough attempt at fairness that a family might improve on. They are limits set by Allah, allotted by Him with regard to closeness of kinship and to dependency. A limit is not a suggestion. You are either inside it or outside it.

## The two ends

The passage then splits into two parallel halves, and the parallelism is the point.

**Ayah 13** — "whosoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, will be admitted to Gardens under which rivers flow, to abide therein, and is the great success" (*al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm*).

**Ayah 14** — "whosoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, and transgresses His (set) limits, He will cast him into the Fire, to abide therein; and he shall have a disgraceful torment" (*ʿadhāb muhīn*).

Obedience against disobedience; Gardens against Fire; abiding against abiding. The mirror is deliberate: there is no third place to stand in relation to a limit.

Notice also that in ayah 14 the wording is fuller than a simple opposite. It is not only "whoever disobeys" but "and transgresses His limits" — *wa yataʿadda ḥudūdah*. Disobedience here is described not as falling short but as **transgressing a limit that had already been set**. That matters, because it names the specific sin of the passage: not ignorance of the shares, but going past them.

## What obedience looks like here — and what disobedience looks like

Ibn Kathir reads "whosoever obeys Allah and His Messenger" as meaning, concretely, obedience **regarding the inheritance** — the person who "does not add or decrease any of these fixed shares by use of tricks and plots. Rather, he gives each his appointed share as Allah commanded, ordained and decided."

Two things in that sentence deserve attention.

First, the phrase **"tricks and plots."** Ibn Kathir does not restrict the violation to an open refusal of Allah's division; adding to or subtracting from the fixed shares by trickery falls under the same warning. What is judged is whether each heir received his appointed share, not how the outcome was arranged.

Second, the reason the punishment in ayah 14 is so severe. Ibn Kathir explains: "This is because he changed what Allah has ordained and disputed with His judgment. Indeed, this is the behaviour of those who do not agree with what Allah has decided and divided, and this is why Allah punishes them with humiliation in the eternal, painful torment."

So the gravity is not merely financial. To rearrange the shares is, in Ibn Kathir's words, to change what Allah has ordained and to dispute with His judgment — to set one's own sense of who deserves what against Allah's ruling. It is a quarrel with the Judge, conducted through an estate.

**And the punishment answers the crime.** The torment in ayah 14 is called *muhīn* — disgracing, humiliating. Ibn Kathir's word for what Allah does to such a person is exactly that: He "punishes them with humiliation in the eternal, painful torment." The one who reached past his appointed share is met with humiliation.

## From the Sunnah: the deed that undoes seventy years

Ibn Kathir brings two narrations here, and both are about the same terrifying possibility — that a lifetime can be overturned at the very end by an unjust will.

**Imam Ahmad recorded** that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "A man might perform the actions of righteous people for seventy years, but when it is time to compile his will, he commits injustice. So his final work will be his worst, and he thus enters the Fire. A man might perform the deeds of evil people for seventy years, yet he is fair in his will. So his final work will be his best, and he thus enters Paradise."

And then Abu Hurayrah himself said: "Read, if you will, *tilka ḥudūd Allāh* — 'These are the limits set by Allah' — until *ʿadhāb muhīn*, 'a disgraceful torment.'" In other words, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ pointed at precisely these two ayat as the reading that goes with that hadith. Ayah 13 and ayah 14 are the two men in the narration: one ends inside the limit, one ends outside it.

**In the chapter on injustice in the will, Abu Dawud recorded in his Sunan** that Abu Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "A man or a woman might perform actions in obedience to Allah for sixty years. Yet, when they are near death, they leave an unfair will and thus acquire the Fire."

Abu Hurayrah then recited the ayah "After payment of legacies he (or she) may have bequeathed or debts, so that no loss is caused" — up to "and that is the great success." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also recorded by At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, and that **At-Tirmidhi said: "Ḥasan Gharīb."**

Read the two narrations together and the lesson is stark. Sixty or seventy years of worship, and then an unjust will at the end — and, as the first narration puts it, "his final work will be his worst." The reverse is also stated, and it is the mercy in the hadith: a life spent in the deeds of evil people, sealed by a fair will, ends in Paradise. What a person does with wealth he is about to leave behind is, in these narrations, weighty enough to decide the ending.

## Why the passage ends this way at all

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān makes an observation about the Qur'an's method that explains the placement of these two ayat: "It is the consistent style of the Holy Qur'an that whenever it has described the beliefs and injunctions prescribed by Allah, it is followed by promises of reward or warnings of punishment."

That is what is happening here. The rules of inheritance have been given; now come the promise and the warning, "to stress upon Muslims to obey these injunctions." Law in the Qur'an is not left as bare law. It is anchored at both ends to the Hereafter, so that a question about fractions of an estate is never only a legal question.

## Some further rules of inheritance

Under the heading "Some additional rules of inheritance," Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets out here a number of rulings that the earlier ayat did not spell out.

**Difference of religion.** The distribution of inheritance is based on nearness of kinship, but there are exceptions — the first being that the deceased and the heir should not be of two different religions. So a Muslim does not inherit from a *kafir*, nor a *kafir* from a Muslim, whatever the lineal relationship between them. The Prophet ﷺ said, as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites from *Mishkat* (p. 263): "The Muslim does not inherit the kafir, nor does the kafir inherit the Muslim." This rule relates to a person who is Muslim or *kafir* by birth. For a man who was a Muslim, turned away from Islam, and died or was killed in that state of apostasy, whatever he earned while a Muslim goes to his Muslim heirs, and what he earned after his apostasy is deposited in the *Bayt al-Māl* (the public treasury). For a woman who becomes an apostate, all her property — from either period — goes to her Muslim heirs. An apostate, man or woman, inherits neither from a Muslim nor from another apostate.

**The killer does not inherit.** If someone kills a person from whose property he was entitled to a share, he no longer remains his heir and is excluded from that inheritance. The Prophet ﷺ said, again cited from *Mishkat* (p. 263): "The killer shall not inherit." Some forms of *qatl al-khaṭaʾ* (accidental or unintended homicide) are excepted from this rule, with the details in the books of fiqh.

**The unborn child.** If a person leaves children and his wife is pregnant, the unborn child is also counted among the heirs. Since the sex and number cannot be known with certainty, it is appropriate to postpone distribution until the birth. If distribution must be made, then as an expedient measure one supposes the two cases — a boy or a girl — gives the heirs the lesser of the two resulting portions, and holds the remainder for the child to be born.

**A woman in her ʿiddah (waiting period).** If a man divorces his wife revocably and dies before the divorce is revoked and before her waiting period expires, she inherits, because the marriage is in force. If he divorces her during the sickness that culminates in his death — even irrevocably, even by a threefold pronouncement — and dies before her waiting period expires, she still inherits; and in order that she may inherit, the longer of the two waiting periods is taken as operative (the waiting period after a divorce is three menstrual periods; after the death of the husband it is four lunar months and ten days). But if he divorced her irrevocably, or by pronouncing it thrice, *before* any sickness culminating in his death, and then died during her waiting period, she does not inherit — though she does if the divorce was revocable. And if the wife herself secured the separation by *khulʿ* during the sickness that culminates in his death, she is not an heir, even though he may die during her waiting period.

**Aṣḥāb al-furūḍ and ʿaṣabāt.** Twelve heirs have shares settled and fixed by the Sharīʿah, known as *farāʾiḍ*; these heirs are called *aṣḥāb al-furūḍ*, the possessors of obligatory shares as determined in the Qur'an. If there is no heir from that category, or if property remains after their shares are given, the residue goes to the *ʿaṣabāt* (agnatic heirs, or residuaries). There are times when one person alone inherits in both capacities; and there are situations in which the children of the deceased and his father, and the offspring of the father — that is, the brother — also become *ʿaṣabāt*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives a worked example. Zayd dies leaving four heirs: a wife, a daughter, a mother and an uncle. The estate is divided into twenty-four shares: twelve (one half) to the daughter, three to the wife against her one-eighth, four to the mother against her one-sixth, and the residue of five shares to the uncle in his capacity as *ʿaṣaba*, the nearest male agnate.

Two further rulings: if there are no *ʿaṣabāt*, the residue left after the fixed shares are distributed is also given to the *aṣḥāb al-furūḍ*, in proportion to their shares — known in the terminology of *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ* (the science of inheritance) as **Radd**, "Return," since the residue returns to them — except that the husband or the wife is not entitled to this return and receives no more than the specified share. And if there is no one from the *aṣḥāb al-furūḍ* and no *ʿaṣaba* either, the inheritance goes to *Dhawī al-Arḥām*, the maternal kinsmen: a large list that includes maternal grandsons and granddaughters, the offspring of sisters, paternal aunts, and maternal uncles and aunts. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that the subject has far more detail than can be taken up in this context.

## Living it

For most people this passage becomes real at exactly two moments.

**When you write your will.** The narrations Ibn Kathir cites — from Imam Ahmad and from Abu Dawud's Sunan — do not describe rare monsters. They describe a man who performed the actions of righteous people for seventy years, and a man or woman who obeyed Allah for sixty, and then were unjust in the will. Ayah 13 promises Gardens to the one who gives each heir "his appointed share as Allah commanded, ordained and decided." Ayah 14 warns of the alternative. Write the will inside the limit.

**When an estate is being divided.** Ibn Kathir's warning is against adding to or decreasing any of the fixed shares "by use of tricks and plots" — that is, the outcome is what is judged, however it is reached. To alter the shares is, in his reading, to change what Allah has ordained and to dispute with His judgment.

The mercy in the passage is that the limit is **knowable**. Allah did not leave a family to guess where fairness lies and then punish them for guessing wrong. He allotted the shares Himself, with regard to the heirs' closeness to the deceased and their dependency on him, and told us where the line runs. Ayah 13 then calls staying inside it *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* — the great success. It is a striking thing to say about the act of handing someone else their share. But that is how the Qur'an frames it: a person who lets Allah's division stand, when he had both the power and the motive to bend it, has won.
