passages.title: Punishing indecency and the repentance Allah will accept
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the courtroom to the heart. Ayah 15 lays down the earliest Islamic response to indecency committed by women — a demanding standard of proof, and a punishment that the verse itself announces will one day be replaced. Ayah 16 turns to "the two" who commit it, commands that they be punished, and then closes by pointing them toward repentance. Ayat 17 and 18 pick up that thread: whose repentance does Allah accept, and when does the door close? Law that restrains, then mercy that reclaims — that is what holds the passage together.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places them in a run of passages correcting the customs of jāhiliyyah — after orphans and inheritance come the cruel treatment of women and other evil customs of that age, such as marrying prohibited women.

## Ayah 15: four witnesses, and why the bar is set so high

The word for the offence is **al-fāḥishah** — the shameful, indecent act. Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: *yaʿnī al-zinā*, meaning unlawful sexual intercourse.

Then the demand: *fastash-hidū ʿalayhinna arbaʿatan minkum* — "take the evidence of four witnesses from among you against them." Maʿārif explains that the case must go before the executive authority, which calls for four qualified witnesses; all four must be men, the testimony of women not being valid in this particular matter.

Why so severe a standard? Because, Maʿārif says, zinā is a crime of extremely grave nature: it violates honour and modesty, and it brings a bad name to the family. The condition, Maʿārif observes plainly, is very hard to meet; it is something which can very seldom take place. And that difficulty is the point — this strict approach was taken so that a husband, his mother, another wife or a sister could not level undue accusations out of personal spite, and so that other ill-wishing people could not use the charge to release their private hostility.

And the protection has teeth: if fewer than four testify, the evidence is invalid, and the complainant and the witnesses may all be charged as liars — the ḥadd of *qadhf*, the punishment for false accusation, becomes operative against them for having falsely accused a Muslim. Maʿārif cites Sūrah al-Nūr (24:13), which means that those who cannot produce four witnesses are liars.

Maʿārif also passes on a reflection from some revered elders on the wisdom of the number four: because the case involves two individuals, a man and a woman, one case here effectively covers two — and since each would require two witnesses, four become necessary.

## "Until death comes to them, or Allah ordains for them some other way"

The punishment prescribed is confinement to the home. Ibn Kathir states it directly: at the beginning of Islam, if a woman's adultery was established by sufficient proof, she was confined to her home, without leave, until she died.

But the verse leaves a door ajar — *aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā*, "or Allah ordains for them some other way." Ibn Kathir explains that this "way" is the abrogation of the ruling that came later. Ibn ʿAbbās said the early ruling was confinement, until Allah sent down Sūrat al-Nūr, which abrogated it with the ruling of flogging for fornication and stoning to death for adultery; Ibn Kathir reports that similar was narrated from ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, Zayd bin Aslam and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, calling it a matter that is agreed upon. Maʿārif records the same gloss of the word "way" from Ibn ʿAbbās — stoning to death for the married, lashing for the unmarried (al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-Tafsīr).

There is a striking report of that moment. Ibn Kathir writes that Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿUbādah bin al-Ṣāmit that when revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ it would affect him and his face would show signs of strain. One day a revelation came down, and when he ﷺ was relieved of its strain he said: "Take from me: Allah has made some other way for them… The married gets a hundred lashes and stoning to death, while the unmarried gets a hundred lashes then banishment for a year." Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan recorded the same from ʿUbādah, and al-Tirmidhī said of it, *Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ*. Notice what he ﷺ announces first: *Allah has made a way* — the promise of ayah 15, kept.

Maʿārif adds that this "way" stands proved through the Prophet's ﷺ own clear statements — the ḥadd he ﷺ pronounced upon Māʿiz ibn Mālik and a woman of the tribe of Azd, both of them married and both stoned — while Sūrah al-Nūr states the hundred lashes for the unmarried explicitly (24:2). Maʿārif also notes that a verse concerning *rajm* was revealed and its recitation later abrogated while the injunction itself remained operative, citing Sayyidnā ʿUmar: the Prophet ﷺ stoned, "and we stoned after him" (al-Bukhārī and Muslim, as in Mishkāt).

So the ruling of ayah 15 is not the standing law of Islam. It was the measure of an early stage, and the verse announced its own replacement before it came.

## Ayah 16: "and the two of you who commit it"

**The punishment.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd bin Jubayr that this punishment included cursing them, shaming them, and beating them with sandals, and that this was the ruling until Allah abrogated it with flogging or stoning. Maʿārif adds a careful point: no definite *ḥadd* is described in these two ayat. The text says only "punish them" and "confine them," with no particular method specified — that was left to the discretion of the authorities, and Ibn ʿAbbās's description appears to be illustrative rather than exhaustive. In the order of revelation, Maʿārif notes, the command to punish came first, and the confinement of the women to their homes came afterwards.

**A difference over who is meant.** Ibn Kathir reports Mujāhid's view that the verse "was revealed about the case of two men who do it," as if referring to the actions of the people of Lūṭ — adding, "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif treats this as a genuine disagreement: some commentators, including Qāḍī Thanāullāh Pānīpatī, read ayah 16 of an act between two males, since the Arabic pronoun used is masculine and presumes males on both sides; those who read both verses of zinā between a man and a woman refute this on the principle that in general usage masculine expressions include the feminine as well. Maʿārif does not force a verdict, saying that the possibility cannot be ruled out.

## "Then if they repent and correct themselves, turn away from them"

Ayah 16 closes on mercy, and the wording is exact. Ibn Kathir explains *fa-in tābā wa aṣlaḥā* as refraining from that evil act, so that thereafter their actions become righteous — repentance is not a word said; it is a stopping and a mending. And *fa-aʿriḍū ʿanhumā* means, in his words, do not verbally abuse them after that — "since he who truly repents is just like he who has no sin." He supports this with what is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs: "When the slave-girl of one of you commits illegal sexual intercourse, let him flog her and not chastise her afterwards" — because the lashes she receives erase the sin that she has committed.

**A grammatical detail worth catching.** Maʿārif draws attention to the connecting *fāʾ* ("then"). Because repentance is mentioned *after* the punishment in the verse's sequence, the act of repentance does not absolve them of the penalty; it means that once they have been punished and have repented, they should not be disgraced or punished any further — whereas in case repentance has not been made, reproach is in order even after punishment. The law ends when the punishment ends, and so must the shaming.

The verse seals it with two of Allah's names: *innallāha kāna Tawwāban Raḥīmā* — Allah is Ever the One who accepts repentance, Most Merciful.

## Ayah 17: what "in ignorance" actually means

Read quickly, *bi-jahālah* looks like a narrow door: only sins done in ignorance are forgivable. Maʿārif dismantles that impression using the explanation given by the noble Companions. *Jahālah* here does not mean that the person was unaware of a sin as sin, nor that he lacked intention or volition. It means the insensitivity and heedlessness of a person toward the evil end of sin and its ultimate punishment — the very thing that gave him the audacity to venture into it, though he knew it was a sin and approached it deliberately. The word is used, Maʿārif says, in the sense of carelessness or stupidity.

The proof is inside the Qur'an. In Sūrah Yūsuf, Yūsuf (peace be upon him) says to his brothers, "Do you know what you did to Yūsuf and his brother when you were ignorant?" (12:89) — though what they did was not error or forgetfulness but knowing and fully deliberate, they are called *jāhilūn* because of their heedlessness toward the evil end of their act.

The early authorities agree, and Ibn Kathir stacks up the reports. Mujāhid: "Every person who disobeys Allah, even wilfully, is ignorant while committing the act of disobedience" — to which Maʿārif adds the telling qualifier: even though, on the outside, he may appear to be a person of great learning. Qatādah reported from Abū al-ʿĀliyah that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say, "Every sin that the servant commits, he commits out of ignorance." By a separate chain — ʿAbd al-Razzāq from Maʿmar from Qatādah — Ibn Kathir records that the Companions agreed that every sin committed, by intention or otherwise, is committed in ignorance; Maʿārif reports that same agreement from Abū al-ʿĀliyah and Qatādah. And ʿIkrimah said that everything one does in this world outside the framework of obedience to Allah is *jahālah* — for one who accepts an everlasting punishment in exchange for short-lived pleasures cannot be called rational, sensible or smart.

This matters enormously for an ordinary struggling believer: since every sin, deliberate or not, is *jahālah*, the verse excludes no one. Maʿārif states the settled position — there is a consensus of the entire Muslim ummah that the repentance of a person who commits a sin deliberately can also be accepted (*al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*).

One more phrase needs care: acceptance of repentance is said to be *ʿalā-llāh*, "upon Allah." Maʿārif clarifies it precisely — this is a form of promise whose fulfilment is certain; otherwise the truth is that Allah does not necessarily owe anything to anyone. The certainty flows from His own undertaking, not from any claim His creation holds over Him.

## "And repent soon afterwards" — how soon is soon?

Ibn Kathir lines up the early answers, and they converge generously. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah: "until just before he looks at the angel of death." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: "Just before his last breath leaves his throat." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "Everything before death is 'soon'." ʿIkrimah went furthest: "All of this life is 'soon'."

The Prophet ﷺ fixed the limit himself. Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger ﷺ said: "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as the soul does not reach the throat" — also collected by al-Tirmidhī, who said *Ḥasan Gharīb*, and by Ibn Mājah. Ibn Kathir cites too, from Imam Ahmad, Abū Dharr's narration that Allah accepts the repentance of His servant "as long as the veil does not drop," which the Prophet ﷺ explained as the soul being removed while one is a polytheist. Maʿārif adds a report of Muḥaddith Ibn Marduwayh from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar: a believing servant who repents a month before his death, or a day, or a moment earlier, has his repentance accepted — provided it is genuine and sincere.

Maʿārif draws the practical conclusion: the Prophet's ﷺ own explanation tells us that virtually a person's whole lifetime comes under "soon," so any repentance offered well before death is acceptable; only repentance made in the throes of death is not. Maʿārif adds a distinction from Maulānā Ashraf Thānavī's *Bayān al-Qurʼān*: a dying person passes through two conditions — first, the state of conscious suffering, when all medicines and efforts have failed and he realises death is round the corner; and then the state of total despair, when the pangs of the soul's departure begin and the time of *ghargharah* draws near — the rattling sound from the throat that heralds approaching death, a state in which the angels and the things of the Hereafter may start appearing before him. The first still falls within *min qarīb*; the second does not. A warning is tucked inside the phrase too: Maʿārif notes that *min qarīb* serves to indicate that a person's very lifespan is limited in time, and that death, which he may think is far away, may actually be quite near.

## Ayah 18: the repentance that arrives too late

Ayah 18 draws the boundary from the other side: repentance is of no effect for those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death faces one of them, he says, "Now I repent" — nor for those who die as disbelievers.

Ibn Kathir describes the moment: when hope in continued living diminishes, the angel of death comes forth, the soul reaches the throat, approaches the chest, and arrives at the state where it is being gradually pulled out — and then there is no accepted repentance, nor a way out of that certain end. He connects this to those who said, on seeing Allah's punishment, "We believe in Allah alone" (40:84), and to the day when some of the signs of the Lord come and faith no longer benefits a soul that did not believe before (6:158). Maʿārif adds the parallel of Pharaoh and his people, who called out while drowning that they now believed in the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn, and were told that their declaration at that time was of no consequence, because the time set for it was over. The tragedy was not that Allah's mercy ran out; it was that they kept running wild with their lives and wasted every opportunity to repent while there was still time.

On the final clause, Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ bin Anas that it was revealed about the people of shirk. Such a person's sorrow and repentance shall not avail him; were he to ransom himself with the earth's fill of gold, it would not be accepted from him. Of the torment prepared for them Ibn Kathir says: torment that is severe, eternal and enormous.

## What tawbah actually is

Maʿārif closes by drawing on Imam al-Ghazālī's *Iḥyāʾ al-ʿUlūm*, which identifies three different situations with regard to sin:

1. **Total sinlessness** — no sin ever committed: the hallmark of the angels, or of the prophets, peace be upon them.
2. **Sinning, then repeating and persisting** — never feeling ashamed or regretful, never thinking of stopping and abandoning it: the degree of the devils.
3. **Sinning, then immediately regretting it** and resolving firmly never to go near it again: the station of the children of Ādam.

Failing to repent after sinning, then, is exclusively the style of devils — hence the consensus of the entire ummah that tawbah is obligatory. Allah says: "O you who believe, repent before Allah, a sincere repentance; may be your Lord removes from you your sins and admits you to gardens beneath which rivers flow" (66:8). A man may spend a whole lifetime in disobedience, yet on repenting sincerely before death he is not only forgiven but admitted into the circle of Allah's favoured servants and made an inheritor of Paradise. Maʿārif cites a ḥadīth in Ibn Mājah that one who repents from sin is loved by Allah, and one who has repented from a sin is like one who had never committed a sin. Maʿārif adds that according to some narrations, when a repentance is accepted, even the written record posted by the angels is erased from the book of deeds, so that the servant may not be disgraced.

**The three pillars of a real repentance**, as Maʿārif lays them out:

- **Regret** — feeling shame and remorse over what one has done. According to a ḥadīth, repentance is remorse itself.
- **Leaving it now** — abandon the sin immediately, and firmly resolve to stay away from it in future.
- **Making amends**, as far as one is able: missed prayers and fasts made up as *qaḍāʾ* — if the number is not remembered, calculate an estimate and begin in all seriousness, offering one missed prayer alongside each daily prayer, commonly called *ʿumrī qaḍāʾ*; unpaid zakāh of previous years paid off, all at once or gradually; a right usurped returned to its owner; a person hurt asked for forgiveness.

If a person does not regret what he has done, or, despite being regretful, will not leave the sin for the future, this is no repentance at all, though it be said a thousand times. Maʿārif quotes a Persian verse: repentance on the lips, a rosary in the hand, and a heart full of the taste of sin — sin laughs at our style of seeking forgiveness.

But if you break your repentance, renew it at once, in the fond hope that Allah, being Most-Forgiving, will relent toward you again. Maʿārif ends with a Persian couplet worth carrying: this is the Court of My Presence, not the Court of Despair — even if you have broken your repentance a hundred times, come again.

passages.title: Women are not inherited; honour the dowry
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat dismantle, in one movement, the idea that a woman is a possession. Ayah 19 forbids treating a widow as part of her dead husband's estate, forbids squeezing a wife to make her hand back what is hers, and then — having cleared away the abuse — commands something positive: *live with them honourably*. Ayat 20 and 21 press the same principle onto money: if a man wants out of a marriage, he leaves with nothing of what he gave her, however large it was.

What holds the unit together is a single target. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the root evil was that "men used to act as owners of the life and property of women." Every abuse the passage names grows from that one assumption, and the passage attacks the assumption itself rather than trimming its branches.

## The world these ayat walked into

Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas explained the occasion of ayah 19: "Before, the practice was that when a man dies, his male relatives used to have the right to do whatever they wanted with his wife. If one of them wants, he would marry her, give her in marriage, or prevent her from marriage, for they had more right to her than her own family. Thereafter, this Ayah was revealed about this practice."

Read that slowly. A woman's husband dies — and she finds that she has been transferred, not to her own family and not to her own choice, but to whichever male relative of the deceased moves first. He may marry her himself. He may marry her off to someone else and take payment for it. Or he may simply freeze her: refuse to marry her, refuse to release her, and wait.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out how that one assumption bred a whole family of injustices:

- **Her property was swallowed.** If she inherited something from her parents or received a gift, "the poor thing stayed deprived of it. Everything received in her name was devoured by men at her husband's home."
- **She was locked in place.** If she did somehow hold her share, men would block her from remarrying so that her wealth could not leave the house — "they wanted her to die right there where she was," leaving property they could then take.
- **She was starved into surrender.** A husband who had tired of his wife for no fault of hers would neither live with her nor divorce her. He would harass her until she handed back the jewellery and dower, or waived what he still owed. Some men divorced a wife and then still obstructed her remarriage until she broke and returned the dower.
- **Her in-laws held her hostage.** After a husband's death his heirs would refuse to let the widow remarry — out of a false sense of family prestige, or simply to extract something for themselves in the bargain.

The Qur'an does not legislate against each of these one by one. It goes to the trunk: *it is not lawful for you to inherit women*.

## "It is not lawful" — the shape of the prohibition

Two features of the Arabic in ayah 19 repay attention.

**First, the word *karhan* — "against their will."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: this is not a condition, as though inheriting a woman *with* her approval would be acceptable. It is a statement of fact. Taking charge of a woman's life and property as a self-appointed owner, with no legal or rational basis whatsoever, could only ever happen by force. Quoting al-Bahr al-Muhit: how could a woman in her normal senses ever agree to such a proposition? And so, Maʿārif adds, the Sharīʿah does not treat her approval as effective here at all. If some woman were so out of her mind as to approve being owned, Islamic law refuses to concede the position. Some things cannot be consented into legitimacy.

**Second, why "it is not lawful" rather than "do not."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ordinary way to stop a wrong is a prohibitive command. Here the Qur'an instead negates the lawfulness of the act: *lā yaḥillu lakum*. Beyond stressing how grave the sin is, this may also point to a legal consequence — that if a man does marry an adult woman without her consent and permission, the marriage is not merely sinful but null and void. No husband–wife relationship comes into being, and none of the rulings of inheritance or lineage follow from it. The same logic extends to money: if a man forces a woman to return her dower or to waive what is still outstanding, that forced return or waiver is not valid in the sight of the Sharīʿah. The wealth does not become lawful to him, and the right is not actually forgiven.

## "Do not squeeze them"

The next clause — *wa lā taʿḍulūhunna li-tadhhabū bi-baʿḍi mā ātaytumūhunna* — is rendered by the two commentaries from slightly different angles, and both belong to the meaning. Ibn Kathir reads it as harassment: "Do not treat the woman harshly so that she gives back all or part of the dowry that she was given, or forfeits one of her rights by means of coercion and oppression." Maʿārif reads it as obstruction: do not prevent women from marrying at their choice, with the intention of taking back what you or a relative already gave them as dower or gift.

Maʿārif draws a practical line. Whatever was given to the wife as her own — dower, gift, anything she was made the owner of — cannot be reclaimed by the husband or his heirs. But if something was handed to her only for temporary use, jewellery or another article she was never made owner of, that never entered her ownership, and asking for its return is not forbidden. The rule protects property, not pretexts on either side.

**The exception: "unless they commit open *fāḥishah*."** Here the early scholars genuinely differed, and Ibn Kathir records the difference rather than flattening it. A long list — Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, ash-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Muhammad bin Sīrīn, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abū Qilābah, Abū Ṣāliḥ, as-Suddī, Zayd bin Aslam and Saʿīd bin Abī Hilāl — held it refers to illicit sex. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk are also reported as saying *fāḥishah* means disobedience and defiance. Ibn Jarīr chose the general reading: the word covers all of it — adultery, disobedience, defiance, rudeness — and Ibn Kathir comments that this view "is good, and Allah knows best." Maʿārif reports the same split, attributing the "disobedience to the husband and indecent abuses against him" reading to Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah and Ḥaḍrat Ḍaḥḥāk and others, and the "immodesty and adultery" reading to Abū Qilābah and Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

The exception is narrow by design: the fault must be hers, and it must be *mubayyinah* — open, evident. Ibn Kathir connects it to Sūrat al-Baqarah: "it is not lawful for you to take back any of what you have given them, except when both parties fear that they would be unable to keep the limits ordained by Allah" (2:229).

## "And live with them honourably"

Then the ayah turns. Having sealed off the exits, Allah commands the actual standard: *wa ʿāshirūhunna bi'l-maʿrūf*. Maʿārif notes that husbands are specifically the ones addressed in this word.

Ibn Kathir unpacks *maʿrūf* concretely: "by saying kind words to them, treating them kindly and making your appearance appealing for them, as much as you can, just as you like the same from them." That last clause is the measure — the standard is reciprocity, not indulgence. He cites alongside it: "And they have rights similar over them to what is reasonable" (2:228).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ saying: "The best among you is he who is the best with his family. Verily, I am the best one among you with my family." And he describes what that looked like: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was kind, cheerful, playful with his wives, compassionate, spending on them and laughing with them. He used to race ʿĀ'ishah, the Mother of the Faithful, as a means of kindness to her. She said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ raced with me and I won the race. This occurred before I gained weight, and afterwards I raced with him again, and he won that race." He said: "This [victory] is for that [victory]." Sometimes all his wives would gather and eat together at the house of whichever one he was staying with, then go back to their homes. He would talk with the wife whose night it was after praying ʿIshāʾ, before he went to sleep. Ibn Kathir then quotes: "Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example to follow" (33:21).

**"And if you dislike them…"** The ayah does not pretend every marriage is easy: *it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah brings through it a great deal of good.* Ibn Kathir explains that patience in keeping a wife one dislikes carries good reward in this life and the Hereafter, and cites Ibn ʿAbbās: the husband may come to feel compassion towards her, and Allah may give him a child with her, a child carrying tremendous goodness. He also cites the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ: "No believing man should hate his believing wife. If he dislikes a part of her conduct, he would surely like another."

## Ayah 20: even a *qintar* stays with her

Ayah 20 takes the hardest case for the man: he simply wants a different wife. Maʿārif frames it exactly so — the woman has shown no contumacy and no immodesty; the husband, "following his own physical desire and pleasure," intends to marry another woman in her place. Even then, he may claim nothing from her in exchange for the divorce, however much wealth he gave her, and he may not force her to forgo an unpaid dower.

The Qur'an names the sum as a *qintār*. Ibn Kathir refers the reader to his tafsir of Sūrah Āl ʿImrān for the word's meaning and simply draws the ruling: even if the dowry was a *qintār* of money, not a portion of it may be taken back — and, he notes, "this Ayah is clear in its indication that the dowry could be substantial."

**ʿUmar and the woman from the Quraysh.** Ibn Kathir attaches a famous incident to that last point. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abū al-ʿAjfāʾ as-Sulamī heard ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb say: "Do not exaggerate with the dowry of women, had this practice been an honour in this world or a part of Taqwa, then the Prophet ﷺ would have had more right to practise it than you. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never gave any of his wives, nor did any of his daughters receive a dowry more than twelve Uwqiyah. A man used to pay a substantial dowry and thus conceal enmity towards his wife!" Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad and the collectors of Sunan collected it through various chains, and that at-Tirmidhī said, "Hasan Sahih."

Then the second report, which Ibn Kathir says al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā recorded from Masrūq, with a chain he calls strong. ʿUmar stood on the minbar of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and told the people not to exaggerate in dowries: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions used to pay up to four hundred dirhams or less, and he did not want to hear of anyone paying more. He came down — and a woman from Quraysh challenged him. "Have you not heard what Allah sent down in the Qur'an?" "Which part of it?" She recited: *and you have given one of them a qintār*. ʿUmar said, "O Allah! Forgive me…" He went back up the minbar and announced: "I had prohibited you from paying more than four hundred dirhams in a dowry for women. So, let everyone pay what he likes from his money."

The Leader of the Faithful, corrected in public by a woman citing an ayah, and reversing himself on the spot. Ibn Kathir's own summary of ʿUmar's position is that he "used to discourage giving a large dowry, but later on changed his view."

## Ayah 21: three arguments, each heavier than the last

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 20–21 as building the case against seizing the dower in three stages.

**First — *buhtānan wa ithman mubīnan*, "wrongfully and with a manifest sin."** This is subtler than it looks. Maʿārif points back to ayah 19: the only ground on which a husband may take back the dower is that his wife committed a shameful act. So if he takes it back when she has done no such thing, his very claim asserts a slander against her. He is, in effect, imputing to her a shameful act, because that is the only situation in which his claim could be rightful. That is *buhtān* — a false imputation — and an open sin.

**Second — *wa qad afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ*, "you have gone in unto each other."** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, as-Suddī and several others said this means marital intimacy. Ibn Kathir puts the question as the ayah does: how can you take back the dowry from a woman with whom you have shared this? Maʿārif adds the reasoning: the cause that made the dower due has already been fulfilled; she certainly deserved it, and she owns it. And if what he gave was a gift rather than dower, that too cannot be recovered, "because what a husband and wife give to each other as gift cannot be taken back" — such a claim is neither permissible in Sharīʿah nor legally enforced.

Notice the reciprocity in the Arabic: *baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ*, "each of you to the other." Ibn Kathir's own paraphrase keeps it mutual — the woman with whom you had relations and who had relations with you. The verse refuses to describe this as something a man did to a woman.

Ibn Kathir illustrates the principle with a striking case. The Two Sahihs record that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said three times to the spouses who said the *mulāʿanah* (the mutual oath-swearing between a husband and wife over an accusation): "Allah knows that one of you is a liar, so would any of you repent?" The man said, "O Messenger of Allah! My money" — meaning the dowry he had given his wife. The Messenger ﷺ answered: "You have no money. If you are the one who said the truth, the dowry is in return for the right to have sexual intercourse with her. If you are the one who uttered the lie, then this money is even farther from your reach." Either way, the money is gone. There is no arrangement of the facts under which he gets it back.

**Third — *wa akhadhna minkum mīthāqan ghalīẓan*, "and they have taken from you a firm and strong covenant."** Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr said this refers to the marriage tie. Maʿārif describes it as the bond of marriage, "solemnly attested to with the name of Allah before a gathering of people following a khutbah."

Consider the grammar: *they* took it *from you*. The covenant is not something the husband holds over his wife; it is something she holds over him, and she took it in Allah's name before witnesses. Ibn Kathir places beside this the words the Prophet ﷺ spoke in the Farewell Hajj — Muslim recorded in his Sahih, from Jābir: "Be kind with women, for you have taken them by Allah's covenant and earned the right to have sexual relations with them by Allah's word."

## Living it

Maʿārif's own summing-up of the passage is the right note to end on: once this marital covenant has been made and mutual privacy has brought the couple close together, forcing the woman to return what was given to her is "open injustice and tyranny. All Muslims must abstain from it."

For a believer today, the passage asks four concrete things.

**Nothing about a woman's marriage is anyone's asset.** Not her family's, not her in-laws', not a widow's late husband's relatives'. Her remarriage is hers to decide. Blocking it to keep wealth in the family is precisely what ayah 19 was revealed to end.

**What is hers stays hers.** Dower given, gifts given, property inherited — they do not return. Pressure applied to make her "voluntarily" give them back does not launder the taking; Maʿārif says the forced return or waiver is simply not valid in the sight of the Sharīʿah.

**Do not use the exception as a door.** The permission in ayah 19 turns on an *open* fault of hers. Ayah 20 warns that invoking it without cause is itself a false imputation against her.

**And the standard is not merely restraint.** *Live with them honourably* is a positive command, and the model given for it is a man who spoke kind words, kept his appearance pleasing for his wives, laughed with them, and raced one of them as a means of kindness to her.

passages.title: Women forbidden in marriage
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat draw the boundary line of marriage: they name the women a man may never marry, the women he may not marry while another man holds them, and then throw the door open to everyone else. One movement runs through them — from abolishing an ugly practice of Jahiliyyah (ayah 22), to a complete register of permanently forbidden degrees (ayah 23), to closing the list and declaring that "all others are lawful" (ayah 24).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that these verses continue the dismantling of Jahiliyyah practices already begun, and sets out the architecture: some women are forbidden **permanently** — by kinship, by fosterage (the milk-tie), and by marriage-relation — and some only **temporarily**, such as a woman already bound in marriage to another.

## Ayah 22 — the stepmother, and three words for one sin

"And marry not women whom your fathers married, except what has already passed; indeed it was shameful and *maqtan*, and an evil way."

Ibn Jarir records from Ibn ʿAbbas that in Jahiliyyah the Arabs already prohibited most of what Allah prohibits in marriage — with two exceptions: marrying the stepmother, and keeping two sisters as co-wives. These verses came down at precisely the two points where pre-Islamic custom had gone wrong; similar was reported from ʿAtaʾ and Qatadah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the outrage in a sentence: how can a man call a woman his mother for years and then, once his father dies, stoop to making her his wife? Ibn Kathir gives a complementary wisdom — the prohibition honours the fathers, so that a man's sons may not have access to his wives after he is gone.

The verse does not merely say "forbidden." It piles up three words:

- ***Fāḥishah*** — a shameful, obscene act. Ibn Kathir links it to "Come not near to *al-fawāḥish*, whether committed openly or secretly" (6:151).
- ***Maqtan*** — the word *added* here beyond those other verses. Ibn Kathir glosses it as offensive, loathsome: the act is vile in itself, and it plants hatred in the son toward his own father, since a man naturally dislikes whoever married his wife before him. ʿAtaʾ bin Abi Rabah read it as meaning that **Allah will hate** the one who does it.
- ***Sāʾa sabīlā*** — "an evil way," meaning, as ʿAtaʾ said, evil for all who take this road afterwards.

From that *maqt* of son toward father Ibn Kathir draws a striking consequence: it is one reason the Mothers of the Faithful were not permitted to anyone after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — they are mothers of the believers because they married him, and he is as a father to the believers, indeed with a right greater than a father's.

**The ruling.** The verse says "whom your fathers married" and says nothing of consummation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore rules (citing Ibn ʿAbidin) that the father's contract alone forbids her to the son forever; equally, a father may not marry his son's wife even if that marriage never went beyond the contract; Ibn Kathir says the same and reports consensus. Maʿārif adds that if the father fell into an illicit relationship with a woman, she too is forbidden to the son.

**How seriously was this taken?** Imam Ahmad and the collectors of Sunan record from al-Baraʾ bin ʿAzib that his uncle Abu Burdah was sent by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to a man who had married his stepmother, to execute him and confiscate his property. Ibn Kathir explains the severity: doing this once the ruling is known amounts to turning away from the religion itself.

**"Except what has already passed"** is mercy at the seam between two eras. What happened in Jahiliyyah, says Maʿārif, is not called to account — but from the moment the ruling came, such a marriage had to be dissolved.

## Ayah 23 — the register: seven and seven

Ibn Kathir opens with two reports from Ibn ʿAbbas that make the same count in different words. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded him saying, "(Allah said) I have prohibited for you seven types of relatives by blood and seven by marriage." At-Tabari recorded him saying, "Seven degrees of blood relation and seven degrees of marriage relation are prohibited (for marriage)." In both reports he then recited the ayah itself.

**By blood (*nasab*).** Mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, brothers' daughters, sisters' daughters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens each out: "mothers" includes every grandmother upward; "daughters" includes granddaughters and downward without end, and a daughter born of *zina* is governed by the rule of a daughter. Adopted children are not covered — marriage with them or their offspring is permissible unless forbidden for another reason. Sisters, aunts and nieces are forbidden in all three forms: full (*ḥaqīqī*), half through the father (*ʿallātī*), half through the mother (*akhyāfī*).

**By suckling (*raḍāʿah*).** "Your foster mothers who suckled you, your foster milk-suckling sisters." Ibn Kathir: just as the mother who bore you is forbidden, so is the mother who nursed you. Al-Bukhari and Muslim record from ʿAʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Suckling prohibits what birth prohibits," and in another narration reported by Muslim, "Suckling establishes prohibited degrees just as blood does."

The milk-tie builds a family tree of its own: Maʿārif traces how the nursing woman becomes the child's foster-mother, her husband its foster-father, her children its siblings, and so outward through aunts and uncles — marriage barred across all of them.

The sources record genuine scholarly difference here:

- **How many feeds?** Ibn Kathir holds that fewer than five sucklings do not establish the prohibition, citing Muslim's report from ʿAʾishah that ten sucklings were revealed, then abrogated to five. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, glossing the same phrase, holds that "the quantity or the frequency of feed makes no difference" — the prohibition stands in every case.
- **Up to what age?** Ibn Kathir holds it must occur before two, connecting it to "the mothers should suckle their children for two whole years" (2:233). Maʿārif reports that Imam Abu Hanifah set the period at two and a half years, while other jurists — including his own leading students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad — said two years only.

The shared principle is the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Fosterage is only from hunger" (al-Bukhari and Muslim): the tie is created when the child genuinely lives on that milk, not by a sip in later life.

**By marriage (*muṣāharah*).** The verse treats two of these differently:

- **The wife's mother** becomes forbidden the moment the contract is made, consummated or not. Ibn Kathir states it plainly, and Maʿārif rules the same: the marriage bond in itself renders the wife's mother unlawful, even if the husband never slept with his wife. Ibn Kathir also records, through Ibn Abi Hatim, that al-Hasan bin Muhammad called two provisions of this ayah "encompassing" — "the wives of your sons" and "your wives' mothers" taken together — meaning both clauses cover these women whether the marriage was consummated or not. The same explanation is given from Tawus, Ibrahim, az-Zuhri and Makhul, and there is consensus on the ruling.
- **The stepdaughter** is forbidden only if he has consummated the marriage with her mother; if he divorces the mother before that, her daughter remains lawful. That is the plain sense of "born of your wives unto whom you have gone in — but there is no sin on you if you have not gone in unto them." Ibn ʿAbbas and others explain "gone in unto" as sexual relations.

**"Under your guardianship" — description, not condition.** The majority, Ibn Kathir reports, hold the stepdaughter forbidden whether or not she was raised in his house. In the Two Sahihs, when Umm Habibah mentioned that people said the Prophet ﷺ wished to marry Abu Salamah's daughter, he replied that even were she not his stepdaughter under his guardianship she would still not be lawful, since she was his niece through suckling — Thuwaybah had nursed both him and Abu Salamah. In another narration in al-Bukhari: had he not married Umm Salamah, her daughter would not have been lawful to him anyway — which, Ibn Kathir notes, makes the marriage the real cause.

**The wives of your sons "who spring from your own loins."** That phrase is deliberate. Ibn Kathir: it excludes the wives of adopted sons, adoption being a Jahiliyyah institution — hence Allah's words about Zayd, "so that there may be no difficulty to the believers in respect of the wives of their adopted sons" (33:37). Maʿārif adds that "son" reaches down to grandsons, and that a foster-son is treated like a natural son though an adopted son is not — a point Ibn Kathir answers with the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Suckling prohibits what blood relations prohibit."

**Two sisters at once.** The second Jahiliyyah exception. Ibn Kathir reports consensus among the Companions, their followers and the Imams that it is forbidden, and that a man who accepts Islam while married to two sisters must keep one and divorce the other. Imam Ahmad records from ad-Dahhak bin Fayruz that his father said, "I embraced Islam while married to two sisters at the same time, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded me to divorce one of them." Maʿārif reports the same episode from Ibn Firoz Dailami on his father's authority (Mishkat), and extends the principle: a woman may not be combined with her paternal or maternal aunt either, for the Holy Prophet ﷺ has said, "Do not combine a woman with her paternal aunt, nor a woman with her maternal aunt" (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Once one sister is divorced the other becomes lawful — but only after her ʿiddah has expired. (*ʿIddah* is the waiting period a woman must observe after divorce or the death of her husband before she may marry again.)

**"Except what has already passed; verily Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Notice where that pair of names lands: at the close of a long list of prohibitions. Maʿārif reads it as reassurance to new believers — what was done in ignorance before Islam is overlooked and the reach of His mercy is vast — while the separation the verse requires must still be made now.

## Ayah 24 — married women, and then the open door

"Also forbidden are women already married, except those whom your right hands possess."

Maʿārif states the plain rule: so long as a woman is married to one man, no other may marry her. He argues it chiefly from lineage: where several men share one woman, no child's fatherhood can be established, and with lineage unproven the structure of parental rights and duties collapses. So carefully is this guarded that even after divorce or a husband's death a woman may not remarry until her ʿiddah — that waiting period — has passed.

The exception concerns women taken captive in a valid war. Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said: "We captured some women from the area of Awtas who were already married, and we disliked having sexual relations with them because they already had husbands. So we asked the Prophet ﷺ about this matter, and this ayah was revealed." Ibn Kathir notes this wording is collected by at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasaʾi, Ibn Jarir, and by Muslim in his Sahih, and adds a condition: only after making sure they are not pregnant — Maʿārif specifies a wait of at least one menstrual cycle, or until delivery if she proved pregnant.

**"Thus has Allah ordained for you"** — *kitāb Allāhi ʿalaykum*. Ibn Kathir: this prohibition is Allah's own decree; adhere to His Book and do not transgress His limits. Maʿārif: the unlawfulness here is something *He* determined, not a human construction.

**"All others are lawful."** After the long list, the door opens. ʿAtaʾ and others said this means every woman besides the prohibited types. Maʿārif gives examples — a cousin, a deceased or divorced uncle's wife, a deceased wife's sister — provided no other cause of prohibition applies. He cautions that "all others" does not cancel the limit of four wives set earlier in the sūrah, nor prohibitions established in the Sunnah.

**Chastity, not appetite.** "Provided you seek them with your property, desiring chastity, not fornication." Maʿārif, citing Abu Bakr al-Jassas in *Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, draws a ruling from "with your property": a marriage cannot exist without a dower of real value, even if both parties agree to waive it. The two words that follow set the intention: *muḥṣinīn* — men making themselves chaste through marriage — *ghayra musāfiḥīn* — not men pouring themselves out in lust; the root of *musāfiḥ*, Maʿārif notes, carries the sense of flowing water, of release sought for its own sake.

**The dower is hers.** "So with those among them whom you have enjoyed, give them their required due." Ibn Kathir: having enjoyed them, surrender their rightful dower. Maʿārif adds the detail — the full dower falls due once the marriage is consummated; if he divorces before that, half is due; and if it was stipulated as prompt (*muʿajjal*), the wife may decline to move to him until it is paid. The figure is a floor, not a ceiling: "if you agree mutually after the requirement has been determined, there is no sin on you." Ibn Kathir relays from Ibn Jarir that al-Hadrami described men who would name a dower and then fall into financial difficulty — hence Allah's word that there is no harm in what the two sides mutually agree afterwards, so a husband may accept it if she forgives part of it. Maʿārif adds that a husband may equally add to the dower of his own accord.

**Mutʿah.** Mujahid held that "those among them whom you have enjoyed" was revealed about mutʿah — a marriage ending on a predetermined date. Ibn Kathir gives what closed the matter: in the Two Sahihs, ʿAli bin Abi Talib said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited mutʿah marriage and eating the meat of domesticated donkeys on the day of Khaybar." And Muslim records in his Sahih from ar-Rabiʿ bin Sabrah al-Juhani, on his father's authority, that at the conquest of Makkah the Prophet ﷺ announced: "O people! I allowed you the mutʿah marriage with women before. Now Allah has prohibited it until the Day of Resurrection" — telling those who held such women to let them go, and to take back nothing they had given them.

Maʿārif answers the argument from the word itself. *Istamtaʿtum* comes from the root *m-t-ʿ*, "to derive benefit" — any benefit from a person or property is *istimtāʿ* — and the whole Ummah from the early elders onward read it in that plain sense. The verse refutes the other reading in its own words: *muḥṣinīn ghayra musāfiḥīn* describes exactly the permanent, chastity-seeking bond that mutʿah is not, since it creates no lasting rights, no household, no lineage. Although Ibn ʿAbbas held it permissible for a time, at-Tirmidhi reports him saying it existed only in the earliest period, and he revoked his earlier view on the counsel of ʿAli.

## "Surely Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise"

Ibn Kathir remarks how fitting this ending is, and Maʿārif draws out both names. *ʿAlīm*: He knows — even where no judge or ruler would ever discover a breach — so fear Him in every circumstance. *Ḥakīm*: each injunction rests on a wisdom too deep for everyone to grasp. Some people, Maʿārif warns, hunt for the cause behind a divine command, fail to find it, and conclude the command is unsuited to the age; the answer is that the lack is in the seeker, not in the law — "You lack understanding. Allah is All-Wise. Do not make your reason the touchstone of the Truth."

Read whole, the passage is quietly protective. By naming precisely who is permanently off-limits, it turns the extended family into a place of safety — in-laws, milk-relations, a father's household, a son's home, all beyond the reach of desire. Then ayah 24 refuses to leave the believer with only prohibitions: "all others are lawful," sought with one's own wealth, aimed at chastity rather than appetite, with the woman's dower handed over as a right and not a favour.

passages.title: Marrying believing bondwomen; Allah lightens burdens
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat pick up a thread that has been running for some time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its comment on ayah 25 by noting that "it is in continuation of the injunctions relating to marriage which have been appearing earlier that the text now takes up the option of marriage with bondwomen," and that the ruling on the ḥadd punishment is attached to it "since the status of a bondman and bondwoman is different from a free man and a free woman." Then the tone shifts. Of ayat 26 to 28 Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says: "Mentioned in the previous verses were details of injunctions. Now, in the present verses, Allah Almighty points to his blessings and favours saying that your being obligated with these injunctions is for your own good." So: one more difficult ruling, and then the divine intention behind the whole body of rulings — to clarify, to guide, to accept repentance, and to lighten.

## Ayah 25: the concession, and what it costs

The verse opens with a condition — "whoever of you have not the means." The Arabic word is **ṭawl**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that ṭawl "signifies power, capability and means"; Ibn Kathir glosses it as **financial capability**. The women in the first clause are **al-muḥṣanāt al-muʼmināt** — Ibn Kathir: "free faithful, chaste women" — and the alternative is believing **fatayāt** from among those the right hands possess, meaning "believing slave girls owned by the believers."

By framing the permission as a fallback, the conditional has already told you what the norm is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "This clearly indicates that one should, as far as possible, marry only a free woman and simply not marry a bondwoman. But, should it be that one has to marry a bondwoman, he should look for a Muslim bondwoman."

**Why the reluctance?** The reasons given in these two sources concern the children, not the woman's worth. Ibn Kathir gives one: it is "better to refrain from marrying slave girls and to observe patience, for otherwise, the offspring will become slaves to the girl's master." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the same reason — "the offspring from a bondwoman becomes automatically bonded to the owner of the bondwoman" — and adds a second of its own: with a non-Muslim bondwoman "there remains the danger that the offspring from the non-Muslim bondwoman could adopt a religion other than Islam following the example of the mother." Hence its conclusion: "in order to rescue the children from bondage and to ensure that they remain Muslims, it is necessary that the mother of the children should be free. If she is a bondwoman, let her, at the least, be necessarily a Muslim."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then reports a related view held by others rather than asserting it in its own voice: "for this reason, respected scholars have said that marrying a free woman from the people of the Book is, no doubt, correct, but, staying away from doing so is better."

## "Allah knows best your faith; you are one from another"

Immediately after permitting the marriage, the ayah says something that is not law at all: **wa Allāhu aʻlamu bi-īmānikum, baʻḍukum min baʻḍ**. Ibn Kathir reads the first half as a check on human judgement: "Allah knows the true reality and secrets of all things, but you people know only the apparent things."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses further. Faith, it says, "is the criterion of precedence. It is very likely that a bondman or bondwoman may be far ahead of free men and women on the scale of faith. Therefore, the option of marriage with a Muslim bondwoman should not be taken as absolutely contemptible." Instead, "the fact that she has faith in Islam should be appreciated." And **baʻḍukum min baʻḍ** — "you are similar to each other" — means "that human beings, free or in bondage, all come from one species, the children of Adam and all were born of only one soul. That one is better than the other depends on ʼĪmān (faith) and Taqwā."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes al-Tafsīr al-Maẓharī on why these two sentences sit exactly here: they are placed "for people to get familiarized with and become acceptance-prone to marriage with bondwomen and get rid of any attitude of contempt for such marriage." That is the shape of the ayah: it grants the permission, then works on the heart of the man who would sneer at it.

## Permission, and a dower paid in full

**"Wed them with the permission of their own folk."** Ibn Kathir: this indicates "that the owner is responsible for the slave girl, and consequently, she cannot marry without his permission." The same holds for a male slave — and he cites a hadith (the source names no collection for it) that any male slave who marries without his master's permission is a fornicator. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees: without that permission "the marriage of the bondwoman will not be correct because the bondwoman does not possess the control over her person," and "the same rule governs the bondman as he too cannot marry without the permission of his master."

Ibn Kathir adds that where the owner is herself a woman, those who would give *her* away in marriage become responsible for her bondwoman too, citing a hadith (again with no collection named): "The woman does not give away another woman, or herself in marriage, for only the adulteress gives herself away in marriage."

**"And give them their due in a good manner."** Ibn Kathir: "pay them their dowry with a good heart, and do not keep any of it, belittling the matter due to the fact that they are owned slaves." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is equally insistent — the mahr must be paid "promptly, honestly and gracefully... without hedging and delaying, and making sure that the payment is made in full, and that no trouble is caused to the bondwoman in this matter just because she happens to be a bondwoman."

On who owns that payment the jurists differed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that **Imam Mālik** held the mahr to be the bondwoman's own right; **other Imams** held that her master becomes the owner of what is paid.

## Chaste — in the open and in secret

Three phrases describe the woman being married: **muḥṣanāt** (chaste), **ghayra musāfiḥāt** (not fornicators), **wa lā muttakhidhāti akhdān** (nor taking secret lovers). Ibn Kathir: muḥṣanāt means "honorable women who do not commit adultery"; musāfiḥāt refers to "dishonorable women, who do not refrain from illicit sexual relations with those who ask." He reports Ibn ʻAbbās saying the fornicating women are those "who do not object to having relations with whomever seeks it," while *muttakhidhāti akhdān* "refers to taking boyfriends" — the private, exclusive arrangement rather than the open one. Abū Hurayrah, Mujāhid, ash-Shaʻbī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʻAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī, Yaḥyā bin Abī Kathīr, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and as-Suddī said much the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the pair the same way — the woman should be neither an "open fornicator" nor a "keeper of clandestine paramours." Public licence and concealed attachment are both excluded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that although bondwomen are the subject here, "it is also much better to stay away from marrying a fornicating free woman as well."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from the verse an argument against **mutʻah** (temporary marriage): if a man who cannot afford a free woman is directed to a bondwoman as his second option, mutʻah cannot be lawful — had it been permitted, it "would have gratified his sexual desire" at a far smaller cost, and would have been the obvious alternative to name. Beyond that, *muḥṣanāt ghayra musāfiḥāt* describes a woman bound in marriage and no fornicator, whereas mutʻah "is all 'safh'." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the consequences: one woman used by several men in short spans, offspring who "cannot be credibly ascribed to anyone," and the benefit of procreation lost.

## The half punishment

"And after they have been taken in wedlock, if they commit *fāḥishah*, their punishment is half that for free women." Ibn Kathir, following Ibn ʻAbbās and others, reads **fa-idhā uḥṣinna** as referring to when the believing slave girls get married — the verse concerns the bondwomen the whole ayah has been discussing.

Then a point of legal reasoning. Ibn Kathir: "half of that for free (unmarried) women" indicates "that the type of punishment prescribed here is the one that can be reduced to half, lashes in this case, not stoning to death, and Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works it out in numbers: the unmarried free man or woman receives one hundred lashes (Sūrat an-Nūr, 24:2); the married adulterer's penalty is rajm, death by stoning, which cannot be halved. "Since this particular punishment cannot be reduced to half, all four Imams agree on the position that the punishment of zinā committed by a bondman or bondwoman, married or unmarried, is fifty lashes." The ayah names only bondwomen; the bondman's case "becomes clear from the obvious analogy of the text."

## Where the scholars differed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a genuine disagreement:

- **Imam Abū Ḥanīfah**: marrying a bondwoman — especially one from the People of the Book — while having the power and means to marry a free woman is **makrūh**, not desirable.
- **Imam ash-Shāfiʻī and other Imams**: doing so while having the means is **unlawful (ḥarām)**, and marrying a bondwoman from the People of the Book is "absolutely impermissible."

Both converge in practice: "to avoid marrying a bondwoman is, under all conditions, certainly better for a free man. However, if one has to do so under personal lack of choice, marrying a Muslim bondwoman is better."

## "For him who fears hardship — but to be patient is better"

**Dhālika liman khashiya al-ʻanat** — rendered in Ibn Kathir as "for him among you who is afraid of being harmed in his religion or in his body." Ibn Kathir: marrying slave girls, "providing one satisfies the required conditions, is for those who fear for their chastity and find it hard to be patient and refrain from sex. In this difficult circumstance, one is allowed to marry a slave girl." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the permission is "for a person who apprehends that he might fall into the sin of fornication."

Then the verse refuses to let the concession become a recommendation: **"but it is better for you that you practice self-restraint."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: if a person, "despite the apprehension of falling into zinā, exercises restraint and keeps himself morally pure rising above the pull of his sexual desire, then, this state of being is better."

The ayah closes on two Names: **al-Ghafūr, ar-Raḥīm**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads them against the ruling just given: marrying bondwomen is makrūh, "yet, should one go on to do something in this line, Allah Almighty will still forgive him. Then, He is Very-Merciful too, because He allowed marriage with bondwomen and did not make it totally prohibited." Forgiveness for the one who takes the lesser path; mercy that the path exists at all.

## What "bondwoman" refers to

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān appends a "Special Note" essential for reading this ayah today. The bondmen and bondwomen of these rulings are *sharʻī* bondmen and bondwomen: men and women from among the disbelievers taken prisoner during Jihad, "given to the Mujahidin as part of the distribution of spoils by the... Amir al-Muʼminin, the Chief Executive of Muslims." On Maʿārif's own assessment that institution has lapsed — Muslims, it says, have "forsaken taking up Jihad in the manner prescribed by the Sharīʻah of Islam," have "entrusted the options of peace and war in the hands of the enemies of their religion," and since then "they ended up being deprived of what was known as a bondman and bondwoman." Two consequences follow, stated flatly:

- "Common domestic servants in our own time are not 'bondmen' and 'bondwomen' because they are free."
- "In some parts of the world, children are sold out or enslaved. This is absolutely and totally Ḥarām (forbidden). They do not become 'bondmen' and 'bondwomen' by doing that."

## Ayat 26–28: four wills

Three times we are told what **Allah wills**, and once — in the middle — what a rival party wills.

**Ayah 26 — He wills to clarify, to guide, to relent.** Ibn Kathir: "Allah explains to the believers what He has allowed and prohibited for them in this and other Sūrahs." *And to show you the ways of those before you* — "meaning their righteous ways and how to adhere to the commandments that He likes and is pleased with." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the consolation: Allah "is putting you in line with the ways of the noble prophets and the righteous who have come earlier. Do not think that these details of what is unlawful and what is not are there for you alone. The fact is that communities, earlier than you, were also charged with such injunctions. Those who acted in accordance with them were rewarded with Allah's favour." Then *wa yatūba ʻalaykum* — to accept your repentance "from sin and error." The ayah seals with **ʻAlīm, Ḥakīm** — All-Knowing, All-Wise, says Ibn Kathir, "in His commands, decrees, actions and statements." The law you have just read is the speech of One who knows completely and places everything exactly.

**Ayah 27 — the counter-will.** Allah wills to turn to you; "those who follow their lusts wish that you should deviate tremendously away." Ibn Kathir identifies them as "the followers of Shayṭān among the Jews, Christians and the adulterous," who "wish that you would take the horrendous path of falsehood instead of the truth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens this to fornicators and adulterers and to "nations and peoples adhering to false creeds who just do not recognize the restrictions of ḥalāl and ḥarām," and names contemporary forms: creeds in which "it is all right to marry women — marriage with whom is not proper"; atheists who "favour the very elimination of the institution of marriage as something out of tune with modern times"; people "talking about women as a shared item of enjoyment." Its sharpest observation concerns the believer's inner life — Muslims "subscribing to Islam yet weak in their faith," keeping such company, "begin to think that their own religion is out-dated and that the position of the enemy is the very epitome of human progress," and start wishing their own religion could have permitted it. "Refuge with Allah from such spineless surrendering!" Note the contrast between the two wills: that you be forgiven, against that you tilt — **maylan ʻaẓīmā**, a tremendous swerve.

**Ayah 28 — He wills to lighten.** Ibn Kathir: Allah wishes to lighten "His legislation, orders, what He prohibits and what He decrees for you. This is why Allah has allowed free men to marry slave girls under certain conditions, as Mujāhid and others have stated." The concession of ayah 25 is thus named for what it was: an easing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the easings of this section together — permission to marry a bondwoman when free women are unaffordable, the right of the parties "to settle the dower by mutual consent," and the right "to marry more than one woman under circumstantial necessity, of course, on condition that justice is not compromised." Its summary of *yukhaffifa ʻankum*: Allah "prescribes injunctions which can be carried out by everyone obligated with them."

## "And man was created weak"

The closing clause of ayah 28 is the reason for everything above it. Ibn Kathir: "this is why it is suitable in his case that the commands are made easy for him, because of his weakness and feebleness." He records, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that **Ṭāwūs** said of *wa khuliqa al-insānu ḍaʻīfā*: "Concerning women." And **Wakīʻ** said: "Man's mind leaves when women are involved."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way and follows the thought to its constructive end: man "is weak by nature, and constituted desire-prone. If man was asked to stay away from women, totally and absolutely, he would have been a hopeless performer when it came to obeying the injunctions of Allah." So he was not merely permitted marriage but induced toward it — a bond that gives a couple "the blessings of a sight that is untainted and a character that is unalloyed," a mutual purity that "increases the moral quality of life for both of them, making them strong, self-reliant and happy." "A peerless method indeed."

## Living it

Allah did not legislate marriage law because human beings are strong enough to bear anything; He legislated it because they are not. Three things follow.

**Do not despise a believer for their station.** The ayah that permits the marriage is the same ayah that says *baʻḍukum min baʻḍ* — one species, one soul, children of Adam — and, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, ranks people by faith and taqwā alone. Quoting al-Tafsīr al-Maẓharī, it says these words sit here precisely to rid people of "any attitude of contempt for such marriage."

**Pay what you owe, fully and gracefully, especially to those who cannot press you for it.** Ibn Kathir's warning against "belittling the matter" because of the woman's status is a general principle in a particular case: weakness on the other side is never a discount.

**Take a concession without mistaking it for the goal.** Ayah 25 permits, and in the same breath says patience is better. And the One who opened that door named Himself, right there, Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Devouring wealth unlawfully and the major sins
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat draw a protective line around the two things a person cannot live without — his wealth and his life — then close with a promise that changes the whole mood: keep clear of the great sins, and Allah will wipe away the small ones and bring you in through a noble door.

One movement holds them together: a prohibition (ayah 29), a warning for whoever breaks it deliberately (ayah 30), an encouragement for whoever holds the line (ayah 31). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this as a habit of the Qur'an — a warning of punishment is generally followed by something drawing the heart towards obedience. Citing Tafsīr al-Mazharī, it also places the passage in the sūrah's argument: after orphans, women, inheritance and marriage, the frame widens to protect life and property in general — for people "related or unrelated, Muslim or non-Muslim with whom there is a no-war pact in force."

## "Do not eat" — the reach of one verb

The verb in ayah 29 is *lā taʼkulū*, literally "do not eat." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as idiom: taking what belongs to someone else without authorisation is called "eating up," even when the thing is not edible. The prohibition covers taking, using and consuming by any route.

The object is *amwālakum baynakum* — "one another's wealth," though the literal sense is "your property in between you." Commentators agree, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, that nobody may devour another's property by false means. But Abū Ḥayyān, in Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, notes the phrasing also reaches a man devouring *his own* property that way — on what is religiously sinful, or in sheer extravagance. The wording folds the community's wealth, your own included, into one protected fund.

Then the decisive word: *bi'l-bāṭil*, "by false means." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ that in the view of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and the majority of the blessed Companions, this one word covers every form of acquisition the Sharīʿah forbids — "theft, robbery, usurpation, breach of trust, bribery, interest, gambling and all false transactions." Ibn Kathir names *ribā* (interest) and gambling here too, along with "wicked methods that appear to be legal, but Allah knows that, in reality, those involved seek to deal in interest."

The Qur'an gave that one word; the Prophet ﷺ was entrusted with the detail — which is why, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, the hadith rulings on impermissible trade are an elaboration of this single Qur'anic injunction.

Ibn Jarīr records Ibn ʿAbbās applying the verse to a sharp practice of the day: a man buys a garment on the understanding that if he likes it he keeps it, and if not he returns it *along with an extra dirham*. That dirham, said Ibn ʿAbbās, is what Allah meant — wrongful gain need not be large to be *bāṭil*. Some of the first Muslims drew the line further out still: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that they said food is our best property, so none may eat from another's, and stopped accepting hospitality — until *"There is no restriction on the blind…"* (24:61) permitted it.

## The door left open: trade by mutual consent

Ayah 29 closes the false routes and opens one: *"unless it be a trade amongst you, by mutual consent."* Ibn Kathir reads it as: do not revert to illegal ways of getting money — but there is no harm in dealings between buyer and seller with mutual consent. Mujāhid glossed the exception as "by selling and buying, or giving someone a gift" (Ibn Jarīr).

Why single out trade, asks Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, when borrowing, gifts, charity and inheritance are also lawful? Because trade is the most recognised and commonly practised way property passes from one person into another's hands — and because trade and labour are, out of all the means open to man, the best way to earn a living. And it is broader here than shopkeeping: according to al-Tafsīr al-Mazharī, service, labour and tenancy are included, since in a sale (*bayʿ*) property is exchanged for property, while in hire (*ijāra*) property is received for labour.

Asked which mode of earning was purest and most lawful, the Prophet ﷺ answered — in the report of Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj — "Man's work with his own hands, and all honest sale transactions" (al-Mundhirī, al-Targhīb, and Mazharī). But that honour is conditional: in a narration from Muʿādh ibn Jabal he ﷺ called the cleanest earning that of traders, provided they do not lie, commit no breach when trusted, do not run down goods they buy or oversell goods they sell, and neither evade a debt nor harass a debtor (Isfahānī, via Mazharī).

## Two conditions hidden in one phrase

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān finds two separate requirements packed into this phrase.

**First, it must actually be trade** — an exchange of property for property. Where one side has a commodity and the other nothing real, this is deception, not trade. Interest fails here, because the extra is a return for *time*, and time is not a commodity. Gambling and speculation fail because the counter-value's existence is doubtful. Forward dealing in a commodity that does not exist fails because one side holds goods and the other only a promise. Jurists call such a contract *al-bayʿ al-bāṭil*, a void sale.

**Second, the exchange must be by genuine mutual consent.** Where both properties exist but consent is absent, it is an invalid trade — *al-bayʿ al-fāsid*. Both forms fall under "eating up each other's property by false means." Ibn Kathir gives the mechanism: agreement is attained when both parties retain the right to uphold or dissolve the deal before they part. In the Two Sahihs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The seller and the buyer retain the right to change their mind as long as they have not parted."

**When "consent" is not consent.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then presses on a third case: both sides have real goods, the deal *looks* consensual, but one party's agreement was extracted by pressure — and such consent is null and void. A company corners the market in daily necessities and drives prices up; the customer walks in on his own legs, but since the goods are available nowhere else his "consent" is an outcome of compulsion. A husband makes life with his wife so thorny that she gives up her due dower; that surrender is not consent in any real sense. A man pays a bribe because legitimate business will not otherwise get done; that too is not free will.

This one phrase, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, is "the key to the wonderful treasure of Muslim jurisprudence" on sales (*al-buyūʿ*) and hire (*al-ijāra*) — the jurists did not invent those rules; they codified the forms established on the authority of the ahadith of the Prophet ﷺ.

## "And do not kill yourselves"

The third clause of ayah 29 turns from property to life: *wa lā taqtulū anfusakum*, literally "and do not kill yourselves." By consensus of the commentators, reports Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, this covers both suicide and unjustly killing one another. Ibn Kathir adds a layer: do not destroy yourselves by committing Allah's prohibitions, falling into sin, and devouring one another's property unjustly.

Why does property come *before* life, when unjust killing is graver? Because, answers Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, injustice and negligence in matters of property are extremely common while murder is customarily far rarer — the Qur'an addresses the frequent danger first.

Among the warnings Ibn Kathir gathers against taking one's own life is the narration of Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk, collected by the Group, that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever kills himself with an instrument will be punished with it on the Day of Resurrection."

**ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and the freezing night.** Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, sent by the Prophet ﷺ for the battle of Dhāt al-Salāsil, said: "I had a wet dream during a very cold night and feared that if I bathed, I would die. So I performed *tayammum* (purification with pure earth) and led my company in the Dawn prayer." On his return the Prophet ﷺ asked, "O ʿAmr! Have you led your people in prayer while you were in a state of sexual impurity?" ʿAmr explained the cold, the fear of perishing, and that he had remembered Allah's words: *"And do not kill yourselves. Surely, Allah is Most Merciful to you."* "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled and did not say anything" (reported by Abū Dāwūd). That smile is the commentary: a Companion took the verse's mercy at its word and was not corrected.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah's closing words as meaning that Allah is merciful to you *in what He commanded you and prohibited you from* — the commands themselves are the mercy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees: they guard us from punishment in the life to come and from harm here.

## Ayah 30: the words that narrow the threat

*"And whoever does this sinfully and unjustly, We will burn them…"* — the Arabic is *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman*, aggression and injustice. Ibn Kathir explains: whoever commits what Allah has forbidden him, *while knowing that it is forbidden for him, yet still dares to commit it*. He calls the ayah "a stern warning and a truthful promise."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the corresponding relief from those same two words: the qualification shows that if such a thing happens out of forgetfulness or mistake, it is not included in the warning, which is aimed at the one who knows and proceeds anyway.

## Ayah 31: the great arrangement

Ibn Kathir's reading is direct: avoid the major evil deeds you were prohibited, and We will forgive the minor ones and admit you into Paradise — which is what *mudkhalan karīman*, "a noble entrance," means. *Kaffārah*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means what makes amends, an expiation. Righteous deeds serve as *kaffārah* for minor sins, which are written off; authentic ahadith describe how, in *wuḍūʼ* — the washing of face, mouth, arms and feet that precedes the prayer — the washing of each limb expiates the sins of that limb, and how every step towards the masjid carries expiation with it. Ibn Kathir cites the same principle: Imam Ahmad recorded that the Prophet ﷺ told Salmān al-Fārisī that whoever bathes and cleans himself as much as he can, then goes to the Friday prayer and stays quiet until the Imam finishes, will have his sins between that Friday and the next forgiven — "**as long as major sins were avoided**."

That last clause is the hinge, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic: **major sins are not forgiven without *tawbah*, repentance.** Wuḍūʼ and prayer expiate the minor, and only for one who has made the effort to stay clear of the major; for someone who stays involved in major sins, those acts "will not at all expiate for even his minor sins, let alone the major ones."

One expansion is easily missed: avoiding major sins *includes* fulfilling all obligations, since neglecting or abandoning what is *farḍ* or *wājib* is itself a major sin. The promise is not for someone who merely refrains from spectacular wrongs while leaving his duties undone.

## What makes a sin "major"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to let "minor" become a soft word. Sin, in the absolute sense, is an act against the command and will of Allah; seen that way, a so-called minor sin is no minor thing. On this basis many scholars have held that *every* disobedience is a *kabīrah*, and that the distinction between *kabīrah* (major) and *ṣaghīrah* (minor) is made only when sins are compared with one another — the sense of the report from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās: "Any act forbidden by the Sharīʿah is a major sin." A minor sin done with nerve or heedlessness stops being minor at all, and Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said, "The lighter you take a sin to be, the greater it will become with Allah as a crime."

Still, a working distinction is needed, since sins differ in the corruption they cause and the harm they produce. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the definition drawn from the Qur'an, Sunnah and the revered elders: a *kabīrah* is a sin for which a *ḥadd* (fixed punishment) has been prescribed in this life, or upon which a curse (*laʿnah*) has been pronounced, or against which a stern warning of Hell has been issued — likewise any sin whose evil outcome equals or exceeds that of a major sin, and any sin done with a rebellious attitude or as a permanent habit.

As for number: someone said before Ibn ʿAbbās that the major sins were seven. He replied, "Not seven. Say seven hundred, which is better." In *al-Zawājir*, Ibn Ḥajar al-Makkī listed those meeting the definition and reached four hundred and sixty-seven. Since the Prophet ﷺ named them in threes and sixes and sevens on different occasions, the scholars concluded that no fixed number is intended — each figure suited the occasion on which it was given.

## The lists from the Sunnah

In the Two Sahihs, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Avoid the seven great destructive sins." Asked what they were, he said: "To join others in worship along with Allah, to kill the life which Allah has forbidden except for a just cause, magic, to consume *ribā*, to consume an orphan's wealth, to turn away from the enemy and flee from the battlefield when the battle begins, and to accuse chaste women, who never even think of anything that would tarnish their chastity and are good believers."
