And notice Ibn Kathir's own heading here — the Prophet ﷺ will be a witness *against, or for*, his ummah. Testimony can go either way.

**An argument for the finality of prophethood.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a further inference from the wording. This textual style of the noble Qur'an, it says, tells us that there is to be no prophet after him who could appear as a witness over a possible community of his — otherwise the Qur'an would have mentioned him, his community, and the testimony he would give. Seen from that angle, the commentary concludes, this verse is a proof of the finality of prophethood as well.

## Ayah 42: wishing to be levelled with the earth

Now the camera turns to those on trial. *"On that day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that they were buried in the earth, but they will never be able to hide a single fact from Allah."*

Ibn Kathir explains: they will wish that the earth would open up and swallow them, because of the horror of the gathering place and the disgrace, dishonour and humiliation they will suffer on that Day. He links it to *"The Day when man will see that (the deeds) which his hands have sent forth"* (78:40).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the wording, and renders the phrase literally — *"shall wish that the earth be levelled with them"* — precisely in order to preserve, in some measure at least, the power and poignancy of the original Qur'anic expression. It describes the state of utter despair the disbelievers face on the Last Day: they would wish to go extinct rather than face its ordeal, to become a patch of the earth underneath, or wish that the earth would crack open and suck them in, leaving nothing on top but dust mingled with dust, so that they would be delivered of the scrutiny and retribution of that fateful time. The commentary notes that the same wish appears elsewhere in the Qur'an, where the disbeliever wishes he had been dust. On the plains of Resurrection the disbelievers will see that all the animals have been turned into dust after exchanging the retribution of each other's excesses — and they too would pine for an end like that, wishing to have become all dust.

## "They will not conceal a single fact from Allah"

The passage ends by closing the last exit. Ibn Kathir says this indicates that they will admit to everything they did and will not hide any of it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists what makes concealment impossible: their own hands and feet will confess, the prophets will testify, and everything is there on record in their Books of Deeds.

But there is an obvious difficulty here, and the sources meet it head on rather than sidestepping it. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Saʿīd bin Jubayr said: a man came to Ibn ʿAbbās and said, "There are things that confuse me in the Qur'an." Ibn ʿAbbās said, "What things do you have doubts about in the Qur'an?" He said, "Not doubts, but rather confusing things." Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Tell me what caused you confusion." He said: I hear Allah's statement, *"There will then be no test for them but to say: 'By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah'"* (6:23) — but He also says, *"but they will never be able to hide a single fact from Allah."* They have indeed hid something.

Ibn ʿAbbās answered: when they see on the Day of Resurrection that Allah does not forgive except the people of Islam, and that He forgives sins no matter how big they are, except *shirk*, then the *mushriks* will lie. They will say, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not those who joined others in worship with Allah," hoping that Allah will forgive them. However, Allah will then seal their mouths, and their hands and feet will disclose what they used to do. And *then* comes this ayah — they will wish that they were buried in the earth, and they will never be able to hide a single fact from Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same resolution: seeing that none but true Muslims are being admitted to Paradise, they decide to refuse point-blank that they ever committed *shirk* or any other evil deed, in the hope that the plan works; but the very parts of their body then testify against them, which totally frustrates the plan — and that is when they confess everything. So the two ayat describe two moments in one trial, not two contradictory claims. The lie is real; it just does not survive contact with the evidence.

## Living it

**Never despise a small deed.** If Allah will not let a *dharrah*'s weight of wrong be added to your account, He will not let a *dharrah*'s weight of good fall out of it either. The mustard seed of faith in a heart was enough to bring people out of the Fire. Nothing you do sincerely is too small to be worth doing.

**Do not calculate your reward; you cannot.** The floor is ten. What the Companions passed on speaks of a million, and of two million. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's summary is the right posture: who can dare calculate the incalculable? Act, and leave the arithmetic to al-Karīm.

**Live now as someone who will be witnessed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls ayah 41 an invitation to visualise the gravity of that Day. Take up the invitation. As al-Qasṭalānī explains it, the Prophet ﷺ wept because the ayah brought the Hereafter before his eyes and he thought of those in his community who were short on good deeds. The kindest response to those tears is to be someone he can testify *for*.

**Concealment has an expiry date.** Every private thing has a day on which the mouth is sealed and the limbs speak. That should frighten anyone living a double life — and it should comfort anyone whose good was never seen by a soul. Both are on record.

passages.title: Approaching prayer in a fit state: sobriety, purity, and tayammum
passages.tafsir:
## What this ayah is about

This single, long ayah is a law about *readiness*. Before you stand before Allah in prayer you must be in a fit state — awake to your own words, and ritually pure. Then it makes that high bar reachable: if water is out of reach, clean earth will do. **Sanctity, then mercy.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note on placement: the verses just before this stressed *taqwā* in how people deal with one another, and here come rules of worship — because prayer and purity "instill man with fear of Allah, promote concern for the life-to-come and help in seeing that dealings come out right and smooth."

---

## Part one: "Do not approach prayer while intoxicated"

### The night that occasioned it

Two incidents are reported. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Abi Hatim: Saʿd said, "Four Ayat were revealed concerning me." A man of the Ansar prepared food and invited men from the Muhajirin and Ansar; they ate and drank until intoxicated, then boasted about their status. A man took up a camel's bone and injured Saʿd's nose, which was scarred ever since. This occurred before khamr was prohibited. Muslim recorded this hadith, as did the collectors of the Sunan except Ibn Majah.

The second, told in full by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān and recorded by Ibn Kathir from Ibn Abi Hatim on the authority of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn ʿAwf invited some Companions to a meal and, as was then customary, liquor was served before dinner. When everyone had eaten, the time for Maghrib came and ʿAli was asked to lead the prayer. Under the effect of intoxication he made a grave error while reciting the well-known Sūrat al-Kāfirūn. Ibn Kathir's narration renders what came out as: "Say, 'O disbelievers! I do not worship that which you worship, but we worship that which you worship'" — with a bracketed note pointing to the correct wording of Sūrah 109. At-Tirmidhi also collected it and said it is *Ḥasan [Gharīb] Ṣaḥīḥ*. The error fell in the very declaration *"I do not worship that which you worship"* — that is what drink did to a tongue standing before Allah.

### "Until you know what you are saying"

Allah does not say "until you are sober." He says **ḥattā taʿlamū mā taqūlūn** — *until you know what you are saying*. Ibn Kathir calls this "the best description for when one is intoxicated, that is, when he does not know the meaning of what he is saying." The measure is your own speech: can you follow it?

Ibn Kathir names two consequences: a drunk person "makes obvious mistakes in the recitation and will not be able to be humble during the prayer."

Because the wording is about awareness rather than alcohol, it reaches further. Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"If one feels sleepy while he is praying, let him sleep for a while so that he knows the meaning of what he is saying."* This was also recorded by Al-Bukhari and An-Nasa'i. In some of the narrations of this hadith the Messenger ﷺ said, *"…For he might want to ask for forgiveness, but instead curses himself!"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same teaching from Qurtubi and draws a ruling: since praying while intoxicated is forbidden, some commentators hold that it is also not correct to pray when one feels so sleepy that one cannot control what one says.

### A stage in a gradual prohibition

Ibn Kathir is explicit: "This Ayah was revealed before alcohol consumption was completely prohibited." He recalls the hadith mentioned in Sūrat al-Baqarah: the Prophet ﷺ recited to ʿUmar the ayah on alcoholic drink and gambling (2:219), and ʿUmar said, "O Allah! Explain the ruling about Khamr for us in a plain manner." When this ayah (4:43) was revealed and recited to him, ʿUmar said the same thing again. After that, they would not drink alcohol close to the time of prayer. Then came *"alcoholic drinks, gambling, Al-Ansab, and Al-Azlam are an abomination of Shayatan's handiwork. So avoid that in order that you may be successful"* through *"So, will you not then abstain?"* (5:90–91) — and ʿUmar said, **"We abstain, we abstain."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wisdom of the staging. Drinking was "an old addiction in Arabia," a national habit involving everyone but a few whom Allah had given a distaste for liquor all along — one such was the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself, who never touched liquor even before he was called to prophethood. And any habit is difficult to leave; this one most of all: "It so overpowers man in its clutches that he just cannot think otherwise. To him a farewell to drinking means a welcome to death."

So the Sharīʿah moved in stages. Drinking has always been unlawful in the sight of Allah, but had it been declared unlawful all of a sudden, people "would have found obedience to this command extremely hard to carry out." The first step was partial: people were warned of the evil effects of drinking, and the instruction in this verse was limited to asking people not to go near prayer while intoxicated. The purpose was to emphasize that prayer is *farḍ* — when its time comes, one must rise, intend and offer it as due — and that one should not be drunk during prayer timings. This helped Muslims realize that drinking is really something bad, for it stops them from praying properly. Some made a spot decision to abandon the habit once and for all; others began thinking seriously about its evils. Finally, when the verse of Sūrat al-Mā'idah carrying the absolute command was revealed, drinking was forbidden under all conditions.

### Enforced publicly

Ibn Kathir records that when the ayah in Sūrat an-Nisā' was revealed, at the time of prayer the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have someone proclaim: *"Let not any drunk approach the prayer."* This is the wording collected by Abu Dawud.

---

## Part two: "Nor while junub, except while passing through"

**Janābah** is major ritual impurity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as the state caused by sexual intercourse or seminal discharge, in passion or in dream, after which it becomes obligatory to take the prescribed bath, *ghusl*. Distinguish it from **minor impurity** (*al-ḥadath al-aṣghar*), caused by any act that breaks wuḍūʼ, such as easing oneself; that is lifted by wuḍūʼ alone.

### What does "except while passing through" mean?

Here the scholars genuinely differed.

**The first reading — it concerns the mosque.** Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Abi Hatim that Ibn ʿAbbas explained it as: "Do not enter the Masjid when you are Junub, unless you are just passing by, in which case, you pass through without sitting down." Ibn Abi Hatim said that similar is reported from a long line of early authorities — among them ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd, Anas, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAṭāʼ, Mujāhid, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah. On this reading, "do not approach the prayer" carries the sense of the place of prayer.

Ibn Jarir records Yazid ibn Abi Habib giving it a concrete setting: some men of the Ansar had doors that literally opened into the Masjid; when they became sexually impure and had no water, their only way to get water was to pass through the Masjid — so Allah sent down *"nor while junub, except while passing through."* Ibn Kathir notes what supports this: al-Bukhari's report in his Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Close all the small doors in this Masjid, except that of Abu Bakr."* This the Prophet ﷺ commanded at the end of his life, knowing that Abu Bakr would be Khalīfah after him and would need to enter the Masjid on numerous occasions to manage the important affairs of the Muslims. (Ibn Kathir adds that some of the Sunan compilers recorded the Prophet ﷺ saying that only ʿAli's door should remain open, "but this is an error, what is in the Sahih is what is correct.")

Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that ʿA'ishah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her, *"Bring me the garment from the Masjid."* She said, "I am having my period." He said, ***"Your period is not in your hand."*** Muslim also collected a similar narration from Abu Hurayrah. Ibn Kathir draws from it that a woman is allowed to pass through the Masjid during menses or post-natal bleeding — and Allah knows best.

**The second reading — it concerns the traveller.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to most commentators, including the Hanafi jurists, "traversing a way" refers to the state of travelling when water is not available: one cannot go near prayer in a state of major impurity without having taken ghusl, *except* that if he is on a journey and does not find water, he can pray after making tayammum — which is what the next sentence of the ayah explains.

Imām al-Shāfiʿī, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, interprets the exception in a totally different manner: "going near salah" means "entering a mosque," which is forbidden to a person in major impurity, though if he intends to go somewhere else and passes through the mosque as a passer-by, he may do so. The Hanafi jurists do not accept this view; they say the verse refers to offering prayers, as is evident from the background in which it was revealed, and that the prohibition of entering a mosque in a state of impurity is based on some other sources.

---

## Part three: tayammum — the mercy at the end

### Who it is for

**Illness.** Ibn Kathir: the illness that permits tayammum is one that a person fears would be aggravated by using water, which could be detrimental to a part of the body, or when doing so would prolong the illness. Some scholars said that any type of illness warrants tayammum, because of the general indications of the ayah.

**Travel.** "It is known, regardless of its length."

**The two causes of impurity, named delicately.** *"Or one of you comes from the ghāʼiṭ"* — the word is, literally, the flat land; Ibn Kathir notes that this part of the ayah refers to the minor impurity. *"Or lāmastum women"* — recited both *lamastum* and *lāmastum* — refers to sexual intercourse. Ibn Kathir supports this from the Qur'an's own idiom, where "touching" stands for intimacy: *"And if you divorce them before you have touched them…"* (2:237) and *"O you who believe! When you marry believing women, and then divorce them before you have touched them…"* (33:49). Ibn Abi Hatim records this interpretation from Ibn ʿAbbās, and it was reported that ʿAli, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, al-Ḥasan, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ash-Shaʿbī and Qatādah said similarly.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the same two: *"or one of you has come after easing himself"* refers to minor impurity, *"or you have touched women"* to sexual intercourse causing major impurity. In both, if someone is too sick to use water, or is on a journey where he does not find water, he can have recourse to tayammum.

### The word itself

**Tayammum** linguistically means *to intend*. Ibn Kathir gives the Arab expression: "May Allah *tayammamaka* — direct at you — His care." **Ṣaʿīdan ṭayyiban**, "clean earth," Ibn Kathir explains as dust.

### How it is done, and what it is

Ibn Kathir draws a point from *"rubbing your faces and hands"*: it "indicates that Tayammum is a substitute for normal ablution, not that it involves cleaning the parts that normal ablution does. Therefore, it is sufficient in Tayammum to just wipe the face and hands, as the consensus concurs." The face and hands are wiped with one strike on the sand.

Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdur-Rahman ibn Abza said that a man came to ʿUmar and said, "I am Junub, but there is no water." ʿUmar said, "Then, do not pray." ʿAmmār said, "Do you not remember, O Leader of the Faithful! You and I were on a military expedition when we became Junub and did not find water. You did not pray, but I rolled myself in the sand and then prayed. When we went back to the Prophet, we mentioned to him what had happened. He said to me, *'This would have been sufficient for you'*, and the Prophet ﷺ stroked his hand on the earth once, blew into it and wiped his face and hands." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same procedure: strike the hands on clean dust, then wipe the face and the wrists.

### The Prophet ﷺ teaching it in the field

In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, it is recorded that ʿImrān ibn Ḥusayn said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ saw a person sitting away from the people and not praying with them. He asked him, *"O so-and-so! What prevented you from offering the prayer with the people, are not you Muslim?"* He replied, "Yes, O Allah's Messenger! I am Junub and there is no water." The Prophet ﷺ said, ***"Perform Tayammum with clean earth and that will be sufficient for you."***

### A privilege of this Ummah

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stress that this allowance distinguishes the community of Muhammad ﷺ — Ibn Kathir: "The Muslim Ummah, rather than all other nations, was favored with the allowance of Tayammum"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "It appears in a hadith that this is a convenience bestowed upon the community of Muhammad ﷺ exclusively."

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim recorded that Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"We were given preference over people in three things. Our lines (in prayer) were arranged in rows to resemble the rows of the angels, all of the earth was made a Masjid for us, and its dust was made clean for us when there is no water."*

And in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, Jābir ibn ʿAbdullah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"I have been given five things which were not given to any (Prophet) before me: Allah made me victorious with fright that covers a month's distance. The earth has been made for me (and for my followers) a place for praying and an object to perform purification with. Therefore let my followers pray wherever the time of a prayer is due"* — and in another narration, *"he will have his means of purity and his Masjid"* — *"The spoils of war have been made lawful for me and it was not made so for anyone else before me. I have been given the right of intercession. Every Prophet used to be sent to his nation exclusively, but I have been sent to all mankind."*

Ibn Kathir argues from Hudhayfah's hadith that the Messenger ﷺ mentioned the favour of making **dust** a purifier for us, "and if there were any other substance to replace it for Tayammum, he would have mentioned it."

The allowance is not a stopgap for an afternoon. Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan, with the exception of Ibn Majah, recorded that Abu Dharr said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Clean earth is pure for the Muslim, even if he does not find water for ten years. When he finds water, let him use it for his skin, for this is better."* At-Tirmidhi said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: after tayammum one is held to be purified for a temporary period, until he is able to use water.

### When tayammum was given: the lost necklace

Al-Bukhari recorded that ʿA'ishah said: "We set out with Allah's Messenger ﷺ on one of his journeys until we reached Al-Bayda' or Dhat-ul-Jaysh, where a necklace of mine was broken (and lost). Allah's Messenger ﷺ stayed there to search for it, and so did the people along with him. There was no water source or any water with them at that place, so the people went to Abu Bakr As-Siddiq and said, 'Don't you see what ʿA'ishah has done! She has made Allah's Messenger and the people stay where there is no source of water and they have no water with them.' Abu Bakr came while Allah's Messenger ﷺ was sleeping with his head on my thigh. He said to me, 'You have detained Allah's Messenger and the people where there is no source of water and they have no water with them.' So he admonished me and said what Allah wished him to say and hit me on my flank with his hand. Nothing prevented me from moving (because of pain) but the position of Allah's Messenger on my thigh. Allah's Messenger ﷺ got up when dawn broke and there was no water. So Allah revealed the verses of Tayammum, and they all performed Tayammum. Usayd bin Hudayr said, **'O the family of Abu Bakr! This is not the first blessing of yours.'** Then the camel on which I was riding was moved from its place and the necklace was found beneath it." Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded this hadith.

Out of one awkward night came a lasting ease for the Ummah.

---

## "Truly, Allah is Ever Oft-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving"

The ayah closes on two names: **ʿAfuwwan Ghafūrā**. Ibn Kathir reads the seal against what precedes it: "a part of His pardoning and forgiving is that He allows you to use Tayammum and to pray after using it when there is no water, to make things easy for you." As he puts it, the ayah sanctifies the position of the prayer — too sacred to be performed in a deficient manner, whether in a state of drunkenness until one becomes aware of what he is saying, or sexually impure until he bathes, or after answering the call of nature until he performs ablution — and then, in the exceptions of illness and of finding no water, Allah allows tayammum "out of His mercy and kindness for His servants, and to facilitate them." As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, land mass and dust "are available everywhere."

**What it asks of you.** Come to prayer awake — if drowsiness is scrambling your words, sleep a while and pray with a mind that knows what it is saying. Take the states of purity seriously; they are the door. And never let the absence of water become a reason to miss a prayer: the man sitting apart was not excused, he was taught.

passages.title: Scripture people who twist words and buy misguidance
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah an-Nisāʾ 4:44–46 — Words Twisted, and a Protector Who Suffices

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up this unit precisely: these verses "take up the matter of dealings with enemies," bringing "into sharp focus the wicked tricks, in word and deed," and then setting beside them "a view of what is true and correct." The people described here were handed real knowledge from Allah and traded it away — and then went to work on the believers, not with swords, but with language.

What holds the three ayat together is a single movement. **Ayah 44** names the charge and its motive. **Ayah 45** breaks in with reassurance before the believer has time to be afraid. **Ayah 46** returns and shows the receipts — the actual sentences these people spoke, quoted back at them.

Ibn Kathir titles his treatment of the whole passage: *Chastising the Jews for Choosing Misguidance, Altering Allah's Words, and Mocking Islam*.

---

## Ayah 44 — A portion of the Book, sold cheap

*"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book, purchasing the wrong path…"*

Notice what Allah credits them with before He indicts them: they **were given a portion of the Book**. This is not ignorance being described. It is knowledge being misused. Ibn Kathir explains that they "ignored what Allah sent down to His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ" and also "ignored the knowledge that they inherited from previous Prophets, about the description of Muhammad ﷺ." The description had been handed down to them, and they turned from it.

**The image is commercial.** The Qur'an does not say they *fell* into misguidance; it says they are *purchasing* it. A purchase is deliberate, and every purchase has a price. Ibn Kathir names what they got in exchange: "a small amount of the delights of this life." That is the whole return on the transaction. They handed over prophetic knowledge and received pocket change.

**And then the second clause turns toward you.** *"…and wishing that you should go astray from the right path."* It was not enough to be lost; they wanted company. Ibn Kathir spells out the wish in plain terms: "they would like that you disbelieve in what was sent down to you, O believers, and that you abandon the guidance and beneficial knowledge that you have."

Read those two halves together and the logic is stark. Having thrown away *their* portion of guidance, they set to work on *yours*. Misguidance is not content to be private.

---

## Ayah 45 — Two sufficiencies

*"Allah has full knowledge of your enemies, and Allah is sufficient as a Waliyy (Protector), and Allah is sufficient as a Helper."*

This ayah is the mercy folded into the middle of the passage, and its placement is everything. The believer has just been told that there are people who actively wish him astray. The natural response is anxiety: *who exactly are they?*

Allah does not answer by handing over a list of names. He answers with Himself.

**"Allah has full knowledge of your enemies."** Ibn Kathir: "Allah has better knowledge of your enemies, and He warns you against them." Two things sit inside that. First, His knowledge is *better* than yours — you will not identify every hostile intention around you. Second, He does not keep that knowledge to Himself; He warns you. This very ayah is the warning arriving.

**Then two descriptions, each with the word "sufficient" attached.** Ibn Kathir distinguishes them by what each one meets in you:

- **Waliyy** — the Protector, the one who takes charge of your affair. "He is a Sufficient Protector for those who seek refuge with Him."
- **Naṣīr** — the Helper, the one who comes to your aid. "A Sufficient Supporter for those who seek His help."

One is for when you need shelter; the other is for when you need backing. And in both, the operative word is *sufficient* — not "an additional resource," not "a help alongside your own precautions." Enough. Note also the condition embedded in Ibn Kathir's gloss: this sufficiency is described for *those who seek refuge with Him* and *those who seek His help*. The protection is real, and it is entered through asking.

---

## Ayah 46 — The evidence: four sentences

Now Allah quotes them. This is the longest of the three ayat, and it is essentially a transcript.

### First, the method: *yuḥarrifūna al-kalim ʿan mawāḍiʿih*

*"…there are some who displace words from their right places."*

The image is physical: a word lifted out of the spot where it was set and put down somewhere else, so that it now says something it was never placed there to say. Ibn Kathir removes any suggestion of innocent error — they "**intentionally and falsely** alter the meanings of the Words of Allah and explain them in a different manner than what Allah meant."

Note carefully what is being altered here in Ibn Kathir's explanation: **the meanings**. This is distortion by interpretation — the text left standing while its sense is bent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "laboured falsification," a phrase worth sitting with. Twisting scripture is *work*. It takes effort, cleverness, and sustained bad faith to make a revealed word mean its opposite. As Ibn Kathir says, it is done intentionally; nobody does it by accident.

### Second, the sentences themselves

Ibn Kathir walks through them one at a time:

**"We hear your word — and we disobey."** (*samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā*) — Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd explained this as: "We hear what you say, O Muhammad, but we do not obey you in it." Ibn Kathir comments that this "demonstrates the Jews' disbelief, stubbornness and disregard for Allah's Book **after they understood it**, all the while aware of the sin and punishment that this behaviour will earn." That is the aggravating detail throughout this passage — comprehension without compliance. They knew exactly what they were refusing.

**"Hear — and may you never be made to hear."** (*wasmaʿ ghayra musmaʿ*) — a phrase built to be deniable. On the surface it is a request: *listen to us*. Ad-Daḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that the intended sense is: "hear our words, may you never hear anything." Ibn Kathir calls it plainly what it is: "the Jews' way of mocking and jesting."

**"Rāʿinā."** — the sharpest of the three, because it exploits the seam between two languages. Ibn Kathir explains that "they pretend to say, 'Hear us,'" using a word that in Arabic means *listen to us* — while in Hebrew it functions as an insult. "Yet, their true aim is to curse the Prophet ﷺ."

This is why the ayah adds *layyan bi-alsinatihim wa ṭaʿnan fī al-dīn* — **"with a twist of their tongues, and as a mockery of the religion."** The twist is the whole technique: a mouth shaped so that what leaves it can be read two ways, one respectful and one contemptuous, with the speaker safely able to claim the first. Ibn Kathir ties the phrase directly to "their cursing the Prophet ﷺ."

Allah closed that loophole in an earlier revelation. Ibn Kathir refers the reader back to Sūrah al-Baqarah: *"O you who believe! Say not Rāʿinā, but say Unẓurnā"* (2:104). The believers were told to drop the ambiguous word altogether and use the clear one, *unẓurnā* — "make us understand." **A phrase that has been turned into a vehicle for insult is not worth defending.**

### Third, what they should have said

*"And if only they had said: 'We hear and we obey,' and 'Do make us understand,' it would have been better for them, and more proper."*

The correction is exact, word for word:

| What they said | What they should have said |
|---|---|
| *samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* — "We hear and disobey" | *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā* — "We hear and obey" |
| *wasmaʿ ghayra musmaʿ* — "Hear, may you hear nothing" | *wasmaʿ* — "Hear" |
| *rāʿinā* — the double-edged word | *unẓurnā* — "Do make us understand" |

Barely anything separates the two columns. A consonant here, a dropped clause there. The distance between mockery and submission was, in terms of syllables, almost nothing — and in terms of the heart, everything.

And what is offered for making that small change is generous: it "would have been **better for them**, and **more proper**." Better *for them* — Allah is not the one who stands to gain.

### Fourth, the outcome

*"…but Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they believe not except a few."*

Ibn Kathir explains the state this describes: "their hearts are cast away from the path of righteousness and therefore, no beneficial part of faith enters it." He links it to the earlier verse *"so little is that which they believe"* (2:88), which, he notes, "means they do not have beneficial faith."

That is the sober point. The problem was never a shortage of information — they had "a portion of the Book." It was a heart turned in such a way that nothing useful could land in it. Knowledge poured into a vessel tipped over runs straight back out.

---

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson the passage was building toward, and it is aimed at us, not at them. After showing the tricks "in word and deed," the verses "give a view of what is true and correct" — and this, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "is in a way an exhortation to Muslims that they should be careful in choosing the words they use to say what they have to say, **for mincing words is not their style**."

Three things follow directly from the passage:

**Say what you mean.** The sin catalogued in ayah 46 is not rudeness — it is the deliberately double-edged sentence, the phrase engineered so it can be defended if challenged and enjoyed if it lands. A believer's speech should not require a decoder. If a word has been loaded with insult, drop it and use the clear one, exactly as the believers were told to say *unẓurnā*.

**Beware of hearing without obeying.** *Samiʿnā wa ʿaṣaynā* is the shape of every attendance at a reminder that changes nothing. Ibn Kathir's aggravating factor — disregard for Allah's Book *after they understood it* — is a warning to anyone with access to knowledge. The counter-phrase given in the same ayah is the believer's posture: *samiʿnā wa aṭaʿnā*, "we hear and we obey."

**Do not carry the anxiety yourself.** Between the accusation in ayah 44 and the evidence in ayah 46 stands ayah 45. You will not always know who wishes you ill or how cleverly they have phrased it. Allah knows your enemies better than you do, He warns you, and He is enough — as Protector for the one who seeks refuge with Him, and as Supporter for the one who seeks His help.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this description of a stance "which ranged from flat denial to laboured falsification, something born out of the desire to misrepresent, alter and ridicule," is not where the passage ends. What follows next in the sūrah addresses these same people directly and "commands them to believe in the final revelation and demonstrate their confirmation" — a door held open even after all of this has been said.

passages.title: Called to the confirming Book, they claim their own purity
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single summons with a single answer. Allah calls the People of the Book to believe in the Qur'an — a Book that *confirms* the scripture already in their hands — and warns them of what follows refusal (ayah 47). He then closes the one door they imagined would always stay open for them: the sin of shirk is not forgiven (ayah 48). And He exposes the root of their refusal: they had already decided they were pure, already acquitted themselves in advance (ayat 49–50). The thread running through all four is this — **a claim of guaranteed salvation, met by a Book that says salvation is Allah's to give, not yours to assume.**

## Ayah 47: "Believe in what We have revealed, confirming what is with you"

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here commands the People of the Scriptures to believe in what He sent down to His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ — "the Glorious Book that conforms to the good news that they already have about Muhammad ﷺ."

Notice the argument packed into one word. The Qur'an is not presented to them as a foreign object demanding they abandon everything they know. It is *muṣaddiqan li-mā maʿakum* — "confirming what is with you." Their own scriptures already carried good news about this Prophet ﷺ. So belief in the Qur'an is not a betrayal of what they held; it is the completion of it. Refusing it means refusing the very thing their own books pointed toward.

## The warning, and what it means

Then comes the threat: *before We efface faces and turn them backwards, or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath.*

**On "effacing" (ṭams).** Al-ʿAwfi said that Ibn ʿAbbas said that "effacing" here refers to blindness.

**On "turn them backwards."** Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as meaning: "We put their faces on their backs, and make them walk backwards, since their eyes will be in their backs." He notes that Qatadah and ʿAtiyah al-ʿAwfi said something similar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Arabic phrase admits two possibilities (citing Mazhari and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī): either the features of the face are eliminated and the whole face turned around toward the back, or the face is flattened like the nape of the neck, devoid of all features — "effaced."

**Why this image?** Ibn Kathir draws out the point. This makes the punishment even more severe, and it is a *parable* Allah set for ignoring the truth, preferring the wrong way, and turning away from the plain path for the paths of misguidance. So the punishment mirrors the crime: **people who turned their backs on guidance are made to walk backwards.** In the same way, he notes, some read Allah's words in Sūrat Yā-Sīn — "Verily, We have put on their necks iron collars reaching to the chins, so that their heads are raised up. And We have put a barrier before them" (36:8–9) — as a parable Allah gave for their deviation and their being hindered from guidance.

**"Or curse them as We cursed the people of the Sabbath."** Ibn Kathir identifies these as those who breached the sanctity of the Sabbath, using deceit, for the purpose of doing more work — and Allah changed these people into apes and swine, a matter he says will be explained in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

## Did this punishment actually happen?

This is the question every honest reader asks, and the commentators asked it too. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that commentators discussed this deconfiguration (*ṭams*) and transmutation (*maskh*) at length: some said this punishment will come upon the Jews before the Day of Doom, while others said it did not come to pass, because some of the Jews entered the fold of faith.

Maulana Ashraf Thanavi cut through the debate with a point about the wording itself. In his view the question simply does not arise, **because there is no single word in the Qur'an here suggesting: if you do not believe, the punishment of *ṭams* and *maskh* will definitely materialize.** It suggests a *probability*: given their crime, they do deserve this punishment — and should Allah spare them from it, that would be His mercy.

This is worth sitting with. Allah's threats are statements of what wrongdoing merits. Being spared is not the threat failing; it is mercy arriving.

**"And the commandment of Allah is always executed."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and heavy: when Allah commands something, no one can dispute or resist His command. The window for repentance stays open only because He keeps it open — not because anyone could hold it open against Him.

## The man who heard this ayah and submitted

Ibn Kathir preserves a report that turns this warning from a historical curiosity into something felt. It was reported that Kaʿb al-Aḥbar became Muslim when he heard this very ayah. Ibn Jarir recorded that ʿIsa bin al-Mughirah said: we were with Ibrahim when we talked about the time when Kaʿb became Muslim. Kaʿb became Muslim during the reign of ʿUmar. He passed by Madinah intending to visit Jerusalem, and ʿUmar said to him, "Embrace Islam, O Kaʿb." Kaʿb answered with a verse: "Do you not read in your Book, *The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Tawrah…* (62:5)? I am among those who were entrusted with the Tawrah." ʿUmar left him alone.

Kaʿb went on to Ḥimṣ in Syria. There he heard one of its inhabitants recite this ayah — while feeling sad — *O you who have been given the Scripture! Believe in what We have revealed, confirming what is with you, before We efface faces and turn them backwards.* And Kaʿb said: **"I believe, O Lord! I embraced Islam, O Lord!"** — for he feared that he might be struck by this threat. He then went back to his family in Yemen and returned with them all as Muslims.

An argument had not moved him. A recited warning did. That is what this ayah is designed to do.

## Ayah 48: the one sin that is not forgiven

Why does the discourse turn suddenly to shirk? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the link. The previous ayah carried an admonition for those who refused to believe — but since some of those addressed could finally be forgiven, one might infer that perhaps *all* of them may be forgiven too. So the text goes on to explain that this group will not be forgiven, because of their kufr. **It also refutes the Jewish claim that they shall be forgiven.**

Ibn Kathir's reading of the words is precise: *He forgives not that partners should be set up with Him* means He does not forgive a servant **who meets Him while he is associating partners with Him**. Ibn Kathir titles the section, "Allah Does not Forgive Shirk, Except After Repenting From it." Shirk is unforgivable at the meeting; repentance before that meeting is the way out. And *He forgives what is less than that* — meaning other sins — *for whom He wills*, of His servants. Both halves must be held together: no shirk gets through, and no other sin is guaranteed to be blocked or guaranteed to be waved through. It is His will.

**And whoever sets up partners with Allah has indeed invented a tremendous sin.** Ibn Kathir places this alongside "Verily, joining others in worship with Allah is a great *ẓulm* (wrong) indeed" (31:13). In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, it is recorded that Ibn Masʿud said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Which is the greatest sin?' He said: **'To make a rival with Allah, while He Alone created you.'**" That last clause is the whole argument — the offence is not merely a rule broken; it is turning to another the One who alone brought you into existence.

## What shirk looks like in practice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this ayah a working definition: the set articles of faith relating to the Being and Attributes of Allah are the indispensable foundation of religion, and holding any belief similar to these in favour of *whoever and whatever He has created* is shirk. It then lists forms it takes:

- **Shirk in knowledge (ʿilm)** — ascribing a partner to Allah in matters of knowing: believing that a certain pious person, a spiritual master or the head of a mystical order knows about everything in this universe all the time; asking an astrologer, fortune-teller or diviner about things going to take place in a person's life, things belonging to the unseen, an exclusive domain of Allah; taking an omen (*fāl*) from words written by a pious person and believing it has got to happen; calling someone from a considerable distance and believing that person has become aware of the call; or keeping a fast dedicated to someone other than Allah.
- **Shirk in power** — ascribing to others the powers and rights that are the exclusive domain of Allah: taking someone to have the power and authority to provide gain or inflict loss; asking someone to grant wishes, or to ask them for sustenance and children.
- **Shirk in worship (ʿibādah)** — ascribing a partner to Allah in acts of worship, which are His sole due: prostrating (*sajdah*) to anyone; releasing an animal dedicated in the name of somebody; making ceremonious offerings for a person or thing, living or dead; making a vow (*nadhr*, *mannat*) in someone's name; making *ṭawāf* around someone's grave or house; giving preference to someone else's word or custom as against Allah's own command; bowing before anyone in the manner of *rukūʿ*, the bowing position peculiar to Muslim prayer; slaughtering an animal in someone's name; taking the affairs of this world as subservient to the effect and influence of the stars; or regarding some month as ill-omened.

The list is uncomfortable precisely because so much of it is quiet and cultural rather than loud and theological.

## From the Sunnah: how wide the forgiveness is

Because ayah 48 is severe, the Sunnah cited here is expansive on the other side of it.

**Imam Ahmad recorded** that Abu Dharr said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah says: *"O My servant! As long as you worship and beg Me, I will forgive you, no matter your shortcomings. O My servant! If you meet Me with the earth's fill of sin, yet you do not associate any partners with Me, I will meet you with its fill of forgiveness."* Ibn Kathir notes that only Ahmad recorded this hadith with this chain of narration.

**Imam Ahmad also recorded** — and Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs recorded this hadith as well — that Abu Dharr said: I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he said, *"No servant proclaims, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah,' and dies on that belief, but will enter Paradise."* I said, "Even if he committed adultery and theft?" He said, *"Even if he committed adultery and theft."* I asked again, and again — and the fourth time he said, *"Even if Abu Dharr's nose was put in the dust."* Abu Dharr departed while pulling his *izār*, saying, "Even if Abu Dharr's nose was put in the dust." Ever after, he would narrate the hadith and then add that same comment.

The exchange is almost humorous, and deeply human: Abu Dharr's own moral instinct kept resisting the sheer scope of the mercy, and the Prophet ﷺ kept refusing to narrow it.

**Al-Bazzar recorded** that Ibn ʿUmar said: "We used to refrain from begging Allah for forgiveness for those who commit major sins, until we heard our Prophet ﷺ reciting *Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives except that to whom He wills*, and heard him ﷺ say: *'I have reserved my intercession on the Day of Resurrection for those among my Ummah who commit major sins.'*"

Note what that does to the believer's posture: it stopped the Companions writing off other people.

## Ayat 49–50: "Have you not seen those who claim sanctity for themselves?"

Now the Qur'an names the disease underneath the refusal. **They had already certified themselves.**

Al-Ḥasan and Qatadah said this ayah was revealed about the Jews and Christians when they said, "We are Allah's children and His loved ones." Ibn Zayd also said it was revealed concerning that statement — *We are the children of Allah and His loved ones* (5:18) — and their statement, *None shall enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian* (2:111).

Against this Allah says: **"Nay, but Allah sanctifies whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir's comment goes to the heart of it: the decision in this matter is with Allah alone, **because He has perfect knowledge of the true reality and the secrets of all things.** The verdict belongs to the One who has that knowledge — not to the one issuing the claim.

**"And they will not be dealt with injustice even equal to the extent of a *fatīl*."** Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that He does no injustice with anyone's compensation in any part of his reward, even if it were the weight of a *fatīl*. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah and others among the Salaf said that *fatīl* means "the scalish thread in the long slit of the date-stone" — a deliberately minute measure. Removing the guarantee of salvation is not the removal of justice. Allah shortchanges no one's reward by a hair.

**Ayah 50: "Look, how they invent a lie against Allah — and enough is that as a manifest sin."** Ibn Kathir lists exactly what the lie consists of: claiming purity for themselves; their claim to be Allah's children and His loved ones; their saying *None shall enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian* (2:111); their saying *The Fire shall not touch us but for a number of days* (3:24); and their reliance on the righteous deeds of their forefathers. On that last point he cites Allah's own decree that the good actions of the fathers do not help the children: *That was a nation who has passed away. They shall receive the reward of what they earned and you of what you earn.*

And "enough is that as a manifest sin" means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that these lies and fabrications of theirs are sufficient. **Inherited righteousness is not a transferable asset, and a self-issued certificate of purity is not a small vanity — the Qur'an classes it as a lie invented against Allah**, because it puts words in His mouth about whom He accepts.

## Living it: the ban on praising yourself

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses this ayah on us rather than leaving it with the Jews of Madinah, noting how strange a spectacle it is: a people attributing sanctity to themselves and then having the audacity to tell others that this is so. From here, it says, we learn that **it is not permissible for anyone to claim and broadcast his or her own sanctity, or that of others.** It gives three reasons:

1. **The cause of self-praise is mostly pride and arrogance.** So what is really being forbidden is pride and arrogance.
2. **Nobody knows how they will end.** Only Allah knows whether a person's end will come in a state of *taqwā* and *ṭahārah* — still fearing Allah spiritually, and free of impurity physically. Claiming sanctity for oneself is therefore contrary to fearing Allah. Maʿārif cites here (from Mazhari) the narration of Sayyidah Zaynab, daughter of Abu Salamah, that the Prophet ﷺ asked her, "What is your name?" Her name at that time was **Barrah** — which means pure from sins — and that is what she told him. He ﷺ then said: *"Do not claim sanctity for yourselves, for it is Allah alone who knows best who among you is of the righteous"* — and he named her **Zaynab** instead. (Maʿārif cites this as reported by Muslim, via Mishkāt.)
3. **It misleads others.** Such a claim gives people the false idea that the person making it is nearer to Allah because he is free of all faults — and that is a lie, for no mortal man is free of one or another shortcoming. (Maʿārif cites Bayān al-Qurʾān here.)

**The ruling that balances it.** Maʿārif is careful not to turn this into false modesty: if the impediments mentioned above do not exist, a person may speak about a trait of his character **as an expression of gratitude for Allah's blessing** (citing Bayān al-Qurʾān). The line is intention. Naming a gift in order to thank the Giver is not the sin; naming it in order to rank yourself is.

## Holding the passage together

Read as one unit, the logic is exact. Believe in the Book that confirms your own (47). Do not imagine an automatic pardon — the one thing not forgiven at the meeting with Allah is associating partners with Him, and everything else is His to forgive as He wills (48). And stop grading yourself: sanctification is His verdict, issued with perfect knowledge of the true reality and the secrets of all things, and issued without cheating anyone of a hair's weight (49–50).

The believer who reads this and only sees the failings of an earlier community has missed the arrow. The safe posture is the one the passage prescribes: hope that reaches "the earth's fill of forgiveness," fear that refuses to write your own reference letter, and a name — like Zaynab's — that does not announce a purity only Allah can see.

passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These seven ayat expose a scandal: scholars who knew the Scripture prostrated to idols and told the pagans of Makkah that idolatry was better guided than the message of the Prophet ﷺ. The arc: **a claim (51) → a verdict (52) → the motive interrogated, envy of a bounty Allah gave to someone else (53–54) → the precedent in their own history (55) → the two ends (56–57).**

Ibn Kathir notes that from ayah 49 Allah addresses those who "claim sanctity for themselves." Al-Hasan and Qatadah said that ayah was revealed about Jews and Christians who said, "We are Allah's children and His loved ones"; Ibn Zayd connected it also to their claim that none enters Paradise but a Jew or a Christian. Allah answered: *bal Allāhu yuzakkī man yashāʾ* — rather, **Allah** sanctifies whom He wills; the decision, says Ibn Kathir, is Allah's alone.

## The story behind ayah 51

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās that after the battle of Uhud two chiefs of the Jews, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, came with a group of their people to the Quraysh at Makkah, and Kaʿb promised Abū Sufyān to collaborate against the Prophet ﷺ. The Makkans, suspicious, said his people were known for cheating by false promises, and challenged them, if they meant it, to prostrate before two particular idols — Jibt and Ṭāghūt, Maʿārif says. To reassure them, he did. Kaʿb then proposed that thirty of you and thirty of us declare before the Lord of the Kaʿbah that all of us will jointly fight Muhammad ﷺ; the Quraysh liked it, and so a united front against the Muslims was opened.

Abū Sufyān then asked the question the ayah answers: *You are learned people; you have the Book of Allah with you. We are totally ignorant. Tell us — are we on the right path, or is it Muhammad?* Kaʿb asked what their religion was. Abū Sufyān said: we slaughter our camels for the Hajj, offer their milk to the pilgrims, entertain guests, keep good relations with our kin, make ṭawāf of the House of Allah and perform ʿUmrah — whereas Muhammad ﷺ has abandoned his ancestral religion, cut himself off from his own people, and challenged it by bringing a new religion of his own. Kaʿb answered: **"You people are on the right path. Muhammad ﷺ has gone astray."**

Ibn Kathir preserves a second telling, from ʿIkrimah (Ibn Abī Ḥātim): Ḥuyayy and Kaʿb came to the people of Makkah, who said, "You are people of the Book and knowledge, so judge between us and Muhammad." Asked to describe both sides, the Makkans said they keep relations with kith and kin, slaughter camels for the poor, release the indebted and provide water for the pilgrims, while Muhammad ﷺ is without male children, severed our relations, and is followed by the thieves who rob pilgrims, the tribe of Ghifār. "So who is better, we or him?" The answer: "You are more righteous and better guided." Ibn Kathir adds that the story is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and several others among the Salaf.

Not one word of scripture was consulted. On "These people are better guided on the way," Ibn Kathir writes that they preferred the disbelievers over the Muslims "because of their ignorance, un-religious nature and disbelief in Allah's Book which is before them."

## Jibt and Ṭāghūt

Ayah 51 says they *believe in Jibt and Ṭāghūt*; the sources give a spread of meanings. Maʿārif: *Jibt* was originally the name of an idol, later used for every false god and for sorcery; *Ṭāghūt* literally signifies the arrogant, and is used for Satan and for evil and falsehood. Commentators, Maʿārif adds, have explained *Jibt* as from the Ethiopian language, meaning a magician, and *Ṭāghūt* as a soothsayer.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said — through Muhammad ibn Isḥāq from Ḥassān ibn Fāʾid — "Jibt is sorcery and Ṭāghūt is the Shayṭān." Al-Jawharī in *aṣ-Ṣiḥāḥ* gives *al-Jibt* as idol, soothsayer and sorcerer. Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, asked about Ṭāghūt, said: "They are soothsayers upon whom the devils descend" (Ibn Abī Ḥātim). Mujāhid said Ṭāghūt is a devil in the shape of a man, whom they refer to for judgement. Imām Mālik said Ṭāghūt is **every object that is worshipped instead of Allah**.

Imam al-Qurṭubī, Maʿārif notes, generally preferred Mālik's view as more inclusive, since the Qur'an supports it: *"Worship Allah and avoid Ṭāghūt"* (16:36). But Maʿārif adds, following Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, that there is no real contradiction; the views can all be implied in one sense or another, since Jibt was essentially the name of an idol and only later applied to other things worshipped besides Allah.

## Ayah 52: the verdict, and what a curse is

*Ulāʾika alladhīna laʿanahum Allāh* — those are the ones Allah has cursed, and whoever Allah curses, you will find for him no helper. Ibn Kathir: they have no supporter in this life or the Hereafter, because they sought the help of the idolaters. That statement was made to lure the disbelievers into supporting them, and they ultimately gathered their forces for the battle of al-Aḥzāb, forcing the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions to dig a defensive trench around Madinah. But Allah saved the Muslims from their evil: *"And Allah drove back those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no advantage. Allah sufficed for the believers in the fighting. And Allah is Ever All-Strong, All-Mighty"* (33:25).

**What laʿnah means.** "Curse" only approximates it, Maʿārif says: *laʿnah* is **being far removed from the mercy of Allah**, extremely debased and disgraced. In Sharīʿah terminology, applied to disbelievers it means being far off from Allah's mercy; applied to Muslims, having fallen from the level of the righteous (Shāmī from al-Quhistānī). Anyone under it cannot be close to Allah.

**Who falls under it.** The Prophet ﷺ cursed the giver, receiver and consumer of interest, its writer and its witness — all equally involved in the sin (Muslim, as in Mishkāt). Bukhārī, from Mishkāt: "Allah curses the eater of interest, and its feeder, and the woman who tattoos another woman and the woman who has herself tattooed, and the picture-maker." Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah, from Mishkāt: Allah curses liquor and everyone in its chain — consumer and server, seller and purchaser, squeezers, handlers, transporters, and those who order it. Baihaqī in *al-Mudkhal*, from Mishkāt, records six the Prophet ﷺ said he had cursed and Allah has cursed too: one who commits excess in the matter of Allah's Book; one who rises to power by force and terror, then honours whom Allah has disgraced and disgraces whom Allah has honoured; the denier of Allah's determined destiny; one who takes as lawful what Allah made unlawful; the person in his progeny who treats the forbidden as lawful; and the one who gives up his sunnah.

**A warning about using it.** Because of the evil it releases, Maʿārif says, heavy restrictions attach to invoking laʿnah. Ibn Masʿūd narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said, "A true Muslim is no taunter or imprecator, nor is he foul-mouthed" (Tirmidhī, from Mishkāt). Abū al-Dardāʾ heard him ﷺ say that when a servant of Allah curses something, the curse rises to the sky and its doors close against it, comes down to the earth and its doors close against it, takes a right and a left, and finding no access returns to the one cursed — if he really deserves it, on him it falls; otherwise it returns to the one who uttered it (Abū Dāwūd, via Mishkāt). Ibn ʿAbbās reported that a man cursed the wind after it swooped away his cloak; the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not curse it, for it is under orders, and whoever curses something that does not deserve it, the curse returns to none but him" (Tirmidhī, via Mishkāt).

Maʿārif's rulings: invoking laʿnah on a **particular** person is not permissible unless it is known that he died in disbelief, even if he was sinful — on this basis ʿAllāmah Ibn ʿĀbidīn advised against cursing Yazīd; where death in disbelief is certain, as with Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab, it is permitted. Cursing without naming anyone — "Allah's curse upon liars" or "upon tyrants" — is permissible. And since laʿnah applied to a Muslim means a fall from the level of the righteous, praying that a Muslim's good deeds decrease is likewise not permissible.

## Ayat 53–54: two questions that take the motive apart

Maʿārif frames these two ayat as one argument in two moves against an unreasonable envy: a first reason in 53, a second in 54, both with the same outcome.

**First move (53).** *Am lahum naṣībun min al-mulk* — do they have a share in the kingdom? Ibn Kathir: merely a rebuke, since they have no share in the dominion at all. Allah continues, *then they would not give people even a naqīr* — the **naqīr**, per Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of the scholars, being the speck on the back of a date-stone. Ibn Kathir: if they had a share in sovereignty they would give no one anything, especially not Muhammad ﷺ, not even that much. He compares 17:100 — those who possessed the treasure of Allah's mercy would withhold it for fear of spending, fear that what they have might run out, though with Allah's treasures no such possibility exists — a verse ending *"and man is ever qatūr"*, which he glosses as *bakhīl*, stingy. Maʿārif's reading: if your envy rests on thinking you are the real inheritors of the kingdom and that what he was given is actually yours, that is simply wrong — you have no kingdom now, and even if you came to have some, you are not the kind to give anything to anybody.

**Second move (54).** *Am yaḥsudūna al-nāsa ʿalā mā ātāhum Allāhu min faḍlih* — or do they envy people for what Allah gave them of His bounty? Ibn Kathir: this is their envy of the Prophet ﷺ for the great prophethood Allah entrusted him with, an envy that made them reject him **because he was an Arab and not from the Children of Israel**. At-Tabarānī recorded Ibn ʿAbbās explaining their attitude: "We are the worthy people, rather than the rest of the people." The answer: *"Then, We have already given the family of Ibrāhīm the Book and al-Ḥikmah, and conferred upon them a great kingdom."* Ibn Kathir: We gave prophethood to the tribes of the Children of Israel, who are among Ibrāhīm's offspring, and sent down the Books to them; these Prophets ruled them by the prophetic tradition, and We made kings among them. Maʿārif's rebuttal: if the complaint is not that the kingdom passed from you to him but why it went to *him* at all, the answer is that he too comes from the family of prophets who ruled over kingdoms before him. The kingdom has not come to a stranger; your envy is unreasonable.

**On envy itself.** ʿAllāmah al-Nawawī, the commentator on Muslim, defines *ḥasad* as **the desire to see another person's blessing somehow disappear** — and it is forbidden. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not hate and do not envy and do not turn your backs on each other. Instead, become servants of Allah, as brothers. And it is not lawful for a Muslim that he abandons his brother for more than three days" (Muslim). He said, "Beware of envy, for envy eats up good deeds as the fire eats up wood" (Abū Dāwūd, via Mishkāt). And az-Zubayr narrated that he ﷺ said, "Stealthily creeping into you is the disease of earlier peoples — envy; and hatred, which is a shaver. I do not say that it shaves hair, but it does shave the religion off" (Ahmad and Tirmidhī, via Mishkāt). Maʿārif draws a fine point from the wording: envy is forbidden over worldly and spiritual excellence alike — *a share in the kingdom* (53) pointing to the worldly, *the Book and the wisdom* (54) to the spiritual.

## Ayah 55: the precedent inside their own history

*"Of them were some who believed in it, and of them were some who rejected it; and enough is Hell for burning."* Ibn Kathir gives two readings. The pronoun may refer to Allah's favour and bounty just mentioned — the Prophets, the Books, the kingship — so that some of the Children of Israel believed in that favour while others rejected it by disbelieving, ignoring it and hindering people from its path, although this bounty was from and for them. They disputed with their own Prophets; so what about you, O Muhammad ﷺ, especially since you are not from the Children of Israel? Mujāhid read the pronoun as the Prophet ﷺ himself: some believed in him and some turned away — and therefore, Ibn Kathir continues, their rejection of you is even more severe, and they are even further from the truth you brought them.

Even here the Qur'an says *some… and some*. Ibn Kathir says the Fire is a just punishment for them because of their disbelief, rebellion and defiance of Allah's Books and Messengers.

## Ayat 56–57: the two ends

Maʿārif notes the shift: particular believers and disbelievers were mentioned before; now the reward and punishment of a believer and a disbeliever are stated **as a universal rule**.

**The Fire (56).** Ibn Kathir: Allah will place them in a Fire encompassing every part of their bodies, and their punishment and torment are everlasting — *"as often as their skins are roasted through, We shall change them for other skins, that they may taste the punishment."* Al-Hasan said the skins are roasted through seventy thousand times every day, and that whenever the Fire has roasted them through and consumed their flesh they will be told, "Go back as you were before," and they will; Maʿārif reports the same from al-Hasan al-Baṣrī (al-Baihaqī, as quoted by Mazharī) and adds Muʿādh's word that the skin is replaced as soon as it is burnt out, with such speed that it is replaced a hundred times in a single moment.

The ayah itself gives the reason — *li-yadhūqū al-ʿadhāb*, "that they may taste the punishment." Maʿārif cites al-Bukhārī and Muslim: the lightest punished among the people of the Fire will be a man in the soles of whose feet there are two smouldering embers, from whose heat his brain keeps boiling like a cauldron. And the ayah seals it with two of Allah's names: *ʿAzīzan Ḥakīmā*, Ever Most Powerful, All-Wise.

**The Garden (57).** *"But those who believe and do deeds of righteousness, We shall admit them to Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever."* Ibn Kathir describes rivers flowing through all its areas, spaces and corners, wherever they desire and wish; they will reside there for eternity, never transferred or removed from it, nor would they ever want to move. The two conditions are in the ayah itself: faith and righteous action together.

*Azwājun muṭahharah*, purified mates: Ibn Kathir explains them as free of menstruation, postnatal bleeding, filth, bad manners and shortcomings. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are "purified of filth and foul things," and ʿAṭāʾ, al-Hasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, an-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ṣāliḥ, ʿAṭiyyah and as-Suddī said the like; Mujāhid said they are free of urine, menstruation, spit, mucus and pregnancies, and Maʿārif adds from him that they are also pure from procreation and seminal impurity (Mazharī).

*Ẓillan ẓalīlā*, "shade, deeply shading." Maʿārif: placing *ẓalīl* after *ẓill* conveys that the shade of Jannah will be dense and ever-present — like *shamsun shāmis* or *laylun layīl* — indicating that the blessings of Paradise last forever. Ibn Kathir renders it wide, extensive, pure and elegant shade; Rabīʿ ibn Anas said it is "the shade of the Throne, which will never decline." Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said there is a tree in Paradise such that if a rider travels under its shade for a hundred years he will not cross it — the Tree of Everlasting Life (Ibn Jarīr); in Maʿārif's version he ﷺ added, "Read, if you wish: *wa ẓillin mamdūd* — a shade, ever-extended."

## Living it

Maʿārif draws the sharpest lesson from Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf: a distinguished scholar among the Jews, who believed in Allah and worshipped none but Him, yet who let the ghost of overweening personal desire overpower his mind and heart and swallowed the bitter pill of prostration to achieve his personal end. He stooped to what was contrary to his own religion and did not show the courage to part ways with the Quraysh on so crucial an issue.

Maʿārif compares this with Balʿam ibn Bāʿūr, of whom the Qur'an says: *"Recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, then he eased out from them, and Satan followed him, and he became one of those who go astray"* (7:175). Commentators say he was a great scholar and a mendicant who wielded spiritual powers; but when he launched his sinister plans against Mūsā (peace be upon him) to achieve his own desires, he achieved nothing — instead he himself ended up accursed and went astray.

Maʿārif's conclusion: **religious knowledge culled from a book is not enough to guarantee the desired benefit.** What is needed is the action that knowledge calls for, and that is not possible unless one abstains altogether from material greed and carnal desires; otherwise a man will not stay strong enough to resist sacrificing his religion on the altar of his desires. In our own time, Maʿārif adds, there are people who would abandon their true creed for material and political goals, some dressing up secular beliefs in the garb of Islam, caring little for the grave covenant between Allah and man or for what will happen to them in the Ākhirah.

Watch, then, the moment you are asked to certify something false because certifying it pays; it arrives quietly. Which is why ayah 57 names the two things Allah accepts: faith, and righteous deeds.

passages.title: Render trusts to their owners, and judge with justice
passages.tafsir:
## What this ayah is about

Ayah 58 lays down two commands: hand back what has been entrusted to you, to the one it belongs to; and when you judge between people, judge fairly. It then praises the counsel itself — "how excellent is the teaching which He gives you!" — and grounds it in the fact that Allah is All-Hearer, All-Seer. One idea holds it together: authority of every kind, from a coin held for a neighbour to the highest office of state, is *held on behalf of someone else*.

## The key of the Ka'bah

The custodial service of the Ka'bah was an office of great honour even before Islam. Its various services were distributed over different people, all of them regarded as figures of great prestige in the community. From the time of *Jāhiliyyah* — the era before Islam — the *siqāyah*, providing Zamzam water to pilgrims during Hajj, was entrusted to the Prophet's ﷺ revered uncle Sayyidunā ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him); some other services were in the charge of Abū Ṭālib, another uncle of the Prophet ﷺ. And the custody of the key to the House of Allah — opening and closing it on fixed days — had been given to ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah.

By ʿUthmān's own account, the Ka'bah was opened every Monday and Thursday then, and people would come to have the honour of entering it. Once, before the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ came with some Companions wanting to enter. ʿUthmān had not yet accepted Islam. He blocked him, and his manner was very rude. The Prophet ﷺ bore the harsh words with great restraint and said: "O ʿUthmān, a day will come when you would perhaps see this key to the Baytullāh in my hands, when I shall have the power and choice to give it to anyone I choose." ʿUthmān shot back that if that ever happened, the Quraysh would all be uprooted and disgraced. The Prophet ﷺ answered: "No, the Quraysh will then be all established and very honourable indeed."

ʿUthmān later said that on some soul-searching he became convinced that whatever this man had said was bound to happen, and he made up his mind to embrace Islam then and there — but his own people opposed the idea vehemently and everybody joined in to chide him out of it.

Then Makkah was conquered. The Prophet ﷺ called for the key, and ʿUthmān presented it — in some narrations he had climbed up over the Baytullāh with the key, and it was Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) who, in deference to the Prophet's ﷺ order, **forcibly** took it from his hand. Handing it over, ʿUthmān said: "I hand over this article of trust to you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the remark was not technically correct — it was the sole right of the Prophet ﷺ to take whatever course he deemed fit — yet the Qur'an took the nature of the trust into account and directed that the key go back to none other than ʿUthmān.

And it mattered, because both ʿAbbās and ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them) had asked that, since the offices of water supply and custodial service were already in their respective charge, the Key-Bearing of the Ka'bah be entrusted to them as well. These were not strangers making the request — ʿAbbās was his own uncle. He set it aside and followed the instruction of the ayah.

He went into the House, offered his prayers there, came out, and returned the key: "Here, take it. Now this key will always remain with your family right through the Last Day. Anyone who will take this key from you will be a tyrant." He also instructed him to use whatever he received in return for this service in accordance with the rules set by the Sharīʿah.

ʿUthmān says he started walking off, delighted, with the key in his hand — and was called back. "Remember, ʿUthmān, did I not tell you something way back? Has it come to pass, or has it not?" He remembered the words spoken before the Hijrah, and answered: "Yes, there is no doubt about it. Your word has come true." And that was the moment he recited the *Kalimah* — the declaration of faith by which a person enters Islam — and entered the fold. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from Mazharī, from Ibn Saʿd.)

Sayyidunā ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) said that as the Prophet ﷺ came out of the Baytullāh that day he was reciting this very ayah — "Verily, Allah commands that you should render back the trusts to those to whom they are due" — adding, "I never heard him recite this ayah before that." Ibn Jarīr records both this and Ibn Jurayj's report that the ayah was revealed concerning ʿUthmān ibn Ṭalḥah, from whom the Prophet ﷺ took the key on the day of the victory of Makkah and to whom he then gave it back.

**A rule, not just a story.** Ibn Kathir notes that although this occasion of revelation is well known, the ayah's application is general — which is why Ibn ʿAbbās and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said, "This ayah is for the righteous and the wicked," meaning a command that encompasses everyone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the principle as a point of consensus: even where a verse is revealed in a particular background, the rule it lays down in general terms must be taken as of universal application and must not be restricted to that event.

## "Trusts" — why the plural

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to a feature of the wording: *amānāt* is plural. The commonly understood picture of an *amānah* is cash or goods left with someone for safekeeping until asked for; the plural is a cue that this is only one kind. The proof is the occasion of revelation itself: the key of the Baytullāh was no financial asset. It was the symbol of an *office*.

Ibn Kathir spreads the word wider still. The command covers all things a person is expected to look after — including Allah's rights over His servants: praying, zakāh, fasting, the penalties for sins, vows and so forth. And it covers the rights of servants over one another: whatever they entrust each other with, **including the cases that are not recorded or documented**.

Ibn Kathir adds that those who do not implement this command in this life will have it extracted from them on the Day of Resurrection, and cites what is recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The rights will be rendered back to those to whom they are due, and even the sheep that does not have horns will take revenge from the horned sheep."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives further shapes the trust can take. **"Meetings are a kind of trust"** — anything said in a gathering is a matter of trust restricted to it, and reporting or publicising it without the participants' permission is not permitted. **"The consultant is a trustee"** — one who is asked for advice is bound to give the counsel that in his best judgment is most beneficial for the one asking; if he gives advice he knows is not in that person's best interest, he has committed a breach of trust right there. And a secret confided to you becomes an article of trust kept on the other person's behalf; disclosing it without permission is *khiyānah* — betrayal of a trust.

## How heavily this weighs

Ibn Kathir cites the narration of al-Ḥasan from Samurah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Return the trust to those who entrusted you, and do not betray those who betrayed you" — recorded by Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan. Their treachery does not license yours.

Sayyidunā Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said it must have been a rare sermon indeed in which the Prophet ﷺ did not say: "One who does not fulfil trust obligations has no faith (*īmān*) with him; and one who does not stand by his word of promise has no religion (*dīn*) with him." (Reported by al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān*.)

And in the narrations of Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them) appearing in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, when the Prophet ﷺ described the signs of hypocrisy, one of them was: *give him an amānah and he will do khiyānah* — entrust the hypocrite with something and he will breach it.

## Offices of authority are trusts from Allah

If the key of the Ka'bah was an *amānah*, then — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses — offices and ranks of government, whatever they may be, are all handed over as a trust from Allah, and whoever receives one is its *amīn*, its trustee. That covers all officials and everyone else in authority who wields the power to appoint and dismiss.

It is therefore not permissible for them to give any office, job or responsibility to anyone undeserving of it in terms of relevant practical expertise or intellectual capability; it is incumbent on them to make a *serious search* for the most deserving person for every job and every office. Where no perfectly qualified candidate can be found, preference goes to whoever is superior-most among those available in both **capability and trustworthiness** — the two are named together.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that if a person charged with some responsibility relating to the general body of Muslims gives an office to someone simply on the basis of friendship or connection of some sort, without finding out the person's capability or merit, the curse of Allah falls upon him, and neither his obligatory (*farḍ*) nor his voluntary (*nafl*) worship is accepted from him, all the way until he enters the Fire (*Jamʿ ul-Fawāʾid*, p. 325). Some narrations report that whoever entrusts a person with an office while knowing that someone else is more suited and more deserving has committed a breach of trust against Allah, against His Messenger, and against all the Muslims.

And from *Kitāb al-ʿIlm* of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the responsibility of affairs is placed under the charge of those who are not deserving of and fit for it, then wait for the Day of Doom."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies this to the chaos and corruption in many systems of governance today: offices distributed on the basis of connections, recommendations and bribes, so that undeserving people usurp posts they are not fit to occupy, harass ordinary people, and destroy the very edifice of the system.

It also challenges a widespread constitutional idea: that government offices are the *right* of a country's people, to be distributed by regional or population quota, so that a more deserving man from elsewhere is barred while a less deserving local is installed. The Qur'an, it argues, has openly proclaimed that these are not rights to be claimed by anybody, but trusts given only to those who deserve them. There may well be beneficial reasons for preferring someone from the area itself — but only on the condition that the appointee's essential ability and trustworthiness are checked first and found satisfactory.

## "Between people" — not "between believers"

The second command: **"and when you judge between people, judge with justice."**

Ibn Kathir reports that Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, Zayd ibn Aslam and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said this ayah was revealed about those in authority — those who judge between people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees this is the obvious first reading, and notes that some commentators took their cue from it and read the *first* command as addressed to rulers too. Its own conclusion: the addressees are *primarily* those in authority, but *secondarily* everyone who keeps a trust or has been appointed to arbitrate in a case — since among ordinary people the usual practice is to appoint a neutral arbitrator between disputing parties. On the first sentence it is more direct: what is more obvious is that it addresses **everyone who holds anything in trust**, masses and those in authority alike.
