Then Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a word. Allah said *bayna'n-nās* — "between **people**" — not "between Muslims" or "between believers." The hint is that all human beings are equal in the sight of the one deciding a case: Muslim or non-Muslim, friend or enemy, from the same country or another, of the same colour and language or different. Those responsible for judging are duty-bound to cast all such connections aside and decide by whatever truth and justice dictate.

Ibn Kathir cites a hadith on the judge's position: Allah is with the judge as long as he does not commit injustice; when he does, Allah leaves him reliant on himself. (The source records this simply as "a hadith" without naming a collection, so it is given here as the teaching, without attribution.) He also records a statement: "One day of justice equals forty years of worship."

## Why trusts come before justice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks why the ayah puts trusts first, and answers: a system that guarantees equity and justice across a country is simply not possible without it. Those who hold power must first discharge their trust obligations — appointing only those who prove the best of the lot in ability to perform the job and in trustworthiness and honesty, with no back doors opened for friendship, relationships, connections, recommendations or bribes. Otherwise the offices fill up with the undeserving, the incapable, the usurpers and the tyrants, and then even those at the highest level of power, however genuinely they wish for an era of justice, can do nothing about it — because these very officials are the functionaries through whom a government acts.

The same section draws out four basic principles:

1. The opening words — *inna'llāha ya'murukum*, "Surely, Allah commands you" — clearly indicate that the real command and rule is from Allah. All rulers of the mortal world are carriers of His command; the supreme authority, the ultimate sovereignty, belongs to none but Him.
2. Government offices are not the rights of a country's residents to be distributed by population ratio; they are trust obligations placed on our shoulders by Allah, to be given only to those capable and deserving of them.
3. Man's rule on this earth can be legitimate only as a deputy or trustee, bound in his lawmaking by the principles Allah has laid down and given to man through revelation.
4. It is the standing duty of those in authority to judge with equity and justice whenever a case comes to them, without discrimination on the basis of race, country of origin, colour, language, or even religion and creed.

## Who should not take the seat

A further point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives from "judge with fairness": a person who does not have the ability and the power to maintain equity and justice should not become a *qāḍī* (judge), because judging fairly is itself an *amānah* — a great charge that a weak and incapable person cannot guard, defend and fulfil.

The case cited is Sayyidunā Abū Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who requested that the Prophet ﷺ appoint him governor of some place in the Islamic state. The reply: "O Abū Dharr, you are weak, and this is an office of trust, which may, on the Day of Doom, become the cause of disgrace and remorse — except for one who has fulfilled all his trust obligations, fully and duly." (Muslim, in Mazharī.) He was not refused for any fault of character, but because the office needs a particular strength.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reports a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the just person is loved by Allah and is the closest to Him, while the unjust person is cast far away from the mercy and grace of Allah. And in another hadith, he asked his Companions who would be the first to go under the shade of Allah. They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: those who, when truth appears, hasten to accept it; who, when asked, spend their wealth; and who, when they judge between people, do it as fairly as they would have done for themselves.

## "Truly, Allah is Ever All-Hearer, All-Seer"

The ayah first praises its own counsel: "Verily, how excellent is the teaching which He gives you!" Ibn Kathir explains this as referring to His commands to return the trusts to their owners and to judge between people with justice — and to all of His complete, perfect and great commandments and laws.

Then the seal: *innaʾllāha kāna samīʿan baṣīran*. Ibn Kathir explains it simply — He hears your statements and knows your actions.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the pastoral point out: this counsel is good counsel, as good as counsel can be, *because Allah hears everyone*. He observes the state of a person who does not have the ability to speak, not even the power or the means to protest — exactly the person a corrupt trustee or a crooked judge counts on being unheard. And because the One who legislated this hears him, the principles He made are workable in every country and every age, unlike principles made by human minds, which are restricted within the parameters of their environment and have to be changed when circumstances change.

## Living it

- Whatever is in your hands on someone else's behalf — money, information, a role, a key — belongs to them, and the fact that nothing was written down changes nothing.
- Betrayal does not earn betrayal: "do not betray those who betrayed you."
- Appoint on capability and trustworthiness, not on friendship, kinship or a recommendation you owe someone; and if you must decide between two people, decide as you would want it decided for yourself.
- And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own reading of *amānah* is worth holding onto: a trust is not charity. It is not permissible to give away what is held in trust to someone needy out of pity, or to a relative or friend out of affection. It goes back to its rightful owner. That is the whole command.

passages.title: Obey Allah, the Messenger, and those in authority
passages.tafsir:
## What this ayah is about

This single ayah lays down the architecture of authority: whom a believer obeys, in what order, on what condition — and where he goes when Muslims disagree. It moves in two halves that belong together. The first half commands obedience: "Obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and those of you who are in authority." The second half tells you what to do when obedience is contested: "If you differ in anything among yourselves, refer it to Allah and His Messenger, if you believe in Allah and in the Last Day. That is better and more suitable for final determination."

The link between the halves is the point of the ayah. Authority is real and must be obeyed — but it is never the final word. There is always a court of appeal above it, and that court is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ.

## The occasion of revelation

Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said this ayah "was revealed about 'Abdullah bin Hudhafah bin Qays bin 'Adi, who the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent on a military expedition." Ibn Kathir notes that this statement was collected by the Group, with the exception of Ibn Majah, and that At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan, Gharib."

## A commander, an order, and a fire

Under the heading "The Necessity of Obeying the Rulers in Obedience to Allah," Ibn Kathir then brings a separate narration — recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Ali — which shows with unusual clarity the kind of crisis this ayah speaks to.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent out a troop under the command of a man from the Ansar. Once they had left, the commander became angry with them over something and said, "Has not the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded you to obey me?" They said, "Yes." He said, "Collect some wood" — and then he started a fire with the wood, saying, "I command you to enter the fire."

The people almost entered the fire. Then a young man among them said something worth memorising: "You only ran away from the Fire to Allah's Messenger. Therefore, do not rush until you go back to Allah's Messenger, and if he commands you to enter it, then enter it." When they went back and told the Prophet ﷺ what had happened, he said:

> "Had you entered it, you would never have departed from it. Obedience is only in righteousness."

Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs.

Notice the shape of what the young man did, because it is the same shape the second half of the ayah gives to every believer. A dispute arose over the limits of a commander's authority. He settled it neither by his own reasoning nor by simple defiance — he took it back to the Messenger ﷺ.

## Three objects of obedience — and one is not like the other two

Read the Arabic closely: *aṭīʿū Allāha wa aṭīʿū ar-Rasūla wa ulī al-amri minkum*. The command "obey" is stated twice — once for Allah, once for the Messenger — and then "those of you who are in authority" is joined on without a third repetition of the verb. Ibn Kathir glosses each of the three in turn, and the third arrives with a condition the first two do not carry:

- **"Obey Allah"** — meaning, in Ibn Kathir's words, adhere to His Book.
- **"and obey the Messenger"** — adhere to his Sunnah.
- **"And those of you who are in authority"** — obey them, says Ibn Kathir, "in the obedience to Allah which they command you, not what constitutes disobedience of Allah, for there is no obedience to anyone in disobedience to Allah."

Ibn Kathir grounds this reading in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in the Two Sahihs, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever obeys me, obeys Allah, and whoever disobeys me, disobeys Allah. Whoever obeys my commander, obeys me, and whoever disobeys my commander, disobeys me." Obedience here runs along a chain: obedience to the commander is reached through obedience to the Messenger ﷺ, and obedience to the Messenger ﷺ is itself obedience to Allah. And a chain is only as strong as what it is fastened to — which is why Ibn Kathir immediately adds that there is no obedience to anyone in disobedience of Allah.

## Hear and obey: how heavily the Sunnah weights this

It would be a serious misreading to take that condition as a licence for easy disobedience. The narrations Ibn Kathir gathers under this ayah press obedience hard, and in deliberately unflattering circumstances:

**When you dislike it.** Abu Dawud recorded from 'Abdullah bin 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Muslim is required to hear and obey in that which he likes and dislikes, unless he was commanded to sin. When he is commanded with sin, then there is no hearing or obeying." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs. Personal distaste is explicitly not an exemption; only sin is.

**When you are being wronged.** 'Ubadah bin As-Samit said: "We gave our pledge to Allah's Messenger to hear and obey (our leaders), while active and otherwise, in times of ease and times of difficulty, even if we were deprived of our due shares, and to not dispute this matter (leadership) with its rightful people." Then the Prophet ﷺ named the exception: "Except when you witness clear Kufr about which you have clear proof from Allah." This hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs. Note how narrow the exception is drawn: not suspicion, not grievance, not being cheated of what you are owed — but *clear* disbelief, with *clear proof from Allah*.

**When the leader is socially beneath you.** Anas narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Hear and obey (your leaders), even if an Ethiopian slave whose head is like a raisin, is made your chief." Al-Bukhari recorded this. Umm Al-Husayn heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say during his Farewell Hajj speech: "Even if a slave was appointed over you, and he rules you with Allah's Book, then listen to him and obey him" — Muslim recorded this, and in another narration with Muslim the wording is "Even if an Ethiopian slave, whose nose was mutilated..."

Two things are being dismantled at once. Pride of standing is dismantled — the man the world would rank lowest is to be heard and obeyed. And the basis of authority is relocated: in the Farewell Hajj wording, what makes him worth obeying is that "he rules you with Allah's Book."

So the Sunnah builds a discipline here with exactly one door out of it, and the door is sin. Within the lawful, obedience holds even when it is unpleasant, even when it is costly, even when it wounds your sense of status. Beyond the lawful, obedience simply ceases — not because the believer has appointed himself judge, but because the command has stepped outside the only authority that could have licensed it. As Ibn Kathir concludes, quoting the authentic hadith again: **"Obedience is only in righteousness."**

## "Refer it to Allah and His Messenger"

Under the heading "The Necessity of Referring to the Qur'an and Sunnah for Judgment," Ibn Kathir turns to the second half: "If you differ in anything among yourselves, refer it to Allah and His Messenger."

What does referring to Allah and His Messenger mean in practice? Mujahid and several others among the Salaf answered plainly: the ayah means "(Refer) to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger." Ibn Kathir explains that this is a command from Allah covering whatever areas the people dispute about, "whether major or minor areas of the religion" — no dispute is too small to be brought to the texts, and none is too large. He supports it with another ayah: "And in whatsoever you differ, the decision thereof is with Allah" (42:10). His conclusion is uncompromising: "whatever the Book and Sunnah decide and testify to the truth of, then it is the plain truth. What is beyond truth, save falsehood?"

**The condition attached to faith.** The ayah adds, "if you believe in Allah and in the Last Day." Ibn Kathir reads this as more than encouragement. It means, he says, refer the disputes and conflicts that arise between you to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ for judgment — and it "indicates that those who do not refer to the Book and Sunnah for judgment in their disputes, are not believers in Allah or the Last Day."

**"That is better and more suitable for final determination."** On *dhālika khayr* — "that is better" — Ibn Kathir says that referring to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger for judgment in various disputes is better. On *wa aḥsanu ta'wīlā*, he reports two readings from the early authorities: As-Suddi and several others said it means it "has a better end and destination," while Mujahid said it "carries a better reward." The two readings sit comfortably together: settling a quarrel by the texts is better in where it lands, and better in what it earns.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: this ayah is the proof of ijtihad and qiyas

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a further point out of the phrase *fa-ruddūhu ilā Allāhi wa'r-Rasūl* — "Then, if you quarrel about something, revert it back to Allah and the Messenger." This reverting back, it explains, takes two forms:

1. **Revert to the aḥkām** — the code of commands as mandated in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is the direct case: a text exists, and you follow it.
2. **Where the textually-mandated aḥkām do not exist**, the act of reverting back "will be accomplished by analogical deduction (Qiyas) as based on their precedents" — that is, by reasoning from the rulings the texts *did* give to the new case that resembles them.

The argument turns on a point of Arabic: the words *fa-ruddūhu* — "revert it back" — are **general**, "thus being inclusive of both forms." The ayah does not restrict itself to the case where an explicit text is found. It says revert it back; and a scholar who derives a ruling by sound analogy from the Book and Sunnah is still reverting the matter back to Allah and His Messenger, not going around them.

This is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān titles the discussion "The Proof of Ijtihad and Qiyas." *Ijtihād* here is that disciplined effort of the scholar to reach the ruling where no text directly settles the case; *qiyās* — analogical deduction — is the method by which he does it. Far from being an alternative to revelation, they are how a new question is brought back under revelation's authority.

## Living it

**Obedience has a shape, not just a volume.** The ayah asks for genuine, patient obedience to those in authority over you — in what you like and in what you dislike — and it asks you to know, without hesitation, the one place that obedience stops. The commander at the fire was owed obedience right up to the moment he commanded a sin, and not one step further.

**Learn the young man's instinct.** When an order and the religion seem to collide, the answer is neither blind compliance nor self-appointed rebellion. It is: *do not rush* — take it back to the Messenger ﷺ, which today means taking it back to the Book and the Sunnah, and to those who know them.

**Take your disagreements to the same place.** The ayah does not confine itself to disputes with rulers. "If you differ in anything among yourselves" — in the major matters of the religion and the minor ones alike — the referral is the same. And the ayah ties that habit directly to belief in Allah and the Last Day, and promises that it is *better*: better in its end and destination, as As-Suddi and several others said, and better in its reward, as Mujahid said.

passages.title: Seeking judgment from false authority
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat expose a counterfeit faith: a person professes belief in everything Allah has revealed, yet the moment a real dispute touches his own interests he takes it anywhere but to Allah's Messenger ﷺ. The movement runs from the accusation (60), through the diagnosis (61–63), to why a Messenger is sent (64), and finally to Allah's oath that faith is not valid without willing submission to the Prophet's ﷺ verdict (65).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the join: the previous verses commanded returning every matter to Allah and His Messenger; these censure the opposite — turning to rulings that contradict the Sharīʿah.

## The dispute that lies behind these verses

Ibn Kathir reports the occasion as a quarrel between a man of the Ansar and a Jewish man. The Jew said, "Let us refer to Muhammad to judge between us." The Muslim said, "Let us refer to Kaʿb bin Al-Ashraf" — whom Ibn Kathir identifies simply as a Jew. He also reports that the ayah concerned hypocrites who pretended to be Muslims yet sought the judgment of Jāhiliyyah, and that other occasions were reported. Then the decisive point: **the ayah has a general meaning.** It censures everyone who declines to refer to the Qur'an and Sunnah and prefers whatever falsehood he chooses — what fits the description of *Ṭāghūt* here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells it at length, naming the hypocrite Bishr and adding that Kaʿb ibn Ashraf was a tribal chief among the Jews and a sworn enemy of the Prophet ﷺ and his followers. The oddity is the point: the Jew wanted the Prophet ﷺ; the man who called himself a Muslim wanted the Jewish chieftain. Maʿārif explains the inversion: both were certain the Prophet's ﷺ judgment would be true and just, free of any tilt or favour. The Jew was in the right, so he trusted the Prophet ﷺ over his own chief; Bishr was in the wrong, so he knew the verdict would go against him. **Neither doubted the Prophet's ﷺ integrity. One was drawn to it; the other fled from it.**

They did go to the Prophet ﷺ. He investigated, found the Jew in the right, and ruled for him. Bishr, dissatisfied, talked the Jew into taking it to Sayyidinā ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) — another calculation: he assumed ʿUmar was hard on disbelievers and would rule for him. The Jew laid out the case and mentioned the Prophet's ﷺ prior judgment and this man's dissatisfaction. ʿUmar asked Bishr, "Is this what really happened?" He confessed. ʿUmar told him to wait, went inside, came out with a sword and struck him down, saying: "This is the decision for him who is dissatisfied with the decision of the Holy Prophet ﷺ." Maʿārif's source: Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, from Sayyidinā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, as narrated by Thaʿlabī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

The heirs of the slain man then sued ʿUmar for killing a Muslim without lawful authority, arguing interpretations to establish that the man had been a believer. Maʿārif adds a detail easy to miss: when the case came before the Prophet ﷺ, the words from his blessed lips were, *"I never thought ʿUmar would ever dare to kill a believing man."* From this Maʿārif draws a governance lesson — a higher authority hearing an appeal must not side with his subordinate but rule on justice alone. The revelation then disclosed that the man killed was a hypocrite, and ʿUmar was absolved.

Ibn Kathir records a second occasion, from the Tafsīr of Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm bin ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Ibrāhīm bin Duhaym, narrated by Ḍamrah: a man who lost a dispute the Prophet ﷺ had judged said, "I do not agree." Abū Bakr Aṣ-Ṣiddīq told him, "Then the decision is that which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ issued." He still refused and demanded ʿUmar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb, who confirmed the story with the other party, fetched his sword and struck him dead. Allah then revealed *"But no, by your Lord, they can have no faith."*

Ibn Kathir also records from At-Ṭabarānī that Ibn ʿAbbās said Abū Barzah Al-Aslamī used to be a soothsayer who judged between the Jews in their disputes; when some Muslims came to him for judgment, Allah sent down *"Have you not seen those who claim that they believe…"* through *"We meant no more than goodwill and conciliation!"* Maʿārif notes other incidents of the kind, where people bypassed a clear Islamic verdict for a soothsayer's or astrologer's ruling — the verse may have come down about all of them.

## The word *Ṭāghūt*

Ayah 60 does not say they sought judgment from another judge but from **Ṭāghūt**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves the word untranslated and explains it: lexically, *one who exceeds the limits*; in usage, Shayṭān is called Ṭāghūt. So carrying the dispute to Kaʿb ibn Ashraf is equated with carrying it to Shayṭān himself — either because Kaʿb was a satan personified, or because the impulse to bypass a ruling given by Allah and prefer one contrary to it can only come from Shayṭān's teaching. Either way, he has taken his case to no court but Shayṭān's — which is why the verse ends warning that those who follow Shayṭān, Shayṭān will mislead them to a remote wrong way.

Note too the opening verb: they *claim* they believe. Ibn Kathir directs the whole rebuke at those who claim belief in what Allah sent down to His Messenger ﷺ and to the earlier Prophets, then refer disputes elsewhere. Maʿārif adds that their claim to have believed in the Torah, the Gospel and now the Qur'an was verbal camouflage; their hearts held the same old disbelief, which the dispute brought into the open.

## Ayah 61: the tell

*"And when it is said to them: 'Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger,' you see the hypocrites turn away from you with aversion."*

Ibn Kathir explains *yaṣuddūna ʿanka ṣudūdan* — they turn away from you **in arrogance**. He sets it beside Allah's description of the polytheists in Sūrah Luqmān, who when told to follow what Allah revealed answer, *"Nay! We shall follow what we found our fathers following"* (31:21) — and against the believers in Sūrah An-Nūr, whose only speech when called to Allah and His Messenger is, *"We hear and we obey"* (24:51).

Maʿārif is blunt: turning away from a Sharīʿah-based decision of the Prophet ﷺ in a private quarrel can never be a Muslim's response. One who does it is a *munāfiq* — a hypocrite.

## Ayah 62: the disaster, and the beautiful excuse

*"How then, when a catastrophe befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, they come to you swearing by Allah, 'We meant no more than goodwill and conciliation!'"*

Ibn Kathir: how will it be when disasters strike them for their own sins and they find themselves compelled to come to you, in need of you? Then they arrive apologising, swearing that in going elsewhere they had only wanted goodwill and reconciliation — not that they believed in that other authority, as they claim. He connects them to those in Sūrah Al-Mā'idah, *"those in whose hearts there is a disease, they hurry to their friendship, saying: 'We fear'"* … who end up *"regretful for what they have been keeping as a secret in themselves"* (5:52).

Maʿārif unpacks the excuse. Their plea: we did not bypass the Messenger of Allah out of doubt about his station or the truth of his rulings; there were simply *expedient considerations*. A case before him would have been decided strictly, legally, justly — leaving no room for a mutual patch-up, none for the "other factors" a settlement can accommodate. So, they said, we took it elsewhere hoping good would come to both sides through conciliation.

**The excuse is the sharpest thing here.** They did not attack the Sharīʿah; they praised it — and then routed around it, in the name of harmony. Maʿārif notes the timing: these interpretations surfaced only *after* their secret was out and their man had been killed. Allah's verdict is plain: they are liars in their oaths and interpretations, and everything they did, they did out of disbelief and hypocrisy.

## Ayah 63: Allah knows — so speak to them

*"They are those of whom Allah knows what is in their hearts; so turn aside from them, but admonish them, and speak to them an effective word to reach their inner selves."*

Ibn Kathir: Allah knows what is in their hearts and will requite them accordingly, for nothing escapes His watch — so let Allah suffice you here, O Muhammad ﷺ; He knows perfectly their outward and hidden affairs. Then three instructions, each precise in his reading:

- *Turn aside from them* — do not punish them for what is in their hearts.
- *Admonish them* — advise them against the hypocrisy and evil in their hearts.
- *Speak to them an effective word to reach their inner selves* — counsel them privately, in words that might actually benefit them.

Maʿārif adds that the ayah tells the Prophet ﷺ to disregard their excuses and reject their charge of excess against ʿUmar, since this man's disbelief had become manifest — and that the closing command is counsel to *the remaining* hypocrites: warn them of what lies beyond this life and invite them to sincere Islam, or remind them that a long-kept hypocrisy may be exposed, and they may meet the same end.

## Ayah 64: why a Messenger is sent at all

*"We sent no Messenger but to be obeyed by Allah's leave."*

Ibn Kathir: obedience to the Prophet was ordained upon those to whom Allah sends him. On *bi-idhnillāh* — "by Allah's leave" — he cites Mujāhid: *"None shall obey except by My leave."* The Prophets are thus obeyed only by those whom Allah directs to obedience. He compares the same word in Āl ʿImrān 3:152, where "with His permission" means by His command, decree and will.

Maʿārif draws the consequence: since every Messenger is sent to be obeyed, whoever sets himself against the Messenger's rulings is dealt with as disbelievers are — which is why ʿUmar's act turned out to be correct.

*"If they, when they were unjust to themselves, had come to you and begged Allah's forgiveness, and the Messenger had begged forgiveness for them, indeed, they would have found Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* Ibn Kathir reads this as direction to sinners and wrongdoers: when you fall into error, come to the Messenger ﷺ, seek Allah's forgiveness in his presence and ask him to supplicate for you — and Allah will forgive and grant mercy and pardon.

Maʿārif observes two things binding for this repentance: that they present themselves before the Prophet ﷺ, and that he prays for them. Its suggested reason: their offence was against the station of prophethood itself — they wounded him by discarding his verdict.

Maʿārif then extends the ruling beyond the occasion: "presenting oneself" before the Prophet ﷺ retains its effect today through visiting the Prophet's Mosque. In support it relates from Sayyidinā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), cited from *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, that three days after the burial a villager fell down close to the blessed grave, wept, recited this verse and asked for the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for his forgiveness — and those present said a voice came from the sanctified mausoleum: *"You have been forgiven."*

Two cautions: our source gives this report only as Maʿārif relates it from *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, with no chain and no grading of authenticity, so hold it lightly rather than lean on it as established; and the extension is Maʿārif's own position, argued from the generality of the wording, on which Ibn Kathir goes no further than coming to the Messenger ﷺ and asking his supplication.

## Ayah 65: Allah swears

*"But no, by your Lord, they can have no faith, until they make you judge in all disputes between them, and find in themselves no resistance against your decisions, and accept them with full submission."*

Ibn Kathir: **Allah swears by His Glorious, Most Honorable Self** that no one attains faith until he refers to the Messenger ﷺ for judgment in all matters; thereafter whatever the Messenger ﷺ commands is the plain truth, to be submitted to inwardly and outwardly. The ayah names three stages: *make him judge*, then *find no ḥaraj* — no tightness, no inward resistance — then *submit with full submission*. Ibn Kathir: they adhere to the judgment, feel no hesitation over it, and submit with no rejection, denial or dispute.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: nobody becomes a Muslim unless he accepts the Prophet's ﷺ verdict willingly, calmly and fully, until not the slightest strain remains in his heart. People ordinarily accept an arbitrator they chose themselves more readily than a government-appointed judge — and this ayah asks the disputing parties to make the Prophet ﷺ their own chosen arbitrator. But his authority never depended on litigants: he exercises authority given by Allah over his community as the Messenger of Allah. He is not only the ruler of a state; he is protected by Allah against sins, sent as a mercy for the worlds, and a loving father to his community. So the instruction is compassionate, not a bare demand.

**Does this end with his lifetime?** No — commentators, Maʿārif reports, say the command is not restricted to the years he graced this world; after him, the verdict of the sacred Law he left behind is nothing but his own verdict. Guidance was sought by turning directly to him in his lifetime; after him, one turns to his Sharīʿah — in reality a return to him ﷺ.

## From the Sunnah

**Al-Bukhari** records that ʿUrwah said: Az-Zubayr quarrelled with a man over a stream both used for irrigation. Allah's Messenger ﷺ said, *"O Zubayr! Irrigate your garden first, and then let the water flow to your neighbour."* The Anṣārī became angry and said, "O Allah's Messenger! Is it because he is your cousin?" The face of Allah's Messenger ﷺ changed colour, and he said, *"Irrigate your garden, O Zubayr, and then withhold the water until it reaches the walls; then release the water to your neighbour."* Ibn Kathir explains: the Prophet ﷺ had first given a generous ruling beneficial to both men; when the Anṣārī angered him, he gave Az-Zubayr his full legal right. Az-Zubayr said, "I think this verse was revealed concerning that case" — *"But no, by your Lord, they can have no faith, until they make you judge in all disputes between them."*

## Living it

**The scope is wider than lawsuits.** From *fīmā shajara* ("in the disputes which arise") — citing *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* — Maʿārif derives that the ayah is not confined to dealings and rights; it covers articles of belief, ideas and many other theoretical problems. Where differences arise, the duty is not to prolong the argument but for both sides to return to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he is not with them personally, to his Sharīʿah.

**A tool for self-examination.** Maʿārif reads *"they find in themselves no resistance"* as a rule of self-assessment: doing something established from the Prophet ﷺ with a heavy heart is a sign of weakness in faith. Its example: the Sharīʿah permits *tayammum*, dry purification, in place of washing with water on certain occasions. If someone feels uneasy at making tayammum instead of the ablution he would rather perform, that unease is not *taqwā*, the piety of fearing Allah, but spiritual sickness. Likewise for insisting on standing through unbearable hardship when the Prophet ﷺ allowed — and himself performed — prayer while sitting. Who can fear Allah more than the Prophet ﷺ?

Maʿārif adds the balance: someone whose need is not that acute may decline the concession (*rukhṣah*) and take the path of high determination (*ʿazīmah*), correct and in accordance with the Prophet's ﷺ own teaching. What is not *taqwā* is feeling *strain* at using the concessions the Sharīʿah grants, as though avoiding them were an absolute rule. The source relates here the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ that just as Allah is pleased with what is done by high determination, so is He pleased with what is done by using the concessions He has granted.

**Where to find the pattern.** Maʿārif closes: the best method of the general acts of worship, of *adhkār* (remembrances of Allah), *awrād* (voluntary recitations kept privately at set hours), *durūd* (asking Allah's peace and blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ) and *tasbīḥ* (glorification of Allah) is no different from what the Prophet ﷺ practised and his Companions consistently followed — and every Muslim should, as a personal obligation, find these out from the authentic and sound narrations of hadith and make them part of daily life.

## The station this passage establishes

Maʿārif's closing note: these details show the Prophet ﷺ was not only a reformer and moral leader but a just ruler, of such standing that his judgment was declared **the very criterion of belief and disbelief**, as the incident of Bishr made visible. Hence Allah pairs obedience to him with obedience to Himself in place after place: *"Obey Allah and obey the Messenger"* (3:32; 3:132; 4:59; 5:92; 24:54; 47:33; 64:12), and *"Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah"* (4:80). That authority was demonstrated when Allah sent His Law down to him so he could decide cases by it: *"We revealed to you the Book with the truth so that you may judge between people by what Allah makes you see"* (4:105).

Read as a whole, ayat 60–65 close off a very human escape route: affirming the Sharīʿah in principle while taking one's own case elsewhere when the ruling will hurt. Faith is not in the affirmation but in the hearing, the accepting, and the heart that finds no tightness in what has been decided.

passages.title: Had they obeyed: the company of the prophets
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer a taunt. A hypocrite had refused the Prophet's ﷺ verdict, the Jews of Madinah mocked the Muslims for it, and Allah replies not with a rebuke alone but with the most extraordinary promise in the sūrah: that ordinary obedient believers will find themselves in the company of the prophets. Ayah 66 imagines a command so severe that almost nobody would obey it; ayat 67 and 68 name what obedience would have bought; ayah 69 opens the door to everyone; ayah 70 reminds us who is really paying.

## The taunt behind ayah 66

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places these verses with the ones just before them, in the affair of Bishr the hypocrite. He had first proposed Kaʿb ibn Ashraf, a Jewish man, as the one to judge his dispute; mutual discussions later forced him to bring the case to the Prophet ﷺ instead. When the judgment went against him he would not accept it and went to Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) for a totally fresh decision.

Word of this got around Madinah, and the Jews used it to chide the Muslims: *What sort of people are you? You believe in a Messenger of Allah and claim to follow him, yet you do not accept his decisions. Look — in order that their repentance be accepted, the Jews were commanded to kill each other. That was a severe command, but we obeyed it, so much so that seventy thousand of our people were killed. If you were given a command like that, what would you have done?*

Ayah 66 is the reply. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, if these hypocrites — or all common people, disbelievers or believers — were charged with some severe command, such as that of self-killing or migration like Banī Isrāʼīl were ordered to do, very few of them would have, being what they are, obeyed this command.

So the ayah cuts two ways at once. On the one hand it is a stern warning to people who seek the solution of their disputes somewhere other than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Law and Way. On the other, it answers the chiding of the Jews: this state of affairs fits the hypocrites, and certainly not those firm in their faith as true Muslims.

## "Kill yourselves, or leave your homes"

The two hypothetical commands in ayah 66 are the two heaviest things a community can be asked for: your life and your home. Ibn Kathir renders the first with a gloss inside the translation itself — "Kill yourselves (i.e. the innocent ones kill the guilty ones)" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the pair as "self-killing or migration like the Banī Isrāʼīl were ordered to do."

Ibn Kathir draws a striking point from the wording. Allah is telling us what would have happened had He given a command He did not in fact give. "Allah has complete knowledge of what has not occurred, and how it would be if and when it did occur." His knowledge is not limited to what actually happens; He knows the shape of every road not taken. And what He tells us about human nature is unflattering: even if people were commanded to do what they had been prohibited from, "most of them would not submit to this command, for their wicked nature is such that they dispute orders."

## The Companions answered back

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the verse produced an immediate reaction among the believers, and that reaction is itself part of the tafsir. Someone from among the noble Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all) said: "Allah did not put us through this trial." When this statement was relayed to the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "There are people in my community in whose heart Faith is entrenched firm like mountains." Ibn Wahab says the statement was made by Sayyidnā Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

According to another narration, when Abū Bakr heard this verse he said: had this command been prescribed, by Allah, I would have been the first to sacrifice myself and my family to obey. And according to some other narrations, when this verse was revealed the Prophet ﷺ said that if this command to self-kill or migrate had come from Allah, Umm ʿAbd — meaning Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) — would have definitely acted accordingly.

Then Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point that closes the argument with the Jews entirely: as for migration, the noble Companions acted faithfully and selflessly. They left their homes in Makkah, left their properties and businesses, and migrated to Madinah. The hypothetical of ayah 66 had already been lived out by the very people being mocked.

## What obedience would have bought (66–68)

The end of ayah 66 and the two ayat after it stack four gifts on top of each other, and they are worth taking slowly.

**"It would have been better for them."** Ibn Kathir: better than disobeying the command and committing the prohibition. Obedience is being described as *in your own interest*, not as a debt you pay.

**"And would have strengthened their conviction"** — *ashadda tathbītā*. Ibn Kathir explains it, on the authority of As-Suddī, as stronger *taṣdīq*, stronger conviction of faith; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says obedience "will make their faith more firm." This is the quiet law inside the passage: faith is not steadied first and then obeyed; it is steadied *by* obeying.

**"A great reward from Ourselves"** (ayah 67). Ibn Kathir notes the phrase *min ladunnā* — "from Us," from Allah Himself — and identifies the great reward as Paradise.

**"And We would have guided them to the straight way"** (ayah 68). Ibn Kathir: in this life and the Hereafter. Guidance appears here not only as what starts obedience but as what obedience earns; the obedient are given more of the very thing that made them obedient.

## Ayah 69: the promise widens to everyone

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the shift precisely. In the verses appearing immediately earlier, the promise of a great reward was made to special addressees; what appears now "is a universal promise, that those who obey Allah and His Messenger shall be rewarded as a standing rule."

Ibn Kathir sums it up: whosoever implements what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have commanded him and avoids what they have prohibited, Allah will grant him a dwelling in the Residence of Honour, and will place him in the company of the Prophets, and those who are lesser in grade, the true believers, then the martyrs and then the righteous.

**The four ranks.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes them in order:

- **The Prophets** — the highest stations of Paradise. Imam Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī notes that the station of prophethood is something which can never be acquired by effort and struggle; but there is still something one gets to have, and that is the *company* of the prophets.
- **The Ṣiddīqīn** — *ṣiddīq* lexically means "very truthful." In Islamic usage it normally refers to those Companions of a prophet who excel all others in their submission to Allah and His Messenger, enjoying the highest status of piety after the prophets: the great Companions who came forward to believe at the very initial stage without any hesitation or hostility, like Sayyidnā Abū Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).
- **The Shuhadāʼ** — people who sacrificed their lives and wealth in the way of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān deliberately declines to translate the word as "martyr," because "martyr" is also applied to persons killed in ethnic or racial wars who may not be termed *shuhadāʼ* in Islamic terminology.
- **The Ṣāliḥīn** — the righteous, who, in Ibn Kathir's phrase, are righteous inwardly and outwardly; people who restrict themselves, outwardly and inwardly, to doing only what is good and right.

**Are these four separate people or four qualities?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a genuine difference among the commentators. Some say all four ranks can be found in one person, since the Qur'an itself says of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) "Surely, he was a man of truth, a prophet" (19:41), of Yaḥyā (peace be upon him) "and a prophet from among the righteous" (3:39), and of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) that he "shall be one of the righteous" (3:46) — though the four attributes are distinct in meaning, they can combine in one person, and by common practice a person is identified with whichever attribute dominates his life's work. Imam Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī determined instead that all four ranks are genuinely different, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the same in Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and Mazharī. On Rāghib's reading the four are gradations in how much a servant knows his Lord: the prophets like someone seeing something from close range; the ṣiddīqīn like someone seeing it from a distance; the shuhadāʼ like someone seeing it in a mirror from close range; the ṣāliḥīn like someone seeing something in a mirror from a distance. He connects the last two to the famous hadith — "That you worship Allah as if you are seeing Him," and "And if you cannot see Him, then, He sees you anyway."

## *Rafīq*: the word that answers a broken heart

"And how excellent these companions are" — the ayah closes by praising this company. The occasion of revelation shows exactly whose ache the word was sent to heal.

Ibn Jarīr records from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: "An Anṣārī man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while feeling sad. The Prophet ﷺ said to him, 'Why do I see you sad?' He said, 'O Allah's Prophet! I was contemplating about something.' The Prophet ﷺ said, 'What is it?' The Anṣārī said, 'We come to you day and night, looking at your face and sitting by you. Tomorrow, you will be raised with the Prophets, and we will not be able to see you.' The Prophet ﷺ did not say anything, but later Jibrīl came down to him with this Ayah… and the Prophet ﷺ sent the good news to the Anṣārī man." Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was narrated in *mursal* form (a report in which the link back to the Prophet ﷺ is not fully named) from Masrūq, ʿIkrimah, ʿĀmir ash-Shaʿbī, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and that this is the version with the best chain of narrators.

Abū Bakr ibn Marduwyah recorded it with a different chain from ʿĀʼishah, who said a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah! You are more beloved to me than myself, my family and children. Sometimes, when I am at home, I remember you, and I cannot wait until I come and look at you. When I contemplate about my death and your death, I know that you will be with the Prophets when you enter Paradise. I fear that I might not see you when I enter Paradise." The Prophet ﷺ did not answer him until this ayah was revealed. (Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿAbdullāh al-Maqdisī collected this in his book *Ṣifat al-Jannah* and commented, "I do not see problems with this chain." And Allah knows best.)

So the ayah is not primarily about rank. It is about not losing the people you love.

**And the Prophet ﷺ wanted that company too.** Al-Bukhari recorded that ʿĀʼishah said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying, (Every Prophet who falls ill is given the choice between this life and the Hereafter.) During the illness that preceded his death, his voice became weak and I heard him saying, (in the company of those on whom Allah has bestowed His grace, the Prophets, the true believers (Ṣiddīqīn), the martyrs and the righteous). I knew then that he was being given the choice." Muslim recorded this hadith too. Ibn Kathir points out that this hadith explains the meaning of another: the Prophet ﷺ said before his death, "(O Allah! In the Most High Company)" three times, and he then died, may Allah's best blessings be upon him. The dying Prophet ﷺ was saying the words of ayah 69.

## Meeting, across the ranks

If the ranks of Paradise differ, how is "with" real? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the answers, having first noted that the Prophet ﷺ gave the questioner the glad tidings that despite the relative precedence of ranks in Paradise, there will be occasions of meeting and sitting together.

One form: people will see each other from where they are. As reported in the *Muwaṭṭaʼ* of Imam Mālik from Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The inmates of Paradise will see those in the strata above them like you see stars in the physical world."

Another form: visits. Ibn Jarīr reports from Sayyidnā Rabīʿ that the Prophet ﷺ, while explaining this very verse, said: "Those of the strata above will come down to those of the strata below to meet and sit with them." And it is also possible that those of the lower strata have permission to visit those above — which is why the Prophet ﷺ, on the basis of this verse, gave many people the glad tidings of being with him in Paradise.

## How the doors were actually opened

The sources attach a striking set of narrations to this ayah — all of them practical, none of them heroic:

- Muslim recorded that Rabīʿah ibn Kaʿb al-Aslamī said: "I used to sleep at the Prophet's house and bring him his water for ablution and his needs. He once said to me, 'Ask me.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah! I ask that I be your companion in Paradise.' He said, 'Anything except that?' I said, 'Only that.' He said, **(Then help me (fulfill this wish) for you by performing many prostrations.)**" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, relating the same report from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, adds that this happened at the time of Tahajjud, and explains the elegant prophetic expression to mean: your wish shall be granted, but you can also help me in this by offering plenty of prostrations — that is, plenty of voluntary prayers (*nawāfil*).
- Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAmr ibn Murrah al-Juhanī that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ declaring that he bore witness to the testimony of faith, prayed the five daily prayers, gave the zakāh due on his wealth and fasted Ramadan. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "(Whoever dies in this state will be with the Prophets, the truthful and martyrs on the Day of Resurrection, as long as — and he raised his finger — he is not disobedient to his parents.)" Ibn Kathir notes that only Ahmad recorded this hadith.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites another hadith from Tirmidhī: "The businessman who is truthful and trusty will be with the prophets and the Ṣiddīqīn and the Shuhadāʼ."

Notice the list: night prayer, the five obligations, kindness to parents, honesty in business. This is the "obedience" of ayah 69 in ordinary clothes.

**And then the widest door of all.** Ibn Kathir says there is greater news still — in the authentic hadith collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ and Musnad compilations, in *mutawātir* form (that is, through so many chains that error is inconceivable), narrated by several Companions; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports it from Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī on the authority of many uninterrupted chains from a large body of the noble Companions. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the person who loves a people but whose status is not close to theirs. He said: **(One is with those whom he loves.)** Anas commented, "Muslims were never happier than with this Hadith." In another narration Anas said: "I love the Messenger of Allah, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and I hope that Allah will resurrect me with them, even though I did not perform actions similar to theirs."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places one more narration here, under the heading "The company of the Holy Prophet is not restricted to any colour or race." Al-Ṭabarānī reports in *al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr*, from Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, that an Ethiopian man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said that the Prophet ﷺ was distinct from him in the beauty of his physique and the colour of his skin, and had besides the distinction of being a prophet and messenger of Allah — "Now, if I were to believe in what you believe and do what you do, can I too have the honour of being with you in the Paradise?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Definitely yes." Later the man asked whether his own eyes would see the same blessing the Prophet's ﷺ blessed eyes would witness, and again he was told: "Definitely yes." Hearing this, the newly converted Muslim from Ethiopia began to weep, and wept until he died in that very state. The Prophet ﷺ performed his last rites — the bathing, the shrouding, the funeral prayer and the burial — all with his own blessed hands.

## Ayah 70: whose bounty this is

"Such is the bounty from Allah." Ibn Kathir's comment is the necessary last word after everything above: it is "from Allah by His mercy, for it is He who made them suitable for this, not their good deeds." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is right that deeds will be the criterion in the ranks of Paradise — but the capacity to obey, the love that carries you into good company, the invitation itself: all of it is a gift, not a wage. Ayah 66 already told us what human nature does when the command gets hard.

"And Allah is sufficient as All-Knower." Ibn Kathir: He knows those who deserve guidance and success. Nobody is misplaced in that company; nobody who longs for it is overlooked.

**What the passage asks of you.** Obey in the small, unglamorous places — the five prayers, zakāh, the fast, honesty in your work, your parents, extra prostrations at night — because obedience is what makes faith firm rather than the other way round. And love the people you want to be with, because the sad man of the Anṣār was not told to become a prophet. He was told he would not be left behind.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends its treatment of this verse with a duʿāʼ, and it is a fitting place to stop: may Allah Almighty bless us all with this love. Āmīn.

passages.title: Marching out and those who lag behind
passages.tafsir:
This passage turns the sūrah's call to obedience into something concrete: a community told to arm itself, organise itself, and march — and then shown the man inside that community who will not move. What holds ayat 71–76 together is a single question of loyalty: when the believers go out, who goes with them, who hangs back and calculates, and what exactly is each side fighting *for*.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubi, sets the seam precisely: before this came the command to obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ; now jihād is prescribed for the obedient and faithful, so that they can vitalise their faith and raise the word of Allah high and supreme. Obedience is not left as a sentiment. It is given a body — a march, a formation, a cost.

## Ayah 71: "Take your precautions"

Ibn Kathir reads *khudhū hidhrakum* — "take your precautions" — as a command from Allah to His faithful servants to take precautions against their enemies by being prepared with the necessary weapons and supplies, and by increasing the number of troops fighting in His cause. Preparation here is not vague vigilance; it is logistics.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two lessons from the shape of the ayah, where the command to ensure the supply of weapons comes first and the launching of the action comes after.

**First, using means is not the opposite of tawakkul.** Getting together functional means to achieve a good purpose is not contrary to *tawakkul* — trust in Allah. The believer who secures his weapons has not thereby stopped relying on his Lord.

**Second — and this is the subtler point — the ayah commands the means but promises nothing from them.** Notice what is absent: the text commands the supply of weapons, yet it does not promise that because of this support the Muslims will have any guaranteed security against their enemies. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that the choice of using means is for nothing but a certain peace of mind; the use of means as such does not carry any operational gain or loss. It cites the Qur'an's own words: *"Nothing will befall us except what Allah has prescribed for us"* (9:51). So the believer prepares fully and leans on none of it — he leans on Allah.

## "In groups, or all together" — the word *thubāt*

*Fa-nfirū thubātin aw infirū jamīʿā.* ʿAli bin Talhah reported that Ibn ʿAbbas explained *thubātin* as "In groups, expedition after expedition," and *aw infirū jamīʿā* as "all of you." Ibn Kathir notes that similar was reported from Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, As-Suddi, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, ʿAta' Al-Khurrasani, Muqatil bin Hayyan and Khusayf Al-Jazari — a striking convergence of the early authorities. Ibn Kathir's own gloss: group after group, party after party, and expedition after expedition.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up further. *Thubātin* is the plural of *thubatun*, meaning a small group, used to denote a military company — what was called a *sariyyah* in the military campaigns of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. So the ayah is not merely saying "go out." It is a marching plan with two options: set out in the formation of small groups, or march as one large army. What is ruled out is the third option — starting off all alone. In fighting, going alone is very likely to hurt, because the enemy is not going to let that opportunity slip out of their hands.

**Beyond the battlefield.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that although this instruction was given for the particular occasion of jihād, even in normal circumstances the Sharīʿah teaches the same thing: do not travel alone. It cites a hadith in which a lone traveller is called one satan, two of them two satans, and three of them become a group or party (the source conveys this teaching without naming a collection). And it cites another narration — "The best companions are four and the best military company is that of four hundred and the best army is that of four thousand" — which it gives from Mishkāt, as reported by Al-Tabarani.

## Ayat 72–73: the man who lags behind

*Wa inna minkum la-man la-yubaṭṭi'ann* — "There is certainly among you he who would linger behind."

Mujahid and others said this ayah was revealed about the hypocrites. Muqatil bin Hayyan explained *layubaṭṭi'ann* as staying behind and not joining jihād. Ibn Kathir adds a second possibility that makes the word heavier: it is also possible that this person himself lingers behind while luring others away from joining. He names the case: ʿAbdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul, may Allah curse him, who used to linger behind and lure other people to do the same, as Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Jarir stated.

**Why "among you"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious difficulty: seen outwardly, the words seem to address the believers, although the characteristics described later cannot be taken to be those of the believers. Al-Qurtubi's answer is that they signify the hypocrites — and since they were the ones who used to claim being Muslims, at least outwardly, they have been identified as a group from among the believers. The phrase is not a slur on the community; it is a warning that the danger is internal, wearing the same face.

**The two speeches.** What follows is one of the Qur'an's most devastating character sketches, and it works by quoting the man twice.

*If a misfortune befalls you* — Ibn Kathir lists what this covers: death, martyrdom, or, by Allah's wisdom, being defeated by the enemy — he says, *"Indeed Allah has favored me that I was not present among them."* He calls his own absence a favour from Allah. Ibn Kathir's comment cuts to the bone: he considers this one of Allah's favours on him, unaware of the reward that he might have gained from enduring war or martyrdom, if he was killed. He is congratulating himself on missing the very thing that would have made him.

*But if a bounty comes to you from Allah* — such as victory, triumph and booty — then, as ayah 73 puts it, he speaks *"as if there had never been ties of affection between you and him."* Ibn Kathir explains that phrase as: as if he was not a follower of your religion. And what does he say? *"Oh! I wish I had been with them; then I would have achieved a great success."* Ibn Kathir tells us plainly what that "great success" means in his mouth: being assigned a share of the booty and taking possession of that share. This is his ultimate aim and objective.

Read the two speeches side by side and the man is exposed. In defeat he voices no grief for his brothers — only relief for himself. In victory he voices no gladness for them — only regret at the share he missed. And Ibn Kathir's gloss on the missing *mawaddah*, the ties of affection, names what is really absent: it is as if he was not a follower of their religion at all.

## Ayah 74: the command, and the guarantee

*Fal-yuqātil fī sabīli-llāh...* Ibn Kathir reads the opening command *"So fight"* as addressed to the believer who has an aversion to fighting — the honest one who finds it hard, as against the hypocrite of the previous ayat who finds it convenient to avoid. The believer's reluctance is met not with rebuke but with an offer.

The phrase *alladhīna yashrūna al-ḥayāta ad-dunyā bil-ākhirah*, "those who trade the life of this world with the Hereafter," Ibn Kathir takes as naming those who are to be fought: those who sell their religion for the meagre goods of the world, and who do this only because of their disbelief and lack of faith.

Then the guarantee: *"And whoever fights in the cause of Allah, and is killed or gets victory, We shall bestow on him a great reward."* Ibn Kathir: whoever fights in the cause of Allah, whether he was killed or triumphant, he will earn an immense compensation and a great reward with Allah. Both branches pay. There is no losing outcome for the one who goes out in Allah's cause — which is precisely the calculation the man in ayah 72 could not see.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites the Two Sahihs: *"Allah has guaranteed the Mujahid in His cause that He will either bring death to him, admitting into Paradise; or, He will help him return safely to his home with whatever reward and booty he gained."* Set this beside ayah 73: the hypocrite wanted the booty and nothing else, and got neither. The believer is promised Paradise or a safe return — and is not shamed for the reward or booty that comes with it.

## Ayah 75: the cry rising out of Makkah

Here the passage stops arguing and starts pleading. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah encouraged His believing servants to perform jihād in His cause and to strive hard to save the oppressed Muslims in Makkah — men, women and children who were restless because of having to remain there. "This town whose people are oppressors" is Makkah; Ibn Kathir compares Allah's words elsewhere, *"And many a town, stronger than your town which has driven you out"* (47:13). Their two requests — *"raise for us from You one who will protect, and raise for us from You one who will help"* — mean, in Ibn Kathir's words, send protectors and helpers for us.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the human detail. Left behind in Makkah were Muslims who were unable to migrate because of physical weakness and insufficiency of resources. Later the disbelievers themselves stopped them from going and started hurting and harassing them in all sorts of ways, so that they would turn away from their faith in Islam. Citing al-Qurtubi, it preserves some of their names: Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbas and his mother, Sulyma ibn Hisham, Walid ibn Walid, and Abu Jandal ibn Sahl, may Allah be pleased with them all. These blessed people kept facing tyranny and torture because of their unflinching faith, showing no sign that they would ever surrender their firm stand on Islam — and they kept praying to Allah Almighty for deliverance.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I and my mother were from the oppressed (in Makkah)." He counted himself among them.

**The two requests, both answered.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they asked Allah for two things — to be rescued from that town, and to be blessed with some supporter and helper — and that Allah granted both. Some were provided the opportunity to move out from there: the first wish fulfilled. Others remained right there until the Conquest of Makkah, when the Holy Prophet ﷺ appointed Sayyidnā ʿAttab ibn Asid as their caretaker, and he had the oppressed Muslims delivered from their oppressors: the second wish fulfilled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson directly: one of the reasons the command to fight came at all was the prayer made by these weak Muslim men and women. Allah responded to their prayer and commanded the Muslims to wage jihād against their oppressors, which put an end to their hardships.

**Why the question rather than the command.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the Qur'an here, rather than giving a straightforward command to fight, says instead: *"What has happened to you that you do not fight in the way of Allah?"* The hint is that fighting under such conditions is a natural duty — not doing which is certainly far from a reasonable man.

## Ayah 76: two banners, and only two

*"Those who believe, fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve, fight in the cause of the Taghut."* Ibn Kathir states the contrast simply: the believers fight in obedience to Allah and to gain His pleasure, while the disbelievers fight in obedience to Shaytan.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the objectives on each side. The purpose for which a believer strives is that the Divine Law becomes operative in this world and the authority of Allah Almighty reigns supreme — because He is the Master of all, He created the universe in His infinite wisdom, and His Law is based on pure justice; and when the rule of justice is established, there will be peace which sustains. The disbelievers, by contrast, seek to spread the message of kufr, give it the widest possible currency, and work to bring about the ascendency of disbelief; they are eager to see satanic powers rule the world, so that everything that constitutes kufr and shirk can be enforced in the universal order and given the sheen and glamour of something seemingly positive. Since kufr and shirk are the ways of Shaytan, the disbelievers help him in doing his job. That is why the ayah calls them *awliyā' ash-Shayṭān*, the friends of Shaytan.

## "Ever feeble indeed is the plot of Shaytan"

The passage ends on reassurance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the deceptive plans made by Shaytan are weak and insubstantial, so that he cannot harm or hurt true Muslims in any way whatsoever. Muslims should therefore not demur when it comes to fighting the friends of Shaytan, because their helper is none other than Allah Himself, and with Allah on their side Shaytan's game plan is not going to work.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān illustrates this with Badr, citing Mazharī. Shaytan stood by the side of the disbelievers, dishing out his tall claims before them, telling them *"this day, nobody is going to over-power you"* — because, he said, *"I am your helper by your side. I shall be there with my armies to support you."* When the actual fighting began he did advance with his army, but no sooner did he notice that the angels had arrived to help the Muslims than all his plans were frustrated and he took to his heels, saying to his disbelieving accomplices: *"I bear no responsibility for you. I see what you do not see. I fear Allah for Allah is severe when punishing."* Big words before the battle; flight the moment reality arrived. That is the measure of his *kayd*, his guile.

**But read the conditions.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful: calling Shaytan's guile feeble here is not an isolated, unconditional statement. Two conditions emerge from the ayah itself. The first, from *alladhīna āmanū* ("those who believe"): the person against whom Shaytan tries his guile must be a Muslim. The second, from *fī sabīli-llāh* ("in the way of Allah"): the effort that Muslim makes must be for the pleasure of Allah alone, with no selfish motive behind it. If either of the two conditions stops existing, then it is not necessary that Shaytan's guile remains feeble against him. Faith plus sincerity is what makes the enemy small.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with a word from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbas, reported by al-Qurtubi: "When you see Satan, do not think twice. Attack him" — after which he recited this very ayah, *"No doubt, the guile of Satan is feeble."*

## Living it

The passage asks for three things at once, and they belong together.

**Prepare properly, and trust only Allah.** Take every means the situation requires — and hold none of them as your security. The means are for peace of mind; nothing will befall us except what Allah has prescribed for us.

**Do not stand outside the community's burdens.** The mark of the one Allah exposes in ayat 72–73 is not weakness but detachment: no grief when they suffer, no gladness when they are given, only an eye on his own share of the spoils. Ask honestly which of the two speeches your heart makes when news of your brothers reaches you.

**Let the cry of the oppressed reach you.** The most affecting thing in these ayat is that Allah quotes the duʿā of the powerless — and then answers it. For those able to help, ayah 75 presents helping as the natural, reasonable duty, and asks what could possibly excuse the refusal. For those who are themselves powerless, the same ayah is the proof that a prayer made under persecution in Makkah was heard, recorded in the Qur'an, and granted in both of its two requests.

passages.title: Those who dread fighting once it is ordained
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat expose a very human moment: people who had begged for permission to fight back, and then, once the command came, found their courage had gone quiet. Allah answers on three fronts — the shortness of this world (ayah 77), the inescapability of death (ayah 78), and the confused theology of blaming the Messenger ﷺ for misfortune (ayat 78–79). One question holds the passage together: **where do you think safety actually comes from?**

## The moment this passage speaks into

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. In the earliest years the Muslims in Makkah were commanded to establish the prayer and give some charity so the poor among them would be comforted, and to be forgiving and forbearing with the idolaters and patient under their abuse. But they were eager for the day they would be allowed to fight and punish their enemies. The circumstances did not permit armed conflict: they were few against many, and their city was the sacred one, the most honoured place on earth — which is why the command to fight was never revealed in Makkah. Only later, once the Muslims had a town of their own in Madinah with strength, power and support, was jihad legislated. And then, when the command came exactly as they had wished, some of them became weary and were very fearful of facing the idolaters in battle.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ruh al-Maʿani) fills in the human texture. Harassed Muslims would come to the Prophet ﷺ complaining of what was being done to them and asking permission to fight back in self-defence. He held them back: he had not been commanded to fight, but to be patient and to pardon, and they should keep to the instructions of salah and zakah already given. And he explained why — unless a person is first trained to fight his own desires in obedience to Allah, and is used to bearing pain and financial sacrifice, he will find it very hard to go out and offer his life.

Ibn Kathir then gives the narration behind the ayah. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said that ʿAbdur-Rahman bin ʿAwf and several of his companions came to the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah and said, "O Allah's Prophet! We were mighty when we were pagans, but when we embraced the faith, we became weak." The Prophet ﷺ replied, *"I was commanded to pardon the people, so do not fight them."* When Allah moved the Prophet ﷺ to Madinah and commanded him to fight the idolaters, some of the Muslims held back — and this ayah was revealed. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was collected by **An-Nasa'i and Al-Hakim**.

## Prayer and zakah first, then fighting

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) draws attention to the order inside ayah 77. Allah mentions first the command to establish salah and pay zakah — the instruments of **self-correction** — and only then fighting, the instrument of political and collective correction, by which the forces of coercion and injustice are removed so peace can prevail. The lesson: long before worrying about correcting others, start with yourself. The relative weight matches the order — salah and zakah are *fard al-ʿayn*, binding on every individual, while fighting is *fard al-kifayah*, an obligation which, if enough people carry it out, lifts from the rest.

## "Why have You ordained fighting for us?"

The ayah reports that when fighting was ordained, "a section of them fear men as they fear Allah, or even more" — and they say, *Our Lord, why have You ordained fighting for us? If only You had granted us respite for a short while.* Ibn Kathir reads their meaning plainly: we wish jihad had been delayed, because it means bloodshed, orphans and widows. He compares Allah's words, "Those who believe say: Why is a surah not sent down? But when a decisive surah is sent down and fighting is mentioned in it…" (47:20).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful not to let the reader condemn these people too quickly. The wish for respite, it says, was not an *objection* to the command of jihad but a benign and subtle complaint, following an ordinary pattern of human psychology. When a person is hurt and harassed to the extreme, he is quick to flare up and want revenge. But *once man is used to a life of physical comfort and peace, he does not feel like going out to fight.* In Makkah they had longed for the command; in Madinah they found the peace they had missed for years, and when the command arrived in that state the old fire was no longer in them. To read that wish as an objection and attribute sin to those Muslims is not correct.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further point (abridged from Bayan al-Qurʼan of Maulana Thanavi). All of that applies if they voiced the complaint aloud. If it was only a thought crossing the mind, then thoughts in the mind and doubts in the heart are not counted as sins by the Shariʿah at all. Both possibilities stand open; the word *qālū* ("they say") can mean they said it within themselves. According to some commentators (Tafsir Kabir), on that reading no explanation is even needed. The Qur'an is naming a real weakness, but notice that the commentators refuse to turn it into a condemnation. Read it as a mirror, not a verdict on someone else.

## "Short is the enjoyment of this world"

Allah answers their fear not with a rebuke but with a comparison. *Say: short is the enjoyment of this world; the Hereafter is far better for whoever has taqwa* — Ibn Kathir: the destination of the one with taqwa is better for him than this life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing al-Tafsir al-Kabir) gives four reasons the Hereafter is the better bargain:

1. The blessings of this world are **few**; those of the Hereafter, **many**.
2. The dunya's blessings are **perishable**; the Akhirah's are **eternal**.
3. The dunya's blessings come **laced with troubles**; the Akhirah's are free of such impurities.
4. Getting the dunya's blessings is **never certain**; the Akhirah's will certainly reach everyone who has taqwa.

Then the ayah closes: *and you will not be wronged even by a fatīl.* Translations tend to leave the word transliterated, but Ibn Kathir's gloss makes its force clear — not the smallest fraction of reward for your good deeds will be withheld; you will earn your full reward. He notes what this promise does: it turns the believers' focus away from this life and makes them eager for the Hereafter, steadying them for the fight.

## Ayah 78: no wall keeps death out

Then comes the line that dismantles the calculation: *Wherever you may be, death will overtake you — even if you were in fortified towers.*

Ibn Kathir: you shall certainly die, and none of you will escape it. He gathers the Qur'an's other statements — "Whatsoever is on it (the earth) will perish" (55:26); "Everyone shall taste death"; "And We granted not to any human being immortality before you." Nothing saves anyone from death, whether he went out to fight or not; everyone has an appointed time and a limited term of life. As for *burūj mushayyadah*, the fortified towers — Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as entrenched, fortified, high and towering. No caution and no fortification can ever avert death.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion for the man avoiding the battlefield: he imagines that by dodging jihad he can dodge death too. But the day of death must come, and it will come exactly where you are. Once that is settled, backing out is senseless.

Both commentaries bring the same witness: **Khalid bin Al-Walid**, in the illness that preceded his death, said from his bed, "I participated in so and so number of battles, and every part of my body sustained an injury due to a stab or a shot. Yet here I am, I die in my bed! Let not the eyes of the cowards ever taste sleep." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Khalid — Saifullah, the Sword of Allah — went from one jihad to the next longing for martyrdom and praying to be spared death in bed, and yet died in his own house, exactly as Allah decreed.

The reverse case is as striking. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays an account Ibn Kathir reports on the authority of Mujahid, narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim, of a woman of an earlier community foretold at birth that she would die by a spider. Every attempt to avert it failed; in the end she was housed in a grand palace kept free of spiders' webs. One day a spider appeared on the wall; she leapt up and crushed it underfoot — and its poison entered her foot and killed her. A woman in a spotless palace killed by a spider; a man who spent his life among swords dying in his bed. The lesson: life and death are in our Creator's hands and His decisions are final. If He wills, He gives death on a luxury bed at the hands of a spider; if He wills to preserve someone, He keeps him alive amid swinging swords and raging fires.

## Strong walls are not a failure of trust

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi) notes that "even if you were in fortified castles" does not condemn building well. Constructing a good, strong house so that your person and property are secure is **not** contrary to tawakkul — trust in Allah — nor against the Shariʿah. Tawakkul means knowing the walls do not decide the hour of death; not that you should live without walls.

## The omen-readers

The second half of ayah 78 turns to a different sickness. *If something good comes to them they say, "This is from Allah"; and if something bad befalls them they say, "This is from you."*

Ibn Kathir gives the picture. The "good" means fertile years and abundant fruit, produce and children — so said Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Al-ʿAliyah and As-Suddi. The "evil" means drought, famine, shortages of produce, the death of their children or animals — as stated by Abu Al-ʿAliyah and As-Suddi. And "this is from you" means: because of you, because we followed you and embraced your religion.

Ibn Kathir places this in a line running through history. Allah says of the people of Firʿawn: "whenever good came to them, they said, 'Ours is this'; and if evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to evil omens connected with Musa and those with him" (7:131). And: "among mankind is he who worships Allah as it were upon the edge" — in doubt (22:11). This, Ibn Kathir says, is the speech of the hypocrites, who took on Islam outwardly while disliking it inwardly, so that when calamity struck they laid it at the door of following the Prophet ﷺ.

Hence the answer: *Say: all is from Allah* — everything occurs by the decision and decree of Allah, and His decree comes to pass for righteous and wicked, believer and disbeliever alike. Then the reproach: *what is wrong with these people that they fail to understand any word?*

## Ayah 79: all from Allah, and evil from yourself

Ayah 79 seems at first to say the opposite of ayah 78: *Whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.* Ibn Kathir notes that Allah addresses the Messenger ﷺ here while the meaning refers to mankind in general.

The two statements answer different questions. "All is from Allah" in ayah 78 is about **creation and decree**: nothing occurs outside His decision. "From yourself" in ayah 79 is about **cause**: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it exactly — although calamities are created by Allah, their cause lies nowhere else but in the misdeeds of man himself. Ibn Kathir reads "from yourself" as "because of you and due to your actions," citing the parallel, "whatever of misfortune befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned. And He pardons much." As-Suddi, Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd said it means because of your errors; Qatadah, as a punishment for you, O son of Adam, because of your sins.

So the hypocrite's error was never in tracing events to Allah's decree — that much is true. It was in exempting himself and blaming the Messenger ﷺ.

## Every blessing is grace, never wages

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) notes that *hasanah* in ayah 79 means "blessing," and draws out the implication: no good reaches a person as a matter of right. It is nothing but the grace of Allah — His *fadl*. However much worship a person performs, he cannot claim to have earned it, because the very ability to worship is itself from Allah, what is called *tawfiq*.
