And Allah's blessings are countless; how could limited acts of obedience purchase them, when whatever we manage in the name of worship is hardly worthy of the Lord of all the worlds?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the Prophet ﷺ as having said that no one will enter Paradise except by the mercy of Allah — and when the narrator asked, "Not you either?" he said, "Not me either." (The commentary reports this without naming a collection.)

## Every affliction carries a mercy inside it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) says *sayyi'ah* here means *musibah*: hardship, misfortune, calamity. Its outcome depends on who receives it. For the disbeliever, the evil striking him in this world is only an ordinary sample of the far greater punishment to come. For the believer, misfortune becomes an **expiation (kaffarah)** for his sins, and thereby a cause of his salvation in the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites two hadith here, from Mazhari, from **Tirmidhi**:

- "No evil ever touches a Muslim, but it becomes a source of forgiveness for him — even the pinch of a thorn in his feet."
- On the authority of Abu Musa: "No hardship befalls a servant of Allah, be it light or tough, but it is always due to his sin — and the sins Allah forgives (without afflicting with a calamity) are much more."

Notice the mercy in the second narration: far more is quietly forgiven than is ever brought to account.

## "And We have sent you as a Messenger to mankind"

The passage ends by re-anchoring everything in the Messenger ﷺ they had been blaming. Ibn Kathir: he was sent to convey to them Allah's commandments — what He likes and is pleased with, and what He dislikes and refuses. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) draws out "to mankind": these words prove that the Prophet ﷺ was sent as a Messenger for all the peoples of the world, not the Arabs alone. His prophethood is universal — open to all human beings, those present now and those yet to come, right up to the Day of Judgement.

And then: *and Allah is sufficient as a Witness.* Ibn Kathir: a Witness that He has sent you, and a Witness over you and over them, with full knowledge of what you convey and of the disbelief and rebellion with which they meet the truth.

## Living it

- **Order your reform correctly.** Salah and zakah before campaigning to fix everyone else: what binds you personally comes before what binds the community.
- **Test where you locate your safety.** Ayah 78 does not tell you to stop building strong walls; it tells you to stop believing they are what keeps you alive.
- **Watch the reflex to blame.** "Good is from Allah" is easy to say. The harder discipline of ayah 79 is to look first at yourself when things go wrong.
- **Recalculate the trade.** Whatever the dunya offers to keep you from obedience is *qalīl*, a small thing — and nothing of your good deeds will be shortchanged by even a fatīl.

passages.title: Obedience professed by day, undone by night
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are best read as a single argument. Ayah 80 lays down the principle — obedience to the Messenger ﷺ simply *is* obedience to Allah — and then turns to comfort him about those who refuse. Ayah 81 shows what that refusal can look like from people who never openly refuse at all: a profession of obedience by day, undone by night. Ayah 82 asks why such people never sat with the Qur'an long enough to be changed by it. And ayah 83 shows the practical fruit of that shallowness: people who broadcast every rumour instead of taking it to those who actually know.

## The principle: his obedience is Allah's obedience

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the movement in the surah here: what came before affirmed prophethood; ayah 80 now establishes *the right* of prophethood — it calls for compulsory obedience. Obedience to Allah is obligatory, even on purely rational grounds; and since obedience to the Prophet ﷺ has here been equated with obedience to Allah, obedience to the Prophet ﷺ turns out to be equally obligatory. Whoever disobeys him has, by that act, disobeyed the command of Allah.

Ibn Kathir grounds this in the nature of what the Prophet ﷺ says: whatever he utters is not of his own desire but a revelation inspired to him. He cites a narration Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever obeys me, obeys Allah; and whoever disobeys me, disobeys Allah. Whoever obeys the Amir (leader, ruler), obeys me; and whoever disobeys the Amir, disobeys me."

Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was recorded in the Two Sahihs.

## The profession, and what happens after dark

**"And they say, 'We obey.'"** Ibn Kathir: the hypocrites pretend to be loyal and obedient. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it a policy of double-dealing — they say one thing with the tongue while something else sits hidden in the heart.

**"But when they leave you."** Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: when they depart and are no longer with you. The force of the ayah is in that transition — one person inside the Prophet's ﷺ gathering, another the moment the door closes.

**"A group of them spend the night planning."** Ibn Kathir: they plot at night among themselves for other than what they pretend when they are with you. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the human picture: these men would come face to face with the Holy Prophet ﷺ and declare themselves obedient, accepting whatever he commanded — then leave his company, gather together, and conspire over how to disobey him. This duplicity, it says plainly, *caused him great pain*.

**"But Allah records what they plot by night."** Ibn Kathir explains: He has full knowledge of their plots, and records it through His command to His scribes, the angels who are responsible for recording the actions of the servants. This is a threat from Allah — He knows what the hypocrites try to hide, their night-time scheming to defy the Messenger ﷺ and oppose him even while professing loyalty, and He will certainly punish them for it. Ibn Kathir points to a parallel in Surah al-Hajj, where they say, "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey" (22:47).

The believer often cannot see behind the smiling face. Allah does — and the record is already being kept.

## What the Prophet ﷺ was told to do about them

**"We have not sent you as a watcher over them."** Ibn Kathir explains it as: *do not worry about him.* Your job is only to convey. Whoever obeys you gains happiness and success — and you gain a reward like his. Whoever turns away gains failure and loss, and you carry no burden for what he does. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point (citing Maulana Ashraf Thanavi's *Bayān al-Qurʼān*): the Prophet ﷺ is not duty-bound to stand guard over their behaviour, nor charged with the mission of stopping people from disbelieving. His mission is to deliver the Message; once delivered, his duty as a Prophet stands fulfilled. Ibn Kathir adds a further prophetic saying to the same effect — that whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will acquire guidance, and whoever disobeys them harms only himself.

**"So turn away from them, and put your trust in Allah."** Ibn Kathir unpacks *fa-aʿriḍ ʿanhum* in five strokes: pardon them, be forbearing with them, do not punish them, do not expose them to the people, and do not fear them. And *wa kafā billāhi wakīlā*: He is sufficient as Protector, Supporter and Helper for those who rely on Him and return to Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way — Allah told him to ignore them and continue with his mission, placing his trust in Allah, because Allah is all-sufficient for him.

### An instruction for anyone who leads

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a lesson for anyone in a position of leadership: one who leads people has to go through all sorts of hardships. People tend to level absurd allegations against him. There will be enemies in the garb of friendship and trust standing close by. Despite all such obstacles, the leader must display determination and steadfastness and devote himself to the mission with full trust in Allah. If his objective and orientation are right, he will — in shāʼ Allah — succeed.

## Beneath it all: a Book they never pondered

**Tadabbur, not just tilāwah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the exact word chosen in ayah 82. Allah does not say *a-fa-lā yaqraʼūn* — "do they not recite?" He says *a-fa-lā yatadabbarūn* — "do they not ponder, deliberate?" The hint is delicate and deliberate: it is only by looking into the Qur'an *deeply* that a person finds no discrepancy in its words and meanings. A plain recitation, devoid of deliberation and deep thinking, may lead someone to start seeing contradictions which really are not there at all.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a command to contemplate the Qur'an and a prohibition against ignoring it — or ignoring its wise meanings and eloquent words. He cites the parallel: "Do they not then think deeply in the Qur'an, or are their hearts locked up?" (47:24).

**The argument from the absence of contradiction.** Ibn Kathir: had it been fraudulent and made up — as the ignorant idolaters and hypocrites assert in their hearts — they would have found in it discrepancies and inconsistencies *in abundance*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the phrase "a great deal of contradiction" (citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*): if there were contradiction even within one subject, then across many subjects the contradictions would obviously have become a great deal. But in fact there is no contradiction anywhere in it — so it is the word of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds why that is so remarkable. The speech or writing of man is affected by circumstances; it varies with peace and distraction, with happiness and sorrow. The Qur'an's eloquence never tapers. It talks about the Oneness of Allah and the disbelief of men and lays down rules for the lawful and the unlawful — with no inconsistency in the process. It offers information about the unseen, and not one bit of that information fails to match reality. Its very order retains the quality of its diction all along, never once touching a low pitch.

**Muhkam and mutashābih.** Ibn Kathir connects this to those firmly grounded in knowledge who say, "We believe in it, all of it is from our Lord" (3:7). The *muhkam* sections are the entirely clear ones; the *mutashābih* are those not entirely clear. Both are true. Those firmly grounded understand the not-entirely-clear from the clear, and thus gain guidance. Those in whose heart is the disease of hypocrisy do the reverse — they understand the *muhkam* from the *mutashābih*, and thus gain only misguidance.

### The Prophet's ﷺ anger at quarrelling over the Book

Ibn Kathir records from Imam Ahmad, on the authority of ʿAmr bin Shuʿayb from his father from his grandfather, that some of the leaders of the Companions were sitting close to a door of the Prophet's ﷺ room. They mentioned an ayah and began disputing until they raised their voices. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was so angry that when he went out his face was red. He threw sand on them and said:

> "Behold, O people! This is how the nations before you were destroyed, because of their disputing with their Prophets and their contradicting parts of the Books with other parts. The Qur'an does not contradict itself. Rather, it testifies to the truth of itself. Therefore, whatever of it you have knowledge in, then implement it, and whatever you do not know of it, then refer it to those who have knowledge in it."

Ibn Kathir also cites Ahmad's narration from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, who saw two men dispute over an ayah until their voices became loud, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Verily, the nations before you were destroyed because of their disagreements over the Book." Ibn Kathir notes Muslim and An-Nasaʼi recorded this hadith.

Notice how that first hadith ends — refer what you do not know to the one who knows. Ayah 83 says something very close.

### Who may ponder the Qur'an?

Because the Qur'an itself demands that *every* human being ponder its meanings, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds it incorrect to suppose that pondering the Qur'an is the exclusive domain of its highest and ablest exponents, the Imams and mujtahids. But the levels of *tadabbur* differ according to different levels of knowledge and understanding. The deliberation of the great exponents deduces the solution of thousands of problems from a single verse; that of a common scholar reaches only as far as comprehending those problems and their solutions. And when common people recite the Qur'an and deliberate on its meanings through a translation and explanation in their own language, this impresses upon their hearts the greatness of Allah, develops love for Him, and implants there a concern for the Ākhirah — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the master key to success.

Its practical counsel: so that common people stay safe from doubts and misunderstandings, it is better to study the Qur'an lesson by lesson under the guidance of an ʿālim; if that cannot be done, take up the study of some authentic and reliable tafsir. And if a doubt arises during such study, the wiser course is not to resolve it on the basis of personal opinion — one should consult expert scholars.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān illustrates with everyday analogies: no one objects that only trained doctors may treat patients, or that contracts for canals, bridges and dams go to expert engineers, or that legal experts alone interpret and apply the law of the land — because all accept that these require years of education, training and recognised competence. Yet when the same standard is applied to the interpretation and application of Qur'an and Sunnah — an intricate and delicate job indeed — the ʿulamāʼ meet a barrage of taunts that they hold a "monopoly" over it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes (citing Qurtubi) that this verse yields an important rule: when we find no explicit statement in the Qur'an and Sunnah on a certain problem, we should make the best of efforts to find a solution by serious deliberation within them — the method technically known as *qiyās*, analogical deduction.

## The tongue that repeats what it has not verified

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 83 as chastising those who indulge in things before being sure of their truth — disclosing them, making them known, spreading their news, even though such news might not be true at all.

**The background of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas, Dahhak and Abu Muʿadh, the ayah was revealed about the hypocrites; while according to Sayyidna Hasan and many others, it was revealed about weak Muslims (*Rūh al-Maʿānī*). It then stresses, following Ibn Kathir, the hadith of Sayyidna ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, collected in the Two Sahihs. Word had spread that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had divorced his wives. ʿUmar left his house for the Masjid, and while still at its doorstep heard the people inside already talking about it. He said that this was something that must first be investigated. He went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him directly: "Have you divorced your wives?" The Prophet ﷺ said, "No." In the narration Muslim collected, ʿUmar says: I stood by the door of the Masjid and shouted with the loudest voice, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not divorce his wives" — and then this ayah was revealed. "So," ʿUmar concludes, "I properly investigated that matter."

**From the Sunnah on careless speech.** Ibn Kathir gathers several narrations here:

- Imam Muslim recorded in the introduction to his Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Narrating everything one hears is sufficient to make a person a liar." Ibn Kathir notes this is the same narration Abu Dawud collected in the section of *Adab* (manners) in his Sunan.
- In the Two Sahihs, it is recorded from Al-Mughirah bin Shuʿbah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited "It was said" and "So-and-so said" — which Ibn Kathir explains as referring to those who often convey the speech that people utter without investigating its reliability and truth.
- The Sahih also records: "Whoever narrates a hadith while knowing it is false, then he is one of the two liars" — that is, the one who invents the lie and the one who spreads it.

## Referring it back: the road to knowledge

**"If only they had referred it to the Messenger and to those in authority among them."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up *istinbāṭ*, the word behind "those of them who could draw it out." Literally (from Qurtubi) it refers to the act of drawing out water from the depth of a well; when a well is dug, the water that oozes out first is called *mustanbaṭ*. But in this context the usage means to get to the bottom of something and find out the truth of the matter.

**Who are "those in authority" (ulū'l-amr)?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a genuine difference among the scholars. Sayyidna Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Layla held that it refers to Muslim scholars and jurists. Al-Suddi held that it means rulers and officials. Abu Bakr al-Jassas, after reporting both, takes the general view that it means both — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers this the correct approach, since the expression applies to all of them. It also records the objection some scholars raise: that *ulū'l-amr*, in its literal sense, means people whose orders are carried out administratively, which is not what jurists do. The answer given is that the implementation of authority takes two forms — by force and coercion, which belongs to those in political authority; and by reliance and trust, which is precisely what the general body of Muslims has, by its own free will and choice, reposed in the jurists in every age, taking their determinations as the mandatory mode of action in matters of religion.

**Ijtihad in new problems.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out (from al-Jassas) that since the ayah carries the command to turn to the Holy Prophet ﷺ for the resolution of new problems while he is present, and to the ʿulamāʼ and fuqahāʼ when he is not, rulings on matters with no explicit text (*naṣṣ*) in the Qur'an or Sunnah are to be deduced by ijtihad and qiyas — because the scholars have the required ability to extract and formulate injunctions from the authoritative texts. It also notes a subtle point: because the phrase "those of them who could draw it out would have known it" is general and covers *both* parties named — the Messenger ﷺ and those in authority — it shows that the Prophet ﷺ too was entrusted with this function of deducing injunctions.

One might object that ayah 83 is only about war news and rumour, not about legal reasoning. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the ayah makes no mention of an enemy at all: "a matter about peace or fear" is stated universally. The way it relates to an enemy, so it does to day-to-day problems — because when an ordinary person faces a matter on whose lawfulness no textual authority exists, he is thrown into a fix, and the way out the Sharīʿah provides is to turn to those capable of extracting and formulating injunctions and act in accordance with what they lay down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of humility: a ruling extracted by the jurists through istinbāṭ and ijtihad cannot categorically be declared the absolute truth in the sight of Allah; the probability always exists that it might turn out not to be. What one gains is a positive, overwhelming and weightier opinion that it is correct — and that is what one acts upon.

**"Had it not been for the grace and mercy of Allah upon you, you would have followed Shaytan, except a few."** Ibn Kathir reports, from ʿAli bin Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, that "except a few of you" refers to the believers.

## Living it

Read as one argument, this passage asks four things of a believer. That your obedience be the same in private as in the Prophet's ﷺ presence — because what is planned at night is written down. That when you are wronged by two-faced people, you pardon, forbear, refuse to fear them, and hand the matter to Allah, who is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs. That you do not merely recite the Qur'an but sit with it in *tadabbur*, and take what is beyond you to those who know rather than to your own opinion. And that when news reaches you — alarming or reassuring — you do what ʿUmar did: go to the source before you open your mouth.

passages.title: The Prophet's solitary charge, and the words that hold a community together
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from a battlefield to a doorstep: Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ to march out even if he marches alone (84), then turns to the words that knit a community together — the word you put in for another (85), the word of peace you return (86) — before naming the One who will gather all people and requite each (87). One thread holds them: **the believer answers for his own act, not for its outcome**, and even his lightest word is an act Allah records.

## The moment behind ayah 84: Badr al-Sughra

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background, from Qurtubi and Mazhari. After Uhud in Shawwal, the Prophet ﷺ began preparing to meet the disbelievers at Badr on the date they had set, in Dhu al-Qaʿdah — which historians identify as the minor Badr. Some Muslims hesitated: some recently wounded, others unsettled by rumours. Into that hesitation this ayah came down, guiding the Prophet ﷺ to ignore the infirm and the scared and to march on even if he had to go all alone, for Allah is his helper.

He went out to Badr Minor with seventy Companions, as promised to Abu Sufyan after Uhud. There, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, Allah put awe and fear into the hearts of Abu Sufyan and his disbelieving accomplices from Quraysh. Not one showed up, so it was they who turned out false in their solemn promise, and the Prophet ﷺ returned with his Companions safely. That is what *"it may be that Allah will restrain the evil might of the disbelievers"* meant in practice.

## "You are not tasked except for yourself"

The command in ayah 84 is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself: *fa-qātil fī sabīl Allāh*, "so fight in the way of Allah." Ibn Kathir reads it plainly — Allah commands His servant and Messenger Muhammad ﷺ to himself fight in jihad and not to be concerned about those who do not join; *lā tukallafu illā nafsak*, "you are not tasked (held responsible) except for yourself." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the sequence: the direction is given to him personally, implying he should go even if no one goes with him. But the sentence following immediately, *wa ḥarriḍ al-muʼminīn*, "and incite the believers," means he must not surrender the work of inducing other Muslims to join. If they remain unresponsive even after that persuasion, his mission has been accomplished, and from that point he is not responsible for what they do.

**Two questions the Companions put to al-Bara'.** Ibn Kathir preserves two reports. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu Ishaq asked al-Bara' bin ʿAzib "about a man who meets a hundred enemies and still fights them, would he be one of those referred to in Allah's statement, *And do not throw yourselves into destruction* [2:195]?" Al-Bara' answered by quoting this ayah — *"Then fight in the cause of Allah, you are not tasked except for yourself, and incite the believers."* Imam Ahmad recorded, through Sulayman bin Dawud from Abu Bakr bin ʿAyyash from Abu Ishaq, a different question: "I asked Al-Bara', 'If a man attacks the lines of the idolators, would he be throwing himself to destruction?'" He answered explicitly: "No — because Allah has sent His Messenger ﷺ and commanded him, *Then fight in the cause of Allah, you are not tasked except for yourself.* That Ayah is about spending in Allah's cause." So the early community read 4:84 as shielding the lone, outnumbered believer from the charge of recklessness, and 2:195 as a different subject.

**What "inciting" looks like.** Ibn Kathir explains *wa ḥarriḍ al-muʼminīn* as urging them to fight by encouraging them and strengthening their resolve — as the Prophet ﷺ did at Badr while organizing their lines: *Stand up and march forth to a Paradise, as wide as the heavens and Earth.* He then cites hadiths on the merit of jihad: Al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah, that *Paradise has one hundred grades which Allah has reserved for the Mujahidin who fight in His cause, the distance between each two grades is like the distance between the heaven and the Earth. So, when you ask Allah, ask for Al-Firdaws, which is the best and highest part of Paradise*; and Abu Saʿīd al-Khudri, collected by Muslim, that there is a deed for which Allah raises the servant a hundred grades in Paradise — and that deed is jihad in Allah's cause.

**"And Allah is Stronger in might and Stronger in punishing."** Ibn Kathir: He is able over them in this life and the Hereafter, as He said elsewhere — had Allah willed, He Himself could certainly have punished them without you, but He lets you fight to test some of you with others (47:4). For Maʿārif ul Qurʼān this clause removes the danger of fighting alone: the One helping him far exceeds such disbelievers in strength and might at war, so success has got to be his — and His punishment may come on the Day of Judgement or, as some commentators said, in this world.

## Ayah 85: the word you put in for someone else

*Shafāʿah* is usually rendered "intercession," but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. Its literal meaning is to meet or join, or cause to meet or join; from the same root, *shafʿ* means an even number or pair, whose antonym is *witr*, odd. So *shafāʿah* is coupling your strength with that of a weak seeker of justice — giving a helpless solitary person the strength of a pair.

That image sets the conditions. For a recommendation to be fair and permissible, the claim of the person recommended must be true and permissible, and it should be a case where weakness or lack of resource stops him carrying it to those in authority himself. Recommending what is not true and rightful, or forcibly influencing others to accept it, is bad recommendation; so, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says bluntly, is pressure exerted through one's connections and influence, because that is injustice. Anything taken in return — money, or a job-related favour such as harnessing someone to a personal chore — turns it into a bribe, which the hadith declares ill-gotten and forbidden. Tafsir al-Kashshaf adds that a good recommendation aims at fulfilling the right of a Muslim, bringing him permissible benefit or shielding him from harm; it must be free of worldly expediency, sought purely for the pleasure of Allah, and never aimed at winning pardon for a proven crime whose punishment stands fixed in the Qur'an.

**Two words for "share."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices a fine choice of word: *naṣīb* for the good share, *kifl* for the bad. Lexically both mean a share, but in usage *naṣīb* is a good share and *kifl* more often a bad one — though *kifl* is sometimes used for a good share too, as in the Qur'anic phrase about two shares of His mercy.

**The reward is for making it, not for winning it.** Ibn Kathir cites what is recorded in the Sahih: the Prophet ﷺ said: *Intercede and you will gain a reward of it. Yet, Allah shall decide whatever He wills by the words of His Prophet.* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this hadith to Sahih al-Bukhari.) The lesson is exact: if a weak person cannot carry his problem to a higher authority, or cannot explain what he needs, do it for him — then what happens is none of your business. Do not interfere in the decision, and if the outcome goes against you, never end up displeased or disgusted. Al-Bahr al-Muhit and Bayan al-Qur'an take *minhā* as indicating cause, and al-Tafsir al-Mazhari reports from Mujahid that one who recommends is rewarded for it even if it is not accepted.

**Barirah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān illustrates: Barirah, a bondwoman freed by ʿA'ishah, had dissolved her marriage to Mughith, who was deeply disturbed because he loved her, and the Prophet ﷺ recommended she think of remarrying him. She said: "Ya Rasulallah, if this is your command, I am all for it; but if this is a recommendation, then I just do not feel like accepting it at all." He said it was a recommendation, not a command; she declined, and he let her stay as she was. If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not press a recommendation, no one may.

**A word is a deed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the Prophet ﷺ as saying that one who brings someone around to a good deed gets a reward like the doer's; and, from Abu Hurayrah in Ibn Majah, that whoever helps in the killing of a Muslim even by part of a word will face Allah with a sign written between his eyes: *deprived from the mercy of Allah*. So prompting to good is itself a good deed with an identical reward; prompting to evil, a sin of equal gravity. And again: *Allah keeps helping His servant as long as he keeps helping his brother.* Even a prayer counts — Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit and al-Mazhari include praying for a Muslim's need under "good recommendation," and according to a hadith, when someone prays for the good of his brother-in-faith the angel says *wa laka bi-mithl*, "and may the same be yours."

**Muqīt.** On *"And Allah is Ever Muqit over everything,"* Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', ʿAtiyah, Qatadah and Matar al-Warraq said it means "Watcher," Mujahid "Witness," and in another narration "Able to do." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives three lexical senses — powerful, observer, dispenser of sustenance — and lets all three stand: He is able to requite both the one who recommends and the one who acts on his word; He is ever-present, knowing with what intention a recommendation is made — sincerely for Allah's sake, or to make a brother a target of self-interest; and He alone dispenses provision, so a recommendation does not leave Him choiceless. Whatever He has written for a person has got to reach him — and the maker of a good recommendation gets his reward for free, for extending a hand to the helpless.

## Ayah 86: the greeting

If ayah 85 is about the word you speak *for* someone, ayah 86 is about the word you speak *to* them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *taḥiyyah* lexically means saying *ḥayyāka'llāh*, "may Allah keep you alive," the kind of expression pre-Islamic Arabs used. Islam replaced it with one standard form, *as-salāmu ʿalaykum*, which the common English "peace be on you" translates incompletely: it means *may you remain safe from every pain, sorrow and distress* — not a bland prayer for long life, but for a life secure against calamity and sorrow.

Ibn ʿArabi, in Ahkam al-Qur'an, notes that Salam is one of the good names of Allah Almighty, so the greeting also says Allah is your guardian and caretaker. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it expresses the reality of our relation with Allah — greeter and greeted alike depend on Him at every moment, and no one can bring benefit to another without His will; it is therefore an act of worship in its own right, not a social reflex. And it is a pledge: Ibn ʿArabi reports Imam Ibn ʿUyaynah's saying, *"Do you know what salam is? The greeter by salam says: you are safe from me"* — the greeter making himself the guardian of the other's life, property and honour. Hence, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the Prophet ﷺ said in a sound hadith: *A Muslim is the one from whom all Muslims remain safe — safe from his tongue and safe from his hands* (Tirmidhi, Kitab al-Iman).

**The command, and its two levels.** Ibn Kathir: if a Muslim greets you with the salam, return it with a better salam, or at least equal to what was given — the better salam recommended, returning it equally an obligation. He cites ʿImran bin Husayn: a man came and said "As-Salamu ʿAlaykum"; the Prophet ﷺ returned the greeting and, after the man sat, said "Ten." Another came adding *wa Rahmatullah* — "Twenty." A third added *wa Barakatuh* — "Thirty." (Imam Ahmad; this is Abu Dawud's narration, also recorded by At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Al-Bazzar. At-Tirmidhi said "Hasan Gharib.")

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a complementary narration, from Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim with different chains, in which the Prophet ﷺ explained the ayah by his own action: each time a man greeted him he returned it with one phrase more — but when a third combined all three phrases in his opening salam, he replied only *"wa ʿalayk,"* and upon you. When the man's heart sank, the Prophet ﷺ explained he had been left nothing to add, so he returned it like for like as the Qur'an teaches. Three rulings follow. First, a salam should be returned with more words added. Second, the addition stops at three phrases as the sunnah practice — ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas reported that the Prophet ﷺ stopped a man who went beyond, saying the salam ends at *barakah* (Mazhari from al-Baghawi; also Ibn Kathir) — the occasion calling for brevity, so any excess that interrupts business or burdens the listener is out of place. Third, a brief "wa ʿalayk" answering the full three-phrase greeting is correct and satisfies *aw ruddūhā*, "or return the same" (Tafsir Mazhari).

**Returning is a duty; starting is a great sunnah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up: returning a salam is obligatory, and one who fails without a valid excuse admitted by the Shariah becomes a sinner — though he may choose the mode: better words or identical ones. The ayah is not explicit about offering salam first, but the passive *idhā ḥuyyītum*, "and when you are greeted," leaves the greeter unnamed, suggestive of salam being something Muslims already do habitually. According to Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit, the majority of scholars hold the initial salam to be *sunnah muʼakkadah*. Hasan al-Basri put it exactly: the initial salam is voluntary, returning it is an obligation.

**Why the Prophet ﷺ pressed it so hard.** Abu Dawud recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *By He in Whose Hand is my soul! You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love each other. Should I direct you to an action that would direct you to love each other? Spread the Salam among yourselves.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same from Sahih Muslim, adding that it should include every Muslim, acquaintance or stranger. From ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, in Bukhari and Muslim: asked which practice of Islam is worthiest, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Feed people and spread the practice of salam, whether you know or do not know a person." The Musnad of Ahmad, Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud report from Abu Umamah: "Nearest to Allah is the person who is the first one to offer salam." From Ibn Masʿud, in Musnad al-Bazzar and al-Muʿjam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: salam is one of the names of Allah which He has blessed the people of the earth with, so make it common among you — and if a gathering does not return a man's greeting, others better than them will respond, namely the angels. And from Abu Hurayrah, in al-Tabarani's al-Muʿjam al-Kabir: *A big miser is the man who acts miserly in offering salam.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, from Tufayl ibn Ubayy ibn Kaʿb in the Mu'atta' of Imam Malik, that ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar would go to the bazaar for the single purpose of meeting a Muslim and offering him salam, so deserving the reward of an act of worship — never intending to buy or sell.

**Practicalities**, from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the rider offers salam to the one walking, the one walking to the one sitting, and a small group passing a larger one offers it first (Bukhari and Muslim); a man entering his house should greet his family, a grace that brings blessing on him and them (Tirmidhi); one should greet a Muslim every time he meets him (Abu Dawud), and greeting on taking leave is likewise sunnah and a source of reward (Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud, from Qatadah and Abu Hurayrah). Replying has exceptions: someone in salah owes no answer, since replying would spoil the prayer; and a person delivering a sermon, reciting the Qur'an, calling the adhan or iqamah, teaching religious texts, or occupied with a human necessity should not be greeted at all, nor is he obliged to answer. Ibn Kathir adds that with *ahl adh-dhimmah*, non-Muslims under Muslim protection, the salam is not initiated nor added to when returning it; as recorded in the Two Sahihs, their greeting is returned equally.

**"Surely, Allah is the Reckoner over everything."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: with Allah rests the reckoning of everything, including human and Islamic rights as apparently small as a salam and its answer. These too will have to be accounted for before Allah Almighty.

## Ayah 87: the ground under all of it

*Allāhu lā ilāha illā hū* — Ibn Kathir: He is singled out as the sole deity of all creation. Then the oath: *He will surely gather you together on the Day of Resurrection about which there is no doubt* — Allah, says Ibn Kathir, is swearing that He will gather the earlier and the later generations in one area, rewarding or punishing each according to his or her actions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: believe in Him as the only object of your worship, and let whatever you do be done with the intention of worship. The final clause seals it: *wa man aṣdaqu min Allāhi ḥadīthā* — who is truer in statement than Allah? Ibn Kathir: no one utters more truthful statements than Allah, in His promise, His warning, His stories of the past and His information of what is to come.

## Living it

One discipline runs through all four ayat: **act, and leave the outcome to Allah.** Go out even if you go alone (84); put in a word for the one who cannot speak for himself, then release it — no pressure, no payment, no resentment if it is refused (85); return the greeting you are given, fuller if you can (86). None of it is small: the courage of the man who rides out alone and a passer-by's "wa ʿalaykum as-salām" are weighed on the same scale.

passages.title: How to treat the two-faced and the neutral
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah an-Nisāʾ 88–91: How to treat the two-faced and the neutral

**What this passage is about.** A group of people had attached themselves to the Muslim community without truly belonging to it, and the Companions could not agree on what to do with them. These four ayat settle the question. They begin by rebuking the believers for splitting into two camps over people whose position Allah had already exposed (ayah 88), then lay down a rule for those who turn back and make their disbelief plain (ayah 89), then carve out two protected exceptions (ayah 90), and finally identify a third group who play both sides and are treated like the first (ayah 91).

What holds the four together is a single question with a single answer: **the deciding factor is not what someone claims, but where they stand in relation to war and peace.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums the whole passage up as three groups of people and two injunctions: *fighting in the absence of peace, and not fighting in the event of peace.*

---

## The moment of revelation

Ibn Kathir notes that there are conflicting opinions over the reason behind the revelation of ayah 88, and he reports several accounts side by side.

**The march to Uhud.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Zayd bin Thābit said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ marched towards Uhud, and some of the people who had accompanied him went back to Madinah. The Companions divided into two groups concerning them — one saying they should be killed, the other objecting. Allah sent down, *"Then what is the matter with you that you are divided into two parties about the hypocrites?"* And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "She (Al-Madinah) is Ṭaybah, and she expels filth, just as the billow expels rust from iron."

Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs also recorded this Hadith. It is worth noticing where the saying falls. The dispute was about which men deserved the sword; the Prophet's ﷺ words are about the city itself, Ṭaybah, and what she does to what is impure in her.

**The Makkans who never left.** Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the ayah was revealed about some people in Makkah who said they had embraced Islam, yet gave their support to the idolaters. One time these people went out of Makkah to fulfil some needs, saying to each other, "If we meet the Companions of Muhammad, there will be no harm for us from their side." When the believers got news that they had gone out, some said: "Let us march to these cowards and kill them, because they support your enemy against you." But another group of the believers said: "Glory be to Allah! Do you kill a people who say as you have said, just because they did not perform Hijrah or leave their land? Is it allowed to shed their blood and confiscate their money in this case?" So they divided into two groups — and, this detail is striking, the Messenger ﷺ was with them and *did not prohibit either group from reiterating its argument*. Only thereafter did Allah reveal the ayah. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this Hadith.

**The traders who never came back.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites ʿAbdullāh ibn Ḥamīd narrating from Mujāhid: some disbelievers of Makkah came to Madinah, pretended to have become Muslims, and claimed to have come as emigrants. Later they turned apostate. They went to the Holy Prophet ﷺ and told him of their plan to go to Makkah to buy merchandise; having made their false excuse, they departed and never returned. A difference of opinion then arose about them among the Muslims of Madinah, some saying they were believers. It was in ayah 88 that Allah declared them disbelievers.

Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānavī explains why the Qurʾān calls them *munāfiq* (hypocrite): they were hypocrites in claiming to have become Muslims while never having believed in their hearts. The fact was that hypocrites were **not** killed, because they concealed their inner disbelief; but the case of these people was different, as their apostasy had come out in the open. As for those who took them to be Muslims, they may perhaps have taken a benign view of their action under some interpretation — but that interpretation was based on sheer opinion, not supported by any proof from the Sharīʿah, and that is why no reliance was placed on it.

---

## Ayah 88: the words that end the argument

**"Allah has cast them back because of what they have earned"** — *wa-Llāhu arkasahum bimā kasabū*. Ibn Kathir explains this as: He made them revert to, and fall into, error. Ibn ʿAbbās said that *arkasahum* means "cast them."

Note the second half: **"because of what they have earned."** Ibn Kathir explains this as their defiance and disobedience to the Messenger ﷺ and their following of falsehood. This matters for anyone troubled by the first half. What the ayah joins together, the Companions were pulling apart: Allah's casting them back is stated in the same breath as what their own hands earned.

**"Do you want to guide him whom Allah has made to go astray?"** Ibn Kathir explains *"you will never find for him a way"* as meaning there will be no path for him, or way to guidance. The rebuke lands on both parties of Companions. They were arguing about who these men really were; Allah tells them the question has already been answered.

---

## Ayah 89: why the wish for your disbelief matters

**"They wish that you reject faith, as they have rejected, and thus that you all become equal."** Ibn Kathir explains: they wish that you fall into misguidance, so that you and they are equal in that regard — and this is because of their extreme enmity and hatred for you. This single line reframes everything. These are not passive neighbours who happen to disagree. What they want is the erasure of the difference between you.

That is why the verse continues: **"So take not Awliyāʾ from them, till they emigrate in the way of Allah."** The test set here is Hijrah: emigration in the way of Allah.

Then: **"But if they turn back."** The early authorities read this in two ways, and Ibn Kathir gives both. Al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās: it means if they abandon Hijrah. As-Suddī: it means, "If they make their disbelief public." Both readings turn on something they do, not on a suspicion we form.

**"and do not take from them a friend or a helper."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from these words that seeking help from disbelievers is forbidden (ḥarām) — so what is in view is not merely personal warmth but alliance and support. Pursuant to this, it cites a narration (Mazharī) that the Anṣār of Madinah sought the permission of the Holy Prophet ﷺ to seek help from the Jews to offset the disbelievers, and his answer was that they were not needed.

## Hijrah then and now

Because ayah 89 makes emigration the dividing line, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on it. Emigration from the homeland of disbelief (*Dār al-kufr*) was enjoined on all Muslims during the early period of Islam — which is for this reason that Allah here prohibited treating those who failed to carry out that obligation as Muslims. In those days, anyone who did not emigrate despite having the ability to do so was not taken to be a Muslim.

That era ended. When Makkah was conquered, the Holy Prophet ﷺ declared: **"There is no Hijrah after the Victory"** — meaning that now that the Conquest of Makkah had made it the Abode of Islam, emigration from there was no longer obligatory. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that this injunction was later abrogated, and this mode of emigration has ceased to exist. Muhammad Taqi Usmani adds the qualification in a footnote: emigration no longer remained a pre-requisite of a person's being Muslim, but if a Muslim lives in a non-Muslim country where he cannot fulfil his religious obligations, it is incumbent on him to emigrate if he has the means to do so.

But a second Hijrah remains open. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies it in a hadith of Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī: Hijrah — not in the sense of abandoning one's homeland, but in the sense of abandoning one's sins — will continue to exist until there remains the time to repent. ʿAllāmah ʿAynī, the commentator on al-Bukhārī, said of this enduring Hijrah that what is meant is the abandonment of sins. And the Holy Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that a *muhājir* (emigrant) is one who emigrates from everything Allah has prohibited (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Mirqāt). So the word carries two senses: to leave one's homeland in order to save one's faith, as the Companions did when they left Makkah for Madinah and Ethiopia; and to leave one's sins.

---

## Ayah 90: the two exemptions

Ayah 90 is the mercy in this passage. Ibn Kathir heads this section **"Combatants and Noncombatants,"** which is exactly the distinction being drawn: Allah excluded some people.

**First exemption: those inside a treaty.** *"Except those who join a group, between you and whom there is a treaty."* Ibn Kathir explains: except those who join and take refuge with a people with whom you have a pact of peace, or people of Dhimmah — then treat them as you treat the people with whom you have peace. This is the saying of As-Suddī, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Jarīr. The protection of a treaty extends to those who shelter under it.

In his Ṣaḥīḥ, Al-Bukhārī recorded the story of the treaty of Al-Ḥudaybiyyah, where it was mentioned that whoever liked to have peace with Quraysh and conduct a pact with them was allowed to, and those who liked to have peace with Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions and enter a pact with them were likewise allowed.

Ibn Kathir then relays a report that Ibn ʿAbbās said this ayah was later abrogated by Allah's statement, *"Then when the Sacred Months have passed, kill the idolaters wherever you find them"* [9:5]. He gives it as a report from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies a treaty that this exemption fits. Ibn Abī Shaybah narrated from Ḥasan that Surāqah ibn Mālik al-Mudlajī visited the Holy Prophet ﷺ after the events of Badr and Uhud and requested him to make peace with his tribe, Banī Mudlaj. The Prophet ﷺ sent Sayyidnā Khālid ؓ to conclude the treaty, whose terms were: *"We will not support anyone against the Holy Prophet ﷺ. If the Quraysh become Muslims, we too shall become Muslims. All tribes who enter into alliance with us, they too shall become a party with us in this treaty."*

**Second exemption: those whose chests are constricted.** *"or those who approach you with their breasts restraining."* Ibn Kathir describes them as another type of people covered by the exclusion from fighting: those who approach the Muslims with hesitation in their hearts because of their aversion to fighting the Muslims, and who do not have the heart to fight alongside the Muslims against their own people. **They are neither with nor against the Muslims** — and the Qurʾān makes room for them.

**"Had Allah willed, indeed He would have given them power over you, and they would have fought you."** Ibn Kathir: it is from Allah's mercy that He has stopped them from fighting you. The believers are being told that this neutrality is not a weakness in the enemy to be exploited; it is a mercy from Allah to be received with gratitude.

**"So, if they withdraw from you, and fight not against you, and offer you peace"** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, they revert to peace — **"then Allah has made no way for you against them."** Ibn Kathir is direct: *you do not have the right to kill them, as long as they take this position.*

**Al-ʿAbbās at Badr.** Ibn Kathir gives a living example: this was the position of Banū Hāshim, whom he identifies as the tribe of the Prophet ﷺ — men such as Al-ʿAbbās, who accompanied the idolaters in the battle of Badr, for they joined the battle with great hesitation. This is why the Prophet ﷺ commanded that Al-ʿAbbās not be killed, but only captured. The exemption of ayah 90 had a face and a name.

---

## Ayah 91: the ones who play both sides

*"You will find others that wish to have security from you and security from their people."*

Ibn Kathir notes that on the surface these appear to be like the type just mentioned — but the intention of each type is different, for these latter are hypocrites. They pretend to be Muslims with the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, so that they attain safety among the Muslims for their blood, property and families; yet they support the idolaters in secret and worship what they worship, so that they are at peace with them also. Ibn Kathir connects them to Allah's description in Sūrah al-Baqarah: *"But when they are alone with their Shayāṭīn, they say: Truly, we are with you"* [2:14].

**"Every time they are sent back to Fitnah, they yield thereto."** The word used of them here, *urkisū*, is the same one used of them in ayah 88, *arkasahum*. Ibn Kathir explains this phrase as: they dwell in fitnah. As-Suddī said that the *fitnah* mentioned here refers to shirk. Not one slip, then: every time they are returned to it, they settle in.

Ibn Jarīr recorded that Mujāhid said the ayah was revealed about a group from Makkah who used to go to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah pretending to be Muslims, but who reverted to worshipping idols when they went back to Quraysh. **They wanted to be at peace with both sides.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it has been narrated from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ that the people meant here are those of the tribes of Asad and Ghitfān, who professed Islam outwardly when they came to Madinah but confided to their own people that they had really believed in monkeys and scorpions, while before the Muslims they piously declared that they followed their faith. Ḍaḥḥāk, according to a report from Ibn ʿAbbās ؓ, ascribes this conduct to the tribe of ʿAbd al-Dār instead.

**And yet the door is still open.** Even for this group, the ruling is conditional. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah commanded they be fought against *unless* they withdraw from combat and resort to peace — *"If they withdraw not from you, nor offer you peace, nor restrain their hands"* — and only then does the command follow. He glosses each clause: to withdraw means to revert to peaceful and complacent behaviour; to restrain their hands means to refrain from fighting you; *fa-khudhūhum* means capture them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the inference explicitly: since the fighting is commanded should these people refuse to leave you alone and insist on fighting, it can be deduced that **in the event they make peace, there should be no fighting against them.**

**"In their case, We have provided you with a clear warrant against them"** — *sulṭānan mubīnā*. Ibn Kathir: an unequivocal and plain warrant. And that is the answer to the situation ayah 88 opened with. The Companions had been arguing from their own reading of who deserved what. Where there is a warrant, Allah states it unequivocally; where there is none — as with the man sheltering under a treaty, and the man who approaches with his breast restraining — He says just as plainly, *Allah has made no way for you against them.*

---

## The passage as a whole

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the three groups cleanly:

1. **Those who did not emigrate** despite their ability to do so, in a period of time when emigration was a pre-requisite of faith in Islam — or who, after emigrating, went out of the abode of Islam (*Dār al-Islām*) and returned to the abode of disbelief (*Dār al-kufr*). The injunction governing them is similar to that which governs the disbelievers in general.
2. **Those who themselves enter a no-war pact** with the Muslims, or who join hands with those entering into such a pact. **Exempted from being arrested and killed.**
3. **Those who make peace to buy time**, ready to throw all treaty obligations to the winds and join the enemy camp once an occasion to fight arises. They deserve the same as is fixed for the first.

And the two injunctions that run through all of it: **fighting in the absence of peace, and not fighting in the event of peace.**

Two things are worth carrying away. The first is the discipline of the opening rebuke. Two groups of sincere Companions read the same situation in opposite ways, and the Messenger ﷺ was among them and did not prohibit either group from making its case, until revelation came. Zeal on its own did not settle the matter, and Thānavī's remark stands over the whole passage: an interpretation based on sheer opinion, unsupported by proof from the Sharīʿah, carries no reliance, however well-meant.

The second is the shape of the exemptions. In the middle of a passage about enemies and warrants, Allah pauses to protect the man bound by a treaty, and the man who has no heart to fight either side — and tells the believers that his not fighting them is a mercy from Allah. And over all of it stands the word the Prophet ﷺ spoke when the Companions were quarrelling about who should be killed: she is Ṭaybah, and she expels filth, just as the billow expels rust from iron.

passages.title: The blood of a believer: by error, by intent, and by haste
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form a single sustained meditation on the sanctity of a believer's life, examined from three angles in turn: the believer killed **by mistake** and how that wrong is repaired (ayah 92), the believer killed **deliberately** and the terrifying sentence that follows (ayah 93), and the believer nearly killed **by haste** — the soldier who assumes a stranger's profession of faith is a trick (ayah 94). Read together, they teach that Muslim blood is so sacred that even an honest accident demands expiation, deliberate murder is named alongside the gravest of sins, and mere suspicion is never licence to strike.

## "It is not for a believer to kill a believer" (ayah 92)

Ibn Kathir opens by stating the principle absolutely: the believer is not allowed to kill his believing brother under any circumstances. He grounds it in the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, recorded in the Two Sahihs, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The blood of a Muslim who testifies that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah, is sacred, except in three instances: life for life, the married adulterer, and whoever reverts from the religion and abandons the Jama'ah." And even in those three cases, Ibn Kathir stresses, carrying out the penalty belongs to the Muslim leader or his deputy — never to private individuals taking the law into their own hands.

**The occasion of revelation.** The exception "except by mistake" (*illa khata'an*) had a real face behind it. Mujahid and others said the ayah came down about 'Ayyash bin Abi Rabi'ah — Abu Jahl's half-brother through his mother, Asma' bint Makhrabah. 'Ayyash killed a man named Al-Harith bin Yazid Al-'Amiri in revenge, because Al-Harith had tortured him and his brother for their Islam. What 'Ayyash did not know was that Al-Harith had since embraced Islam and made Hijrah. On the day Makkah was conquered, 'Ayyash saw him, took him for the persecutor he remembered, and killed him — and Allah sent down this ayah. It is the perfect illustration of *khata'*: the hand intended the blow, but the heart never intended a believer's blood. A second report, from 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, connects the ayah to a Companion who killed a man who had declared faith just as the sword was raised over him, then excused himself: "He only said that to avert death." The Prophet ﷺ answered, "Have you opened his heart?" Ibn Kathir notes the basis for this story is in the Sahih, though it is not actually about Abu Ad-Darda' as that report claims.

**Two obligations, then the treaty cases.** For killing by mistake the ayah imposes two things. First, a *kaffarah* (expiation) owed to Allah: freeing a believing slave — believing, not any slave, because even an accidental killing of a believer is a great sin needing purification. Imam Ahmad recorded that an Ansari man brought a slave girl to the Prophet ﷺ to test whether freeing her would fulfil this duty. The Prophet ﷺ asked her: Do you testify there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah? That I am the Messenger of Allah? Do you believe in Resurrection after death? When she answered yes to each, he said, "Then free her." Second, the *diyah* (blood money) owed to the bereaved family — unless they remit it, in which case it lapses; a right can be forgiven by its owner. Imam Ahmad and the Sunan compilers record from Ibn Mas'ud — the wording being An-Nasa'i's — that "Allah's Messenger ﷺ determined that the diyah for unintentional murder is twenty camels which entered their fourth year, twenty camels which entered their fifth year, twenty camels which entered their second year, and twenty camels which entered their third year."

Strikingly, this diyah is not paid from the killer's own pocket but by the elders of his tribe — in the Shari'ah's terminology, the *'aqilah*, his kinsmen-guardians. The Two Sahihs record the case Abu Hurayrah relates: two women of Hudhayl quarrelled, one threw a stone killing the other and her unborn child, and the Prophet ﷺ ruled that the fetus's diyah was the freeing of a slave and that the woman's diyah fell on the killer's tribal elders. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wisdom: the guardians are not wholly innocent, for they failed to restrain their member from such recklessness — and the prospect of paying will make them vigilant in future. Ibn Kathir adds a related principle from what Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih from 'Abdullah bin 'Umar: when Khalid bin Al-Walid killed people of Banu Jadhimah who, not knowing how to say "we have become Muslims," cried "Saba'na, Saba'na," the Prophet ﷺ raised his hands and said, "O Allah! I declare my innocence before You of what Khalid did" — then sent 'Ali to pay their diyah and compensate every loss, down to a dog's bowl. The mistake of the leader's deputy is paid from the Muslim treasury.

The ayah then works through three scenarios. If the victim was a believer but his people are at war with the Muslims, only the freeing of a slave is due — combatant disbelievers receive no diyah. If he belonged to a people bound to the Muslims by treaty — Ahl adh-Dhimmah (protected non-Muslim residents) or a peace-pact people — the diyah goes to his family, with the slave-freeing added if the deceased was a believer. And whoever cannot find a slave to free must fast two consecutive months, unbroken; if broken without a valid excuse such as illness, menstruation or post-natal bleeding, the fast begins again. All of this the ayah calls *tawbatan min Allah* — "a repentance from Allah": this is how the accidental killer returns to his Lord, "And Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise."

**The jurists' map.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets these ayat within a complete scheme: victims fall into four classes (Muslim, Dhimmi, peace-pact beneficiary, belligerent disbeliever) and killing is either intentional or accidental — eight forms in all, each with its ruling drawn from this passage, from Surah al-Baqarah's law of *qisas* (even retaliation), or from hadith. It further distinguishes three kinds of homicide: *qatl al-'amd* (intentional, with a weapon that cuts), *qatl shibh al-'amd* (quasi-intentional — deliberate, but without such a weapon), and *qatl al-khata'* (accidental). Both of the latter carry diyah and sin — Maʿārif records the rule that the quasi-intentional killing's diyah is one hundred camels of four types, twenty-five of each, while the accidental killing's is one hundred camels of five types, twenty of each — but the quasi-intentional is more sinful because killing was intended, while the accidental flows from mere heedlessness. And Maʿārif adds a sobering caveat: these categories govern worldly law, but the reality of intention lies in the heart, known to Allah alone — before Him, what courts call accidental may be intentional, and the reverse. Among its practical rulings: the kaffarah must come from the killer himself even though the diyah falls on the 'aqilah; the diyah of a Muslim and a Dhimmi is equal; the diyah is distributed like inheritance, so any heir may forgive his share; and in intentional killing there is no kaffarah at all — only repentance remains.

## The deliberate murderer (ayah 93)

Then comes the most fearsome sentence in the Qur'an on this subject: whoever kills a believer intentionally, "his recompense is Hell to abide therein; and the wrath and the curse of Allah are upon him, and a great punishment is prepared for him." Ibn Kathir observes that this sin is mentioned alongside Shirk itself in several places in Allah's Book — as in Surat Al-Furqan (25:68) and Al-An'am (6:151). From the Sunnah: the Two Sahihs record from Ibn Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Blood offenses are the first disputes to be judged between the people on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dawud recorded from 'Ubadah bin As-Samit that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The believer will remain unburdened in righteousness as long as he does not shed prohibited blood. When he sheds forbidden blood, he will become burdened." And another hadith states that the destruction of this entire world is less significant before Allah than the killing of one Muslim.

**Can such a murderer repent?** Here the Salaf genuinely differed, and Ibn Kathir presents both views. Ibn 'Abbas held that the deliberate murderer's repentance is not accepted: Al-Bukhari records that Ibn Jubayr, finding the scholars of Kufah divided, travelled to Ibn 'Abbas, who told him this ayah "was the last revealed on this subject and nothing abrogated it" (Muslim and An-Nasa'i also recorded it). The majority of scholars, early and later, held that his repentance can be accepted: if he returns to Allah humbly and works righteousness, Allah will change his evil deeds into good ones and Himself compensate the victim by rewarding him for his suffering. They cite Al-Furqan 25:68–70, which excepts "those who repent and believe and do righteous deeds," and Az-Zumar 39:53 — "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves! Despair not of the mercy of Allah" — which Ibn Kathir calls general over every sin, while the ayah "Verily, Allah forgives not that partners should be set up with Him, but He forgives what is less than that to whom He wills" — mentioned, he notes, in this very Surah both before and after this passage to encourage hope in Allah — excludes only Shirk from what Allah may forgive. He also recalls the man of the Children of Israel, confirmed in the Two Sahihs, who killed a hundred people, was told by a scholar "What is there that would prevent you from repentance?", set out for a land where Allah was worshipped, died on the road — and was taken by the angel of mercy. If that door stood open for an Israelite, Ibn Kathir argues, it is even more fitting for this Ummah, relieved of former burdens and sent the easy way of Hanifiyyah.

How then to read the ayah's threat? Abu Hurayrah and several of the Salaf said: this is his recompense *if* Allah chooses to punish him — as with every threatened sin, good deeds or divine pardon may intervene. And even if the murderer does enter the Fire, he does not remain in it forever but only for a long time, for mutawatir hadiths (reports transmitted so widely their authenticity is beyond doubt) state that whoever has the least speck of faith in his heart shall ultimately depart the Fire. The threat is left standing in its full terror — yet the door of mercy is not welded shut.

## "Do not say to the one who greets you: You are not a believer" (ayah 94)

The passage closes by cutting off the sin at its most common root among fighters: haste built on suspicion. Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Ikrimah said that Ibn 'Abbas said — At-Tirmidhi recorded it in his Tafsir and graded it Hasan — that a man of Banu Sulaym, tending his sheep, passed a party of the Prophet's ﷺ Companions and offered them the Salam. They said to one another, "He only said Salam to protect himself from us," attacked him, killed him, and brought his sheep to the Prophet ﷺ — and this ayah came down. Ibn 'Abbas said pointedly: "The goods of this world were those sheep." Imam Ahmad alone also records the account of 'Abdullah bin Abi Hadrad's expedition to Idam, where Muhallam bin Juthamah killed 'Amr bin Al-Adbat after he had greeted them, over an old grudge. And Al-Bukhari (briefly, without a complete chain) with Al-Bazzar (in a connected, detailed chain) record the story of Al-Miqdad, who killed a man who stood his ground reciting "There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah," assuming the words were only to save his wealth. In Al-Bazzar's narration the Prophet ﷺ summoned him: "O Miqdad! Did you kill a man who proclaimed, 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah'? What would you do when you face 'There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah' tomorrow?" Maʿārif notes that the scholars see no contradiction between these reports — all these events together could be the cause of revelation.

The ayah's rebuke is layered. *Fa-tabayyanu* — "verify" — forbids acting on conjecture; Maʿārif quotes the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that acting with deliberation is from Allah and rushing is from Shaytan. "Seeking the perishable goods of the worldly life" exposes the motive underneath the suspicion — the victim's flock, camel, or wealth — and Allah answers it: "There is much more benefit with Allah." Most piercing of all: "so were you yourselves before, till Allah conferred on you His Favors." Sa'id bin Jubayr explained: you too once hid your faith, just as this shepherd hid his. The Prophet ﷺ said the same to Al-Miqdad: the slain man was a believer concealing his faith among disbelievers, "just as you used to hide your faith in Makkah before." The one you cut down may be exactly what you once were. Maʿārif adds that "the Salam" here can be read as the Muslim greeting or, more broadly, as any offer of submission to Allah — either way, it must be taken at face value. The closing words, "Allah is Ever Well-Aware of what you do," are, as Sa'id bin Jubayr said, a threat and a warning.

**The enduring ruling.** From this ayah Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a principle that far outlives the battlefield: whoever professes Islam — by the Kalimah, or by its marked signs such as the Adhan and Salah — must be treated as a Muslim. Peering into hearts is not our business; the Companions were never asked to prove their inner sincerity, and neither may we demand it of others. Even a Muslim who neglects prayer and fasting and falls into sins is not thereby expelled from Islam; Imam Abu Hanifah said, "We do not call the people of the Qiblah Kafirs because of a sin." Only positive, unambiguous proof of disbelief — words or deeds that admit no other interpretation, as with Musaylimah the Liar, who recited the Kalimah yet claimed prophethood and was declared an apostate by consensus of the Companions — changes that judgment. Between those limits, the rule of this passage stands: judge by what is apparent, leave hearts to Allah, and treat every believer's blood as what these three ayat declare it to be — sacred.

passages.title: Those who strive and those who sit at home
passages.tafsir:
# Not Equal: The Ones Who Go Out and the Ones Who Stay Behind (4:95–96)

This short passage draws a line of honour through the community of believers: those who strive in Allah's cause with their wealth and their lives are not on the same level as the able-bodied who stay at home — yet Allah immediately carves out those with a genuine excuse, and promises good to *everyone* who believes. The two ayat work as a single sentence of divine justice: ayah 95 states the comparison and the exception, and ayah 96 unfolds what the preference actually consists of — degrees of rank, forgiveness, and mercy from Him.

## The moment of revelation: an exception written in real time

Few ayat in the Qur'an let us watch revelation being adjusted before our eyes the way this one does.

Al-Bukhari records from Al-Bara' that when the words "Not equal are those of the believers who sit (at home)" came down, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called Zayd and commanded him to write it. Then Ibn Umm Maktum — a blind Companion — came and mentioned his blindness. And Allah revealed the addition: *ghayru ulī al-ḍarar*, "except those who are disabled."

Al-Bukhari also preserves a fuller, more vivid account. Sahl bin Sa'd As-Sa'di relates that he saw Marwan bin Al-Hakam sitting in the masjid and sat by his side; Marwan told him what Zayd bin Thabit had told him — that Allah's Messenger ﷺ was dictating this very ayah to Zayd when Ibn Umm Maktum arrived and pleaded: "O Allah's Messenger! By Allah, if I had power, I would surely take part in Jihad." Then, Zayd relates, Allah sent down revelation to His Messenger ﷺ while his thigh rested on Zayd's own — and it grew so heavy that Zayd feared his thigh would be broken. When it ended, Allah had revealed "except those who are disabled."

At-Tirmidhi records a related report from Ibn 'Abbas connecting the ayah to the battle of Badr: it distinguishes those who went out to Badr from those who did not, and when the battle was about to occur, Abu Ahmad bin Jahsh and Ibn Umm Maktum asked, "We are blind, O Messenger of Allah! Do we have an excuse?" — and the exception was revealed. Of this wording, At-Tirmidhi said "Hasan Gharib."

Ibn Kathir draws out the sequence: the first statement, "Not equal are those of the believers who sit," was **general**. Soon after, the revelation came with the exception. So whoever has a real disability — blindness, a limp, an illness that prevents joining the fight — is *not* placed in the comparison at all. The unfavourable comparison falls only on those who were able and still stayed behind.

Notice what this scene teaches about Allah and His Book. A single blind man's anguished honesty — "if I had power, I would surely take part" — was answered by fresh revelation, and the answer was written permanently into the Qur'an for every excused believer until the end of time.

## Reading the ayat phrase by phrase

**"Those who sit" and "those who strive" (ayah 95).** The passage names the two groups by their posture: *al-qāʿidūn*, the ones sitting at home, and *al-mujāhidūn*, the ones striving in the cause of Allah "with their wealth and their lives." The striving the ayah honours is total — it costs a person both what he owns and what he is, his property and his very life.

**"Unto each, Allah has promised good" (ayah 95).** Before any believer despairs, the ayah itself insists: *both* groups have been promised *al-ḥusnā* — which Ibn Kathir explains as Paradise and tremendous rewards. The difference between them is one of ranking, not of acceptance versus rejection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that this clause "gives peace of mind to those who are engaged in religious duties other than Jihad."

**"Degrees from Him, and forgiveness and mercy" (ayah 96).** Ayah 96 then spells out what the "huge reward" of the mujāhidīn contains: elevated degrees, forgiveness, and mercy — Ibn Kathir describes it as rooms in Paradise, forgiveness, and the descent of mercy and blessing, "as a favor and honor from Him." The passage closes on Allah's names: "And Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" — the whole hierarchy of reward rests finally on His forgiveness and mercy, not on anyone's deserving.

How high do those degrees go? In the Two Sahihs, Abu Saʿid Al-Khudri relates that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are a hundred grades in Paradise that Allah has prepared for the Mujahidin in His cause; between each two grades is the distance between heaven and Earth."

## The excused are not left behind

The exception clause is not a grudging concession — it is a door into one of the most consoling teachings in the Sunnah. Al-Bukhari records in his Sahih from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are people who remained in Al-Madinah who were with you in every march you marched and every valley you crossed." The Companions asked, astonished, "While they are still in Al-Madinah, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes. Only their disability hindered them."

A believer whose body fails him but whose heart is on the road shares in the reward of the road. The ayah excludes the excused from the *comparison*; the Prophet ﷺ includes them in the *company*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the ruling plainly: Jihad is not obligatory on the lame, the crippled, the blind, the sick, and others who are excusable under Islamic law.

## What the scholars derived: a collective duty — Fard Kifayah

Commenting on the clause "Unto each, Allah has promised good," Ibn Kathir states that this ayah indicates that jihad is not *farḍ* on each and every individual, but *Fard Kifayah* — a collective duty.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing the leading exegetes, opens this term up. **Fard Kifayah** ("obligation of sufficiency") stands opposite **Fard ʿAyn** (an obligation on every individual). A Fard Kifayah is fulfilled on behalf of the whole community when enough people discharge it — but if nobody does, everyone shares the sin. Most collective religious duties work this way: teaching and spreading the religious sciences; the funeral prayer, washing, and shrouding of the deceased; building mosques and religious schools; running works of public welfare. The wisdom, Maʿārif explains, is a principle of *distribution of work*: some serve in defence, others in education and daʿwah, others in meeting the community's various needs — and all these labourers are covered by "unto each, Allah has promised good."

But the classification is conditional, not permanent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān maps its limits: jihad is Fard Kifayah *under normal conditions*, when those engaged in it suffice for the defence. If they do not suffice, it becomes Fard ʿAyn on the Muslims of the neighbouring areas; if that is still not enough, the obligation widens ring by ring — until, in the extreme case, every Muslim from the East to the West could be bound by it as a solemn religious obligation.

## Living the passage

Two truths hold this passage in balance, and a believer needs both.

First: sacrifice matters, and Allah does not flatten it. Where real striving with wealth and life is needed and a person is able, comfort is not equal to contribution — "not equal" is Allah's own verdict, and He backs it with a hundred grades of Paradise.

Second: sincerity under excuse loses nothing. The believer kept back by illness, disability, or genuine incapacity — whose longing is that of Ibn Umm Maktum, "if I had power, I would surely take part" — marches, in Allah's record, with those who marched. And over both groups stands the closing promise of ayah 96: Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: Emigration, the excused, and dying en route
passages.tafsir:
# The Reckoning of Those Who Stayed Behind (4:97–100)

This passage is a single, tightly-built unit about hijrah — emigration for the sake of the faith. It moves through three groups in sequence: those who could have emigrated from a land of persecution but stayed until death overtook them (ayah 97); the genuinely helpless who could not leave and whom Allah excuses (ayat 98–99); and those who do set out, for whom Allah promises refuge on earth and — even if they die on the road before arriving — a reward made binding upon Himself (ayah 100). What holds the ayat together is a question of where a believer plants his feet when his faith is at stake, and the answer runs from the sternest warning in the passage to one of the most tender promises in the sūrah.

## The scene at the moment of death

Ayah 97 opens with a scene, not a ruling: the angels are taking souls in death, and they find those souls "wronging themselves" — ẓālimī anfusihim. Ibn Kathir explains that their wrong was precisely their refraining from hijrah: they resided among the idolaters while able to perform hijrah and unable to practice the faith, and he records that such people fall into a prohibition "according to the consensus" as well as by the plain sense of this ayah.

Then comes the interrogation. The angels ask, "In what (condition) were you?" — which Ibn Kathir glosses as: why did you remain here and not perform hijrah? The souls answer, "We were weak and oppressed on the earth," meaning, in his words, that they claim to be unable to leave the land or move about in the earth. And the angels reply with a question of their own: "Was not the earth of Allah spacious enough for you to emigrate therein?" Then the sentence falls: "Such men will find their abode in Hell — what an evil destination."

## The occasion: Muslims in the ranks of the enemy

Ibn Kathir gives the story behind the ayah, and it is sobering. Al-Bukhari recorded from Muhammad bin ʿAbdur-Rahman, Abu Al-Aswad, that ʿIkrimah, the freed slave of Ibn ʿAbbas, related from Ibn ʿAbbas: some Muslims used to go out with the idolaters, increasing the size of their army against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. An arrow would hit one of them and kill him, or he would be struck on his neck with a sword and killed — and Allah sent down this ayah about them. (Abu Al-Aswad recounted this when ʿIkrimah strongly forbade him from enlisting in an army being raised in Madinah — the lesson of the ayah was applied across generations.)

Ad-Dahhak adds that the ayah was revealed about hypocrites who did not join the Messenger of Allah ﷺ but remained in Makkah, went out with the idolaters for the battle of Badr, and were killed among the slain. Either way, the picture is the same: people who professed Islam ended their lives physically standing in the ranks arrayed against the Prophet ﷺ, having never made the break that faith demanded.

Ibn Kathir reinforces the seriousness of residing among the enemies of the faith with a hadith recorded by Abu Dawud from Samurah bin Jundub, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever mingles with the idolator and resides with him, he is just like him."

## The excused — and the certainty hidden in "likely"

Ayah 98 immediately carves out the exception: "Except the weak ones among men, women and children who cannot devise a plan, nor are they able to direct their way."
