Ibn Kathir explains that this is an excuse Allah Himself grants: these people cannot free themselves from the idolaters, and even if they could, they would not know which way to go. Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and As-Suddi all explained "who cannot devise a plan, nor are they able to direct their way" as: they simply do not find the way to emigrate.

Ayah 99 says of them: "These are they whom Allah is likely to forgive them" — ʿasā Allāhu an yaʿfuwa ʿanhum. Ibn Kathir makes a point every reader should hold onto: this means Allah will pardon them for not migrating, "and here, 'likely' means He shall." From the Generous One, what sounds tentative is in fact a promise. The ayah seals it with two of His names: "and Allah is Ever Oft-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving."

Two narrations from al-Bukhari put faces on this category:

**The Prophet's ﷺ prayer for the trapped.** Abu Hurayrah related that while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was praying ʿIsha, he said "Samiʿ Allahu Liman Hamidah," and then, before he prostrated, supplicated: "O Allah! Save ʿAyyash bin Abi Rabiʿah. O Allah! Save Salamah bin Hisham. O Allah! Save Al-Walid bin Al-Walid. O Allah! Save the weak Muslims. O Allah! Be very hard on Mudar tribe. O Allah! Afflict them with years (of famine) similar to the (famine) years of the time of Prophet Yusuf." He named individual believers, one by one, among the weak Muslims — the very mustaḍʿafīn (the oppressed-as-weak) of these ayat — and carried them into the middle of his prayer.

**Ibn ʿAbbas's testimony.** Al-Bukhari also recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said of "Except the weak ones among men": "I and my mother were among those (weak ones) whom Allah excused." The exception in ayah 98 was not an abstraction; a child who would become one of the greatest scholars of this ummah lived inside it.

## What hijrah actually is

Since the whole passage turns on this word, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān pauses to define it. Lexically, hijrah comes from a root meaning "being displeased with something and leaving it." In common parlance it means leaving one's home country; in the terminology of the Sharīʿah it means leaving Dār al-Kufr (a homeland of disbelief) for Dār al-Islām (the abode of Islam) — a definition Maʿārif cites from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī. Mulla ʿAli al-Qari, in Sharh al-Mishkāh, adds that leaving a home country for religious reasons is also included, and from Sūrah 59:8 ("Those who have been driven away from their homes...") we learn that being forcibly expelled for being Muslim counts as hijrah too. What does not count, Maʿārif notes pointedly, is relocating merely to benefit from business or employment opportunities — such a person is not a muhājir in the legal sense.

Then Maʿārif widens the word beyond geography with a hadith from al-Bukhari and Muslim: "Muhajir is one who leaves everything Allah and His Messenger have prohibited" — whose full sense, Maʿārif says, becomes clear from the first sentence of the same hadith: "A Muslim is the one from whom all Muslims remain safe - (safe) from his tongue and (safe) from his hands" (Tirmidh, Kitab al-Iman). The true and successful muhājir does not consider crossing a border the ultimate obligation; he leaves everything the Sharīʿah has declared unlawful. Maʿārif puts it poetically: when you change into the iḥrām garment, better change your heart too.

## Ayah 100: the promise — and dying on the road

Having warned and excused, the passage turns to encourage. "He who emigrates in the cause of Allah, will find on earth many dwelling places and plenty to live by." Ibn Kathir says this encourages the believers to perform hijrah and abandon the idolaters, for wherever the believer emigrates he will find a safe refuge to resort to. The key word is murāgham — Maʿārif explains it as a verbal noun meaning to move from one land to another, also used for the place to which one moves and settles. Ibn Kathir records Mujahid's reading of "many dwelling places": the emigrant "will find a way out of what he dislikes"; and "plenty to live by" refers to provision. Qatadah goes further: "Allah will take him from misguidance to guidance and from poverty to richness." The ayah is answering, point by point, the fears that keep people from leaving — no home, no livelihood — with Allah's guarantee of both.

Maʿārif documents how history vindicated the promise: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) migrated from his homeland in Iraq to Syria and Allah gave him all those things; Musa and the Children of Israel migrated from Egypt and were given the land of Syria, a better homeland — then Egypt too; and when the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions left Makkah, they found in Madinah the best of shelter — honour, power, peace and prosperity, once the transitory hardships of the early period passed. There were many Companions who were poor in their home-city of Makkah whom Allah made rich and happy after hijrah. Abu Hurayrah, when appointed the governor of a province, used to address himself with relish: "O Abu Hurairah, you are the same man, the servant of a tribe," recalling how his salary had been what he could eat, and how "Today, because of Islam, you are here, so high from so low, and they call you the Commander of the Faithful!"

Then the ayah reaches its most consoling clause: "And whosoever leaves his home as an emigrant unto Allah and His Messenger, and death overtakes him, his reward is then surely incumbent upon Allah." Ibn Kathir: whoever starts emigrating and dies on the way will acquire the reward of those who emigrate for Allah. Maʿārif relates that according to some narrations this clause was revealed about Khalid ibn Hizam, who left Makkah intending hijrah to Ethiopia and died of a snakebite on the way. He never arrived — and the Qurʼan declares his wage established with Allah.

Two hadiths in the sources illuminate this clause:

**Deeds are by intentions.** The Two Sahihs, along with the Musnad and Sunan compilers, record from ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions, and every person will be rewarded according to what he has intended. So, whoever emigrated to Allah and His Messenger, then his emigration is for Allah and His Messenger. And whoever emigrated for worldly benefits or for a woman to marry, his emigration is for what he emigrated for." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith is general — it applies to hijrah as well as every other deed. The man who dies en route earns the emigrant's reward because the intention was complete even though the journey was not; the man who arrives with a worldly intention earns only what he sought.

**The man who killed a hundred.** In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that a man who had killed ninety-nine people completed the hundred by killing a worshipper, then asked a scholar whether he had a chance to repent. "What prevents you from repentance?" the scholar replied, and told him to emigrate to a land where Allah is worshipped. He set out — and death overtook him on the way. The angels of mercy and the angels of torment disputed over him: the former said he had gone out in repentance, the latter that he had never arrived at his destination. They were commanded to measure the distance between the two lands, and to whichever land he was closer, he would be counted as its people. Allah commanded the righteous land to move closer and the land of evil to move farther, and he was found to have died a hand-span closer to the land he intended — so the angels of mercy captured his soul. In another narration, when death came to him he moved his chest towards the righteous village. The story is the ayah enacted: a lifetime of sin on one side, a single sincere journey cut short on the other, and Allah's mercy tipping the scale by a hand-span He Himself moved.

Maʿārif also conveys a saying of the Holy Prophet ﷺ that hijrah will undo all sins which may have been committed before it — which is exactly what the murderer's story shows.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a few clear demands. First: faith is not compatible with settling into a situation that makes practising it impossible while a way out exists — "Was not the earth of Allah spacious enough?" is a question the angels themselves will ask. Second: Allah's excuse is real and generous for those genuinely without plan or path — the standard is true inability, like Ibn ʿAbbas and his mother, not mere inconvenience. Third: what sanctifies any departure is its intention; Maʿārif applies this bluntly to emigrants of every era — those who migrate truly for Allah's sake are muhājirūn with all the promised blessings, those who migrate to make money or marry receive exactly what they migrated for, and those living in distress should correct their intention and then witness the truth of Allah's promise with their own eyes. And finally, the passage ends where every believer hopes to end: with a Lord who is "Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful," who counts the journey even when death arrives before the destination.

passages.title: Shortened and fear prayer on campaign
passages.tafsir:
# The Prayer That Never Lapses: Qasr and the Fear Prayer (4:101–104)

This passage answers a question every traveling and campaigning believer must face: what happens to the prayer when life is dangerous, hurried, and uncertain? The answer these four ayat give is remarkable — the prayer is never suspended, not even with an enemy army in sight; instead, Allah Himself adjusts its form to the situation. What binds the ayat together is a single graduated system: ayah 101 gives the concession of shortening the prayer on a journey, ayah 102 gives the extraordinary \"fear prayer\" for when the enemy is actually at hand, ayah 103 commands remembrance afterwards and restores the prayer to its full form once safety returns, and ayah 104 turns from worship to morale, urging the believers not to falter in pursuit of their enemy. As Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes, the preceding verses dealt with jihad and hijrah — and since both involve travel, with a strong likelihood of confronting the enemy on the way, these verses now spell out the concessions granted for prayer under exactly those conditions.

## Ayah 101 — Shortening the prayer: \"a gift from Allah\"

The ayah opens, \"When you travel through the land…\" The Arabic is *wa-idhā ḍarabtum fī al-arḍ* — literally \"when you strike out in the land.\" Ibn Kathir shows this is the Qurʼān's idiom for travel by citing the parallel in 73:20, where Allah speaks of those \"*yaḍribūna* (traveling) through the land, seeking of Allah's bounty.\" The concession itself, Ibn Kathir explains, is to reduce the four-unit prayers to two units. This shortening is called **Qasr** — as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān defines it, the reduction of the four obligatory rakʿāt of Zuhr, ʿAsr and ʿIshāʼ to two while in the state of travel (*safar*).

But the ayah attaches what looks like a condition: \"…if you fear that the disbelievers may put you in trial.\" Does that mean shortening is only allowed when there is danger? This very question troubled the Companions themselves, and the answer they received is the heart of this ayah.

**The question ʿUmar asked.** Imam Ahmad records that Yaʿlā bin Umayyah said, \"I asked ʿUmar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb about the verse… Allah has granted Muslims safety now?\" ʿUmar replied, \"I wondered about the same thing and asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it, and he said: **'A gift that Allah has bestowed on you, so accept His gift.'**\" Muslim and the collectors of the Sunan recorded this hadith; At-Tirmidhi said, \"Hasan Sahih,\" and ʿAli bin Al-Madīnī affirmed its soundness, noting that its narrators are all known. The word the Prophet ﷺ used is *ṣadaqah* — a charity, a gift. Shortening the prayer is not a grudging emergency measure; it is a favour Allah has given, and refusing a gift is poor manners with the Giver.

The same answer came from the next generation. Abu Bakr Ibn Abī Shaybah records that when Abu Hanzalah Al-Hadhāʼ asked Ibn ʿUmar, \"We are safe now\" — why still shorten? — Ibn ʿUmar answered simply, \"This is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.\" And the Prophet's ﷺ own practice confirms it: Al-Bukhari records from Anas, \"We went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from Al-Madinah to Makkah; he used to pray two rakʿahs until we went back to Al-Madinah\" — a journey during which they stayed in Makkah ten days. Imam Ahmad records that Harithah bin Wahb Al-Khuzāʿī said, \"I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ for the Zuhr and ʿAsr prayers in Mina, when the people were numerous and very safe, and he prayed two rakʿahs\" — a hadith recorded by the Group with the exception of Ibn Majah; in Al-Bukhari's wording, \"The Prophet ﷺ led us in the prayer at Mina during the peace period by offering two rakʿahs.\"

**Why then does the ayah mention fear at all?** Ibn Kathir's explanation is a small lesson in how to read the Qurʼān. The fear clause \"refers to the typical type of fear prevalent when this ayah was revealed\": in the early period after the Hijrah, the Muslims experienced fear during most of their travels — most surrounding territory belonged to combatant enemies, and journeys were largely military expeditions. The ayah describes the normal circumstance of its first audience, not a legal condition. Ibn Kathir observes that when the prevailing circumstances cease or a new situation prevails, \"decrees of this nature may not be understood,\" and he adduces two other verses of the same kind: \"And force not your slave girls to prostitution, *if they desire chastity*\" (24:33), and \"And your stepdaughters, under your guardianship, born of your wives whom you have gone into.\" The fear clause here is wording of that nature — it reflects the prevailing situation at the time of revelation. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states the resulting rule plainly: even if there is no fear of danger on a journey, Qasr is still observed.

**Practical rulings.** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān gathers the fiqh: Qasr applies only to the four-rakʿah obligatory prayers — Zuhr, ʿAsr and ʿIshāʼ; there is no shortening of Maghrib or Fajr, nor of Sunnah or Witr prayers. On its reckoning, a journey of less than 48 miles takes the full prayer, and a traveler who intends to stay somewhere fifteen days or more prays in full there, since it has become a place of residence; an intended stay of less than fifteen days keeps the rules of travel in force. And to those troubled by a scruple — the feeling that praying two instead of four must somehow be a deficiency — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān answers directly: this apprehension is misplaced, for Qasr is itself a rule of the Sharīʿah, and following it brings no sin; on the contrary, it brings reward.

## Ayah 102 — The fear prayer: worship under arms

Ayah 102 legislates something more dramatic: congregational prayer with the enemy in view, weapons in hand. \"When you are among them and lead them in prayer, let one party of them stand up with you, taking their arms with them…\" One group prays behind the Prophet ﷺ while the other stands guard; then they exchange places, so that everyone prays and no one leaves the army exposed. The ayah even names the enemy's hope — that the Muslims might grow \"negligent of your arms and your baggage\" so they could \"attack you in a single rush\" — and then grants a concession within the concession: no sin in laying the weapons aside \"because of the inconvenience of rain or because you are ill,\" yet still, \"take every precaution for yourselves.\"

**The occasion at ʿUsfān.** Imam Ahmad records from Abu ʿAyyāsh Az-Zuraqī: \"We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the area of ʿUsfān (a well-known place near Makkah), when the idolators met us under the command of Khalid bin Al-Walid, and they were between us and the Qiblah.\" The Prophet ﷺ led the Muslims in Zuhr, and the idolators — watching an entire army bow and prostrate in unison — realised what they had missed: \"They were busy with something during which we had a chance to attack them.\" They resolved to strike at the next prayer, ʿAsr, \"a prayer that is dearer to them than their children and themselves.\" But between Zuhr and ʿAsr, Jibrīl came down with these very ayat. When ʿAsr came, the Prophet ﷺ arranged the army in two lines behind him: all bowed together, but only the front line prostrated with him while the rear stood guard; then the lines exchanged positions for the second rakʿah, and each took its turn to prostrate while the other watched the enemy. The narration notes he prayed it this way twice — once at ʿUsfān and once in the land of Banu Sulaym. This is the narration recorded by Abu Dawud and An-Nasaʼi, and, as Ibn Kathir notes, it has an authentic chain of narration and many other texts to support it. The scene explains the ayah perfectly: the plotted ambush never came, because revelation arrived first.

**Many forms, one principle.** Ibn Kathir explains that the fear prayer has no single fixed shape, \"for the enemy is sometimes in the direction of the Qiblah and sometimes in another direction,\" and the prayer being protected may be four rakʿahs, three (Maghrib), or two. Al-Bukhari records Ibn ʿAbbās describing one form; Imam Ahmad and An-Nasaʼi record Jabir describing another, in which the Prophet ﷺ prayed two rakʿahs while each group prayed one with him; Ibn Abī Ḥātim records from Sālim, from his father, a form in which each group prayed one rakʿah behind him and then each stood to complete one more rakʿah on its own while the other guarded — a narration the Group collected. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān makes the same point about this last form: the ayah mentions each group praying one rakʿah, and the method of completing the second appears in the hadith.

When battle is actually raging and even this arrangement is impossible, Ibn Kathir says they pray individually, facing the Qiblah or not, riding or on foot — even walking and fighting while performing the acts of the prayer. Some scholars held that in that extremity the prayer becomes a single rakʿah, on the strength of Ibn ʿAbbās's words: \"By the words of your Prophet ﷺ, Allah has ordained the prayer of four rakʿahs while residing, two rakʿahs during travel, and one rakʿah during fear\" — recorded by Muslim, Abu Dawud, An-Nasaʼi and Ibn Majah. Ibn Kathir attributes this view to Ahmad bin Hanbal, and Al-Mundhirī lists ʿAṭāʼ, Jabir, Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Al-Hakam, Qatadah and Hammad with it, Ṭāwūs and Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk preferring it. Ishaq bin Rāhwayh went furthest: in raging battle, one rakʿah with a nod of the head suffices — and if even that is impossible, a single prostration, \"because the prostration is remembrance of Allah.\" The doctrine underneath all these forms is one: the connection to Allah is never severed, however desperate the hour.

**Two clarifications from Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān.** First, the ayah's address — \"when *you* (O Prophet) are among them\" — must not be read to mean the fear prayer lapsed with the Prophet's ﷺ passing. That wording reflects the situation of the time, when no one could excuse himself from praying behind the Prophet ﷺ; after him, whoever leads stands in his place, and all leading religious authorities agree that Ṣalāt al-Khawf remains operative and has not been abrogated. Second, the concession is not limited to human enemies: the fear prayer is likewise permissible for one gripped by fear of a beast — a lion or a python — when little time remains for the prayer.

On the weapons themselves, Ibn Kathir notes that a group of scholars held carrying arms in the fear prayer to be obligatory by the apparent sense of the ayah — and the rain-and-illness exemption testifies to it, for a stated exception implies a standing command. Even those excused must \"take every precaution,\" keeping their weapons within easy reach. The ayah closes with the assurance that gives the whole arrangement its confidence: \"Verily, Allah has prepared a humiliating torment for the disbelievers.\"

## Ayah 103 — Remembrance in every posture, and the prayer's fixed appointment

\"When the prayers are over, remember Allah — standing, sitting, and lying on your sides.\" Ibn Kathir draws out a subtle point: dhikr (remembrance of Allah) is encouraged after every prayer, so why single it out after the fear prayer? Because in the fear prayer the pillars of the prayer are diminished — the movements, the guard duty, the abbreviated form — so the remembrance afterwards compensates for what the circumstances curtailed. He compares it to Allah's saying about the Sacred Months, \"wrong not yourselves therein\" (9:36): injustice is forbidden all year, but the prohibition is emphasised where the sanctity is greatest. \"Standing, sitting down, and on your sides\" means, he says, *in all conditions* — remembrance has no posture and no battlefield exemption.

Then the counterweight to every concession in the passage: \"But when you are secure, establish the prayer.\" When safety returns and fear subsides, the prayer returns to its full form — \"performing it as you were commanded; fulfilling its obligations, with humbleness, completing the bowing and prostration positions.\" The concessions were for the circumstance, never a downgrade of the prayer itself.

The ayah ends with the reason none of this could simply be postponed: \"Verily, the prayer is *kitāban mawqūtan* upon the believers\" — enjoined at fixed hours. Ibn ʿAbbās explained *kitāban* as \"enjoined,\" and added, \"The prayer has a fixed time, just as is the case with Hajj.\" Similar explanations are reported from Mujahid, Sālim bin ʿAbdullah, ʿAli bin Al-Husayn, Muhammad bin ʿAli, Al-Hasan, Muqātil, As-Suddī and ʿAṭiyah Al-ʿAwfī. This single phrase is the key to the whole passage: because the prayer's times are divinely appointed, it cannot be deferred until the war is over — so its *form* bends while its *time* stands.

## Ayah 104 — \"You hope from Allah what they cannot hope for\"

Having secured the army's worship, the passage turns to its resolve: \"Do not falter in pursuit of the enemy.\" Ibn Kathir explains: do not weaken your resolve; pursue them vigorously, fight them, and remain wary of them. The ayah then makes an argument of striking psychological honesty. It does not pretend the believers feel no pain: \"if you are suffering, they too are suffering as you are suffering.\" Wounds, exhaustion, loss — these fall on both sides alike, as Allah says elsewhere, \"If you suffer a harm, be sure a similar harm has struck the others\" (3:140). The difference lies in what the pain is *for*: \"but you have hope from Allah for that which they cannot hope.\" Ibn Kathir: you and they are equal in injury and pain, but you hope for Allah's reward, victory and aid, as He has promised in His Book and by the words of His Messenger ﷺ — and Allah's promise is true — while your enemies have no such hope. Therefore, he concludes, it is you, not they, who should be the more eager, \"so that you establish the Word of Allah and raise it high.\" Equal pain plus unequal hope yields unequal endurance.

The passage seals with two of Allah's names: \"and Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise.\" Ibn Kathir comments that He is most knowledgeable and wise in all that He decides, decrees, wills and enacts of worldly and religious ordainments, and is worthy of praise in all conditions. It is a fitting seal for four ayat of finely calibrated law: the One who shortened the prayer for the traveler, choreographed it for the soldier, and restored it in security knows His servants' circumstances perfectly — and every concession He grants is a gift to be accepted with gratitude.

passages.title: Do not plead for the treacherous
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat command the Prophet ﷺ — and through him every believer — to judge by what Allah has revealed and never to lend advocacy to people who are treacherous, however skilfully they present their case. What binds the passage together is a single dramatic incident in Madinah: a theft, a cover-up, and an attempt to pin the crime on an innocent man — until revelation itself intervened to expose the truth.

## The story behind the revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the episode in full, noting that ayat 105–113 all came down concerning it. The central figure was a man of the clan of Banū Ubayriq in Madinah — named Bashīr in the narration of Tirmidhī and Ḥākim, or Ṭuʿmah in the narration of al-Baghawī and Ibn Jarīr. Outwardly he lived among the Muslims; the narration of Tirmidhī adds that he was in reality a hypocrite who composed insulting verses against the Companions and circulated them under other people's names.

The theft took place in the early period after the Hijrah, when the Muslims lived in real hardship. Wheat flour was scarce in Madinah — the common food was barley bread or dates — and when a consignment came from Syria, Rifāʿah (the uncle of Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān) bought some, put it in a bag, placed some weapons on top, and stored it securely in his house. Ibn Ubayriq somehow came to know of it, broke into the house, and made off with the bag.

When Rifāʿah discovered the theft in the morning, he and Qatādah investigated. Neighbours reported having seen firelight at the Banū Ubayriq house the night before — probably, they said, from cooking what was stolen. Realising they were suspected, Banū Ubayriq went on the offensive. First they accused Labīd ibn Sahl, a man known for sincerity and piety — who came out sword in hand demanding the truth be established, at which they quietly backed down. Then, in the narration of al-Baghawī and Ibn Jarīr, they framed a Jewish man: they made a trail of flour from a slit in the bag leading from Rifāʿah's house to his door, and deposited the stolen arms with him for "safe keeping", so that when the goods were recovered from his house the case seemed closed. The Jew swore that Ibn Ubayriq had given them to him — but appearances were against him.

Qatādah brought the matter to the Prophet ﷺ and voiced his strong suspicion of Banū Ubayriq. They in turn came complaining that a Muslim family was being accused without legal proof while the stolen property had been found with the Jew. The outward evidence was so persuasive that even the Prophet ﷺ inclined towards the probability that the Jew was guilty — according to al-Baghawī's narration, he even intended to carry out the punishment for theft on him — and he admonished Qatādah for accusing a Muslim family without proof. Qatādah was so grieved that he wished he had never raised the matter, even at the cost of his property; Rifāʿah bore it patiently, saying only that Allah is the One from whom all help is sought.

Then this passage came down, showing the Prophet ﷺ the reality behind the case, acquitting the innocent Jewish man, and exposing Banū Ubayriq. Left with no way out, they returned the stolen goods; the Prophet ﷺ restored them to Rifāʿah, who endowed the weapons for use in jihād. Bashīr fled to Makkah and joined the disbelievers — so that if he had been a hypocrite before, he was now an open disbeliever, and if a Muslim, an apostate. Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ adds that even in Makkah he found no peace: the woman who housed him expelled him when she learnt of the affair, and he died breaking into yet another house when the wall he entered through collapsed on him.

## Judging by what Allah has shown — ayat 105–106

In ayah 105 Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ: "We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you might judge between men by that which Allah has shown you — so be not a pleader for the treacherous." Ibn Kathir explains "in truth" to mean that the Book truly came from Allah, and that its narrations and commandments are true. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that, having shown the Prophet ﷺ the reality behind the case of theft, Allah here directs him to use the knowledge and insight gifted to him to decide matters accordingly, abstaining from taking sides with traitors — that is, Banū Ubayriq.

Ayah 106 then says: "And seek the forgiveness of Allah; certainly Allah is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles this with care. The Prophet's ﷺ inclination towards the apparently guilty party was no sin — the obvious circumstances and evidences genuinely pointed that way — yet it was contrary to the actual fact, and the station of the prophets (ʿalayhim as-salām) is so high that Allah does not favour even something this slight issuing from them. Hence the instruction to seek forgiveness — a mark of how exalted the prophetic standard is, not an accusation of wrongdoing.

## A judge rules on what he hears — from the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir brings two hadith here that state the principle underlying the whole passage. In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that Zaynab bint Umm Salamah said that Umm Salamah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard the noise of disputing people close to the door of his room and went out to them saying: "Verily, I am only human and I judge based on what I hear. Some of you might be more eloquent in presenting his case than others, so that I judge in his favor. If I judge in one's favor concerning the right of another Muslim, then it is a piece of the Fire. So let one take it or leave it."

Imam Ahmad recorded from Umm Salamah that two men of the Anṣār came with a dispute over an old inheritance, with no evidence. The Prophet ﷺ told them the same: he is only human, judges by what he hears, and whoever is awarded a piece of his brother's right should not take it — "it is a part of the Fire that I am giving him and it will be tied around his neck on the Day of Resurrection." Both men wept, and each said, "I forfeit my right to my brother." The Prophet ﷺ then told them to go and divide the estate, trying to be just, then draw lots, and each forgive his brother thereafter.

The teaching is sobering: a court verdict does not change reality. A ruling won by eloquence transfers nothing lawfully — it hands the winner a portion of the Fire.

## Hiding from people but not from Allah — ayat 107–108

Ayah 107 repeats the prohibition emphatically: do not argue on behalf of "those who deceive themselves" — "verily, Allah does not like anyone who is a betrayer, sinner." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the reason plainly: Allah does not like such people, so His Messenger must not defend them.

Ayah 108 then exposes the absurdity at the heart of all concealed sin. "They may hide their crimes from men, but they cannot hide them from Allah; for He is with them when they plot by night in words that He does not approve." Ibn Kathir explains that this chastises the hypocrites: they hide their evil from people to escape criticism, yet disclose it before Allah, Who has perfect watch over their secrets and knows what is in their hearts — Ibn Kathir notes that this "withness" is by His knowledge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it strange indeed: they feel shy before people like themselves and feel no shame before Allah, Who is with them all the time and watches over everything they do — especially on the occasion when they conspired together to put the blame on the Jew, then went to the Prophet ﷺ to complain against Rifāʿah and Qatādah and appeal for support against the Jew. "And Allah ever encompasses what they do" — Ibn Kathir reads this as a threat and a warning: nothing escapes Him.

## Who will plead for them before Allah? — ayah 109

The passage closes by turning to those who took up the traitors' cause: "Here you are, arguing for them in the life of this world — but who will argue for them on the Day of Resurrection against Allah, or who will then be their defender?" Ibn Kathir draws out the logic: suppose they win their verdict in this life, since rulers judge by what is apparent. What will their condition be on the Day of Resurrection, before Allah, Who knows the secret and what is more hidden still? Who will be their advocate then? None will support them that Day. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the verse serves two purposes at once: it admonishes those who backed the betrayers, and it reminds them of the perils of the Hereafter — thereby calling them to repent and turn back to Allah.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that although these verses came down about one episode, in the Qur'an's characteristic style the instructions are not confined to it: they are basic principles for all Muslims of every generation. From this passage, as the sources present it: never lend your advocacy, your eloquence, or your influence to someone you know to be in the wrong, whatever their affiliation to you — the guilty party here was outwardly "one of us" and the innocent man an outsider, and revelation sided with the outsider. Remember that winning an argument transfers no right: what is taken by a favourable verdict against the truth is a piece of the Fire. And weigh the strange inversion ayah 108 exposes — being more ashamed before people than before Allah — for He is with those who plot by night, and He encompasses everything they do.

passages.title: Pinning your crime on an innocent man
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Behind these ayat stands a real crime and a real cover-up. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls the episode: the theft was committed by the Banū Ubayriq themselves, and they then went on to put the blame on Sayyidnā Labīd, or the Jew. Out of that specific incident, Allah lays down truths that stand forever. Ibn Kathir titles the section: "The Encouragement to Seek Allah's Forgiveness, and Warning those who Falsely Accuse Innocent People" — and that pairing is exactly what holds the passage together. Ayah 110 opens the door of repentance as wide as it will go; ayah 111 warns that unrepented sin lands on no one but the sinner; ayah 112 names the crime at the heart of the story — sinning and then throwing the sin at an innocent person; and ayah 113 turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself, whom Allah protected from being deceived by the schemers.

## Ayah 110: The door that is never shut

The passage begins not with condemnation but with an offer: "Whoever does evil or wrongs himself but afterwards seeks Allah's forgiveness, he will find Allah Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sees here the wise way of the Qurʼān at work: this ayah was revealed "in order to save sinners from total disappointment." A sin is a sin, big or small; but when a sinner repents and seeks Allah's forgiveness, he finds Him forgiving and merciful. There is an element of persuasion in it for those who have committed sin: they still have the time and the hope to desist and repent sincerely; nothing is lost, Allah will forgive everything.

How wide is this offer? Ibn Kathir relates the comment of Ibn ʿAbbās (through ʿAlī bin Abī Talhah): Allah here informs His servants of His forgiveness, forbearing generosity and expansive mercy — so whoever commits a sin, minor or major, then seeks Allah's forgiveness, will find Him Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful, "even if his sins were greater than the heavens, the earth and the mountains."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad: ʿAlī said, "Whenever I hear anything from the Messenger of Allah, Allah benefits me with whatever He wills of that. Abu Bakr told me, and Abu Bakr has said the truth, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *No Muslim commits a sin and then performs ablution, prays two Rakʿahs and begs Allah for forgiveness for that sin, but He forgives him.*" He then recited this very ayah (4:110) together with its sister verse, "And those who, when they have committed Fāhishah or wronged themselves…" (3:135). So the ayah is not an abstraction; the Prophet ﷺ gave it a concrete practice — wudūʼ, two units of prayer, and a plea for forgiveness.

**What real repentance is.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses a necessary caution here. This ayah covers all sins — whether they violate the rights of Allah (*Huqūqullāh*) or the rights of human beings (*Huqūq al-ʿIbād*) — but only genuine repentance unlocks it. Mere verbal declarations of "Astaghfirullāh" (I seek Allah's forgiveness) and "Wa atūbu ilayhi" (and I turn to Him in repentance) are not, by themselves, acts of genuine repentance. By the consensus of the scholars, the person who is involved in some sin, is not ashamed of it, and does not leave it — or at least does not resolve to leave it in the future — makes of his verbal "Astaghfirullāh" an open mockery of repentance. For tawbah (repentance) to be genuine, three things are necessary:

1. Being ashamed of past sins;
2. Immediately leaving the sin one is in;
3. Resolving to stay away from sin in the future.

And where the sin violated the rights of the servants of Allah, Maʿārif adds a further binding condition: forgiveness must be sought from the wronged party itself, or one should, to begin with, pay what was due or fulfil what was denied. These, it says, are binding conditions of genuine repentance.

## Ayah 111: Sin lands only on the sinner

"And whoever earns sin, he earns it only against himself." The translation's word is *earns* — the sin belongs entirely to the one who committed it. Ibn Kathir explains this by pairing it with another ayah: "And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another." No one will avail anyone else; every soul, and none else, shall carry its own burden.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the other side of the same truth: if these people choose not to repent despite the option given to them, their action brings no harm to Allah, nor to His Messenger ﷺ, nor to the Muslims. The sad nemesis of a person's evil deed shall be faced by the person himself.

The ayah closes: "And Allah is Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise." Ibn Kathir comments that this occurs due to Allah's knowledge, wisdom, fairness and mercy.

## Ayah 112: The double crime of framing the innocent

Now the ayah that names what actually happened: "And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then blames it on someone innocent, he has indeed burdened himself with falsehood and a manifest sin."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this sets forth a general rule of conduct: anyone who himself commits a crime and then puts the blame on an innocent person — as in the episode where the theft was committed by the Banū Ubayriq themselves and they went on to put the blame on Sayyidnā Labīd or the Jew — has done something grave. He has levelled a false accusation of great magnitude against an innocent person, *plus* an open sin weighing heavy on his own shoulders.

The arithmetic of the ayah is worth sitting with. The framer hoped to transfer his sin to someone else; instead, in Maʿārif's words, he *doubles and hardens* it. He has made himself deserving of severe punishment twice over — the punishment of his own sin, then the added punishment for lying and accusing falsely. The man who tried to unload his crime onto innocent shoulders ends up carrying more than he started with — the very truth ayah 111 announced: sin cannot be passed to another; every soul carries its own burden.

## Ayah 113: Allah's grace guarding His Prophet ﷺ

The passage now turns to the Prophet ﷺ directly: "Had not the grace of Allah and His mercy been upon you, a party of them would certainly have made a decision to mislead you, but they mislead none except their own selves, and no harm can they do to you in the least."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the address: it was Allah's grace and mercy that He revealed to the Prophet ﷺ the reality behind the event of the theft; otherwise these people would have misled him into error. But since Allah's grace and mercy is with him, they can never mislead him. On the contrary, they themselves fall into error, and they cannot harm him in any way whatsoever, because Allah has revealed the Book and wisdom to him and taught him what he did not know.

**The Prophet ﷺ and ijtihād.** From verse 105 — "Surely We have revealed to you the Book with the truth" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws rulings about the Prophet's ﷺ judgment. He had the right to arrive at decisions by *ijtihād* — reasoned judgment in situations not covered by an explicit authority in the Qurʼān — and in situations of major importance there were many decisions he took by his ijtihād. But his ijtihād was unlike that done by the Mujtahid Imams, for whom the probability of an error of judgment always remains: when the Prophet ﷺ took a decision on the basis of his ijtihād, any possible error in the judgment would always stand corrected by Allah Himself. And when nothing against it came from Allah, that itself was an indicator that the decision found favour with Him and is correct in His sight. Genuine ijtihād, Maʿārif adds, can be considered trustworthy in the sight of Allah only when it is based on and deduced from Qurʼānic principles and the clear authority of its text — simple opinions or views do not qualify. And a further ruling follows: pursuing or advocating a false case or a false claim, or seconding or supporting them, is totally harām (forbidden).

**"The Book and the Hikmah."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a weighty point from the pairing of *al-Kitāb* (the Book) with *al-Hikmah* (the Wisdom): Hikmah here is the name of the Sunnah — the teachings of the noble Prophet ﷺ — and it too was sent down by none but Allah. The difference is that the Sunnah's words are not from Allah, which is why they are not part of the Qurʼān; but its meanings, like the Qurʼān's, are certainly from Allah — and therefore it is obligatory to act in accordance with both. This explains what some jurists say about revelation (*wahy*) being of two kinds: *matluww* — "recited" revelation, the Qurʼān, whose words and meanings are both from Allah; and *ghayr matluww* — "unrecited" revelation, the hadith, whose words are from the Prophet ﷺ and whose meanings are from Allah.

**"And taught you that which you knew not."** Ibn Kathir explains this as: before this revelation was sent down to you — and connects it to the ayat "You knew not what is the Book" (42:52) and "You were not expecting that the Book would be sent down to you, but it is a mercy from your Lord" (28:86). The Prophet's ﷺ knowledge came by revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a corrective in the other direction: this phrase also resolves the error of those who insist the Prophet ﷺ possessed all-comprehending knowledge of the entire universe equal to Allah's. The truth is that the measure of his knowledge corresponded to what Allah bestowed upon him — while, at the same time, there is no doubt that the knowledge bestowed upon him exceeds the combined knowledge of all created beings. The ayah itself holds both truths: he was *taught* — so his knowledge is a gift, not divine omniscience — and what he was taught was so vast that Allah closes the passage with: "And ever great is the grace of Allah unto you."

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a clear ladder. If you have sinned — even against your own soul, even gravely — the first move is toward Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ showed the way: ablution, two rakʿahs, and sincere istighfār, with real shame, real abandonment of the sin, real resolve, and — where the rights of another person were violated — seeking their forgiveness or paying what was due. What is never an option is the Banū Ubayriq's move: shifting your guilt onto someone innocent. That path does not lighten the burden; by the ayah's own words, the one who does it has burdened himself with falsehood and a manifest sin on top of the original crime. And ayah 113 gives the consolation that closes the whole affair: schemers mislead none except their own selves, and can do no harm in the least to those under Allah's grace.

passages.title: Worthless secrets and defying the Messenger
passages.tafsir:
# Worthless Secrets and Defying the Messenger (4:114–115)

This passage weighs human speech and human allegiance on a single scale. Ayah 114 sifts through all the private conversations people hold and declares most of them worthless — except three kinds of talk that Allah singles out and promises to reward immensely. Ayah 115 then turns from worthless words to something far graver: the person who, after the truth has become plain to him, deliberately breaks with the Messenger ﷺ and abandons the path of the believers. What binds the two ayat together is the theme of the whole preceding section: the sūrah has just recounted the episode of theft and the conspiracies made to cover up the crime with false accusations against others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the text now moves from those conspiracies to the positive counterpart — highlighting the good that can be done through mutual consultation, the kind of consultation that helps a person remain obedient to the Messenger's ﷺ teachings and the command of Allah, without ever going against the ideal path taken by those who believe in Allah and His Messenger.

## "No good in most of their secret talks"

The word in ayah 114 is *najwā* — private, confidential talk, whispered counsel between people. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase simply as "what the people say to each other." The verse does not say there is no good in *any* of it, but in *most* of it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why: most of the talks people hold and the plans they hatch are aimed at transitory worldly gains, made while unmindful of the life to come — and such talk is devoid of good. It cites a hadith teaching that anything a person says works against him in one way or another, unless his words are the remembrance of Allah, or bidding the Fair and forbidding the Unfair. (The bundle records this teaching without naming a collection.)

## The three exceptions

Allah exempts three kinds of private talk, and each one is other-directed — speech that carries benefit beyond the speaker:

**1. Ordering ṣadaqah (charity).** The scholars of tafsir agree, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports as a consensus, that *ṣadaqah* here carries a general sense: it includes the obligatory zakāh, voluntary charities, and everything done to bring benefit to someone.

**2. Ordering maʿrūf.** *Maʿrūf* — rendered "goodness" or "the Fair" — is a technical term worth pausing on. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines *amr bi-l-maʿrūf* (bidding the Fair) as urging every action the Sharīʿah considers good and which those who know the Sharīʿah patently recognise as such; its opposite, *nahy ʿan al-munkar* (forbidding the Unfair), targets every action the Sharīʿah deems undesirable. Bidding the Fair is a broad category: helping the oppressed, assisting the needy with loans, guiding the lost — all fall under it. Charity and reconciliation are technically part of this definition too, yet Allah names them separately, because their benefit passes from one person to another and improves the collective life of a community. Together these two fields cover what is most essential about public service: charity spreads benefit to Allah's creation, and reconciliation stops mutual pain and loss.

**3. Making iṣlāḥ — reconciliation between people.** This third exception receives the richest treatment in the sources, and deserves its own section.

## The graces of making peace

Imam Ahmad recorded that Umm Kulthum bint ʿUqbah — one of the immigrant women who gave their pledge of allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — heard him say: "He who brings about reconciliation between people by embellishing good or saying good things, is not a liar." She added that she never heard him allow untrue speech except in three cases: in war, in bringing peace between people, and in the affectionate speech of a husband and wife to each other. Ibn Kathir notes that "the Group" also recorded this hadith, with the exception of Ibn Majah. The point is striking: reconciliation is so beloved to Allah that smoothing over a quarrel with generous words is lifted out of the category of lying altogether.

Imam Ahmad also recorded from Abu Ad-Dardāʼ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked: "Should I tell you what is better than the grade of fasting, praying and ṣadaqah?" They said, "Yes, O Allah's Messenger!" He said: "Bringing reconciliation between people." And he said: "Spoiling the relationship (between people) is the destroyer." Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi also recorded this hadith, and At-Tirmidhi graded it "Hasan Sahih." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān conveys the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of that last phrase — discord is "what really shaves": it does not shave the head, but it shaves off one's faith.

## The condition: seeking Allah's pleasure

Ayah 114 does not stop at naming the deeds; it attaches a condition — *"and he who does this seeking the good pleasure of Allah."* Ibn Kathir glosses it: with sincerity, awaiting the reward with Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this a significant reminder: bidding charity, fair action, or reconciliation is only worthwhile and acceptable when undertaken exclusively for Allah's pleasure, without any trace of personal or material interest. Only then comes the promise: *"We shall give him a great reward"* — in Ibn Kathir's words, an immense, enormous and tremendous reward.

## Ayah 115: breaking with the Messenger ﷺ

The passage now names its gravest crime. *"Whoever contradicts and opposes the Messenger after the right path has been shown clearly to him"* — Ibn Kathir stresses the deliberateness in this: it refers to whoever *intentionally* takes a path other than the path of the Law revealed to the Messenger ﷺ, after the truth has been made clear, apparent and plain to him. This is not the stumbling of the ignorant or the confused; it is knowing defiance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states plainly that opposing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this way is *kufr* — disbelief — and a terrible curse.

**"And follows other than the believers' way."** Ibn Kathir explains that this second clause is closely related to the first: the contradiction may take the form of opposing a text of the Qurʼān or Sunnah, or of opposing what the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ has unanimously agreed upon. And here he makes a remarkable creedal point: the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ is immune from error when they all agree on something — a miracle granted to increase their honour, due to the greatness of their Prophet ﷺ.

## The proof-text for ijmāʿ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the juristic weight of this ayah. Just as following the injunctions of the Qurʼān and Sunnah is obligatory, when the Muslim Ummah agrees about something universally, following that consensus (*ijmāʿ*) becomes equally obligatory, and opposing it is a grave sin. It records the Prophet's ﷺ warning that the hand of Allah is upon the Muslim community, and whoever breaks away and separates himself from it will himself be separated for consignment to Hell. (The bundle records this teaching without naming a collection.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates a famous story about this very verse. Imam al-Shāfiʿī was asked whether the authority of the consensus of the Muslim Ummah could be proved from the Qurʼān itself. He devoted three full days to reciting the Qurʼān — completing three recitals each day and night — searching for the proof. The proof he came up with was this verse. When he cited it before the scholars, they all agreed: this proof is sufficient to confirm the authority of ijmāʿ.

## "We shall keep him in the path he has chosen"

The end of ayah 115 contains one of the most sobering statements in the Qurʼān about how Allah deals with the wilful rebel: *nuwallihi mā tawallā* — "We shall keep him in the path he has chosen, and burn him in Hell — what an evil destination!" Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism of this punishment: when someone persists on the wicked path, Allah punishes him by making that evil path appear good in his heart, beautifying it for him so that he is tempted further along it. The punishment for choosing misguidance is more misguidance — abandonment to one's own choice.

Ibn Kathir gathers parallel ayat to show this is a recurring divine pattern: *"Then leave Me alone with such as belie this Qurʼān. We shall punish them gradually from directions they perceive not"* (68:44); *"So when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away"* (61:5); and *"We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly"* (6:110). And the end of that path in the Hereafter is the Fire, as in *"Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions"* (37:22) and *"The criminals shall see the Fire and apprehend that they have to fall therein, and they will find no way of escape from there"* (18:53).

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a practical audit of speech and allegiance. Before entering into private talk — a group chat, a quiet conversation, a plan made behind closed doors — ask whether it belongs to the three exempted categories: does it move someone toward charity, toward what is right, or toward mending a broken relationship? If it does, do it *for Allah*, not for reputation or advantage, for only sincerity unlocks the "great reward." Take reconciliation seriously as worship: the Prophet ﷺ ranked it above the grade of fasting, prayer and charity, and warned that stoking discord shaves away faith itself. And on the larger scale, hold fast to the Messenger's ﷺ path and the united way of the believers — for the ayah warns that the one who knowingly walks away is left to the road he chose, and that road ends at an evil destination.

passages.title: Shirk and Satan's pledge to mislead humanity
passages.tafsir:
This passage sets out, in one sustained movement, the single sin Allah has declared He will not forgive — shirk, associating partners with Him — and then pulls back the curtain on who is really behind it: Shaytan, who once swore before Allah that he would claim a fixed share of humanity and mislead them by every means. What binds ayat 116–121 together is a descent from the crime, to its true instigator, to his methods, to the end of everyone who takes him as an ally: a Fire from which "they will find no way of escape" (ayah 121).

## Why these ayat come here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayān al-Qurʼān) notes the placement. The preceding verses dealt with the Jews and the hypocrites among the enemies of Islam; now the Qur'an turns to the largest group of antagonists — the pagans — taking up their beliefs and the punishment awaiting them. It also connects backward: the thief mentioned in the earlier verses had become an apostate, and this passage makes plain the lasting punishment such a person earns.

## Ayah 116: the one unforgivable sin

"Surely Allah does not forgive the ascribing of a partner to Him, and forgives anything short of that for whomsoever He wills." Ibn Kathir explains the verse's ending — "whoever associates partners with Allah has strayed far away" — to mean that such a person has left the true path entirely, deviated from guidance, and destroyed himself and his contentment in both this life and the Hereafter.

**What exactly is shirk?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a precise definition: to consider any created being *equal to Allah* — in worship, or in love and reverence, or in His particular attributes such as being the Creator, the Provider, the Absolute Master, the Knower of the seen and the unseen. The subtlety matters. As the same passage observes, even the polytheists did not believe that the idols of their own making were the Creator and Master of the universe. Yet the Qur'an records what the disbelievers will say on entering Jahannam: "By Allah, we were in obvious error when we had equated you with Allah, the Lord of all the worlds" (26:97–98). It was rather under other erroneous assumptions that they had come to regard their idols as equal to Allah in worship or in love and reverence — and this, notes Fath al-Mulhim, was the shirk which caused their being in Jahannam.

**A telling difference of wording.** This ayah is almost identical to ayah 48 of this same surah — except for its final clause. There, the verse ends "has invented a great sin" (iftarā ithman ʿaẓīmā); here, "has strayed far away" (ḍalla ḍalālan baʿīdā). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, relaying the master exegetes, explains: ayah 48 addressed the Jews, People of the Book who knew the truth of tawhid (Allah's oneness) and the falsity of shirk from the Torah itself — so their shirk amounted to a forgery, a false accusation against their own scripture. This ayah addresses the pagans of Makkah, who had no prior Book or Prophet, but for whom the rational case for Allah's oneness was overwhelming: worshipping stones carved by one's own hands is absurd even to plain common sense. Hence their verdict — not "forgery," but "straying far indeed."

**Why is the punishment eternal for a sin committed in a finite life?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers a question many readers feel: should punishment not be proportionate to the deed? The one who commits kufr (disbelief) and shirk does not regard it as a crime at all; he considers it good and proper, and holds to it with the firm intention of remaining that way forever. If he carries that resolve to his last breath, he has — to the full extent of his own choice and volition — committed a *permanent* crime, and so its punishment is permanent.

**Three kinds of injustice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ibn Kathir vide Musnad Bazar) records a threefold division of zulm (injustice): the injustice Allah will never forgive — shirk; the injustice that may be forgiven — falling short in the rights of Allah (ḥuqūq Allāh); and the injustice that meets retribution — violations of the rights people hold against each other (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād).

## Ayah 117: who they really worship

"Instead of Allah, they invoke nothing but female deities — and they invoke nothing but Shaytan, a persistent rebel." Ibn Kathir relates from Ad-Dahhak (through Juwaybir) how the "female deities" worked: the idolators claimed the angels were Allah's daughters and said, "We only worship them so that they bring us closer to Allah." They shaped idols as girls and declared them likenesses of those "daughters" — hence Al-Lat and Al-'Uzza (53:19), and the Qur'an's rebuke that "they make the angels, who are themselves servants of the Most Gracious, females."

Then comes the unmasking. Whatever name is on the idol, the one actually being obeyed is Shaytan — it was he who commanded this worship and made it seem fair and beautiful in their eyes. So in reality they are worshipping him, as Allah says elsewhere: "Did I not command you, O Children of Adam, that you should not worship Shaytan?" (36:60). On the Day of Resurrection the angels themselves will disown their supposed worshippers: "Nay, but they used to worship the jinn" (34:41). This is the passage's deepest insight into false religion: shirk always dresses itself as devotion to something exalted, but the real recipient of the obedience is the rebel who suggested it.

## Ayat 118–119: Satan's pledge

"Allah cursed him" — Ibn Kathir explains the curse (laʿnah) as Allah expelling him and banishing him from His mercy and His grace. And in that state of banishment, Shaytan swore: "I will surely take an appointed portion of Your servants" — a fixed, known share of humanity. Muqatil bin Hayyan commented starkly: "From every one thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine will go to the Fire and one to Paradise."

Then the pledge unfolds into a program, each clause in ayah 119 opening with an oath:

- **"I will surely mislead them"** — turn them off the true path altogether.
- **"I will surely arouse in them false desires."** Ibn Kathir's gloss here is piercingly practical: tempting them to feign repentance, arousing false hopes, encouraging them to delay and procrastinate with righteous deeds. Not dramatic evil — just "later." On this reading, the whispered *tomorrow* belongs to Shaytan's sworn program.
- **"I will surely order them to slit the ears of cattle."** As Qatadah and As-Suddi explained, this refers to the pagan custom of cutting the ears of animals to mark them as Bahirah, Sa'ibah, and Wasilah — beasts dedicated to idols and set apart by superstition. Man-made religion, presented as piety.
- **"I will surely order them to change the creation of Allah."** Al-Hasan al-Basri explained this as tattooing. Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim recorded in his Sahih the prohibition of tattooing the face, in one wording: "May Allah curse whoever does this." And it is recorded in the Sahih that Ibn Mas'ud said, "May Allah curse those who have tattoos and those who do it, who pluck their (facial) hairs and the one who does it for them, and those who make spaces between their teeth for the purpose of beauty, changing what Allah has created" — then defended his words: "Why should I not curse whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has cursed, when the Book of Allah commands it," citing "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, abstain from it" (59:7).

Notice the progression Shaytan himself lays out: from misguidance of the heart, to false hopes, to corrupted religion, to disfiguring the very bodies Allah fashioned. The ayah closes with the verdict: "Whoever takes Shaytan as a walī" — a protector and ally — "instead of Allah has surely suffered a manifest loss." Ibn Kathir: he has lost this life *and* the Hereafter, a loss that can never be compensated or restored.

## Ayat 120–121: the promises collapse

"He makes promises to them and arouses desires in them — but Shaytan promises them nothing but delusion." Ibn Kathir says this verse states the true reality: Shaytan deceitfully assures his followers that they are the winners in this world and the next. And Allah names the entire portfolio of those assurances with one word — ghurūr, deception. On the Day of Return, Shaytan himself will confess it, as the Qur'an records: "Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you. I had no authority over you" (14:22).

Ayah 121 seals the outcome for those who liked and preferred what Shaytan promised them: "Their refuge is Hell, and they will find from it no escape." Ibn Kathir underlines the finality of maḥīṣ — no way to avoid, avert, evade, or elude it. The promises of the deceiver end where they were always headed; his own confession, "I betrayed you," is the last word on every hope he ever sold.

## Living it

The passage equips the believer with Shaytan's own declared playbook. Among the tactics Ibn Kathir draws out of the pledge, one is strikingly undramatic: *postponement* — the feigned or intended-but-delayed repentance, the good deed pushed to tomorrow. Recognizing that whisper as part of an ancient oath is half the defence. The verses also warn that corrupted religion (the slit-eared cattle of every age — pious-looking practices Allah never sanctioned) and tampering with Allah's creation for vanity are his projects too. And beneath it all stands the passage's central question: whom have you taken as your walī? Everything hangs on that single choice.

passages.title: Allah's true promise, not wishful thinking
passages.tafsir:
# Allah's True Promise, Not Wishful Thinking (4:122–124)

This passage sets two promises side by side — the empty promises of Shaytan, which the preceding verses have just exposed, and the promise of Allah, than whose words nothing is truer — and then delivers a ruling that cuts through every religious boast: salvation is not granted by wishes, yours or anyone else's, but by faith proven through deeds. What binds ayat 122–124 together is this single test of truthfulness: a true promise from a true Lord, answered by a true religion of the heart made real in action.

## Two promises: deception versus truth

Ayah 122 lands with full force only when read against what comes just before it. In ayat 119–120 Shaytan swears, "Verily, I will mislead them, and surely, I will arouse in them false desires," and Allah comments: "He makes promises to them, and arouses in them false desires; and Shaytan's promises are nothing but deceptions." Ibn Kathir explains that Shaytan "deceitfully promises his supporters and tempts them into believing that they are winners" in this life and the Hereafter — tempting them, among other things, "to feign repentance… encouraging them to delay and procrastinate with righteous deeds." Ibn Kathir then cites Shaytan's own confession on the Day of Resurrection: "Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you. I had no authority over you" (14:22).

Against that fraud, ayah 122 opens: "And those who believe and do righteous good deeds, We shall admit them to Gardens under which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever." Ibn Kathir describes these believers as people whose "hearts were truthful and their limbs obedient" — inner conviction and outer action together, a pairing the whole passage will insist on. Of the rivers of Paradise he gives a striking detail: the dwellers "will think of where they want these rivers to flow and they will flow there." And "to dwell therein forever" means without end and without ever being removed.

Then comes the seal: **"Allah's promise is the truth (waʿd Allāhi ḥaqqā); and whose words can be truer than those of Allah?"** Ibn Kathir: none is more truthful in statement and narration than Allah; there is no deity worthy of worship, or Lord, except Him. He notes that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to proclaim in his speech: "The most truthful speech is Allah's Speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad. The worst matters are the newly invented (in religion), every newly invented matter is an innovation, and every innovation is a heresy, and every heresy is in the Fire."

## The occasion of ayah 123: a contest of boasts

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān record the setting. Qatadah reported that some Muslims and some of the People of the Scripture began mentioning their virtues against each other. The People of the Scripture said: "Our Prophet came before your Prophet and our Book before your Book. Therefore, we should have more right to Allah than you have." The Muslims answered: "Rather, we have more right to Allah than you — our Prophet is the Final Prophet and our Book supersedes all the Books before it." Al-ʿAwfi relates a similar account from Ibn ʿAbbas: the people of the Tawrah, the people of the Injil, and the Muslims each claimed the best Book and the best Prophet. Then Allah sent down: **"It will not be in accordance with your desires, nor those of the People of the Scripture; whosoever works evil will have the recompense thereof."**

Notice something remarkable, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out: the verse rebukes *both* sides of the argument — "not your fancies, nor the fancies of the People of the Book." The correction falls on everyone, because "nobody becomes superior to anybody simply on the basis of conjectures, fancies and claims. Instead, everything depends on deeds." No matter how noble one's Prophet and Book, it is the adherent's own conduct that counts.

Ibn Kathir distils the principle: religion "is not accepted on account of wishful thinking or mere hopes. Rather, the accepted religion relies on what resides in the heart and which is made truthful through actions." Merely uttering a claim to the truth does not make one its possessor "until his claim gains merit with proof from Allah." Safety lies "in obeying Allah and following what He has legislated through the words of His honorable Messengers."

## "Whoever works evil will be recompensed" — the ayah that shook the Companions

The middle clause of ayah 123 — *man yaʿmal sūʼan yujza bih* — struck the Companions with real fear, and the way the Prophet ﷺ consoled them is one of the most tender chapters connected to this passage.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that ʿA'ishah said, "O Messenger of Allah! I know the hardest ayah in the Qur'an" — and she named this one. He ﷺ replied: "That is what strikes the believing servant, even the problems that bother him." Ibn Jarir and Abu Dawud also recorded this hadith.

Saʿid bin Mansur recorded that Abu Hurayrah said that when this ayah was revealed it was hard on the Muslims, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told them: **"Be steadfast and seek closeness. Everything that afflicts the Muslim, even the thorn that pierces his skin and the hardship he suffers, will be an expiation for him."** This is the wording collected by Ahmad through Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah; Muslim and at-Tirmidhi also recorded it (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an-Nasa'i).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates a narration found in Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi and Tafsir Ibn Jarir: when the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah to Abu Bakr, he felt as if his back had broken. "Ya Rasulallah, there is hardly anyone among us who can claim to have done nothing bad in his life. If every evil deed must be requited, who can hope to escape?" In one narration the Prophet ﷺ answered: "O Abu Bakr, do you not get sick? Are you never tested by distress and sorrow?" He said all of that does happen. "There — this is the requital of whatever evil you may have done." And in a hadith in Abu Dawud, ʿA'ishah reported that a believer's fever, pain, even the pinch of a thorn — even the small trouble of searching one pocket for something found in another — becomes an expiation of sins.

So the recompense the ayah threatens does not have to mean Hell. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah may exact it "either in this life, which is better for him, or in the Hereafter" — and the hardships of this world, borne by a believer, settle the account. As for "he will not find any protector or helper besides Allah," ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports Ibn ʿAbbas adding the crucial rider: "Unless he repents and Allah forgives him." The door of tawbah — repentance — stands open through everything this ayah warns of.

## Ayah 124: the promise made personal — to every believer, male or female

Having stated the rule of justice for evil, Allah states — in Ibn Kathir's words — "His kindness, generosity and mercy" in accepting good deeds: "And whoever does righteous good deeds, **male or female**, and is a believer, such will enter Paradise, and not the least injustice, even to the size of a Naqir, will be done to them."

The explicit "male or female" ensures no one hears the promise as belonging to someone else. And the *naqīr* is the tiny speck on the back of a date-stone — Ibn Kathir notes that alongside it the Qur'an also mentions the *fatīl* (the scalish thread in the long slit of a date-stone) and the *qiṭmīr* (the thin membrane over it): three images of near-nothingness, all deployed to say that not the faintest atom of a believer's good work will be withheld or wronged.

One condition governs it all: "and is a believer." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is direct about the hint given here: people may have genuinely good deeds to their name, but where the faith beneath them is not sound, those deeds are not acceptable. Deeds must issue from true faith — which is exactly the balance the whole passage teaches. Ayah 123 strips away faith-labels without deeds; ayah 124 strips away deeds without faith. Neither claim nor conduct stands alone.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes its commentary on ayah 123 with a reminder aimed squarely at Muslims, not only at others: do not indulge in tall claims and wishful thinking. Attachment to the Final Prophet ﷺ and the Final Book is a truth — but it saves no one as a mere badge. Real prosperity lies in making certain that one's belief is correct and that one is particular about doing good deeds as enjoined.

And the Prophet's ﷺ own prescription for living under this ayah remains the believer's program: *saddidū wa qāribū* — be steadfast and seek closeness — trusting that Allah, whose promise is truth and whose word none can surpass, counts every thorn-prick in your favour and will not wrong you the speck on a date-stone.

passages.title: The best religion: submission like Abraham
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

After warning that salvation rests neither on Muslim wishful thinking nor on the claims of the People of the Scripture, Allah now answers the question that warning raises: if mere labels and hopes count for nothing, what *does* the best religion look like? Ayah 125 gives the answer — a person who surrenders himself wholly to Allah, does good in the right way, and follows the path of Ibrahim, whom Allah took as His intimate friend. Ayah 126 then seals the point with the reason no other religion could possibly be better: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and He encompasses all things. The two ayat belong together as claim and proof — here is the best way, and here is why the One it leads to deserves nothing less.

## The dispute behind the verse

Ibn Kathir preserves the setting. Qatadah reported that the Muslims and the People of the Scriptures had been trading boasts about their own virtues. The People of the Scriptures said, "Our Prophet came before your Prophet and our Book before your Book — therefore we have more right to Allah than you." The Muslims answered, "Rather, we have more right to Allah: our Prophet is the Final Prophet and our Book supersedes all the Books before it." Allah then sent down the verses beginning "It will not be in accordance with your desires, nor those of the People of the Scripture" (4:123) and culminating in ayah 125. Similar accounts are attributed to As-Suddi, Masruq, Ad-Dahhak and Abu Salih, and Ibn 'Abbas described the same kind of three-way dispute between the people of the Tawrah, the people of the Injil, and the people of Islam.

Notice what Allah did *not* do. He did not settle the argument by endorsing anyone's boast. First He levelled the field — "whosoever works evil will have the recompense thereof" — and only then, as Qatadah puts it, "supported the argument of the Muslims" by defining the best religion in terms of what a person actually *is* and *does*, not what community he claims. Ibn Kathir draws the lesson sharply: religion is not accepted on account of wishful thinking or mere hopes; the accepted religion "relies on what resides in the heart and which is made truthful through actions." A claim to truth gains no merit until it is proven — and the proof Allah names is submission and good deeds.

## "Submits his face to Allah" — the two conditions

Ayah 125 stacks two phrases: *aslama wajhahu lillah* ("submits his face — himself — to Allah") and *wa huwa muhsin* ("while he is a Muhsin, a doer of good"). Both classical commentaries in front of us read these as the two conditions on which the acceptance of any deed depends.

**Sincerity (ikhlas).** To "submit one's face" is, in Ibn Kathir's words, to perform good actions "in sincerity for his Lord, with faith and awaiting the reward with Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān phrases it as acting for the good pleasure of Allah "without ever contaminating one's deeds with hypocritical or materialistic motives." This condition belongs to the heart, the innermost human dimension.

**Correctness (following the Sunnah).** Being a *Muhsin* means, per Ibn Kathir, "following the correct guidance that Allah legislated in the religion of truth which He sent His Messenger ﷺ with." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir approvingly, insists the way one acts cannot be "some self-invented way" — it must be the way based on Allah's injunctions and the teachings of His Messenger ﷺ. This condition belongs to the human exterior.

Ibn Kathir then gives the famous formulation: a deed is *sincere* when performed for Allah alone, and *correct* when it conforms to the Shari'ah — outwardly correct by following the Sunnah, inwardly correct by sincerity. Lacking either, the deed is null and void. He even names the failure modes: the one who works without sincerity becomes a hypocrite who shows off for people; the one who abandons the Shari'ah becomes an ignorant, wicked person. Only when both pillars combine do a person's actions become the deeds of the faithful, "whose best deeds are accepted from them and their errors erased."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the lens to the history of nations: every deviant group has failed on one of these two counts. It links them to the two groups of Surah Al-Fatihah — those "who incurred wrath" are the people who lacked sincerity (victims of desires), and those "who have gone astray" are the people who did not act right (victims of doubts). Interior and exterior, heart and limb — the best religion synchronises both.

## Why "better in deed," not "more in deeds"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses a point many believers miss. Everyone understands the need for sincerity; what even many Muslims ignore is that *good conduct itself is defined by the Sunnah*, not by personal choice. It gives a deliberately jarring example: praying three rak'at of Zuhr instead of the prescribed four is a sin — and praying *five* is a sin of exactly the same nature. Doing less than the Prophet ﷺ taught and doing more are both wrong, because the form of worship set by Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is final. Innovations added to the religion — however attractive, however "sincerely" performed — are of this kind; the deed of such a person "goes waste or becomes even sinful."

The commentary supports this from Surah al-Mulk (67:2), where Allah says He tests "who among you is *best* in deed" — *ahsanu ʿamalan*, not *aktharu ʿamalan*, "most in deeds." The Qur'an's concern is quality measured against the Prophet's ﷺ example, not quantity measured against our enthusiasm. So the practical rule Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws: whoever intends any good deed — prayer, fasting, Hajj, zakah, charity, remembrance of Allah, sending salutations on the Prophet ﷺ — must first find out how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did it and taught it, because any deed removed from his course stands unacceptable.

## The creed of Ibrahim, the Hanif

Why does the verse then say "and follows the *millah* (creed, way) of Ibrahim, the *Hanif* (Monotheist)"? Ibn Kathir explains that this describes Muhammad ﷺ and his followers until the Day of Resurrection, and he cites two other ayat to prove the connection: "Verily, among mankind those with the best claim to Ibrahim are those who followed him, and this Prophet" (3:68), and "Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim the Hanif, and he was not of the Mushrikin" (16:123).

The word *Hanif* receives a vivid gloss from Ibn Kathir: the Hanif "intentionally and with knowledge avoids Shirk; he goes attentively to the truth, allowing no one to hinder him or stop him from it." It is not a passive orthodoxy but a deliberate, informed turning: away from associating partners with Allah, toward truth, unstoppably.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is cited here precisely as *the worked example* of the verse's two conditions: he was "absolutely and superbly sincere, and his deed too was sound and correct with intimation from Allah." Following him is not optional decoration on the verse — it has been declared mandatory.

## "And Allah took Ibrahim as a Khalil"

The verse closes with an extraordinary honour: Allah took Ibrahim as a *Khalil* — an intimate friend. Ibn Kathir explains that Ibrahim "attained the grade of Khalil, which is the highest grade of love," and thereby reached "the ultimate closeness to Allah that the servants seek" — not arbitrarily, but *due to his obedience*, on account of the acts Allah loves and prefers. The Qur'an's own descriptions confirm it: "Ibrahim, the one who fulfilled" (53:37), the one whom his Lord "tried with certain commands, which he fulfilled" (2:124), who "was an Ummah, obedient to Allah, a Hanif" (16:120). The mention of this station in our verse, Ibn Kathir says, is itself an encouragement: Ibrahim "was and still is an Imam whose conduct is followed and imitated."

Two reports from the Sunnah illuminate the title.
