Al-Bukhari records from 'Amr bin Maymun that when Mu'adh returned from Yemen and led the people in Fajr prayer, he recited "And Allah took Ibrahim as a Khalil," and a man present exclaimed, "Surely the eye of Ibrahim's mother has been comforted" — such is the honour of the title that hearing it recited moved a listener to marvel at the joy it would bring a mother.

And this station was not Ibrahim's alone. In the Two Sahihs, Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri reports that in his last speech the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O people! If I were to take a Khalil from the people of the earth, I would have taken Abu Bakr bin Abi Quhafah as my Khalil. However, your companion is the Khalil of Allah." Several Companions also narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah had chosen him as His Khalil just as He chose Ibrahim as His Khalil. The community that follows the creed of Ibrahim follows a Prophet ﷺ who shares Ibrahim's own station of divine love — and the door into that path remains what it always was: sincerity and obedience.

## Ayah 126 — the ownership that grounds it all

Why should submission to Allah be the best religion and not merely one option among the religions that were boasting against each other? Ayah 126 answers: "To Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. And Allah is Ever Encompassing all things."

Ibn Kathir unfolds both halves. Everything and everyone are Allah's property, servants and creation; He has full authority over all of it. No one can avert His decision or question His judgment — He is never asked about what He does, because of His might, ability, fairness, wisdom, compassion and mercy. And His knowledge encompasses everything: nothing concerning His servants is ever hidden from Him; not the weight of an atom, nor anything smaller or bigger, escapes His observation in the heavens or the earth.

Set after ayah 125, this changes the temperature of the whole passage. Submitting one's face to the Owner of everything is not a sectarian preference; it is the only posture that matches reality. And because He encompasses all things, the two conditions of the previous verse are guaranteed their full weight: the sincerity hidden in the heart is fully seen, and no deed — however small — is lost from His knowledge.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with a simple, searching audit, drawn straight from the commentaries: for any deed, ask two questions. *For whom am I doing this?* — that is sincerity, the inner condition. *Am I doing it the way the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did it and taught it?* — that is correctness, the outer condition. Neither substitutes for the other; enthusiasm cannot repair a self-invented practice, and technically correct form cannot repair a heart performing for an audience other than Allah. That pairing — heart surrendered, practice anchored in the Sunnah, on the ancient path of Ibrahim — is what the Qur'an here calls the best religion. And it is answerable to no one's boast, because it is lived before the One to whom the heavens and the earth belong.

passages.title: The verdict sought about women, and the answer given
passages.tafsir:
This passage records a question the Companions actually brought to the Prophet ﷺ — a request for a formal ruling about women — and the answer Allah Himself gave. Ayah 127 settles the rights of orphan girls and vulnerable children; ayat 128–130 then walk through the three possible states of a strained marriage: reconciliation on agreed terms, continuing together despite unequal feelings, and, if all else fails, a separation in which Allah promises to enrich both parties. The thread running through the four ayat is the one named in the opening words: they asked about women, and it is Allah who gives the ruling concerning them.

## Why they came asking

The opening word of ayah 127, *yastaftūnaka* — "they ask you for a ruling" — points to a real moment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the background: earlier in this sūrah, revelation had given women and children fixed shares of inheritance and secured the rights of orphans, overturning the practice of Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance). Some people found these rulings so contrary to their custom that they assumed they must be a temporary measure — perhaps they would be abrogated later. Some even waited for that to happen. When no abrogation came, they went directly to the Prophet ﷺ and asked. According to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir (as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Bayān al-Qurʼān), this question was the reason this verse came down.

Notice the shape of the answer: "Say: it is Allah who gives you the ruling concerning them." The Prophet ﷺ does not answer from himself; the fatwā about women comes from Allah directly, and it also points back to "what is recited to you in the Book" — which ʿĀʼishah explained (in a report recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim) as the earlier verse 4:3 about orphan girls. The new ruling reaffirms the old one: it is not going away.

## The orphan girl and her guardian

Al-Bukhari recorded — and Muslim also recorded it — that ʿĀʼishah explained the verse: it concerns a man who is guardian and heir of an orphan girl, whose wealth is so mingled with his that she shares with him "even the branch of a date". If she is wealthy, he wants to marry her himself — cheaply — rather than let another man marry her and gain a claim on that shared property. So he blocks her from marrying anyone else.

The Arabic phrase *wa-targhabūna an tankiḥūhunna* is remarkable because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, it carries two opposite readings, and both were happening. It can mean "whom you desire to marry" — the guardian attracted by the girl's beauty or wealth, marrying her without her full rights or dowry. And it can mean "whom you avoid marrying" — the guardian who finds her plain and poor, will not marry her himself, yet will not release her to marry anyone else, so that her wealth stays in his hands. ʿĀʼishah's commentary, whose basis is recorded in the Two Sahihs, covers both cases: guardians were forbidden to marry orphan girls of property and beauty without justice to them, just as they habitually refused the ones who had neither.

Ibn ʿAbbas (as related by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah) described the Jahiliyyah practice vividly: a guardian would cover an orphan girl with his rope, and once he had done so no other man would marry her. If she was beautiful, he married her and took her wealth; if not, he kept her locked out of marriage until she died — and then inherited her money. Allah prohibited and outlawed this outright.

The verse then widens to "the weak and oppressed children": in Jahiliyyah, young children and females were denied any inheritance at all. Allah's words "you give them not what is decreed for them" abolish that, fixing a share for every heir, young or old, as Saʿid bin Jubayr and others stated. And the command to "stand firm for justice to orphans" cuts both ways — Saʿid bin Jubayr put it sharply: just as you would want to marry her when she is beautiful and wealthy, marry her when she is neither. Justice means the guardian's treatment of her cannot depend on what he stands to gain. Ibn Kathir notes that when a guardian does wish to marry his ward, Allah commands him to give her a dowry equal to what women of her standing receive — and if he will not, then let him marry other women, "for Allah has made this matter easy for Muslims". The passage closes its first movement with a promise: "whatever good you do, Allah is ever All-Aware of it" — every act of fairness toward the powerless is seen and will be rewarded fully.

## Ayah 128: when a wife fears being cast aside

The passage now turns from the orphan to the wife. Ayah 128 addresses the case where a woman fears *nushūz* or *iʿrāḍ* from her husband — harshness, or a cold turning-away. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes something important about this scenario: often neither party is truly to blame. A husband may simply feel no attraction to a wife who is aging, while she can do nothing to change his heart. She cannot be blamed for what she is, nor can he be censured for feelings he does not control.

In that situation the verse opens a door: "there is no sin on them both if they make terms of peace between themselves." The wife may voluntarily give up some or all of her rights — her allotted night, her maintenance, part of her dowry — in exchange for keeping the marriage, and the husband may accept. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the phrase "no sin upon them" is doing real work here: on the surface such a deal could look like a bribe, the husband being paid off with forgone claims. The Qurʼān clarifies that it is not bribery but wise accommodation — both sides stepping back from their full claims to reach a workable middle.

**The story behind the verse.** Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas: Sawdah feared that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ might divorce her, and she said, "O Messenger of Allah! Do not divorce me; give my day to ʿĀʼishah." He did, and Allah then sent down this verse. At-Tirmidhi recorded it and graded it Hasan Gharib, and Ibn ʿAbbas drew the legal principle from it: "Whatever the spouses mutually agree to is allowed." In the Two Sahihs it is recorded from ʿĀʼishah that when Sawdah bint Zamʿah became old she forfeited her day to ʿĀʼishah, and the Prophet ﷺ would spend Sawdah's night with ʿĀʼishah. Ibn Kathir adds the point of this: by keeping Sawdah among his wives after her offer, the Prophet ﷺ made this kind of settlement a model for his Ummah to follow.

**"And settlement is better."** The little sentence *wa-l-ṣulḥu khayr* is stated absolutely, and both commentaries linger on it. Ibn Kathir reads it plainly: settlement is better than divorce — "divorce is not preferred with Allah." (He also records the view related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the verse refers to the husband giving his wife the choice to stay or leave, though he judges the apparent wording to be about the wife's concession.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān goes further: because the wording is general, the principle reaches beyond marriage to every family quarrel, dispute, and lawsuit in worldly life — compromise is better than fighting a claim to the bitter end. It cites in support the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "Every compromise is permissible between Muslims except a compromise in which something unlawful has been made lawful or something lawful has been made unlawful…" (narrated by al-Hakim from Kathir ibn ʿAbdullah, as cited in Tafsir Mazhari). So a wife could not, for instance, secure a settlement on condition that her husband marry her sister — for combining two sisters is forbidden — nor on condition that he neglect another wife's rights.

**"And souls are made to be present with greed."** This striking phrase — *wa-uḥḍirat il-anfus al-shuḥḥ* — is the Qurʼān's psychological realism. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it is precisely each party's self-interest that makes the compromise workable: the wife clings to the marriage for her children's future or her own security; the husband is drawn by the relief of forgone claims. Allah does not pretend the spouses are angels; He legislates for human beings as they are, and turns even their self-regard toward peace.

Two further notes from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān are practical gold. First, the verse says the two should reconcile *baynahumā* — "between the two of them" — and al-Tafsir al-Mazhari draws from this that it is better that no third person interfere in husband-wife matters: outsiders can make compromise impossible, and the couple's weaknesses get needlessly exposed. Second, on the scope of what a wife gives up: rights already due (such as unpaid dowry she forgives) lapse permanently, but future rights — future maintenance, her future share of time — do not lapse forever; she may later declare she is no longer willing to forgo them, at which point the husband must either resume them or release her.

And the verse ends with a third path beyond settlement or divorce: "if you do good and have taqwā" — if the husband, despite his feelings, treats the wife he does not incline to just as he treats the others — "then Allah is ever Well-Acquainted with what you do." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices that the verse does not spell out the reward for this forbearance; the silence itself is the hint that it will be greater than one can imagine.

## Ayah 129: the justice that is demanded, and the justice that is not

Ayah 129 states flatly: "You will never be able to do perfect justice between wives, even if you ardently desire it." This seems, at first, to collide with 4:3, which commanded a man fearing injustice to keep to one wife. The resolution, given by Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUbaydah As-Salmani, Mujahid, Al-Hasan Al-Basri and Ad-Dahhak, is that the impossible justice is the justice of the heart. A man may divide the nights with strict equality, yet love, desire and intimacy will never weigh the same on both sides of the scale — and that is beyond human control.

The Prophet's ﷺ own practice makes the distinction luminous. Imam Ahmad and the collectors of the Sunan recorded from ʿĀʼishah that he used to divide equally between his wives and then pray: "O Allah, this is my division in what I own; so do not blame me for what You own and I do not own" — meaning his heart. (This is the wording Abu Dawud collected; Ibn Kathir notes its chain is Sahih.) Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks the piercing question: who had greater mastery of his own soul than the Prophet ﷺ? Yet even he counted the heart's inclination as outside his control and asked to be excused for it. The lesson: equality is obligatory in everything a man does control — nights, provision, living standards — and not obligatory in what he does not.

Hence the verse's command: "do not incline totally, so as to leave her hanging (*ka-l-muʿallaqah*)." Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Al-Hasan, Ad-Dahhak, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, As-Suddi and Muqatil bin Hayyan all explained *muʿallaqah* the same way: a woman left "neither divorced nor married" — legally bound but practically abandoned. The warning against it is severe: Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever has two wives and inclines to one of them (too much) will come on the Day of Resurrection with one of his sides dragging." And the verse balances warning with mercy: if you do justice and divide equally in what you have power over, while keeping taqwā, "Allah is ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" — Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will then forgive the favoritism a man showed to some of his wives.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also addresses a misunderstanding here: some juxtapose 4:3 ("if you fear injustice, keep to one") with 4:129 ("you will never be perfectly just") to conclude that polygamy is effectively prohibited. It answers that the two verses themselves refute this. Ayah 129 immediately follows its statement with "so do not incline totally" — instructions for a man who *has* more than one wife — and 4:3's conditional "if you fear" shows that workable justice is attainable. It adds an argument from 4:23: the Qurʼān took two full verses to detail which women are forbidden, and prohibited specifically "combining two sisters"; had plural marriage itself been unlawful, that careful restriction would have been redundant.

## Ayah 130: if they must part

Sometimes neither settlement nor patience avails, and the couple separates. Ayah 130 meets that moment not with condemnation but with a promise: "If they separate, Allah will enrich each of them out of His abundance." Ibn Kathir reads it as a concrete pledge — Allah will suffice each of them, giving him a better wife and her a better husband. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a consolation of great tenderness: let each of them remember their life before the marriage. They were once two strangers, and Allah brought them together; the One who did it once can do it again. There is no reason to despair.

The closing Names seal the passage: "Allah is ever All-Encompassing (*Wāsiʿ*), All-Wise (*Ḥakīm*)." His capacity is vast enough to provide for both of them apart, and His wisdom governs even the parting — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes it is quite possible that the separation itself was the wisest solution, and that the life after it will be better for both.

## Living it

Taken whole, the passage teaches a consistent ethic. Toward the orphan under your protection: never let material interest dictate how you treat her — her wealth and her marriage are hers, and justice to her is commanded whether she is wealthy and beautiful or neither. Within marriage: prefer settlement to rupture, and keep the negotiation between the two of you. Accept that your heart is not fully yours to command, but answer for everything that is: your time, your provision, your fairness — and never leave a wife hanging, neither divorced nor married. And if, after all of it, the marriage ends — trust the One whose bounty is wider than the home you are leaving.

passages.title: Allah owns all and needs none of you
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat step back from the detailed rulings that fill this part of the sūrah and lift the reader's gaze to the One who issued them. Three times in quick succession Allah declares that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him — and around that refrain He weaves a command (have taqwa), a warning (He could replace you entirely), and a promise (whoever fears Allah and obeys Him will find his needs fulfilled). What holds the passage together is a single truth turned to catch three different lights: Allah owns all, so He needs nothing from you — but you need everything from Him.

## Why this passage comes here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the placement. The sūrah has just finished stating rules of behaviour concerning women and orphans. Now, in the Qurʼān's usual style, the text turns to the promise of reward for those who abide by these rules and the warning for those who contravene them. In other words, ayat 131–134 supply the reward and the warning that stand behind the rulings just given.

## One refrain, three shades of meaning

The words "to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth" are repeated three times. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the point: repeated thrice, these words signify three shades of meaning, each occurrence carrying its own emphasis.

**First (opening of ayah 131): the limitless scope of His power.** The first mention points to the limitless scope of Allah's power of creation, which lacks nothing. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary the same way: Allah is the Owner of the heavens and the earth and the Supreme Authority over them. Everything that follows in the passage — the command, the threat, the promise — rests on this ownership.

**Second (later in ayah 131): His self-sufficiency.** The refrain returns immediately after the words "but if you disbelieve", and here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the objective is to focus on Allah's attribute of self-sufficiency, self-adequacy, His being need-free. Should anyone disbelieve, deny, or reject the good counsel given, He is in no need of anyone's obedience, for He stands ever-praised in His pristine glory. The ayah seals this with two of His names: *Ghaniyy* — Rich, free of any need — and *Ḥamīd* — Worthy of all praise. Ibn Kathir illuminates the pairing with two parallel passages: Mūsā told his people, "If you disbelieve, you and all on the earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich (free of any need), Owner of all praise" (14:8); and of an earlier people Allah said, "So they disbelieved and turned away. But Allah was not in need (of them). And Allah is Rich (free of any need), Worthy of all praise" (64:6). Ibn Kathir's gloss: He is far too Rich to need His servants, and worthy of all praise in all His decisions and commandments.

**Third (ayah 132): His mercy that carries His servants.** The refrain's final appearance closes with "and sufficient is Allah as a *Wakīl*" — Ever All-Sufficient as a Disposer of affairs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this third mention as a statement of Allah's mercy which makes things work for people: should one fear Allah and be obedient to Him, Allah will fulfil all his needs, because He is the Owner of everything in this universe. Ibn Kathir adds the note of vigilance in the same verse: He has perfect watch over every soul, knowing what it deserves; He is the Watcher and Witness of all things.

## An unbroken chain of counsel: taqwa

In ayah 131, between the first and second mentions of the refrain, comes the heart of the passage: "And verily, We have enjoined upon those given the Scripture before you, and upon you, that you have taqwa of Allah." Ibn Kathir explains: We have recommended to you what We recommended to the People of the Scriptures — taqwa of Allah, by worshipping Him Alone without partners. The same counsel given to the People of the Scripture before this community is given to it: one standing recommendation, carried from those who received revelation before to those who receive it now.

## Ayah 133: the sobering "if He wills"

"If He wills, He can remove you altogether, O humanity, and bring others; and Allah is ever All-Potent over that." Ibn Kathir states the meaning plainly: He is able to take you away and replace you with other people if you disobey Him. He cites the parallel warning: "And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people, and they will not be your likes."

## Ayah 134: aiming too low

The passage closes by diagnosing a failure not of rebellion but of ambition: "Whoever desires the reward of this world — then with Allah is the reward of this world and of the Hereafter." Ibn Kathir addresses the person directly: O you whose ultimate desire is this life, know that Allah owns the rewards of this life *and* the Hereafter — therefore, if you ask Allah for both, He will enrich you, award you, and suffice you. The error is not in wanting well-being in this world; it is in stopping there, asking the Owner of both rewards for only one of them.

Ibn Kathir supports this with a cluster of ayat. Allah contrasts those who say "Our Lord, give us in this world!" — and have no portion in the Hereafter — with those who pray, "Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and save us from the torment of the Fire," for whom there is a share of what they earned. He also cites: "Whosoever desires (by his deeds) the reward of the Hereafter, We give him increase in his reward" (42:20), and "Whoever desires the quick-passing (transitory enjoyment of this world), We readily grant him what We will for whom We like" (17:18), a passage that continues to "See how We prefer one above another (in this world)" (17:21).

The ayah — and the passage — ends: "And Allah is ever All-Hearer, All-Seer" (*Samīʿ*, *Baṣīr*). He hears and He sees — including the petition of the one who asks only for dunyā. After three declarations of ownership, this closing is the fitting seal: the Owner of everything is not a distant proprietor. He hears you and He sees you.

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage asks two things of a believer, both drawn directly from the commentary. First, taqwa of Allah — worshipping Him Alone without partners, and abiding by the rules just stated concerning women and orphans, with the promise of reward for those who abide by them and the warning for those who contravene them. Second, ambition in supplication: since the reward of this world and the Hereafter are both with Allah, ask Him for both — for whoever asks Him for both, He will enrich, award, and suffice.

passages.title: Stand firm for justice, even against yourselves
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 135 is one of the Qur'an's most uncompromising statements on justice: a command to every believer to be a permanent upholder of fairness and a truthful witness for Allah's sake — even when the testimony cuts against your own self, your parents, or your nearest kin. The ayah then systematically dismantles every excuse a person might reach for: family loyalty, the wealth or poverty of the parties, personal desire, and finally the quieter escape routes of twisting one's words or simply staying silent.

## What the ayah is commanding

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here commands His believing servants "to stand up for justice and fairness and not to deviate from it, right or left" — not fearing anyone's blame, not letting anyone prevent them from doing something for the sake of Allah, and helping and supporting one another for Allah's sake.

The phrase **shuhadāʾ lillāh** — "witnesses to Allah" — sets the standard for testimony. Ibn Kathir links it to Allah's words "And establish the testimony for Allah" (65:2): testimony must be delivered precisely and for the sake of Allah, so that it comes out "correct, truly just, and free of alterations, changes or deletions." A witness is not performing for anyone; he is answering to Allah.

## "Even against yourselves, or your parents, or your kin"

This is the ayah's famous edge. Ibn Kathir: give correct testimony and say the truth when asked, *even if harm will affect you as a consequence* — and he adds the consolation that Allah shall make a way out and give relief for those who obey Him in every matter. As for parents and relatives: do not compromise for their sake; give the correct and just witness even if they are harmed in the process, "for the truth presides above everyone and is preferred to everyone."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what "even against yourselves" really means: justice is not something to be demanded from others only — it must be exacted from one's own self. Say nothing against the truth even when the declaration costs you personally, because that loss is "insignificant, tiny and transitory," whereas the one who placates himself with flat lies "has bought for himself the severe punishment of the Day of Retribution."

**"Be he rich or poor, Allah is a better Protector to both."** Two opposite temptations are cut off in one stroke. Ibn Kathir: do not favour someone in your testimony because he is rich, and do not feel pity for him because he is poor. Allah is the caretaker of both parties, "a better Protector of them than you," and He has better knowledge of what is good for them.

**"So follow not the lusts, lest you may avoid justice."** Ibn Kathir reads this broadly: let neither desire, nor lust, nor the hatred you have against others lure you into injustice in your affairs — rather, stand for justice in all situations. He cites here Allah's words in 5:8: "And let not the enmity and hatred of others make you avoid justice. Be just: that is nearer to piety."

## The two Arabic words at the end: Talwū and Tuʿriḍū

The closing warning — "and if you *talwū* or *tuʿriḍū*" — names the two subtle ways a witness fails without openly lying.

- **Talwū** is to *twist* the testimony. Mujahid and several others among the Salaf (the early generations) explained it as distorting and changing one's testimony; Ibn Kathir notes it includes distortion and intentional lying, and compares it to 3:78, where "among them is a party who *yalwūna* (distort) the Book with their tongues."
- **Tuʿriḍū** is to *turn away* — hiding and withholding the testimony altogether, as in 2:283: "Who hides it, surely, his heart is sinful."

So the ayah covers the whole spectrum: the bold lie, the shaded half-truth, and the coward's silence. Against the last of these, Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet's ﷺ teaching that the best witness is he who discloses his testimony before being asked to do so. And the ayah seals all of it with "Verily, Allah is Ever Well-Acquainted with what you do" — Ibn Kathir adds: and He will reward or punish you accordingly.

## "This is the basis on which the heavens and earth were created"

Ibn Kathir relates a striking story alongside this theme. When the Prophet ﷺ sent ʿAbdullah bin Rawahah to collect the tax on the fruits and produce of the Jews of Khaybar, they offered him a bribe so he would go easy on them. He replied: "By Allah! I have come to you from the dearest of the creation to me, and you are more hated by me than an equivalent number of apes and swine. However, my love for him (the Prophet ﷺ) and hatred for you shall not prevent me from being just with you." They answered: "This (justice) is the basis which the heavens and earth were created."

The story is the ayah made flesh: neither his intense love for one side nor his aversion to the other bent his scales by a hair — and even the opposing party recognised that this is the order the universe itself rests on.

## Why "qawwāmīn" and not simply "be just"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the ayah's first word, **al-qisṭ**: justice and fairness, whose true sense is "that every holder of a right should be given his or her due in full" — covering the rights of Allah and every kind of human right. Upholding qisṭ, it explains, includes not wronging anyone, stopping the wrongdoer (*ẓālim*) and supporting the wronged (*maẓlūm*), not dodging the duty of testifying when a victim needs your witness to recover a usurped right, testifying exactly as things are whether for or against anyone, and — for those in authority — treating both parties before them with complete equality, hearing witnesses carefully, investigating thoroughly, and judging with perfect justice.

Then a fine linguistic point. Allah could have commanded justice in a single word — *aqsiṭū*, "do justice," as in 49:9. Instead He chose the longer construction *kūnū qawwāmīna bil-qisṭ*, using **qawwāmīn** — "those who uphold and are steadfast." Maʿārif explains why the longer wording matters: being just in one particular case now and then proves nothing — even the most evil, tyrannical ruler may find himself having done justice in some case. The word *qawwāmīn* establishes that upholding justice "is a constant duty which must be observed at all times, under all conditions, for every friend or foe." Not an act, but a character.

## The twin ayah in Sūrat al-Māʼidah

Both commentaries pair this ayah with 5:8, which Maʿārif renders: "Be steadfast for Allah as witnesses for justice. And malice against a people should not bid you to not doing justice. Do justice. That is nearer to Taqwa." Maʿārif observes that the two ayat together remove the two great impediments to justice:

- **Love** — kinship, friendship, attachment — which pushes a witness to testify in favour of his own people, and inclines a judge toward the party he is linked to. This ayah (4:135) removes it: "even against yourselves, or your parents, or your kin."
- **Hatred** — grudge, malice, enmity — which may take a witness or judge to lean against an opponent. 5:8 removes it: malice against a people must not bid you to abandon justice.

Maʿārif also notes the mirrored word order: here it is "upholders of *justice*, witnesses for *Allah*" (4:135), while 5:8 has "steadfast for *Allah*, witnesses for *justice*." Most commentators say the interchange shows these are two interpretations of one and the same reality — justice done purely for Allah, and standing for Allah expressed as justice.

## Justice is not the government's job alone

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the lens with 57:25: "We have sent Our messengers with clear signs and We have sent with them the Book and the Balance so that people stand firm with justice and we sent the iron in which there is great awe, and benefits for people." The very purpose of sending prophets and scriptures was that justice should prevail — with the mention of iron hinting that where good counsel fails, the compulsive miscreant must be disciplined through legal process and due punishment.

But — and this is the point Maʿārif presses hardest — these ayat clearly state that establishing justice "is not simply the duty of governments and courts." The address *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* obligates the entire Muslim community, and 57:25 ("so that *mankind* stands firm with justice") binds all human beings: each person must be personally firm upon justice within his or her own circle, and strive that others stay equally firm too. Only the enforcement of justice against those who challenge and flout it falls to government, which holds the reins of power.

Maʿārif diagnoses the modern condition sharply: when people come to believe that dispensing justice is the state's business alone — demanding fairness from their governments while feeling no personal duty to be fair — rulers and ruled harden into confronting parties, law stands on hold, and crime rides high no matter how much legislation and policing multiply. Comparing the century from 1857 to 1957, it observes, every increase in law-making and law-enforcement machinery was matched by a more than matching increase in ever-escalating crime, leaving people further deprived of justice.

## The real guarantee: knowing that Allah sees

Why does the ayah end with "Verily, Allah is Ever Well-Acquainted with what you do"? Maʿārif notices that all three justice ayat close the same way — 4:135 with "Allah is all-aware of what you do," 5:8 with the instruction to observe taqwā followed by "Allah is aware of what you do," 57:25 with "Allah is powerful, mighty." The conclusion each time turns the reader from the courtroom to the Hereafter.

Peace in the world, Maʿārif insists, "has never been achieved through penal codes, nor will it ever be." The only guarantee of universal peace is belief in the Hereafter and the fear of Allah — the realization of His power and domain, the thought of having to be present before Him, of reckoning, and of retribution. When that awareness lives in both ruler and ruled, everyone "pulsates with the crucial sense of individual responsibility": the officials enforce law as servants, not thoughtless masters, of Allah's multitudes of people, never selling law for mean desires or paltry gains; and the masses cannot get away by saying that respecting law was the officials' job. In such a society, law was respected by every individual "in bolted homes and in the darkness of nights."

Maʿārif adds that this is no utopia and no fairy tale: the Prophet ﷺ bequeathed it not as an unproven theory but as a practical, functioning system, followed by the rightly-guided Caliphs and rulers who kept strictly to his Sunnah — an order in which, as the saying goes, the lion and the lamb were seen drinking at the same water trough: identical justice for strong and weak, rich and poor. Indeed, one explanation given of the ayah "And for one who fears the high station of his Rabb (Lord), there will be two Paradises" is exactly this — one Paradise in the Hereafter, and one right here in this world, in the shape of a society where justice reigns.

## Living this ayah

Concretely, this single ayah asks the believer to: testify truthfully even when it costs you or harms your family; refuse to tilt for the rich or out of pity for the poor; guard against your own loves and hatreds as the two great corrupters of fairness; never twist your words, and never hide testimony a wronged person needs; and do all of it not as an occasional act but as a settled trait — *qawwām bil-qisṭ* — because the One for whom you witness "is Ever Well-Acquainted with what you do."

passages.title: Wavering faith and allying with disbelievers
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a turning point in Sūrat al-Nisāʼ. Having dealt for many verses with practical rulings, the sūrah now turns — and stays turned almost to its end — to the question of what faith itself is, and what counterfeit faith looks like. Ayah 136 sets out true īmān in full; ayat 137–139 then hold up its opposite: the person whose belief flickers on and off, and who quietly transfers his loyalty to the enemies of the believers in the hope of borrowing their prestige.

## "O you who believe — believe" (ayah 136)

The opening command sounds strange at first: Allah addresses those who *already* believe and orders them to believe. Ibn Kathir explains that this is not redundancy. It is a command to adhere to all the elements of faith — its branches, pillars and cornerstones — and to keep completing and maintaining that faith continually. He compares it to the believer's plea in every prayer, "Guide us to the straight way" (1:6): the one asking is already on the path, yet asks to be made more aware of it, increased in guidance, and strengthened upon it. Faith, in other words, is not a box ticked once; it is something renewed, deepened, and guarded. Ibn Kathir notes that the Qurʼān speaks this way elsewhere too: "O you who believe! Have Taqwa of Allah, and believe in His Messenger" (57:28).

The ayah then lays out what this faith comprises: Allah, His Messenger, "the Book which He has sent down to His Messenger" — the Qurʼān — and "the Scripture which He sent down to those before," meaning the previously revealed divine Books. And it closes with the warning: whoever disbelieves in Allah, His Angels, His Books, His Messengers, and the Last Day "has strayed far away" — Ibn Kathir glosses this as deviating from correct guidance and wandering far from its path.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the structural logic: first comes this description of īmān as it is credible in the sight of the Sharīʿah; then the following verses censure various groups for beliefs — and deeds flowing from those faulty beliefs — that fall short of it.

## The faith that flickers (ayah 137)

Ayah 137 describes people who "believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then went on increasing in disbelief." About such people Allah says He "will not forgive them, nor guide them on the way."

Who are they? Ibn Kathir reads the verse as describing the hypocrites — this is their signature pattern, belief and disbelief in alternation, "and this is why their hearts become sealed." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same primary view, but also relates (from Rūḥ al-Maʿānī) that some commentators held the verse to be about the Jews: they believed, then disbelieved by taking to the golden calf, then repented and believed, then fell back into disbelief by rejecting the prophethood of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), and finally increased further in disbelief by refusing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

What does "increasing in disbelief" mean? Ibn Kathir cites the comment of Ibn ʿAbbās — recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim through his chain, with Mujahid saying similarly — "They remain on disbelief until they die." That gloss controls how the frightening words "Allah will not forgive them" must be understood. Ibn Kathir: whoever keeps reverting and then *remains on disbelief and increases in it until death* will have no chance of accepted repentance after death, no forgiveness, no deliverance to guidance.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of real pastoral importance here. The verse, read as a whole, means that repeated returning to disbelief corrodes the very ability to receive guidance — such a person is left, in the end, without the will to repent or believe. But this does not overturn the general rule established by the definitive texts of the Qurʼān and Sunnah: a disbeliever or an apostate (murtadd), no matter how hardened, has his past sins forgiven if his tawbah (repentance) is sincere and true. The door of amnesty remains open to anyone who actually walks through it. The verse describes those who never do — who toy with faith until death forecloses the question.

## "Good news" of a painful punishment (ayah 138)

Ayah 138 says: "Give the hypocrites the tidings that there is for them a painful torment." The word used is *bashshir* — from *bashārah*, the word for announcing glad tidings. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the bitter irony: everyone looks forward to some good news to brighten his future, but for the hypocrites there is simply no other news than this. The vocabulary of celebration is turned into a sentence.

## Borrowed honour (ayah 139)

Ayah 139 identifies the tell-tale conduct of these hypocrites: they "take the disbelievers as awliyāʼ — allies, protecting friends — instead of the believers." Ibn Kathir says this means they are the disbelievers' supporters *in reality*: they give them loyalty and friendship in secret, and when alone with them they say, "We are with you; we only mock the believers by pretending to follow their religion."

Then comes the question that exposes the whole enterprise: "Do they seek ʿizzah with them?" ʿIzzah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means might and mastery — honour, power, standing. The hypocrites' calculation, the commentary says, is the common one: the disbelievers' outwardly visible influence, power and collective strength will surely rub off on those who keep close to them. Allah demolishes the assumption in one stroke: "then indeed all ʿizzah belongs to Allah." You are seeking honour from people who do not themselves own any; whenever might and mastery appear in any person, it is Allah who gave it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the absurdity: what reasoning is it to chase honour by *displeasing the Owner and Giver of real honour*, scrounging for temporal prestige through His enemies?

Ibn Kathir cites the parallel verses: "Whosoever desires honor, then to Allah belongs all honor" (35:10), and "But honor belongs to Allah, and to His Messenger, and to the believers — but the hypocrites know not" (63:8). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on that second verse: by joining the Messenger and the believers to Allah in it, the Qurʼān teaches that Allah alone possesses real honour, and He bestows a share of it on those dear to Him. Ibn Kathir adds that the declaration "all honour is Allah's" is itself an invitation — meant to encourage the servants to hold fast to their servitude to Allah and be among His faithful servants, who gain victory in this life and on the Day of Resurrection when the Witnesses stand to testify.

Two sayings of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, distil the point. The first, cited via al-Jaṣṣāṣ: "Whoever seeks honour through human beings is disgraced by Allah." The second — as in Mustadrak al-Hakim — was said to Abu ʿUbaydah, the Governor of Syria: you were the fewest and weakest of people, and Allah multiplied you and raised you in honour through Islam; "if you seek honour from any source other than Allah, Allah will disgrace you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a juristic clarification from Abu Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ in Aḥkām al-Qurʼān: what the verse forbids is seeking honour through friendship with disbelievers and sinners; seeking honour and strength through the Muslims is not forbidden, since Allah has Himself placed honour with His Messenger and the believers (63:8). And on what kind of ʿizzah is meant, the commentary offers both readings: if it is the everlasting honour of the Ākhirah, that belongs to the Messenger and believers by definition, for it can never be the lot of a disbeliever; if it is worldly honour, then — barring transitional periods and accidental turns of history — mastery ultimately belongs to Islam and its people, as the early history of the Muslims showed, with present weakness reflecting weakness of faith rather than any defect in the promise.

## Living it

The passage asks two things of the believer. First: treat faith as a living thing — something to be completed and continually maintained, in Ibn Kathir's words, not a past event; its opposite, the flickering faith of ayah 137, is the disease to be feared. Second: locate your sense of worth correctly. The pull toward the powerful — the instinct that closeness to worldly strength confers standing — is precisely what ayah 139 names and dismantles. All honour is Allah's; He gives it to His Messenger and the believers; and the one who hunts for it anywhere else, in ʿUmar's words, is disgraced by the very One who owns it.

passages.title: Hypocrites: fence-sitting and false allegiance
passages.tafsir:
## What This Passage Is About

These five ayat complete the Qur'an's portrait of the hypocrites (munāfiqūn) begun earlier in the sūrah. What binds them together is a single theme seen from several angles: **divided allegiance**. Ayah 140 forbids the believer from sitting comfortably where Allah's verses are mocked; ayah 141 exposes the hypocrite's habit of watching from the sidelines to see who wins; ayat 142–143 lay bare the inner condition that produces such behaviour — a heart that belongs fully to no one, swaying between two camps; and ayah 144 turns to the believers directly with the command that resolves the whole passage: do not take the disbelievers as allies in place of the believers. Ibn Kathir notes that the censure flows on from the preceding verses (137–139), where the hypocrites are described as believing, then disbelieving, then increasing in disbelief until their hearts are sealed — and as seeking honour (ʿizzah) with the disbelievers, when "to Allah belongs all honor."

## Ayah 140: You Cannot Sit Neutrally While Revelation Is Mocked

Ayah 140 says something startling: "It has already been revealed to you in the Book that when you hear the verses of Allah being denied and mocked at, then sit not with them, until they engage in talk other than that; certainly in that case you would be like them."

**"Already revealed" — which earlier revelation?** Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both identify it: the verse of Sūrah al-Anʿām (6:68), revealed in Makkah before the Hijrah — "And when you see those who engage in false conversation about Our verses by mocking at them, stay away from them." So this is not a new rule; it is a reminder that the command had come down much earlier. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the sting of the reminder: these heedless people had been told long ago not even to *sit* with such company — and now they had gone far beyond sitting, establishing friendly relations with the mockers on the assumption that they held honour and power in their own right. (Ibn Kathir also records the view of Muqatil bin Hayyan that this ayah abrogated part of the al-Anʿām verse, alongside 6:69, which had said that those who fear Allah and keep their duty to Him are not responsible for the mockers — their duty is only to remind.)

**"You would be like them" — how far does this go?** Ibn Kathir explains: if you knowingly remain seated where Allah's verses are rejected and mocked, and you sanction that conduct, you have participated in what they are doing and share the burden they earn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two levels. If a person's heart actually approves of the mockery — if he likes and is satisfied with those expressions of disbelief — then he is in reality a disbeliever, "because liking kufr is nothing but kufr." If his heart does not approve but he sits on regardless, he becomes "like them" in the sense of an accomplice: by his presence he abets their assault on the faith.

**What counts as "mocking the verses"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the lens beyond crude ridicule. Citing Ibn ʿAbbas (as reported by Dahhak), it includes those who explain the Qur'an erroneously, distort its meaning (taḥrīf), or invent in the religion what is not there (bidʿah) — meanings contrary to the explanation given by the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions or against the consensus of the Muslim community. From this the commentary derives a practical ruling: attending the teaching sessions of someone who expounds the Qur'an against the understanding of the righteous early generations is itself impermissible — a sin rather than a source of reward. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr al-Muhit, states the underlying principle memorably: what is sinful to say is equally sinful to hear voluntarily — "Protect your ears from hearing the evil / As you protect your tongue from saying it."

**When the talk changes topic, may you stay?** The Qur'an leaves this unstated, and the scholars differed. Some held the prohibition ends when the offensive talk ends. Hasan al-Basri held that sitting with such people is not correct even afterwards, arguing from the al-Anʿām verse's wording "do not sit *with the unjust people*" — the person remains unjust even after he changes the subject. Qadi Thanaullah Panipati, in al-Tafsir al-Mazhari, harmonised the views: even after the talk moves on, sitting with such people *unnecessarily* remains forbidden, but sitting for a genuine religious or worldly need is permissible.

**The limits and the balance.** The obligation to withdraw has its own conditions. Imam al-Jassas writes in Ahkam al-Qur'an that one who witnesses sin in a gathering should stop it by force if able; failing that, he must at least show displeasure — the lowest degree being to rise and leave. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates in this connection — citing al-Bahr al-Muhit — that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdul-ʿAziz punished a man found sitting among wine-drinkers even though the man was fasting and had drunk nothing: mere unexplained presence was blameworthy. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites, from Ibn Kathir's Tafsir, the Prophet's ﷺ words: "One who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not sit to dine where liquor is being served." Yet leaving must not itself entail sin: one does not abandon congregational prayer in the masjid because something objectionable occurs there. Hasan al-Basri warned: "If we were to keep giving up what we must do just because of the sins of other people, we shall be paving the way for all sorts of sinners to come and destroy the Sunnah and Shariʿah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the possible postures towards such company: approving their attacks on the faith is kufr; staying without valid excuse while inwardly disliking it is fisq (sinfulness); staying for a genuine worldly need is allowed; staying to convey Islam is an act of worship; and staying under compulsion is excusable.

## Ayah 141: The Fence-Sitters

"Those who wait and watch about you" — Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites watch for harm to befall the believers, awaiting the day the Muslims' circumstances dissolve and disbelief takes over. Their speech is calibrated to whoever wins. If Allah grants the believers victory, they say "Were we not with you?" — cozying up for a share of the triumph and the booty. But if the disbelievers gain a success — as happened at Uhud, for the Messengers are tested though the final victory is theirs — the hypocrites tell them, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?" Meaning: did we not secretly help you, confuse the believers, and weaken their resolve? Ibn Kathir names the motive precisely: they pretend friendship with both parties so as to be safe from the harm of both — the fruit of weak faith and lack of certainty.

The ayah answers with the Day of Judgment: "Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection." Do not be deceived, Ibn Kathir warns, by the shade of Islamic law that protects the hypocrite outwardly in this life; on that Day the secrets of souls will be disclosed and pretending will avail nothing.

**"Never will Allah grant the disbelievers a way over the believers."** The early authorities read this promise in two registers. ʿAli bin Abi Talib, when asked about it, tied it to the previous clause: Allah will judge on the Day of Resurrection, and *then* He will never grant the disbelievers victory over the believers — a reading also related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Malik al-Ashjaʿi. As-Suddi added that "way" (sabīl) can mean *proof*. Ibn Kathir allows a this-worldly sense too: the disbelievers may sometimes defeat some Muslims, but they will never be enabled to exterminate the believers entirely; the final triumph belongs to the believers in this life and the Hereafter, as Allah says, "Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in the worldly life" (40:51).

## Ayat 142–143: The Anatomy of the Hypocrite Heart

**"They seek to deceive Allah, but it is He Who deceives them."** Ibn Kathir is careful with this expression: there is no doubt that Allah can never be deceived, for His knowledge encompasses every secret the hearts conceal. The hypocrites, out of ignorance and weak minds, imagine that because their act fooled people — Islamic law shielding them as apparent Muslims — the same act will work on Allah on the Day of Resurrection; indeed they will swear to Him then as they swear to people now. "He deceives them" means He lures them further into their misguidance and bars them from the truth in this life and the next — as in the scene of 57:13, where the hypocrites call to the believers, "Wait for us! Let us get something from your light!" and are told to turn back. Ibn Kathir also cites here a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever wants to be heard of, Allah will make him heard of, and whoever wants to be seen, Allah will show him."

**The hypocrite at prayer.** "When they stand up for Salah, they stand with laziness and to be seen of men, and they do not remember Allah but little." Ibn Kathir observes that this is their attitude toward the most honoured act of worship: no true intention, no belief in it, no humility, no understanding — and inwardly, no sincerity, only performance for people. They especially shirk the prayers they can hide from, ʿIsha' and Fajr, prayed in darkness. The hadith in the Two Sahihs records the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying that the heaviest prayers on the hypocrites are ʿIsha' and Dawn — "If they knew their rewards, they would attend them even if they had to crawl" — and that he was moved to have the prayer established and then go with men carrying firewood to the houses of those who stay away. And the vivid hadith reported by Imam Malik from Anas bin Malik — recorded also by Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i, with At-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan Sahih" — has the Prophet ﷺ say three times, "This is the prayer of the hypocrite": he sits watching the sun until it sinks between the two horns of the devil, then stands and pecks out four rakʿahs, remembering Allah in them only a little.

Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi, in Bayān al-Qur'ān, adds an important reassurance for the ordinary believer: the laziness censured here is *doctrinal* laziness — sluggishness born of lacking real conviction. Laziness that exists despite correct belief is outside this censure; and if it comes from a valid excuse such as sickness, fatigue or sleepiness, it is not even blameworthy — though without excuse it is.

**"Swaying between this and that."** Ayah 143 gives the passage its defining image: mudhabdhabīn — belonging neither to these nor to those. Ibn Kathir explains: they are with the believers outwardly and with the disbelievers inwardly, at home in neither camp, some of them seized by fits of doubt, leaning one way and then the other — like those of whom Allah said, "Whenever it flashes for them, they walk therein, and when darkness covers them, they stand still" (2:20). Mujahid identified the two poles: "belonging neither to these" — the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ — "nor to those" — the Jews. And the Prophet ﷺ gave the picture that fixes it in the memory — recorded by Ibn Jarir from Ibn ʿUmar, and by Muslim: the hypocrite is like a sheep wandering between two herds, going now to this one, now to that one, not knowing which to follow.

The verse closes: "he whom Allah sends astray, you will not find for him a way." Ibn Kathir comments that whomever Allah leads astray from the paths of safety will find no guide and no rescuer; none can resist Allah's decision, and He is not asked about what He does, while they all will be asked.

## Ayah 144: The Command That Resolves It

Having exposed the hypocrite, the passage turns to the believers: "O you who believe! Do not take disbelievers as awliyā' (allies and protecting friends) instead of believers." Ibn Kathir spells out what this wilāyah includes: befriending and associating with them, advising them, being intimate with them, and exposing the believers' secrets to them — and he links it to another ayah in which Allah forbids the believers to take the disbelievers as friends instead of the believers, "except if you indeed fear a danger from them," with the warning, "And Allah warns you against Himself."

Then the arresting question: "Do you wish to offer Allah a manifest sulṭān against yourselves?" Ibn Abi Hatim narrates from Ibn ʿAbbas — with an authentic chain, and it is also the view of Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazi, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and An-Nadr bin ʿArabi — that *sulṭān* in the Qur'an means **proof**. That is: do you want to hand Allah clear evidence against yourselves, warranting His punishment? The believer who takes the mockers of revelation as his allies is not merely being imprudent; he is writing the case against himself.

Ibn Kathir's commentary then carries the thought into the verses that immediately follow this passage (ayat 145–147): there the hypocrites are declared to be in the lowest depth of the Fire — Ibn Masʿud said, in sealed coffins of fire — *except* those who repent, do righteous deeds, hold fast to Allah, and purify their religion for Him, replacing showing off with sincerity; they will be with the believers, and Allah will grant the believers a great reward. Those verses lie beyond this passage, but they are the answer the sūrah itself gives to the question ayah 144 raises.

## Living It

The passage draws one line through every scene: allegiance cannot be split. Concretely, it asks the believer to guard his *company* — not to lend his silent presence to gatherings, teaching circles, or conversations where Allah's revelation is denied, ridiculed or twisted, unless he stays for a purpose the Shariʿah itself recognises (necessity, a genuine need, or the work of conveying Islam); to guard his *prayer* — attending it, and attending to it, since a prayer pecked out for show is the very signature of hypocrisy, while honest tiredness in a believing heart is not; and to guard his *loyalty* — never trading the fellowship of the believers for the patronage of those hostile to the faith in hope of their honour or protection, "for verily, to Allah belongs all honor" (ayah 139, which Ibn Kathir reads with 35:10 and 63:8). The sheep wandering between two herds belongs, in the end, to neither — but as the verses that follow this passage declare, the door of repentance, sincerity and firm attachment to Allah stands open even to the hypocrite, and through it he rejoins the believers.

passages.title: The lowest depth, and the way back out of it
passages.tafsir:
# The lowest depth, and the way back out of it

What binds these three ayat together is a single movement from terror to hope: ayah 145 states the sentence — the lowest depth of the Fire — ayah 146 states the exception, and ayah 147 asks a question so tender it reframes everything before it: *why would Allah punish you at all, if you are grateful and believe?*

## Why the punishment is stated only now

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a shift in purpose here. The preceding verses were concerned with pointing out some of the ugly traits of the hypocrites, and their punishment of being in Hell with the disbelievers was mentioned only as a corollary to another subject. From this stage onwards, the purpose is to state their punishment clearly. And the reason, Maʿārif explains, is mercy in disguise: the fear that such an impending punishment generates in a good-natured person usually becomes the very reason for early repentance. That is why the threat in ayah 145 does not stand alone; exemption from punishment is promised immediately in ayah 146 to those who repent, together with the incentive of a good reward. The warning exists to drive the reader toward the exception.

The passage also flows straight out of ayah 144, where Allah forbade the believers from taking the disbelievers as friends and allies instead of the believers — a course of action that, in the ayah's own words, hands Allah "a manifest sulṭān" against oneself, which Ibn Kathir explains as proof against you that warrants receiving His torment. To secretly side with the enemies of faith is to build the evidence for one's own conviction. Ayah 145 then reveals where that road ends.

## Ayah 145 — the lowest depth

"Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire." The phrase is *ad-dark al-asfal* — rendered "the lowest depth (grade)." Ibn Kathir explains that this will be on the Day of Resurrection, due to their tremendous kufr — disbelief. He records, through ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah (al-Wālibī), that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the phrase simply: the bottom of the Fire. Other scholars, Ibn Kathir adds, drew out the structural point: just as Paradise has ever higher grades, the Fire has ever lower depths. Hell is not flat. There is a hierarchy of ruin, and the hypocrite is placed at its floor.

The most vivid picture in the sources comes from the Companion ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd. Ibn Jarir records his explanation of this ayah: the hypocrites will be inside coffins of Fire that surround them, closed and sealed upon them. Ibn Abi Hatim records that when Ibn Masʿūd was asked about the hypocrites, he said: "They will be placed in coffins made of fire and they will be closed in them in the lowest depth of the Fire."

And then the ayah's closing clause: "no helper will you find for them." Ibn Kathir comments that no one will save them from their misery and painful torment. The hypocrite's whole strategy in this life was to keep helpers on every side — believers here, disbelievers there, always hedged. On that Day the hedging yields nothing at all.

## Ayah 146 — the four steps back

Then comes *illā* — "except." The sentence just pronounced is not final for anyone still breathing. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: whoever among the hypocrites repents in this life, Allah will accept his repentance and sorrow, if the repentance is sincere and he follows it with righteous deeds while depending on his Lord.

The ayah lays out four movements, and it is worth walking through them in order, because together they map the road out of the deepest pit:

- **"Those who repent" (tābū)** — the turning itself: renouncing the hypocrisy.
- **"Mend their ways" (aṣlaḥū)** — repentance proven in conduct; the sources stress that sincere sorrow must be *followed by performing righteous deeds*.
- **"Hold fast to Allah" (iʿtaṣamū billāh)** — depending on Him, as Ibn Kathir glosses it. The one who abandoned his double game needs something firmer than his old alliances to hold onto.
- **"Purify their religion for Allah" (akhlaṣū dīnahum lillāh)** — the decisive one, because it strikes hypocrisy at its root. Ibn Kathir explains it as *replacing showing off with sincerity, so that their good deeds will benefit them, even if they were minute*. Note that consolation: once the disease of display is cured, even tiny deeds count.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this fourth step under the heading "The Meaning of Sincerity." A deed, to be acceptable with Allah, has to be free of hypocrisy and exclusively for His sake and pleasure. The word for the sincere person is *mukhliṣ*, and Maʿārif remarks that "sincere" is actually a weaker equivalent of it. The Muslim jurists defined the *mukhliṣ*, as cited from Mazhari: "A sincere person is one who acts for Allah alone and does not like that people praise him for it." That second clause is the sharp edge. It is not enough to act for Allah; the *mukhliṣ* does not even *want* the human applause. Hypocrisy is precisely the appetite for being seen; *ikhlāṣ* — sincerity — is its cure: a deed that would be done identically if no human eye ever fell on it.

And the promise for those who make this turn: "then they will be with the believers" — on the Day of Resurrection, Ibn Kathir specifies. Not merely spared the Fire, but granted membership among the very people they once deceived. "And Allah will grant the believers a great reward" — the former hypocrite, now sincere, is folded into that reward without an asterisk.

## Ayah 147 — the question that changes the register

After this severe threat, Allah asks: "Why should Allah punish you if you are grateful and faithful?" Ibn Kathir draws out what the question reveals: Allah is too Rich to need anyone — He gains nothing from punishing His servants, and He only punishes them because of their sins. Punishment is not divine appetite; it is the consequence of what people themselves choose. Remove the sin — by thanking Him and believing in Him, by correcting your actions and having faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ — and the punishment has no reason to exist.

The ayah seals this with two of Allah's names: "And Allah is Ever All-Appreciative (of good), All-Knowing" — *Shākiran ʿAlīmā*. Ibn Kathir's comment on the first is striking: Allah *appreciates those who appreciate Him*. The servant thanks Allah, and Allah — who needs nothing — responds with appreciation of the servant. And He is All-Knowing: He has knowledge of those whose hearts believe in Him, and He will give them perfect reward. That last point closes the circle of the whole passage. The hypocrite's wager was that hearts are hidden; ayah 147 answers that nothing in the heart is hidden from Allah — which is terrifying news for the insincere, and the best possible news for the sincere, whose unseen, unpraised deeds are seen and repaid in full by the One whose appreciation actually matters.

## Living it

The passage names the hypocrites, but its architecture addresses anyone who finds traces of their disease in himself — acting for an audience, hedging his loyalties, keeping his inside and outside out of step. Its message is double. First, that this disease is not minor: the Qurʼān assigns it the lowest depth of the Fire. Second — and this is where the passage insists on ending — the door out is open and the steps are named: turn, mend, hold fast to Allah, and purify the deed until you no longer even crave the praise. Do that, and the threat of ayah 145 dissolves into the question of ayah 147: why would Allah punish you? He is Appreciative and Knowing — and He is waiting to appreciate you.

passages.title: Speaking ill, being wronged, and choosing to pardon
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat form a small, complete moral law about the words we speak when we have been hurt. Ayah 148 lays down the general rule — Allah does not love that evil speech be uttered openly — then carves out one merciful exception: the person who has been wronged. Ayah 149 immediately lifts the reader above that concession, holding out something better than permitted retaliation: doing good, openly or secretly, and pardoning the one who hurt you. Together, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the two verses "give a law to eradicate injustice and oppression from the world" — a law built not on compulsion alone, but on a combination of justice permitted and forgiveness beloved.

## The rule and its one exception

The default in this religion is restraint of the tongue. Allah does not love that evil — cursing, denouncing, broadcasting another person's wrong — be spoken aloud in public. But the ayah adds: *illā man ẓulim*, "except by him who has been wronged." The victim of injustice is not required to suffer in silence.

The early commentators understood this exception concretely. Ibn Kathir relates, through Ali bin Abi Talhah, that Ibn ʿAbbas explained the ayah to mean that Allah does not like anyone to invoke Him against another person — to call down His punishment on someone — *unless* that person has been wronged. In that case Allah permits the victim to invoke Him against the wrongdoer. And then Ibn ʿAbbas adds the note that colours everything that follows: "Yet, it is better for one if he observes patience."

Al-Hasan al-Basri pressed the point further, steering even the wronged person away from curses. Rather than praying against the oppressor, he taught, one should supplicate: "O Allah! Help me against him and take my right from him." In another narration al-Hasan said that Allah has allowed the wronged person to invoke Him against the oppressor — but "without transgressing the limits." Even the licensed complaint has a ceiling.

ʿAbdul-Karim bin Malik al-Jazari drew the line with a vivid example: "When a man curses you, you could curse him in retaliation. But if he lies about you, you may not lie about him." You may answer like with like; you may never answer wrong with a different wrong. He cited in support the ayah, "And indeed whosoever takes revenge after he has suffered wrong, for such there is no way (of blame) against them."

## The limit on retaliation

The Sunnah seals this boundary. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Abu Dawud, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whatever words are uttered by those who curse each other, then he who started it will carry the burden thereof, unless the one who was wronged transgresses the limit." The sin of the whole exchange falls on the one who began it — a striking mercy toward the person provoked — but only so long as the wronged party stays within bounds. The moment retaliation exceeds the original wrong, the victim forfeits that protection.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this to the parallel ruling in Surah al-Nahl (16:126): if you retaliate, retaliate only with the like of what was done to you — and if you are patient, that is better for the patient. The principle it draws out: an injustice may never be answered with another injustice. Retaliation, where it happens at all, must itself be an act of justice — measured, equal, and no more. Otherwise, in the words of the commentary, "it is you who would turn into the unjust one."

In its commentary on these verses, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes a practical consequence: when an oppressed person goes about complaining to people about the injustice done to him, this is not counted as *ghibah* (backbiting), which is otherwise haram (forbidden) — because it is the oppressor who, by his own act, gave the victim the opportunity to complain. The wronged person may protest, and may go to a court of law to seek redress; this is "the basic demand of justice" and itself a means of eradicating crime.

## Ayah 149: the higher road

Having secured the victim's rights, the passage immediately turns his gaze upward. "Whether you disclose a good deed, or conceal it, or pardon an evil — verily, Allah is Ever Pardoning, All-Powerful." Ibn Kathir explains: when you acknowledge a good favour done to you, or conceal your own good deeds, and forgive those who wrong you, this brings you closer to Allah and increases your reward with Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks why the doing of good — open or secret — is mentioned in a verse whose real concern is pardoning injustice. The answer it gives: to hint that overlooking and forgiving is itself a great act of good, and whoever chooses it becomes deserving of Allah's own mercy and forgiveness.

**Why "Ever Pardoning, All-Powerful"?** The pairing of the two divine names at the verse's close — *ʿAfuwwan Qadīrā* — is the heart of the argument. Ibn Kathir writes that among Allah's attributes is that He forgives and pardons His servants *although He is able to punish them*. His pardon is never weakness; it flows from perfect power. Ibn Kathir relates the report that some of the angels who carry Allah's Throne praise Him saying, "All praise is due to You for Your forbearing even though You have perfect knowledge," while others say, "All praise is due to You for Your forgiving even though You have perfect ability (to punish)." Forbearance joined to knowledge, forgiveness joined to power — this is the divine pattern the verse invites the believer to imitate.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns the same point into an argument addressed to us: Allah is powerful in the absolute sense — He can punish whomever He wills — yet He is All-Forgiving. A human being, by contrast, has little real power; if he sets his heart on revenge, he may not even have the capability to carry it out. For such a creature, how much more fitting is it to overlook and forgive.

And the pardoner loses nothing. Ibn Kathir cites an authentic hadith: "No charity shall ever decrease wealth, and Allah will only increase the honor of a servant who pardons, and he who is humble for Allah's sake, then Allah will elevate his grade." What looks like surrendering a right is, in Allah's accounting, a rise in honour.

## Why this law works

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with a reflection on the wisdom of this two-sided design. Worldly laws are "limited to dictatory formulations" — they command and threaten. This law works instead by "a combination of persuasion and awe." On one side, it upholds justice: the victim may protest, retaliate in equal measure, or seek redress in court. On the other, it holds up the immense gain of the life to come and persuades the victim to make "a little sacrifice" of his legitimate right.

The difference shows in the outcomes. Court decisions and measured revenge do check injustice, the commentary concedes — but the parties usually walk away "saddled with long term grievances and feelings of abhorrence" that seed future disputes. The Qur'an's way of pardon produces something no verdict can: reconciliation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the promise the Qur'an gives at another place (41:34) — "You will see that he with whom you had enmity has become your closest friend." Old enmities, met with forgiveness, can change into close and lasting friendships.

## Living these ayat

The passage leaves the believer with a clear ladder. If you are wronged, you are not condemned to silence: you may complain, you may supplicate against the oppressor — al-Hasan's du'a, "O Allah, help me against him and take my right from him," is a model of restraint even here — and you may seek exact, never excessive, redress. But at every rung the Qur'an whispers that patience is better, and at the top stands pardon: releasing your claim as an act of good done for Allah, in imitation of the One who pardons while fully able to punish. The promise attached to it is not merely peace between people, but nearness to Allah, increase in reward, and honour that only grows.

passages.title: Dividing between Allah and His messengers
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat draw a single, decisive line through humanity. On one side stand those who pick and choose among Allah's messengers — believing in some, rejecting others, and calling that arrangement faith. On the other stand those who receive every prophet Allah ever sent as one unbroken chain. The passage is one sentence of divine judgement in two halves: the verdict on selective belief (ayat 150–151), and the promise to whole belief (ayah 152).

## The illusion of a "middle way"

Ayah 150 describes people who "wish to make distinction between Allah and His messengers," saying, "We believe in some but reject others," and who "wish to adopt a way in between." The wording is telling: they present their position as a reasonable compromise — not outright rejection of Allah, not full acceptance of His messengers, but a path between the two.

Notice how the ayah itself names what they are doing: not merely dividing between one messenger and another, but making "distinction *between Allah and His messengers*" — and Ibn Kathir specifies that this distinction is "in faith." The ayah then refuses to grant their self-description any standing; before their words are even quoted, it has already called them "those who disbelieve in Allah and His Messengers." The supposed middle path is never treated as a path at all.

Ibn Kathir presses on the arbitrariness of it. Those who make this distinction, he says, "do not follow any proof for such distinction, because there is no such proof." What actually drives the selection is desire, prejudice, and the inherited practice of forefathers. He then surveys the landscape of his day as illustration: the Jews accepted the prophets but not ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them; the Christians accepted the prophets but rejected the final and seal of them, Muhammad ﷺ; the Samaritans accepted no prophet after Yushaʿ (Joshua), the successor of Musa bin ʿImran; and the Zoroastrians were said to follow only Zoroaster — while discarding the very law he brought. In every case the dividing line falls exactly where communal loyalty and habit fall, never where evidence does.

## Why partial faith is no faith at all

Ayah 151 delivers the verdict: "they are indeed the true disbelievers" — *al-kāfirūna ḥaqqan*, disbelievers in truth, in reality, whatever they call themselves.

Ibn Kathir explains the logic behind this severe judgement, and it is worth sitting with. If a person truly believed in a messenger, that same reasoning would compel him to believe in every other messenger — "especially if the other Messenger has a stronger proof for his truthfulness. Or at least, they would have strived hard to acquire knowledge of the truth of the other Messenger." The one who rejects a prophet "out of envy, bias and personal whim," Ibn Kathir says, "only demonstrates that his faith in other Prophets is not valid, but an act of following desire and whim." So, in his words, "whoever rejects only one of Allah's Prophets, he will have disbelieved in all of them" — because it is required of mankind to believe in every prophet whom Allah sent to the people of the earth.

The punishment named at the end of ayah 151 — "a humiliating torment" — answers the crime precisely. Ibn Kathir notes it is just recompense for *belittling* the prophets they rejected and for preferring the insignificant possessions of this world. And in some cases the rejection came after knowledge, not before it: he cites the Jewish rabbis of the Prophet's ﷺ time, who envied him the great prophethood Allah gave him, and therefore denied him, defied him, and fought against him — upon which Allah sent humiliation on them in this life, to be followed by disgrace in the Hereafter, as in His saying, "And they were covered with humiliation and misery, and they drew on themselves the wrath of Allah" (2:61). Those who dealt in humiliation of Allah's messengers are repaid in the same coin.

## The believers: one chain, no gaps

Ayah 152 turns to the other camp: "those who believe in Allah and His messengers and make no distinction between any of them." Ibn Kathir identifies them as the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, "who believe in every Book that Allah has revealed and in every Prophet whom Allah has sent," and he anchors this in the parallel verse: "The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord, and (so do) the believers. All of them believe in Allah" (2:285). This is the distinctive mark of this Ummah — every prophet whom Allah has sent, and every Book He has revealed, belongs to a Muslim's creed.

For them, "We shall give them their rewards" — Ibn Kathir speaks of great rewards, tremendous favor, and a handsome bounty prepared for them — and the ayah closes with two names of Allah: "and Allah is Ever Forgiving, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir's comment on this closing is brief and tender: forgiving "for their sin, if they have any." Whole faith does not mean sinlessness; it means the door of mercy stands open over whatever shortfalls remain.

## Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: salvation depends on this faith — and the answer to a common misreading

The commentary Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the doctrinal consequence bluntly: this passage is "a clear verdict" against the idea that a person may keep to a creed that rejects some of the prophets and still look forward to salvation. It addresses a misreading that fuels that idea — Surah al-Baqarah 2:62, "Surely, those who believed in Allah... whosoever believes in Allah and in the Last Day, and does good deeds — they have their reward with their Lord." Some conclude from it that belief in Allah and the Last Day alone suffices, with belief in the prophets optional.
