The answer, Maʿārif explains, is that the Qur'an has its own terminology: "Belief in Allah," wherever the Qur'an credits it, means belief in Allah *together with* belief in His Prophet — otherwise, as Maʿārif observes, even the Satan admits that a single Creator exists and that He is One. And the Qur'an clarifies its own meaning in 2:137: "So, if they believe in the like of what you believe in, they have certainly found the right path." Faith counts when it is the same faith the believers hold — in which belief in the Prophet is indispensable. Maʿārif cites here a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that one part of the Qur'an explains the other, and concludes that it is not permissible to explain the Qur'an in any way contrary to the Qur'an's own tafsir of itself — so 2:62 must be read alongside verses like these, never against them.

Maʿārif adds a test of coherence: had salvation been available through every religion, Islam would have had no right to stake life and property on spreading its message (*tablīgh* — conveying the call of Islam); the mission of the Prophet ﷺ — indeed the revelation of the Qur'an itself — would be rendered, Allah forbid, redundant. The seriousness with which Islam calls people to itself is itself proof that the call matters.

## Firm in creed, generous in conduct

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is equally careful to head off the opposite error. Islam, it states, "stands unmatched in its attitude to non-Muslims in matters of justice and fairness, sympathy and goodwill, favour and tolerance." What it will not do is treat articles of faith as personal property to be gifted away for the sake of appearing broad-minded — "religious principles and articles of faith are not our property which we could donate or present to somebody." The believer is asked to hold both at once: maximum sympathy and tolerance toward people of other faiths, and unbending firmness in the defence of faith's frontiers.

That is the practical weight of these ayat for a believer today. Guard the completeness of your faith: every messenger, every Book, no gaps, no picking by preference. And when tolerance is asked of you, give it generously in your dealings — but never by trimming the creed, for these ayat have already named selective belief for what it is: not a middle way, but disbelief in truth. And for those who hold the whole rope, ayah 152 leaves the last word with Allah's own names — Ever Forgiving, Most Merciful.

passages.title: The covenant at the Mount, and the breach that followed
passages.tafsir:
# The Covenant at the Mount, and the Breach That Followed (4:153–155)

This passage answers a fresh provocation with an old record. Jewish chiefs came to the Prophet ﷺ and demanded that he bring down a book from the heaven, all written from there, like the one that came to Musa (peace be upon him) — only then, they said, would they believe. Allah replies by unrolling the history of their own forefathers: a people who demanded far more than that, were given sign after sign, were bound by a solemn covenant sealed under a mountain raised over their heads, and broke every term of it. What holds these three ayat together is the movement from **demand** (ayah 153) to **covenant** (ayah 154) to **breach and its consequence** (ayah 155).

## The demand behind ayah 153

The commentators preserve the occasion. Muhammad bin Ka'b Al-Qurazi, As-Suddi and Qatadah said the Jews asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to cause a book to come down to them from heaven, just as the Tawrah was sent down to Musa. Ibn Jurayj adds a variant: they asked for books addressed personally to named individuals among them, testifying that he was truly sent. Ibn Kathir is blunt about the motive — this was not sincere inquiry but "stubbornness, defiance, rejection and disbelief," and he notes the disbelievers of Quraysh made the same kind of demand: "We shall not believe in you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us" (17:90).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the purpose the verse served for the Prophet ﷺ himself. The demand was "a device to drag and stall," one excuse in an endless series from a people given to taking the opposite stand; by revealing this verse, Allah made him aware of the real state of affairs, **to give him comfort and peace of mind** in dealing with a people long accustomed to harassing the prophets of Allah.

Then comes the devastating reply: *"Indeed, they asked Musa for even greater than that."* Their ancestors said to Musa, **"Show us Allah openly"** — and for that wickedness, that injustice and rebellion, they were struck by the thunderbolt. The Qur'an had already told this story in Surat Al-Baqarah: "you were struck by a bolt of lightning while you were looking. Then We raised you up after your death, so that you might be grateful" (2:55–56). The point of the comparison is sharp: a written book from the sky is a small thing next to demanding to see Allah Himself — and even the greater demand, when granted its answer, produced no faith, only destruction.

## The calf — and the forgiveness that followed

Ayah 153 continues: *"Then they worshipped the calf even after the clear proofs (al-bayyināt) had come to them."* Ibn Kathir stresses the timing. This was **after** they had witnessed the tremendous miracles at Musa's hand in Egypt, and after they watched Fir'awn and his army drown in the sea. Yet almost immediately, passing a people devoted to idols, they said, "Make for us a god as they have gods" (7:138); and when Musa went to meet his Lord, they took the calf as an object of worship. Ibn Kathir recalls how their repentance was accepted: those who had not worshipped the calf were commanded to kill those who had, they complied, and Allah resurrected them afterwards.

Then the ayah pivots on a single clause: *"Even so, We forgave them."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here: Allah remained forbearing when "the occasion demanded that they be eliminated." Amid a catalogue of crimes, the passage deliberately records divine pardon — and then Allah's continued favour: "We gave Musa a clear proof of authority (sulṭānan mubīnā)."

## Ayah 154: the mountain overhead

*"And for their covenant, We raised over them the Mount (aṭ-Ṭūr)."* Ibn Kathir explains the scene: they had refused to implement the rulings of the Tawrah and rejected what Musa brought them from Allah, so Allah raised the mountain above their heads and they were ordered to prostrate. They did — but even in prostration they kept glancing upward, terrified the mountain would fall on them, as Surat Al-A'raf describes: "when We raised the mountain over them as if it had been a canopy, and they thought it was going to fall on them: 'Hold firmly to what We have given you'" (7:171). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it starkly: the Mount of Tur was suspended over them to compel acknowledgement of the Law of the Torah — accept it, or be crushed beneath the mountain.

Two further commands complete the covenant. First: *"Enter the gate prostrating (or bowing) with humility."* Ibn Kathir relates that they were commanded to enter Bayt Al-Quds (Jerusalem) bowing and saying "Ḥiṭṭah" — a plea meaning, in his gloss, "O Allah, take from us our sin of abandoning Jihad," the sin that had caused their forty years of wandering in the desert of Tih. Instead, they defied the command "in word and action": they entered crawling on their rear ends and twisted the word of repentance into a joke — "Ḥinṭah (a wheat grain) in Sha'rah (the hair)." Second: *"Transgress not on the Sabbath"* — a command to honour the day and what Allah had prohibited on it, which they later violated "by deceit and trickery," the story of the town by the sea told in Surat Al-A'raf.

The ayah closes: *"And We took from them a mīthāqan ghalīẓā"* — a firm covenant, which Ibn Kathir explains as a strong covenant. This was no casual promise but a solemn pledge — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises, "they contravened every single command, one after the other, breaking the solemn pledge with Allah." That commentary closes its account of the covenant with a sobering verdict: because of this, Allah put disgrace on them in the mortal life of this world, and they will have to undergo the worst punishment in the Hereafter as well.

## Ayah 155: the breach and the seal

Ayah 155 opens with *fa-bimā naqḍihim mīthāqahum* — "so, because of their breaking of their covenant..." — and begins a list of the crimes that earned condemnation: breaking the covenant, rejecting the āyāt of Allah (His signs, proofs, and the miracles witnessed at the hands of their Prophets, as Ibn Kathir explains), and *"their killing the Prophets unjustly"* — for, he writes, they killed many Prophets, may Allah's peace be upon them.

Then comes their own self-description: *"Our hearts are ghulf."* Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, As-Suddi and Qatadah all explain **ghulf** as "wrapped with covering." It was offered as an excuse — as Ibn Kathir puts it, it is as if they claimed their hearts could not understand what the Prophet says because they were wrapped with coverings. He notes the idolaters said the very same thing: "Our hearts are under coverings from that to which you invite us" (41:5).

The Qur'an's reply overturns the excuse: *"Nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief."* The sealing was not a prior condition excusing rejection; the ayah names their disbelief as its cause. Their hearts, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "became accustomed to Kufr, transgression and weak faith" — *"so they believe not but a little."*

The passage does not end here in the surah itself: this list of crimes runs on into the following ayat — the slander against Maryam and the claim about 'Isa, peace be upon them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's brief note on this ayah says just that: like the earlier verses, the censure of the Jews continues through the present ones, and their false ideas are also refuted — a refutation taken up in detail in the commentary on the verses that follow.

## What the passage teaches

Read as a whole, these ayat make one argument. Demands for spectacular signs, made in stubbornness rather than sincerity, are a stalling tactic, not a path to faith — the generation that saw the sea close over Fir'awn, the thunderbolt, and a mountain suspended overhead still worshipped a calf and mocked the word of repentance. Faith is not produced by escalating proofs but by a heart willing to receive them; and a heart that persistently refuses is, by Allah's just decree, sealed because of its own disbelief. Alongside the warning stands the mercy: even after the calf, "We forgave them" — Allah's forbearance outlasted crimes that, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, demanded elimination. The covenant at the Mount is remembered not to satisfy curiosity about the past, but so that those who now carry Allah's final revelation hold firmly to what they have been given — and do not repeat the breach.

passages.title: Their slander against Mary and their boast of killing the Messiah
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat continue the indictment that began in ayah 155. Allah is listing, one by one, the crimes for which the Children of Israel forfeited His favour — breaking the covenant, rejecting His signs, killing the Prophets — and now the list reaches its two most shocking entries: a vile slander against a righteous woman, and a boast of having murdered a Messenger of Allah. What holds the pair together is that both are *words* — "their saying against Maryam" in ayah 156, "their saying, 'We killed the Messiah'" in ayah 157 — and the Qur'an treats each spoken outrage as a crime as real as the killing of the Prophets mentioned just before.

## Ayah 156: the slander against Maryam

Allah describes what they said about Maryam as a *buhtān ʿaẓīm* — a grave, outrageous false charge. Ibn Kathir reports through 'Ali bin Abi Talhah that Ibn 'Abbas explained it plainly: the Jews accused Maryam of fornication. This is also the recorded view of As-Suddi, Juwaybir, Muhammad bin Ishaq and several others, and Ibn Kathir notes that this meaning is apparent from the ayah itself: they accused her of unchastity and claimed that 'Isa was an illegitimate son — some of them went so far as to claim that she was menstruating while fornicating.

Notice how the ayah frames it: "for their disbelief **and** their saying against Maryam a grave false charge." The slander is set alongside kufr (disbelief) itself as a cause of their being cursed and sealed away from guidance. To attack the honour of the woman Allah had chosen was not merely cruelty toward her; it was a rejection of the sign Allah had displayed through her and her son.

## Ayah 157: "We killed the Messiah"

The Jews' words are quoted back to them with bitter irony: "We killed al-Masih, 'Isa, son of Maryam, **the Messenger of Allah**." They did not believe he was Allah's Messenger — Ibn Kathir explains that they meant "the one who *claimed* to be the Messenger of Allah," uttering the title in jest and mockery, just as the polytheists said of the Prophet ﷺ: "O you to whom the Dhikr has been sent down! Verily, you are a mad man!" (15:6). So the boast is doubly damning: they confess the intent to murder, and they sneer at the office of messengership while doing so.

Allah's answer comes with two emphatic negations: "they killed him not, nor crucified him — but it was made to appear so to them (*wa lākin shubbiha lahum*)."

## What happened that night — the accounts of the early scholars

Ibn Kathir narrates the background. When Allah sent 'Isa with clear proofs — curing the blind and the leper, raising the dead by Allah's leave, fashioning a bird from clay that flew by Allah's leave — the Jews envied him and tried their utmost to harm him, so that he could not settle in one city and travelled constantly with his mother, peace be upon them both. Finally they denounced him to the king of Damascus of that time, a Greek polytheist who worshipped the stars, alleging that a man in Bayt al-Maqdis was stirring unrest among the king's subjects. The king ordered his deputy in Jerusalem to arrest this "rebel," crucify him, and crown him with thorns.

On a Friday evening the deputy, with a party of Jews, surrounded the house where 'Isa was staying with his companions — twelve, thirteen or seventeen of them. Knowing he would soon be taken, 'Isa asked, "Who volunteers to be made to look like me, for which he will be my companion in Paradise?" A young man volunteered; 'Isa hesitated over his youth and repeated the question a second and third time, and each time the same young man offered himself, until 'Isa said, "Well then, you will be that man." Allah cast the likeness of 'Isa upon him, a hole opened in the roof of the house, and 'Isa was raised to heaven. When the pursuers saw the man who now looked exactly like 'Isa, they seized him at night, crucified him, and set the crown of thorns on his head — then boasted that they had killed 'Isa.

Ibn Kathir also records a fuller report from Ibn Abi Hatim, with what he calls an authentic chain of narration to Ibn 'Abbas (also narrated by An-Nasa'i), containing the same core: the repeated offer of the young volunteer, the casting of the resemblance, and 'Isa's ascent through the roof. That report adds that after the event his followers split into three groups — one saying Allah Himself had remained among them and then ascended (the Jacobites), one saying the son of Allah had been among them (the Nestorians), and one, the Muslims, saying: "The servant and Messenger of Allah remained with us as long as Allah willed, and Allah then took him to Him." The two disbelieving groups cooperated against the Muslim group and killed them, and from then on Islam was veiled until Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the same tradition with its variants. Dahhak's account (cited via Qurtubi) has Iblis himself directing the execution squad — four thousand strong — to the house, and 'Isa giving the volunteer his own shirt and head-cover before the resemblance was cast. Another report (cited via Mazhari) says the man sent in to kill him — known to the Arabs as Teetlanoos — entered the house, found it empty because Allah had already raised 'Isa, and came out bearing 'Isa's likeness, so that the Jews seized and killed their own agent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes a point worth holding onto: the Qur'an itself does not determine which version occurred — "there is room for whichever of the situations came to pass… Allah alone knows what really happened." What all the reports agree on, and what the ayah itself asserts, is the common factor: the enemies of 'Isa were subjected to a compelling delusion. The event's reality was hidden from them.

## "They have no knowledge — only conjecture"

The end of ayah 157 turns from the event to its aftermath: "those who differ therein are full of doubts. They have no certain knowledge; they follow nothing but conjecture. For surely, they killed him not." Ibn Kathir explains that this covers both the Jews who claimed the killing and the Christians who, in ignorance, accepted their claim — all of them "in confusion, misguidance and bewilderment." Even the stories that circulated betray the confusion: it was said that Maryam sat weeping beneath the crucified corpse, and that the dead man spoke to her. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some of the perpetrators themselves woke up to the problem: the man they had killed resembled the Messiah in face but not in body, and they said, "If this man we have killed is the Messiah, where then is our man? And if this is our man, where then is the Messiah?" The closing phrase *wa mā qatalūhu yaqīnan* — "they certainly did not kill him" — nails it down: they never possessed certainty about the one thing they boasted of.

Ibn Kathir observes that all of this was a test from Allah for His servants, out of His wisdom — and that Allah then settled the matter definitively in the Qur'an sent to His Messenger ﷺ, for Allah is the Most Truthful, who knows what the hearts conceal and all that has occurred and will occur. Where human beings had only rumour and sect, revelation gave certainty.

## The promise that was kept

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recalls that in Surah Aal-'Imran (3:55) Allah had already made promises to 'Isa in connection with foiling the Jewish plans against him — among them that the Jews would not be allowed to have their way in their intention to kill him; instead, Allah would lift him towards Himself. This ayah makes explicit that the promise was kept: the truth of the matter, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is that they certainly did not kill the Messiah — rather, Allah lifted him towards Himself. The boast of ayah 157 is answered not by human counter-claim but by the deed of Allah.

## What the passage teaches

Two things stand at its heart. First, the tongue can commit crimes the Qur'an ranks beside the killing of Prophets: the slander of a chaste woman is called a *grave* false charge and listed among the causes of a nation's ruin. Second, certainty belongs to revelation, not to conjecture. The people who "differed therein" built entire positions on *ẓann* — supposition — and Allah's verdict on all of it is that they had no knowledge. Against every human claim stands the serene divine assertion: they did not kill him, they did not crucify him — Allah lifted him towards Himself, and their plot came to nothing.

passages.title: Raised to Allah, and the belief that will come
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the summit of the Qurʼān's answer to the claim, listed among the crimes of the People of the Book in the preceding verses, that they had killed the Masīḥ, ʿĪsā son of Maryam. Ayah 158 declares what actually happened — Allah raised him up to Himself, alive — and ayah 159 declares what is still to come: a day when every one of the People of the Book will truly believe in him before his death, and a Day when he will stand as a witness concerning them. The passage holds together as one movement: a false claim about the past is overturned, and a true promise about the future is sealed.

## "Rather, Allah raised him up to Himself"

Ayah 158 opens with a single decisive word: *bal* — "Rather". The verses before it (155–157) had catalogued a series of offences: breaking the covenant, rejecting Allah's signs, killing the Prophets unjustly, the grave slander uttered against Maryam, and finally the boast, "We killed Al-Masīḥ ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah." The Qurʼān answers: "they killed him not, nor crucified him, but it appeared as that to them" (157) — and then *bal rafaʿahu Allāhu ilayhi*: no, the truth is the opposite of what they claimed. Allah raised him up to Himself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects this back to Sūrah Āl ʿImrān (3:55), where Allah made promises to ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) in the face of the plot against his life — among them that his enemies would not be allowed to have their way, and that Allah would lift him towards Himself. What was promised there is stated here as accomplished fact: they did not kill him, they did not crucify him; Allah took him up.

## How were they "deluded by resemblance"?

Both commentaries relate accounts of how the crucifixion of someone else came to be mistaken for the crucifixion of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him). Ibn Kathir records the report of Ibn ʿAbbās — narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim with what Ibn Kathir calls an authentic chain, and also by An-Nasaʼi — that just before Allah raised him, ʿĪsā was with twelve of his companions in a house. He asked, "Who volunteers that his image appear as mine, and be killed in my place? He will be with me in Paradise." One of the youngest among them kept volunteering until ʿĪsā said, "You will be that man." The resemblance of ʿĪsā was cast over him, and ʿĪsā himself ascended to heaven from a hole in the house. When the pursuers came looking for ʿĪsā, they found the young man and crucified him. Ibn Kathir notes that many among the Salaf related the event in this way: a volunteer accepted death in ʿĪsā's place for the promise of being his companion in Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a similar account from the early exegete Ḍaḥḥāk (through Qurtubi), and also a different report (through Mazhari) in which the man sent to kill ʿĪsā entered the house after Allah had already lifted him, and was himself made to resemble him — so that the pursuers seized and killed their own man. Then Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of scholarly restraint that is worth taking to heart: the Qurʼān itself has not determined which of these situations came to pass, so "Allah alone knows what really happened." What all the reports and the ayah itself agree on is the common factor: those who claimed the killing were subjected to a compelling delusion. The event remained hidden from them, and everything they asserted afterwards was conjecture. That is exactly what ayah 157 says of those who differ over it: "They have no certain knowledge, they follow nothing but conjecture." Ibn Kathir observes that even those who claimed the killing were never sure that the man they killed was really ʿĪsā — they remained in doubt and confusion over the very deed they boasted of.

Ibn Kathir also relates, from the report of Ibn ʿAbbās, what followed: those who had been with ʿĪsā later divided into three groups — the Jacobites and Nestorians, who fell into false beliefs about him, and a third group, the Muslims, who said, "The servant and Messenger of Allah remained with us as long as Allah willed, and Allah then took him to Him." The two disbelieving groups cooperated against the Muslim group and killed them, and ever since, Islam was veiled until Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ.

## "And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise"

The ayah closes with two of Allah's names, and both commentaries pause over why these two. *ʿAzīz* — the Almighty: Ibn Kathir says He is never weak, "nor will those who seek refuge in Him ever be subjected to disgrace." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the contrast: the plot to kill ʿĪsā was insignificant when matched against the power of Allah, who had taken it upon Himself to protect him. *Ḥakīm* — the All-Wise: everything He decides and ordains for His creatures rests on wisdom. Ibn Kathir adds that all of this — even the scene of those who wept believing a beloved Prophet had been crucified — "was a test from Allah for His servants out of His wisdom." And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the modern sceptic gently: if materialists cannot grasp the reality of the lifting of ʿĪsā, that is their own limitation, not a defect in the event.

## Ayah 159: "before his death" — whose death?

Ayah 159 declares emphatically that there is none of the People of the Book but *must* believe in him before "his death" (*qabla mawtihi*). The scholars discussed whom the pronoun in "his death" refers to, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out both readings.

**The first reading** — recorded in Bayān al-Qurʼān by Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi — attaches the pronoun to the People of the Book themselves: those Jews, when they glimpse the realm of *barzakh* (the state between death and resurrection) moments before their death, will readily believe in ʿĪsā — but too late, a belief as useless as the believing of Pharaoh while he drowned.

**The second reading** — adopted, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, by a large number of the Companions and their Successors, and supported by authentic hadith — refers the pronoun to ʿĪsā himself (peace be upon him): before *ʿĪsā's* death. Since he was raised alive and has not yet died, this makes the ayah a promise about the end of time: when he reappears on this earth close to the Day of Judgement, all the People of the Book then alive will believe in him genuinely. Ibn Jarir records this from Ibn ʿAbbās: "before the death of ʿĪsā, son of Maryam." Abu Malik said the same: "This occurs after ʿĪsā returns and before he dies, as then, all of the People of the Scriptures will believe in him."

The second reading has explicit support from the Sunnah. Al-Bukhari records — in the chapter on the Prophets, under "The Descent of ʿĪsā, Son of Maryam" — that Abu Hurayrah related the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying: "By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, the son of Maryam will shortly descend among you as a just ruler, and will break the cross, kill the pig and abolish the Jizyah. Then there will be an abundance of wealth and nobody will accept charitable gifts any more. At that time, one prostration will be better for them than this life and all that is in it." Then Abu Hurayrah said: "Read if you will: 'And there is none of the People of the Scripture but must believe in him before his death…'" Muslim also recorded this hadith.

In another narration recorded by Ahmad — and Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded it — Abu Hurayrah again recited the ayah after a hadith of the descent, and added, "Will believe in ʿĪsā before ʿĪsā dies." Yet the narrator Hanzalah was careful to pass on his own uncertainty about that addition: "I do not know if this was a part of the Prophet's Hadith or if it was something that Abu Hurayrah said on his own." Separately, in the report Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites through Qurtubi, Abu Hurayrah said with stress, "Before the death of ʿĪsā," and repeated it three times; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that this explanation stands proved from so venerated a Companion on the strength of a sound chain of narrators. On this reading, the ayah is conclusive evidence that ʿĪsā's death has not yet come to pass: he will die on this very earth only after his coming, when the wise considerations of Allah behind his descent have reached their fruition.

## What the Sunnah says of his return

Because Abu Hurayrah tied this very ayah to the descent of ʿĪsā, Ibn Kathir gathers here the hadiths of his return; a few carry the heart of it.

Al-Bukhari records (and Imam Ahmad and Muslim also recorded it) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "How will you be when Al-Masīḥ, son of Maryam, descends among you while your Imam is from among yourselves?"

Ahmad records — and Abu Dawud also recorded it — that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The Prophets are paternal brothers; their mothers are different, but their religion is one. I, more than any of mankind, have more right to ʿĪsā, son of Maryam, for there was no Prophet between him and I." The hadith then describes him so that believers may know him when they see him: a well-built man, his colour between red and white, wearing two long, light yellow garments, his head appearing to drip water though no moisture touched it. He will break the cross, kill the pig, banish the Jizyah and call the people to Islam; in his time Allah will destroy all religions except Islam, and will destroy the False Messiah (Al-Masīḥ Ad-Dajjāl); safety will then fill the earth, so much so that wolves will mingle with sheep and children will play with snakes unharmed. "ʿĪsā will remain for forty years and then will die, and Muslims will offer the funeral prayer for him." That last line quietly completes the meaning of ayah 159: the death the ayah speaks of lies still ahead, and it will be the death of a servant of Allah, prayed over by the Muslims.

In the long hadith of An-Nawwas bin Samʿan in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ described the descent itself: at the height of Ad-Dajjāl's trial, ʿĪsā will come down "close to the white minaret to the east of Damascus," his hands placed on the wings of two angels, and will pursue Ad-Dajjāl to the doors of Ludd and kill him — and no disbeliever who finds the scent of his breath will survive it. Ahmad also records — and Muslim also recorded it — that ʿĪsā will pronounce the *ihlāl* (the pilgrim's declaration on entering the rites) from the mountain highway of Ar-Rawḥāʼ, for Hajj, ʿUmrah or both.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the discussion with a statement of creed, citing Ibn Kathir: the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ conveying the tidings of the coming of ʿĪsā before the Day of Judgement as a just ruler have been reported by *tawātur* — uninterrupted mass transmission that removes doubt. These mutawātir narrations, more than a hundred in number, were collected by the author's teacher, Maulana Muhammad Anwar Shah al-Kashmiri; the author of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then compiled the collection in Arabic at his teacher's proposal, and it was published under the title At-Taṣrīḥ bimā tawātara fī nuzūl al-Masīḥ — later republished from Beirut, with additional notes, by the Syrian scholar ʿAbd al-Fattah Abu Ghuddah. The belief in the coming of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) towards the later times is, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, absolute and unanimous as held by the Muslims. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also supports it from Sūrah az-Zukhruf (43:61), "Surely he is a sign of the Hour," which Ibn ʿAbbās explained as referring to ʿĪsā, who will come before the Day of Judgement.

## "And on the Day of Resurrection, he will be a witness against them"

The passage ends beyond even the descent, at the Day of Resurrection. Qatadah explained the witness ʿĪsā will bear: "He will bear witness before them that he has delivered the Message from Allah and that he is but a servant of His." Ibn Kathir points to the similar passage at the end of Sūrah al-Māʼidah (5:116–118), which opens with Allah's question on the Day of Resurrection, "O ʿĪsā, son of Maryam! Did you say unto men…" and closes with His names, "the Almighty, the All-Wise." So the very Prophet whom one community rejected and another deified will himself testify to the truth between the two extremes: a servant and Messenger of Allah.

## What the passage settles

Taken together, ayat 158–159 close off every false path concerning ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and leave one straight one. Against the claim that he was killed: rather, Allah raised him up to Himself. Against those who deified him: he is a servant who will one day die on this earth, be prayed over by Muslims, and testify on the Day of Resurrection that he only delivered his Lord's message. And against every conjecture built on that confused Friday evening in Jerusalem, the passage sets certainty: those who differed "have no certain knowledge, they follow nothing but conjecture" — while the believer rests on the word of the One who is ʿAzīz, whose protection cannot be overcome, and Ḥakīm, whose every decree carries wisdom, even when its unfolding is hidden from human eyes.

passages.title: Good things forbidden as penalty, and the few grounded in knowledge
passages.tafsir:
## When lawful things become forbidden — and who is exempt

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its comment here by noting that earlier verses had already mentioned wrongdoings of the Jews and the punishment they would receive; the present verses take up "some other vices of theirs" and mention yet another kind of punishment — a striking one: because of their wrongdoing, Allah stripped away from them good, pure things (*ṭayyibāt*) that had once been lawful. But the passage refuses to end on condemnation. Ayah 162 turns, with the word *lākin* — "but" — to the exception: those among the very same people who were well-grounded in knowledge and believed. What binds the three ayat together is a single contrast: a people's sins earning a penalty, and the individuals within them whose sincerity earns "a great reward."

## Ayah 160: a punishment unlike any other prohibition

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah prohibited some of the lawful, pure things previously allowed to the Jews "because of the injustice and transgression of the Jews, demonstrated by committing major sins." The ayah itself signals this in its opening: *fa-bi-ẓulmin* — "For the wrongdoing…" The prohibition was not about the food; it was about the people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this matters. In the Sharīʿah brought by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, things declared ḥarām (unlawful) are forbidden because of some physical or spiritual harm in them. What happened to the Jews was the reverse: the good things forbidden to them "had no physical or spiritual harm in them" — they were forbidden purely as punishment for transgression and disobedience. The same commentary notes that while the fuller punishment for their vices awaits the Day of Judgment, this penalty operated right here in the world: they found things that had been lawful for them made unlawful.

**How did the prohibition happen?** Ibn Kathir records two possible readings, without settling on one:

- **A prohibition of decree.** Allah allowed the Jews to falsely interpret their Book, altering what was permitted to them, so that "out of exaggeration and extremism in the religion, they prohibited some things for themselves." Their own distortions became their punishment.
- **A prohibition in the Tawrah itself.** Allah revealed new prohibitions in the Tawrah of things previously allowed.

For the second reading Ibn Kathir marshals two other ayat. Sūrah Āl ʿImrān (3:93) states that all food was lawful to the Children of Israel before the Tawrah was revealed, except what Isrāʼīl made unlawful for himself — Ibn Kathir specifies this was camel's meat and milk. Then Sūrat al-Anʿām records that Allah forbade the Jews every animal with undivided hoof, and the fat of the ox and the sheep except what adheres to their backs or entrails or is mixed with bone — "Thus We recompensed them for their rebellion. And verily, We are Truthful." So the Qurʼan itself names the mechanism: dietary restriction as recompense for rebellion.

**The second charge of ayah 160** — "their hindering many from Allah's way" — Ibn Kathir reads broadly: they hindered both themselves and others from following the truth, "and this is the behavior that they brought from the past to the present." He connects it to their enmity toward the Messengers, the killing of many of the Prophets, and their denial of Muhammad ﷺ and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them.

## Ayah 161: riba and devouring wealth

The indictment continues with two financial sins: taking *riba* (usurious interest) though they had been expressly forbidden from it, and consuming people's wealth wrongfully. Ibn Kathir's comment is brief but pointed: they had been prohibited from riba, "yet they did so using various kinds of tricks, ploys and cons, thus devouring people's property unjustly." The sin was not open defiance alone but legal trickery — dressing the forbidden in permissible-looking forms. The ayah then closes with the sentence for the hereafter: "And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them a painful torment."

## Ayah 162: the ones grounded in knowledge

*Lākin al-rāsikhūna fī al-ʿilmi minhum* — "But those among them who are well-grounded in knowledge…" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the turn plainly: the previous verses referred to Jews who adhered to their disbelief and obstinately continued practising what was blameworthy; the present verse now cites those who were, no doubt, from among the People of the Book, yet believed. Ibn Kathir glosses *al-rāsikhūn fī al-ʿilm* as those "firm in the religion and full of beneficial knowledge." He adds that "the believers" mentioned alongside them refers to these same well-grounded ones: their knowledge and their faith are one description, not two groups.

**Who were they?** Ibn Kathir relates that Ibn ʿAbbās said this ayah was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah bin Salām, Thaʿlabah bin Saʿyah, Zayd bin Saʿyah and Asad bin ʿUbayd — men of the People of the Book who embraced Islam and believed in what Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ with. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in why their story belongs here: these were people who, when the Prophet ﷺ came with his mission, "found in him, fully and unmistakably, all qualities the Last among Prophets was supposed to have according to the prophesies of their Scriptures" — and so they believed. Their honest knowledge of their own Scriptures opened the way to faith, and the words of praise in this verse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, are for these blessed souls.

**What the ayah praises in them**, phrase by phrase:

- *Belief in what was sent down to you and what was sent down before you* — they did not trade one revelation for another; they affirmed the whole chain of prophethood.
- *Establishing the prayer and giving zakah* — Ibn Kathir notes that "give zakah" could refer to the obligatory charity due on wealth, or to those who purify themselves, or both — "Allah knows best."
- *Belief in Allah and the Last Day* — which Ibn Kathir unpacks as believing there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and believing in resurrection after death and the recompense of deeds, good or evil.

And the promise: "it is they to whom We shall give a great reward" — which Ibn Kathir states plainly means Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful theological note on this promise: the great reward is for the combination of faith and righteous deeds, but salvation itself depends on soundness in the essentials of belief — subject always to the condition that one's life ends upon faith (*īmān*).

## Reading the passage whole

Set side by side, the three ayat move from sin to sentence to exception. A people who wronged, hindered, and devoured were recompensed — even in their diet, and in this world before the next — yet within that same people, four named men who read their Book honestly walked straight into Islam and into the promise of Paradise. The passage warns against what sin does — it can draw a punishment that narrows even what is lawful — and it honors what grounded knowledge and sincere faith earn: "a great reward," which Ibn Kathir tells us is Paradise. For the believer, the practical weight falls on ayah 161's phrase about riba taken through "tricks, ploys and cons": prohibition evaded by clever packaging is still prohibition defied, and the passage counts it among the sins that drew a painful torment.

passages.title: Revelation to Muhammad as to earlier prophets
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers a challenge thrown at the Prophet ﷺ by setting his revelation in the same line as the revelation given to the prophets before him. Ayat 163–164 name the prophets to whom Allah sent waḥy (revelation) before him; ayah 165 explains *why* Allah has always sent messengers; and ayah 166 seals the matter with the greatest testimony possible — Allah's own. What holds the four ayat together is a single argument: the revelation given to Muhammad ﷺ is not a novelty to be doubted but the continuation of everything the People of the Book already claim to believe.

## The challenge that prompted these ayat

Ibn Kathir records the occasion with its chain: Muhammad bin Ishaq narrated that Muhammad bin Abi Muhammad said that 'Ikrimah — or Sa'id bin Jubayr — related to Ibn 'Abbas that two men, Sukayn and 'Adi bin Zayd, said to the Prophet ﷺ, "O Muhammad! We do not know that Allah sent down anything to any human after Musa." Allah then sent down the rebuttal: *"Verily, We have inspired you as We inspired Nuh and the Prophets after him"* (ayah 163).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the wider background. The Jews had set a condition: they would believe in the Prophet ﷺ only if he brought them a Book "all written up, from the heavens," like the Torah. The passage exposes the inconsistency in this demand. They accept the great prophets named in the verse — yet they never made such demands before believing in them. They accepted those prophets on the basis of their miracles; and Muhammad ﷺ has his miracles too, so there is no reason why they cannot step forward and believe in him as well. So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, their demand was no quest for truth — it was rooted in prejudice and hostility.

A second, related scene attaches to ayah 166. Ibn 'Abbas narrated that a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and he said to them: "Surely, you do know that I am a true messenger of Allah?" They refused to accept it — and ayah 166 came down: *"But Allah bears witness through what He has revealed to you."* If human witnesses withhold their testimony, the divine Witness does not.

## Why the list begins with Nuh

In ayah 163 the comparison is drawn specifically with "Nuh and the prophets after him," and the exegetical notes of Maulana Shabbir Ahmad 'Usmani (cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) draw out why. In the time of Adam, revelation was at an initial, educational stage; people who strayed were treated as excusable and given time to learn. With Nuh, that stage of instruction reached maturity — and with maturity came accountability. It was from Nuh that the chain of great prophets began, and from his time that the first punishment descended on those who transgressed against revelation: the Great Flood, followed in later generations by the punishments that struck the peoples of Salih, Shu'ayb, and others.

By likening the Prophet's ﷺ revelation to the revelation of Nuh and those after him, then, the ayah serves full warning on the People of the Book and the disbelievers of Makkah: whoever will not believe in the waḥy of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ — that is, the Qur'an — will deserve the greatest punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) adds a striking note on Nuh himself: his very person was a miracle. He was granted nine hundred and fifty years of life, losing none of his teeth, with no white in his hair and no failing of physical strength — and he spent that whole lifetime bearing his people's persecution with patience and fortitude.

## One revelation, many prophets, many modes (ayat 163–164)

Ayah 163 names by name: Nuh, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub and al-Asbat (which Ibn Kathir explains as the offspring of the twelve sons of Ya'qub), 'Isa, Ayyub, Yunus, Harun, Sulayman — and Dawud, to whom Allah gave the Zabur. The Zabur, Ibn Kathir notes, is the name of the Book revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him — known Biblically as the Psalms.

Ayah 164 then widens the frame: *"Messengers We have mentioned to you before, and Messengers We have not mentioned to you."* Ibn Kathir lists the prophets named in the Qur'an: Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Ayyub, Shu'ayb, Musa, Harun, Yunus, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, al-Yasa', Zakariya, Yahya, 'Isa — and their leader, Muhammad ﷺ — with several scholars of tafsir adding Dhul-Kifl. Beyond these, the ayah itself tells us there were prophets whose stories were simply never related in the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the report of Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (which it cites from Qurtubi) that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah sent one hundred and twenty-four thousand prophets, of whom three hundred and thirteen were Shariʿah-bearing Messengers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the decisive lesson from this survey: waḥy comes to prophets in different modes. It may come through an angel bearing a message; it may come as a written Book; and sometimes Allah speaks directly to His Messenger. Whatever the mode, once revelation comes, acting upon it becomes obligatory. So the Jews' insistence that they would believe only if a written Book descended like the Torah was, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, "short on sense and tall on disbelief" — as if the container of revelation mattered more than its Sender. And since waḥy is one command of Allah reaching all His prophets, whoever believed in the revelation sent to past prophets must believe in this one too; whoever rejects it has, in effect, rejected them all.

## "And to Musa Allah spoke directly" — the honour of the Kalim

Ayah 164 closes with a singular honour: *"and to Musa Allah spoke directly."* Ibn Kathir explains that this is an honour to Musa, and this is why he is called *al-Kalīm* — the one whom Allah spoke to directly.

Ibn Kathir then relates a telling incident recorded by al-Hafiz Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah, from 'Abdul-Jabbar bin 'Abdullah. A man came to Abu Bakr bin 'Ayyash and reported hearing someone recite the ayah with the words rearranged so that it would mean "and to Allah, Musa spoke directly" — making Musa the speaker and dodging the affirmation that Allah speaks. Abu Bakr replied, "Only a disbeliever would recite it like this." The report then records the true recitation's pedigree: al-A'mash recited it with Yahya bin Withab, who recited it with Abu 'Abdur-Rahman as-Sulami, who recited it with 'Ali bin Abi Talib, who recited it with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — "and to Musa Allah spoke directly." Abu Bakr bin 'Ayyash was so angry with the man, Ibn Kathir explains, because he had altered the ayah's words and its meanings. That reciter was from the Mu'tazilah — a group who denied that Allah spoke to Musa or that He speaks to any of His creation. When some of them tried the altered recitation elsewhere, a teacher present retorted: what would you do with Allah's statement, *"And when Musa came at the time and place appointed by Us, and his Lord spoke to him"* (7:143)? That ayah cannot be altered or changed at all.

The affirmation, then, stands exactly as Allah revealed it: Allah spoke to Musa directly — and the early reciters guarded even the word order of the ayah against any attempt to unsay it.

## Why messengers at all (ayah 165)

Ayah 165 states the wisdom behind the whole prophetic enterprise: *"Messengers as bearers of good news and warning, in order that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the Messengers."* Ibn Kathir explains the pairing: the prophets bring good news to those who obey Allah, and warn of His punishment those who defy His commandments. Allah sent down His Books and His Messengers, made plain what pleases Him and what displeases Him — so that no one could stand before Him on the Day of Judgement and claim ignorance. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel ayah: had Allah destroyed people without warning, they would have said, "Our Lord! If only You had sent us a Messenger, we should certainly have followed Your Ayat, before we were humiliated and disgraced."

Here Ibn Kathir brings the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, from Ibn Mas'ud, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one is more jealous than Allah. This is why He prohibited all types of sin committed in public or secret. No one likes praise more than Allah, and this is why He has praised Himself. No one likes to give excuse more than Allah, and this is why He sent the Prophets as bearers of good news and as warners." And in another narration: "And this is why He sent His Messengers and revealed His Books."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point to its conclusion: now that Allah has sent messengers with miracles and they have shown the straight path, refusing the true faith cannot be accepted from anyone under any pretext. "Waḥy is an absolute argument, final, conclusive and disarming. No argument stands operative against it." The ayah then closes on the words: *"And Allah is Ever All-Powerful, All-Wise."*

## The witness who cannot be denied (ayah 166)

And if, after all this, the deniers still refuse? Ayah 166 answers: *"But Allah bears witness to that which He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness. And Allah is All-Sufficient as a Witness."*

Ibn Kathir explains: even if they deny, defy and disbelieve in you, O Muhammad, Allah Himself testifies that you are His Messenger, to whom He sent down the Glorious Qur'an — the Book that "falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Allah's witness is borne *through* what He revealed: the miraculous Qur'an is itself the testimony, a perfect message from His Knowledge, revealed to him with full realization that he is deserving of it — and the angels join in that testimony. After the witnessing of the All-Knowing Allah, there is nothing left to argue about.

The phrase *"He has sent it down with His knowledge"* receives a rich comment from Ibn Kathir: the Qur'an carries the knowledge Allah willed His servants to have access to — the clear signs of guidance, what He loves and what He is displeased with, knowledge of the unseen past and future, and knowledge of His honourable attributes that no sent Messenger or illustrious angel could know without His leave — "and they will never compass anything of His knowledge except that which He wills" (2:255).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes where the passage then turns (in the ayat that follow): to those who not only deny but conceal the Prophet's ﷺ description found in the Torah and actively keep others from the faith. For such people there is neither forgiveness nor guidance — which makes clear, by contrast, that guidance itself depends on following the Prophet ﷺ.

## What the passage asks of the reader

Two things stand out from the sources. First, consistency: the People of the Book were faulted for accepting past prophets by one standard and then inventing a new standard for the final Prophet ﷺ. Truth is not served by demands designed never to be met. Second, the end of excuses: ayah 165 teaches that Allah, in His mercy, sent warner after warner precisely so that no soul could plead ignorance — and the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud reveals the tenderness inside that severity: no one loves to give excuse more than Allah, and that is why He sent the prophets at all. The believer who has received this final revelation stands, therefore, with the proof established and the good news extended — and with Allah Himself as witness to the Book in his hands.

passages.title: Barring others from Allah's path, and the summons that answers it
passages.tafsir:
# Barring Others from Allah's Path, and the Summons That Answers It (4:167–170)

This passage sets two things side by side: the fate of those who not only reject the truth but actively block others from reaching it (ayat 167–169), and a sudden, wide-open call to all of humanity to answer the Messenger who has come with the truth (ayah 170). What binds the four ayat together is the image of the *path*. Those who obstruct Allah's path have, by that very act, lost their own way — and the only "way" left to them, in the verse's own words, is the way of Hell. Against that darkness, ayah 170 throws open the door: the road is still here, the Messenger has brought it, so take it.

## Where this passage sits

These ayat do not appear out of nowhere. In the verses just before them (4:163–166), Allah affirmed the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ against those who denied him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas that a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and he said to them: surely you know that I am a true messenger of Allah. When they refused to accept it, the verse came down: "But Allah bears witness to that which He has sent down unto you" (4:166) — Allah Himself testifying to his prophethood through the miraculous Qurʼan, with the angels joining in that testimony. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, after the witnessing of the All-Knowing, All-Aware Allah, there is nothing left to argue about.

Ayah 167 then turns to those who *still* deny — and worse. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes their method: they concealed the Prophet's ﷺ character traits and the indicators of his appearance present in the Torah, and tried to keep others away from the true faith by presenting things that were not there, or things jumbled together to distort the truth. This is what "hindering from the Way of Allah" looked like in practice: the deliberate distortion of knowledge so that seekers could not find the road.

## The double crime — and why it means being "far astray" (ayah 167)

Notice that ayah 167 names two acts, not one: "those who disbelieve **and** hinder others from the Way of Allah." Ibn Kathir draws out the logic: they are disbelievers themselves and do not follow the truth, *and* they strive hard to prevent people from following and embracing Allah's path. Therefore, in his words, they have defied the truth, deviated, and strayed far away from it. That is the force of the Arabic *ḍallū ḍalālan baʿīdan* — not merely that they have strayed, but that they have strayed **far** away.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a principle that flows from this: guidance — the very ability to find the straight path — depends on following the Prophet ﷺ, and straying, whatever form it takes, is at bottom nothing but hostility towards him.

## A road that leads only to one place (ayat 168–169)

Ayah 168 states Allah's judgment against "those who disbelieve and did wrong" — Ibn Kathir explains this wrong (*ẓulm*, wrongdoing, here the wronging of one's own soul) as their disbelief in Allah's Ayat, Book and Messenger, their hindering of others from His path, their sins and their violation of His prohibitions. For such people, Allah will not forgive them, "nor will He guide them to a way."

Then comes ayah 169 with one of the Qurʼan's most sobering turns of expression: "**except** the way of Hell." Ibn Kathir points out simply: "and this is the exception." The people who blocked the way to Allah are not left wayless — they are given a way, but it is the *ṭarīq Jahannam*, the road to Hell, "to dwell therein forever and ever." And the ayah closes: "and that is ever easy for Allah."

## The summons that answers it (ayah 170)

Now the register changes completely. After three ayat about a specific class of obstructors, Allah addresses everyone: *Yā ayyuhā al-nās* — "O mankind!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the significance of this widening: having answered the objections of the Jews and confirmed the prophethood of Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ, the Qurʼan now carries Allah's message to all human beings wherever they may be, as its direct addressees. The essence of the message, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words: your salvation lies nowhere but in belief in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ — so believe and prosper.

Ibn Kathir unfolds the ayah's phrases:

- **"The Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord"** — Muhammad ﷺ has come with guidance, the religion of truth, and clear proof from Allah.
- **"So believe in him; it is better for you"** — believe in what he brought and follow him, for this is better for you.
- **"But if you disbelieve, then certainly to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth."** Ibn Kathir explains: Allah is far too rich — too self-sufficient — to need you or your faith, and no harm could ever touch Him because of your disbelief. He cites the parallel words of Musa: "If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich (Free of all needs), Owner of all praise." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the same point from the human side: those who choose to disbelieve lose everything, while Allah loses nothing — with His limitless dominion and power, who could conceive of bringing any loss or harm to Him? That, it adds, is what the disbelievers should be worrying about.

## "All-Knowing, All-Wise" — the quiet warning in the closing Names

The passage seals itself with two of Allah's Names: *ʿAlīman Ḥakīman* — Ever All-Knowing, All-Wise. Ibn Kathir reads them against everything that came before: Allah knows those who deserve to be guided, and He guides them; and He knows those who deserve deviation, and He leads them to it. And He is All-Wise in His statements, actions, legislation and all that He decrees. Nothing in the fate described in ayat 167–169, and nothing in the open invitation of ayah 170, is arbitrary.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a final, practical warning from this pairing: Allah knows everything about people's believing and disbelieving, so let no one be misled by the delay or lightness of punishment in this world — He is All-Wise, and He does what His wisdom allows to prevail.

## Living it

Two things follow directly from the passage itself. First, the gravity of *hindering*: the ayat treat distorting religious knowledge — presenting what is not there, jumbling truth with falsehood so others cannot find the way — as the crime that compounds disbelief and takes a person "far astray." Honesty about the truth one carries is not optional. Second, the direction of need in ayah 170: belief benefits the believer, and disbelief costs only the disbeliever. Whoever hears the summons "O mankind" is being invited for his own sake — "believe in him; it is better for you."

passages.title: No excess in religion: the Messiah is a servant
passages.tafsir:
# No Excess in Religion: The Messiah Is a Servant (4:171–173)

Having addressed the Jews in the preceding verses, the sūrah now turns to the Christians. These three ayat state, with complete clarity, what Islam teaches about ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace be upon him: he is a true Messenger of Allah, honoured with titles of nearness — "His Word" and "a spirit from Him" — yet he is a servant — not a god, and not a son. What binds the passage together is one idea: *ghuluww*, excess in religion. Ayah 171 forbids it and corrects it; ayah 172 shows that ʿĪsā himself would never resent the servanthood his admirers tried to lift him out of; ayah 173 lays out the two destinations that follow from accepting or scorning that servanthood.

## What "excess in religion" means

The key word of ayah 171 is *lā taghlū* — "do not go to extremes." The Arabic term is *al-ghuluww*, which lexically means to cross the limits or transgress, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Imam al-Jaṣṣāṣ's definition from *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān*: "Excess in Faith is crossing the limit set therein." Both communities of the People of the Book are addressed, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, because excess was the common factor between them — but in opposite directions. The Christians committed the excess of over-estimation: honouring ʿĪsā until they raised him from prophethood to divinity. The Jews committed the excess of under-estimation: not only refusing him as a prophet but imputing a false accusation to his revered mother, Maryam. The Qurʼān's answer to both is the same single truth: the Masīḥ is a human being born to Maryam and a true Messenger of Allah — and the straight path runs between the two ditches of deficiency and exaggeration.

Ibn Kathir adds that the Christians' excess did not stop at ʿĪsā. They extended it to those they believed were his followers, treating their words as inspired whether true or false — which is how, in the words of the Qurʼān he cites (9:31), "They took their rabbis and their monks to be their lords besides Allah." Excess in venerating a prophet becomes, in the next generation, excess in venerating the prophet's (real or supposed) heirs.

## "Do not praise me as the Christians praised ʿĪsā"

Because this disease had destroyed earlier communities, the Prophet ﷺ built defences against it for his own ummah — and the sources for this passage preserve his own words on it.

Imam Ahmad recorded, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from ʿUmar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Do not unduly praise me like the Christians exaggerated over ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. Verily, I am only a servant, so say, 'Allah's servant and His Messenger.'"* Ibn Kathir notes this is the wording of al-Bukhari.

And Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas bin Mālik that a man once addressed the Prophet ﷺ: "O Muhammad! You are our master and the son of our master, our most righteous person and the son of our most righteous person…" He ﷺ replied: *"O people! Say what you have to say, but do not allow Shayṭān to trick you. I am Muhammad bin ʿAbdullāh, Allah's servant and Messenger. By Allah! I do not like that you elevate me above the rank that Allah has granted me."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates the incident at Hajj when the Prophet ﷺ asked Ibn ʿAbbās to gather pebbles for stoning the Jamarāt. When he brought average-sized pebbles, the Prophet ﷺ approved of them, said twice "like these, like these," and then declared: *"It is your duty to avoid excess in Faith for communities before you were destroyed because of being excessive in their Faith."* From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a precise rule: the limit of every religious act is what the Prophet ﷺ fixed by his word and deed, and *ghuluww* is crossing that prophetic limit — even in something as small as the size of a pebble.

## "His Word... and a spirit from Him"

Ayah 171 gives ʿĪsā two remarkable titles, and because Christians historically leaned on them, the commentators open them up carefully.

**His Word (*kalimatuh*).** Ibn Kathir explains that ʿĪsā is called Allah's Word because he was created *by* a word: Allah said "Be" (*kun*), and he was — the word sent with Jibrīl to Maryam taking the place of a father, just as Allah says, "Verily, the likeness of ʿĪsā before Allah is the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then (He) said to him: 'Be!' — and he was" (3:59). He cites Qatādah (through ʿAbdur-Razzāq, from Maʿmar): the meaning is that He said "Be," and he was; and the fine clarification of Shādh bin Yaḥyā recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim: "ʿĪsā was not the word. Rather, ʿĪsā came to existence because of the word." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same understanding from Imam al-Ghazzālī — two factors normally operate in a child's birth, the sperm and Allah's command "Be"; since the first was absent in ʿĪsā's case, he was named after the second — along with two further views: that "word" means the glad tiding Allah sent to Maryam (compare 3:45, "Allah gives you the good news of a word"), or that it means a sign (as in 66:12).

**A spirit from Him (*rūḥun minhu*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers several explanations from the commentators: that *rūḥ* here means "essence," expressing the perfect purity of one created without a father, purely by Allah's will; that ʿĪsā infused spiritual life into dead hearts as the spirit gives life to the body — a sense in which the Qurʼān itself is also called a *rūḥ* (42:52); that *rūḥ* can mean a secret, and his miraculous birth was a sign and secret of Allah; that the phrase means "possessor of a spirit from Him"; or that it refers to the breath (*nafkh*) which Jibrīl, by Allah's command, blew, from which the conception occurred (compare 21:91). None of these meanings — the commentary is explicit — implies that ʿĪsā is a part of Allah or a divine person.

**What "from Him" does and does not mean.** Both commentaries meet on this point. Ibn Kathir explains that "from Him" means from His creation, exactly as in "And has subjected to you all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth; it is all from Him" (45:13); attributing something to Allah — the she-camel of Allah, the House of Allah — is a way of honouring it, not a claim that it is part of Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same comparison with *Baytullāh* (the House of Allah) and *ʿAbdullāh* (the servant of Allah), and even with the Prophet ﷺ himself being honoured as "His servant" in 17:1. It then relates a memorable episode reported by al-Ālūsī in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: in the court of Hārūn al-Rashīd, a Christian physician challenged the scholar ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Wāqidī that "a spirit from Him" proves ʿĪsā is part of Allah. Al-Wāqidī recited 45:13 and asked: if "from Him" means "part of Him," then is everything in the heavens and the earth a part of Allah? The physician was silenced — and chose to become a Muslim.

## "Say not: Three!"

The command "Cease! It is better for you" confronts the doctrine of the Trinity directly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the state of the major Christian sects at the time of revelation: one held that the Masīḥ *is* the Deity Himself appearing in the world; another that he is His son; a third professed a trinity — with some counting Maryam as the third person and others the Holy Spirit. Ibn Kathir relates, from the Christian scholar Saʿīd bin Baṭrīq, Patriarch of Alexandria, the history of the council convened under Constantine, attended by more than two thousand patriarchs who splintered into many factions; the emperor adopted the creed of the largest faction and suppressed the rest, and later councils produced the Jacobites and the Nestorians. All three sects agreed ʿĪsā was divine yet disputed how his divinity related to his humanity, each accusing the others of heresy. Ibn Kathir observes that their creeds so multiplied and contradicted one another that it prompted some people to say that if ten Christians meet, they would end up with eleven sects.

Against all of this the ayah sets one sentence: "Allah is only One — hallowed be He above having a son. To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth, and Allah is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic: when everything is His creation and every being is His servant, who could possibly be His partner or son? And He who is the perennial dispenser of every need, needing nobody — how could He *need* a partner or a child? Ascribing one to Him, it concludes, is the act of one deprived of both faith and reason.

## Ayah 172: servanthood is an honour, not an insult

"The Masīḥ would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the nearest angels." The verse turns the argument over to ʿĪsā himself: the very one the Christians deified would himself confess to being Allah's servant — and so would the angels, which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, includes Jibrīl, whom some alleged to be a person of the Trinity. Ibn Kathir records Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation (via Ibn Abī Ḥātim) that the "pride" rejected here means insolence, and Qatādah's comment that the Masīḥ and the near angels will never be arrogant.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Maulana Shabbir Ahmad ʿUsmani's beautiful observation here: being Allah's servant — devoted to His worship, obedient to His command — is itself an honour, a nobility of the highest class, and the Masīḥ and the close angels know its worth best of all. How could they spurn such an honour? The true disgrace lies in the opposite direction: worshipping other than Allah, as those did who ascribed to Allah the Masīḥ as a son, or the angels as daughters.

This is why the hadith of ʿUbādah bin aṣ-Ṣāmit, recorded by al-Bukhari (and also by Muslim), makes ʿĪsā's servanthood part of the saving testimony itself. The Prophet ﷺ said: *"If anyone testifies that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah Alone Who has no partners, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and that ʿĪsā is Allah's servant and Messenger and His Word which He bestowed on Maryam and a spirit created by Him, and that Paradise is true and Hell is true, then Allah will admit him into Paradise with the deeds which he performed"* — and in another narration, *"through any of the eight doors of Paradise he wishes."* Notice how the testimony holds both truths at once: ʿĪsā's honour (Messenger, Word, spirit) and his servanthood — precisely the balance this passage commands.

## Ayah 173: the two endings

The passage closes with the reckoning. Whoever disdains Allah's worship and is proud — "He will gather them all together unto Himself," which Ibn Kathir explains as the Day of Resurrection, when Allah will judge between them with His just judgment that is never unjust or wrong. Then the two outcomes: those who believed and did righteous deeds receive their rewards in full "and more out of His bounty" — Ibn Kathir glosses this as extra kindness, ample mercy and favour beyond what their deeds earned. But those who refused His worship out of arrogance face a painful torment, "and they will not find for themselves besides Allah any protector or helper." Ibn Kathir pairs this with 40:60: "Verily! Those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation" — the fitting end of pride, which is disgrace.

## Living between the two extremes

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will not let the reader treat this as someone else's history. The Prophet ﷺ, it notes, warned: *"Every Bidʿah is straying and every straying ends in Jahannam."* A *bidʿah* is a self-promoted innovation in established religion — something assumed to be part of the religion which is not found in the Prophet's ﷺ word and deed, clearly or through hint — and Jahannam is the Hellfire. Shah Waliyyullah explained why innovation is treated so seriously: it opens the doors to alteration in religion. Earlier communities added to what their Book said and their prophet taught, generation after generation, until the true religion could no longer be told apart from the additions.

The commentary then applies the lesson to a question every believer faces: whom to follow in religion? One extreme dispenses with scholars altogether — "the Book of Allah is sufficient for us" — producing self-made experts who read translations and dismiss the explanation transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions; yet no one ever became a physician or an engineer from translations alone, and had a book without a teacher sufficed, there would have been no need to send a prophet at all. The other extreme follows just about anyone blindly, never testing a guide's teaching against the Qurʼān and Sunnah — the very road by which earlier communities came to worship their religious leaders. The middle course Maʿārif ul Qurʼān commends: learn the Book of Allah from the people of Allah, and recognise the people of Allah by the Book of Allah.

The same balance governs even worldly life: Islam blames greed, but the Prophet ﷺ fixed the limits by his own example — marriage, children, earning for one's family ("an obligation after the obligation"), trade and labour — while the monasticism the earlier communities invented for themselves was never prescribed by Allah, and they failed to keep even what they had imposed (57:27).

That is the passage's single thread. Religion is not made better by adding to it, and a prophet is not honoured by deifying him. ʿĪsā's glory — and the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ, as he himself insisted — is the glory of *ʿabduhu wa rasūluh*: His servant and His Messenger. To stay within the limits Allah set is not a lesser love; it is the only love that is true.

passages.title: Clear proof and a manifest light
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

After the long argument of this sūrah — culminating, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, in the refutation of beliefs that ascribe divinity to ʿĪsā (Jesus), peace be upon him, with reward promised to those who acknowledge the truth and punishment to those who insist on denying it — the address suddenly widens. In ayah 174 Allah no longer speaks to a sect or a community but to all of humanity: *"O mankind! Verily, there has come to you a convincing proof from your Lord; and We sent down to you a manifest light."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this as a universal address praising the blessed status and mission of His Messenger — who taught the truth revealed to him and conveyed the truth of the Qurʼān admirably — and praising, too, those who believed in and testified to the truth of the Book and the Messenger. Ayah 175 then completes the announcement with its consequence: whoever believes in Allah and holds fast to Him will be brought into His mercy and grace and guided to Him along a straight path. The two ayat form one sentence of the heart: here is the proof, here is the light — and here is what awaits those who take hold of them.

## "A convincing proof" — what is the burhān?

The key word of ayah 174 is **burhān**, which lexically means *proof*. Ibn Kathir explains the force of this: Allah informs all people that a plain, unequivocal proof has come to them from Him, one that *eradicates all possibility of having an excuse, or falling prey to evil doubts*. After the burhān arrives, no honest doubter is left stranded and no denier is left with a defence.

But what exactly is this proof? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, drawing on Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, records that the burhān refers to **the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself**. Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, explained why: the Prophet ﷺ was called *burhān* in consideration of his blessed person, his noble morals, his miracles, and his being the very recipient of the revelation of the Book of Allah. Each of these is an open proof of his prophethood, beyond which no further proof is needed. In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's memorable summation, *his person is, in itself, proof personified*.

## "A manifest light" — the nūr

The second gift named in ayah 174 is the **nūr mubīn**, the manifest light, which "directs to the Truth" (Ibn Kathir). Ibn Jurayj and others said plainly: *"It is the Qurʼān."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān confirms this identification and links it to a parallel verse, Sūrah al-Māʼidah 5:15 — *"There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book."*

That parallel raises a subtle question the commentators address. In Arabic, joining two terms with "and" (the conjunction) normally implies they are two different things — so are the "light" and the "Book" of al-Māʼidah 5:15 two separate gifts? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī) gives two answers. First, a difference in *expression* is enough to justify the conjunction even when the two terms mean the same thing — the Qurʼān can be called both "light" and "clear Book," and Maulānā Ashraf Thānavī's rendering in Bayān al-Qurʼān reads it exactly this way: a light *which is* the clear Book, the Qurʼān. Second, it would also be correct to take the "light" as referring to the Prophet ﷺ and the "Book" as the Qurʼān. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds an important caution: even on this second reading, the verse does not prove that the Prophet ﷺ was light in the *literal* sense — being described as a light is not against his being physically human.

So whichever way the words are distributed, the substance of ayah 174 is the same: Allah has sent humanity the Messenger ﷺ and the Book — a convincing proof and a manifest light.

## Holding fast — ayah 175

Ayah 175 turns from the gift to the response. Two things are asked: to **believe in Allah** and to **hold fast to** — that is, depend on — **Him**. Ibn Kathir explains this holding fast as worshipping Allah and *relying on Him for each and every thing*. Ibn Jurayj said that this part of the ayah means: "They believe in Allah and hold fast to the Qurʼān."

## The threefold promise

For those who respond this way, ayah 175 stacks three promises, each explained by Ibn Kathir:

- **"He will admit them to His mercy and grace"** — He will grant them His mercy and admit them into Paradise, and will increase and multiply their rewards and their ranks. Note the wording Ibn Kathir draws out: this comes *as a favor and bounty from Him*.

- **"And guide them to Himself"** — the destination of the path is not merely safety or reward but Allah Himself. The believer is being led *to his Lord*.

- **"By a straight path"** — Ibn Kathir describes it as a clear way with no wickedness or deviation in it, and then opens up its double meaning: this is the description of the believers *in this life and in the Hereafter*. In this life they travel the straight, safe path in matters of both action and creed — sound belief and sound practice together. In the Hereafter, they are on the straight path of Allah that leads to the gardens of Paradise.

## Living it

The passage addresses every human being, and its demand is correspondingly simple: the proof has come, the light has been sent down — believe, and hold fast. Ibn Kathir's two-part portrait of that holding fast — worshipping Allah and depending on Him in each and every thing — and Ibn Jurayj's gloss — holding fast to the Qurʼān — give the believer a concrete daily shape for it: keep your worship for Allah, keep your reliance on Allah, and keep your grip on His Book. The reward is stated in Allah's own sequence: mercy, grace, and guidance to Him along a straight path — in this life, and in the Hereafter, the path that leads to the gardens of Paradise.

passages.title: Kalāla: inheritance when there is neither parent nor child
passages.tafsir:
## The last ayah of the Qur'an to be revealed

This single ayah — the closing verse of Sūrat al-Nisāʼ — was revealed, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, in answer to a question posed by some Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: how is the estate of a *kalālah* divided? A *kalālah* is a person who dies leaving behind neither children nor parents — no descendants and no ascendants. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary by noting its distinction: Al-Bukhari recorded that Al-Baraʼ said the last sūrah to be revealed was Sūrah Barāʼah (chapter 9), and the last *ayah* to be revealed was this one — "They ask you for a legal verdict…"

## The occasion: Jabir's question from his sickbed

Ibn Kathir relates the story behind the verse. Imam Ahmad recorded that Jabir bin ʿAbdullah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came visiting me when I was so ill that I fell unconscious. He performed ablution and poured the remaining water on me, or had it poured on me. When I regained consciousness, I said, 'I will only leave inheritance through Kalalah, so what about the inheritance that I leave behind?' Allah later revealed the Ayah about Fara'id (inheritance)." The Two Sahihs and also the Group recorded it, and in one of its wordings Jabir said that the ayah revealed was this very one — "They ask you for a legal verdict. Say: Allah directs (thus) about Al-Kalalah." The wording of the ayah, Ibn Kathir observes, indicates that the question was about the kalālah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing the exegetical notes of Tafsīr ʿUsmānī) draws out what this occasion teaches: the Prophet ﷺ would not give a decision on his own in such matters without the guiding command of *waḥy* (revelation). If no revealed guidance existed for a case, he would put his decision on hold and wait; when revelation came, he gave his verdict. And there is a further subtlety here about why the Qur'an came down gradually rather than all at once, as the People of the Book demanded: a Companion could ask a question out of real need and be answered *through the recited revelation itself* — so that a verse revealed in favour of, or in answer to, a particular Companion is treasured as a testament of his virtues, keeping his name and merit alive "right upto the Day of Doom."

## What "kalālah" means — and why even ʿUmar found it hard
