Ibn Kathir explains the word: *kalālah* means the crown that surrounds the head from all sides — and this is why the scholars stated that kalālah pertains to one who dies and leaves behind neither descendants nor ascendants. Some said it pertains simply to one who has no offspring, since the ayah itself says "leaving no child"; but Ibn Kathir shows from the verse's own wording that parents must be absent too — for the ayah gives the sister half the estate, and had there been a surviving ascendant, the sister would not have inherited anything, a point on which there is consensus. So the verse can only be speaking of a person survived by neither.

Even so, Ibn Kathir notes, the meaning and ruling of kalālah was somewhat confusing to the Leader of the Faithful, ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab. It is recorded in the Two Sahihs that ʿUmar said: "There are three matters that I wished the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had explained to us, so that we could abide by his explanation: (the share in the inheritance of) the grandfather, the Kalalah, and a certain type of Riba." Imam Ahmad recorded (in a short narration; Muslim recorded a longer form) that ʿUmar said there was nothing he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about its meaning more than the kalālah, until the Prophet ﷺ stabbed him with his finger in the chest and said: *"The Ayah that is in the end of Surat An-Nisaʼ should suffice for you."* Ibn Jarir recorded — through a chain of narration that is authentic — that ʿUmar once gathered the Companions and said he would give a ruling concerning the kalālah "that even women will talk about it in their bedrooms"; a snake then appeared in the house and the gathering had to disperse, and ʿUmar commented: "Had Allah willed this to happen, it would have happened." And Al-Hakim recorded ʿUmar saying that had he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about three things, it would have been better for him than red camels: who should be the Khalifah after him; about a people who said, "We agree to pay Zakah, but not to you (meaning to the Khalifah)," whether it is allowed to fight them; and about the kalālah.

In the end, Ibn Jarir also reported that ʿUmar deferred: "I feel shy to change a ruling that Abu Bakr issued. Abu Bakr used to say that the Kalalah is the person who has no descendants or ascendants." This, Ibn Kathir says, is what the majority of scholars among the Companions, their followers, and the earlier and later Imams agree with — and it is also the ruling the Qur'an itself indicates, since Allah closes the verse by declaring that He has explained and made plain the matter "lest you go astray."

## The rulings of the ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises the distribution (after preferential rights — debts, wills, burial expenses — are settled):

- **One sister** (a real sister, or a half-sister on the father's side): she receives **half** the estate. The other half goes to the heirs in the category of *ʿaṣabah* (residuary heirs); if none exist, it too reverts to her, so she takes the whole property. (A half-sister on the *mother's* side is not covered here — her share of one-sixth, or a shared third divided equally among two or more, was already given in ayah 12 of this sūrah.)
- **The brother inheriting from the sister:** "he will be her heir if she has no children" — Ibn Kathir explains that the brother inherits all that his sister leaves behind if she has no surviving offspring or parents. He adds the qualification: if someone with a fixed share exists, such as a husband or a half-brother from the mother's side, they take their share first and the rest goes to the brother — as in the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Give the Faraʼid to its people, and whatever is left is the share of the nearest male relative."*
- **Two or more sisters** (real, or half-sisters on the father's side): they share **two-thirds**; the remaining third goes to the *ʿaṣabah*, and in their absence it too returns to the sisters, divided equally. Ibn Kathir notes the scholars reasoned in both directions between this verse and ayah 11: from this ayah they took the ruling that two daughters (or more) share in the two-thirds, just as the share of two or more sisters was taken from the ayah about the daughters.
- **Brothers and sisters together** (real, or from the father's side): the whole estate is divided on the rule *"the male will have twice the share of the female."*

**A case the Companions differed over.** What if the deceased leaves a *daughter* and a sister? Ibn Jarir and others mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Az-Zubayr used to judge that the sister gets nothing — the verse says "leaving no child," and one who leaves a daughter has left a child. But the majority of scholars disagreed, holding that the daughter gets one half and the sister the other half, relying on other evidence. Ibn Kathir relates it from Al-Bukhari: during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Muʿadh bin Jabal gave a judgment that the daughter gets one half and the sister the other half. And when Abu Musa Al-Ashʿari gave the same answer for the case of a daughter, granddaughter and sister, Ibn Masʿud answered by the Prophet's ﷺ own judgment: the daughter one-half, the granddaughter one-sixth (the two shares adding up to two-thirds), and whatever is left for the sister — at which Abu Musa said, "Do not ask me (for legal verdicts) as long as this scholar is still among you."

## "Lest you go astray" — and why this subject came three times

The ayah ends: "Allah makes clear to you (His Law) lest you go astray. And Allah is the All-Knower of everything." Ibn Kathir comments that Allah has perfect knowledge of the consequences of everything and of the benefit each matter carries for His servants — He knows what each relative deserves from the inheritance, according to the degree of relation he or she has with the deceased. The shares are not human bargaining; they are apportioned by the One who knows.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that inheritance appears three times in this sūrah — near its beginning, in its middle, and now at its very end — perhaps because of the prevailing injustice in matters of inheritance before the advent of Islam: by taking the subject up gradually, the addressees would be alerted to the need for justice in this area and enabled to show their maximum concern.

And it closes with a contrast that gives the verse its place in the sūrah's finale. Ayah 170 addressed the condition of the disbelievers; ayah 175 presented the model of those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him. The People of the Book did something terrible when they made the suggestion of a partner and son to Allah an article of their faith and took a blatant position against the Divine revelation. The noble Companions, by contrast, were so surrendered to revelation that even in "subsidiary and commonplace" matters — inheritance, marriage — they would not elect to be ruled by personal desire or reason, but would wait for the command of Allah through *waḥy* and look for the Prophet's ﷺ guidance in everything they did, returning to him until they were satisfied. "Here are two sets of people, so different and so apart!" That a community could be honoured by being addressed by its most exalted Creator, its questions answered through the recited revelation, is — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says — a great honour never granted to any other community. With that, Sūrat al-Nisāʼ ends: *and to Allah belongs all praise, at its beginning and its end.*
